title: From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: The prime minister is promising to crack down on ‘rip-off’ business practices
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: The prime minister is promising to crack down on ‘rip-off’ business practices
Content: Time to retire ‘transaction’ or ‘order processing fees’ on concert/show tickets?Photograph: Mike Lewis Photography/RedfernsView image in fullscreenTime to retire ‘transaction’ or ‘order processing fees’ on concert/show tickets?Photograph: Mike Lewis Photography/RedfernsUK cost of living crisisAnalysisFrom ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of livingHilary OsborneMoney and consumer editorThe prime minister is promising to crack down on ‘rip-off’ business practicesMon 10 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.45 EDTShareAndy Burnham has announced he willban fake discounts and make it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptionsin an effort to improve life for UK consumers.In the long run, these so-called “everyday fixes” may not make as much difference to your wealth as increasing mandatory contributions on pensions or capping rents, but they will get rid of some day-to-day frustrations. Here are six other things he could fix while he is in the mood:Ban booking fees on ticketsBuying a ticket for an event such as a gig or show doesn’t come with as many hidden costs as previously, thanks toconsumer protection laws introduced last year. But the fact the fees are clearer does not make them all more palatable.In the days when you could choose to go to a box office, or between having your tickets posted or emailed, there may have been a justification for some of the add-ons to cover different costs for the promoter, but when there’s no choice, it sticks in the throat. Retailers do not charge “transaction” or “order processing fees”, so why can they still be slapped on tickets?Stop direct debit hikes when your energy bill is in creditYou pay your bill by direct debit and have been careful with your usage, so at the end of the winter, you are in credit – and then your provider tells you it wants to put up your monthly cost by £50. Of course, a rising price cap might mean you need to increase what you pay, but if you have already got a cushion, why should you hand over more?According to the regulator Ofgem,providers held a total of £3.2bn of customers’ moneyin the year to March, with the average household £135 in credit. Yet some households on fixed tariffs with large balances are still told that their supplier wants to increase their direct debit. Yes, you can refuse, but the onus is on you as a customer to make the effort. Providers could be banned from raising direct debits by more than the price change, or when customers have built up a surplus that covers a set percentage of their bills.Cut sneaky shrinkflationWe all know prices have been going up and sometimes a smaller pack for the same price is more welcome than having to shell out more, but when the cuts are sneaky, that’s bad for consumers.In France and Austria, there are rules designed to make it more obvious to shoppers when they are getting less product for the same – or sometimes even more – money. Demanding a simple “new pack size” message on products would at least alert people to the change and mean they are making informed decisions about what they are buying.Force companies to put a phone number on their homepageYou’ve got a problem with a company and you want to get it sorted – and then you realise you cannot find a number for it anywhere. There are communications companies that have no “contact us” link anywhere to be seen, and energy companies that send you all round the houses looking for a way to get in touch.One of the recurring themes of Guardian Money readers’ problems is the struggle to find someone to help when something goes wrong. Clearly, once you have published a phone number, you need staff at the other end answering the phone and offering some joined-up thinking, so this is only the start of the solution – but at least customers would not feel like companies were trying to hide from them.Bring forward plans to improve parkingFines forcharging an electric car, debt notices that shouldnever have been sent, fees when you havetried to pay and the app has let you down… Guardian Money has heard from readers encountering all of these things and more when simply entering a car park. The government has promised to sort it out: a code of practice wasdrawn upseveral years ago but was not introduced, and a new consultation on it ended last September. Meanwhile plans for a nationwide app that would bring together all of the different parking company apps, making it easier to pay while out and about, werewatered down.Bringing forward and enforcing the planned code, so that drivers are not receiving bills for parking crimes they did not commit, would leave a welcome gap in the Guardian Money postbag.Make insurers give you the best deal upfrontA lot has been done to improve the experience of renewing your insurance policies. Insurers are supposed to offer existing customersas good a dealas they do new ones, and your renewal letter tells you how much you paid last year so that you can see if the cost has gone up. And yet the annual dance continues: if you don’t call your insurer and query an increase, shop around or threaten to leave, you will probablyend up paying morethan you need to. It is a system that still penalises those who stay put.Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisConsumer affairsConsumer rightsTicket pricesEnergy billsInsuranceHousehold billsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Lesbians, latex and $2,000 condoms: why are this summer’s movies so obsessed with sex? | Movies | The Guardian
description: From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacy
Content: Olivia Wilde in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesView image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesMoviesLesbians, latex and $2,000 condoms: why are this summer’s movies so obsessed with sex?From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacyRafaela BassiliMon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThefirst alarm bellssounded nearly 10 years ago, and since then, a deluge of books, podcasts androundtableshas tried to get at the bottom of the problem: why is gen Z not having sex?Recently it’s as though culture has been recalibrated to make up for the youth’s apparent frigidity. “Smut” literature is on the rise, prestige TV is nowdepictingOnlyFans models, and indie films have taken a turntowardskink. This summer, through confused young protagonists and their sexual misadventures, the movies are zeroing in on generational attitudes about sex.One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcomRead moreThere is acontradictionbehind gen Z chastity: despite being the most sexually progressive generation ever, zoomers live under the influence of rampant sexual conservatism. After the 2022 overturning of Roe v Wade, for instance, 16% of single gen Z adults are more afraid to date. This tension is at the heart ofOne Night Only, a new romcom that imagines a world in which Congress has outlawed premarital sex. For one night of the year, the government lifts the ban, essentially enacting the purge for single people’s sexual freedom. On this night, after a series of missed encounters and wrong turns, Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (Monica Barbaro) meet cute.View image in fullscreenCallum Turner and Monica Barbaro in One Night Only.Photograph: Nicole Rivelli/Universal Pictures/APDespite its political tenor, One Night Only’s vision of dystopia is not a comment on America’s rapid hurtle toward authoritarianism. It merely presents obstacles for Allie and Owen to overcome – such as the $2,000 price tag for the condoms Owen attempts to procure – much like the missed connection brought about by a busy phone line in a 90s romcom. We know nothing about what these characters’ lives were like before the ban, which means that Allie’s complaints about the difficulty of finding her “Prince Charming” come off generic, indistinguishable from any number of complaints that I, a married zoomer, have heard from my single friends about dating in the age of apps.‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken starRead moreSilly hijinks aside, One Night Only misunderstands today’s sex recession as libidinal, when really, it’s existential. It’s not that zoomers aren’t horny, or can’t find a man: they are the first generation to grow up fully under the influence of the internet, with its attendant alienations; worse, its youngest members came of age during the pandemic. Knowing how to relate to one another is hard enough, let alone how to initiate sex – a process often awkward, if not outright painful, foreveryoneno matter their age (This much, at least, One Night Only gets right.)Other films this summer understand that sex can’t solve the fundamental alienation brought about by modern life. It’s loneliness that ails Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), the flush-cheeked studio assistant to the provocative artist Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde) inGregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex. For the most part Araki’s characters stay in their boxes, with Erika the worldly provocateur to Elliot’s gullible dork. But in the film’s best moment, a doomed threesome with Elliot’s sexually confused roommate Apple (Chase Sui Wonders), that order is disturbed. The arrival of a third person with her own muddled desires – does Apple want Erika, Elliot, or both? Do they wanther? Does she want to be wanted? – leads Erika to lose her grip, and Elliot to rebel against his part. Standing there half naked, they might as well be worlds apart.View image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in The Invite.Photograph: Black Bear/PAI Want Your Sex shares a dynamic withThe Invite(in which Wilde also stars, and which she directed) and Jane Schoenbrun’sTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a younger and less experienced person (or couple) becomes entangled with an older, sexy woman who shows them the path to self-knowledge through desire. But whereas sex is an all-consuming problem for the characters in The Invite and I Want Your Sex, Camp Miasma presents sex, death and art as intertwined human impulses that are impossible to separate from one another. Tasked with rebooting the Camp Miasma slasher franchise that first prompted her “queer awakening”, 29-year-old film-maker Kris (Hannah Einbinder) has one theme on her mind: “DESIRE”, as she scrawls in her journal, in big block letters.By letting us into Kris’s process of self-discovery, Miasma addresses generational concerns in more nuanced ways than its counterparts this summer. Through her relationship with her muse Billy Presley (a wonderfulGillian Anderson), Camp Miasma’s original final girl, Kris learns that to arrive at artistic epiphany or sexual climax, one must let go of control, let the movie play out. To Billy, slashers are as elemental as sexual desire: she teaches Kris that sex, like art, is a visceral experience not easily theorized.View image in fullscreenGillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Ryan Plummer/Mubi/APWhile One Night Only plays threats tobodily autonomyfor laughs and I Want Your Sex’s Erika rolls her eyes at gen Z’s “wokeness”, Camp Miasma strikes a more sincere tone. Kris is initially drawn to reboot the Camp Miasma films to correct the franchise’s transphobia, but only discovers a physical and emotional experience of art when she learns to stop overintellectualizing slashers. It’s only then that she can really connect with Billy, and it’s only through their connection that she can make a film that is true.These movies don’t exactly present zoomers with a model for how to be a young person who has sex; if anything, they’re more like cautionary guides showing what kinds of behavior to avoid. But that’s precisely where their value lies. After decades of unrealistic depictions of sex on screen and a fewworrisome yearswhen it seemed likely that sex would disappear from the movies altogether, it’s a relief to see sex return to screen – messy awkwardness and all.Explore more on these topicsFilmSexOlivia WildeGregg ArakiSeth RogenRoe v WadeRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Prison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him that | Simon Hattenstone | The Guardian
description: Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives, says Guardian writer Simon Hattenstone
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives, says Guardian writer Simon Hattenstone
Content: A new review into indeterminate prison sentences has been announced.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA new review into indeterminate prison sentences has been announced.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianOpinionPrisons and probationPrison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him thatSimon HattenstonePolitical leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own livesMon 10 Aug 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTShareIn January 2015, Tommy Nicol told his family that he was suffering “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years”. Nicol had been given an imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentence six years earlier for stealing a car from a garage and injuring the owner. He was alreadytwo years beyond his four-year tariff– the minimum time you can serve in prison before being considered for release. Nicol was given another two-year knock-back from the Parole Board and was in despair. If and when he got released, he would be on a lifelong licence. Eight months later, aged 37, Nicol hanged himself at The Mount prison in Hertfordshire, England.By the time he took his own life, the inhumane IPP sentence had already been abolished for three years. The problem is, it didn’t apply retroactively. Those already serving IPP sentences stayed on them. This, despite David Blunkett, who devised and introduced them as home secretary in 2005, calling it “the biggest regret” of his political career. And this despite UN special rapporteur on torture Alice Edwardsagreeing with Tommy Nicolthat the sentence was “psychological torture”. Astonishingly, more than 2,000 people are still serving IPP sentences in England and Wales.Last week prime minister Andy Burnham announced anew reviewinto indeterminate sentences as part of his plan to reduce the prison population. Reviewing a sentence that was abolished 14 years ago seems Kafkaesque. And what exactly is left to review? We all know IPPs are wrong – they are no longer handed down, and those serving them should be resentenced. Review after review has said so. Surely it makes more sense to simply introduce legislation to make that happen?IPPs were given to people who didn’t merit life sentences, but were regarded as a risk to society. With an IPP, once prisoners have served their tariff, they have to apply to the Parole Board for release. The Parole Board only grants release if satisfied that the offender no longer poses a risk to the public. This means that an IPP prisoner could be detained indefinitely.It was expected that very few prisoners would receive IPPs (an estimated 900 at any one time) and only for serious crimes.The reality couldn’t have been more different. Between 2005 and 2013 (a handful of people were sentenced after the cut-off of 31 December 2012),8,711 people were given an IPP sentence. While some had long tariffs, most were on low tariffs for minor crimes. Nevertheless, many never got released. Or if they did, they were recalled to prison for the slightest breaches of their licence, such as being late for appointments with probation officers.Often the people who were imprisoned on an IPP were already vulnerable. Not surprisingly, many prisoners lost hope, like Nicol did. Ninety-four peoplehad taken their own lives up to March 2025 while serving the sentence in prison. Forty-four people are known to have taken their own lives while out on licence, though these community-based figures have only been tracked since April 2019, so are likely to be higher.The IPP horror stories are legion, and many concern young people such as Martin Myers, whoserved 18 yearsfor attempting to steal a cigarette, despite having an original tariff of just 19 months and 27 days when sentenced aged 24; Ronnie Sinclair served16 years in jail on a three-year IPP tarifffor stealing a flowerpot at the age of 17; and Wayne Bell was 17 when he was imprisoned on an IPP for punching a boy and stealing a bike in 2007 on a tariff of one year and 350 days. He is still in prison 19 years later.Although the lifelong licence was removed for IPP prisoners in 2024, many are still serving the sentence. As of June 2026, there were2,271 IPP prisonersjailed in England and Wales –856 unreleased prisoners and 1,415 recalled prisoners.This proposed review would be the third since 2022 when the cross-party Justice Committee Inquiry concluded IPP sentenceswere “irredeemably flawed”and recommended resentencing. Nothing was done. Last year the Howard League expert working grouprecommended fixed-release windowsfor IPP prisoners. Nothing was done. A private member’s bill sponsored by (Lord) Anthony Woodley urged a comprehensive, retrospective resentencing exercise forall prisoners still subject to an IPP. The bill passed its second reading in the House of Lords and progressed to the committee stage, but the government blocked it.The campaign groupUngrippfears that any new review will have the same outcome as previous ones. “Each review meant more wasted time, more people on IPP despairing and inevitably, more suicides,” it says. “How can we be confident this will be any different?”Shockingly, all but three of the 2,271 people serving IPP sentences in prison are past their tariff. With resentencing, these three prisoners would be given a fitting determinate sentence, while the 2,268 remaining IPP prisoners would gradually be released with appropriate social care and housing to ensure they were safe within the community and the community safe with them. The£60,000 a year savedin prison costs would go a considerable way towards paying for this.So why hasn’t it yet been done? Simple. Political leaders are terrified of looking soft on crime – so they have consistently kicked the IPP can down the road. Yet IPP sentences are universally recognised as unjust. Not a single mainstream politician defends this barbaric sentence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast year Keir Starmer said: “It is right that the IPP sentence has been abolished”, but he wasn’t brave enough toresentence IPP prisoners. Andy Burnham must be braver.The former supreme court justice Lord Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood called IPP “the greatest single stain on our criminal justice system” in a2020 reportfor the Prison Reform Trust. If Burnham wants to show he means business, he will not bother with another review and will simply legislate to get this shaming stain removed once and for all.Resentencing is too late for Tommy Nicol and the many others IPP prisoners who took their own lives, but it’s not too late for those still behind bars, tortured by not knowing whether their imprisonment will ever end.Simon Hattenstone is a Guardian features writerIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionSentencingUK criminal justicecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s very challenging’: how the Duke of Westminster’s farm is taking on the climate crisis | Farming | The Guardian
description: Amid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethane
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Amid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethane
Content: Grosvenor Farms produces more than 34m litres of milk a year and supplies Müller and Tesco.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGrosvenor Farms produces more than 34m litres of milk a year and supplies Müller and Tesco.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFarming‘It’s very challenging’: how the Duke of Westminster’s farm is taking on the climate crisisAmid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethaneJulia KolleweMon 10 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a distinctive smell of cow manure in the air at theDuke of Westminster’s dairy farm near Chester. It is a world away from the collection of grand West End properties controlled by the duke that form the backbone of his near £10bn fortune, a decade on from becoming Britain’syoungest billionaire.As part of his 349-year-oldGrosvenor empire, Lea Manor Farm on the duke’s Eaton Estate in north-west England has fared better than most dairy farms in recent years.But it has also been hit by declining milk prices and other challenges faced by British farmers. Aseries of heatwavescausing drought, with afifth looming this week– combined with fertiliser shortages triggered by the Iran war, diseases and a scarcity of workers since Brexit – have made farming very difficult.Milk prices are cyclical; higher farm-gate prices in the UK last year encouraged an expansion of production, and oversupply in the UK and overseas has led to price reductions of up to 50% this year, according to Mark Roach, the managing director of Grosvenor Farms. “I can’t imagine any other industries suffering a 50% reduction.”Lea Manor has been an arable and livestock farm for centuries, with a focus on potatoes between 1984 and 2002, when it switched to cows after the realisation that growing potatoes on the heavy Cheshire clay was not sustainable.The farm at Eaton Estate, which is part of Grosvenor’s sprawling portfolio of offices, shops, homes, woods and farmland, has 77 staff and 2,600 Holstein friesian cows; it produces more than 34m litres of milk a year – 13,200 litres a cow – and supplies Müller and Tesco. It is surrounded by fields where animal feed such as wheat, maize, barley and rye is grown, set in 4,685 hectares (11,577 acres) of land.View image in fullscreenMark Roach, the managing director of Grosvenor Farms, says oversupply has led to price reductions of up to 50% this year.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThis year’s heatwaves –supercharged by the escalating climate crisis– have piled more pressure on farmers. When temperatures rise above 25C, cows become more lethargic, eat less and produce less milk. At 36C during the June heatwave, each Grosvenor cow produced up to six litres less milk a day, with the heat partly mitigated by a sprinkler system and the large airy barns.At some other farms, the milk yield was down as much as 10 litres a day for each cow, Roach says. “It’s very, very challenging for farming.”Mark Preston, an executive trustee of Grosvenor, says: “Extreme weather in many parts of the northern hemisphere is affecting crop yields and farm economics. Farmers are adapting where they can, but the full impact is likely to become clearer over the next growing season, reinforcing the importance of building greater resilience into the UK’s food production system.”With almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales officially in drought, wheat half the normal height and the broccoli yield down 50%,the UK is forced to import more foodfrom countries such as Spain toavoid shortages, while global prices are rising.Rural estates are also grappling with labour shortages post-Brexit, which has meant the flow of new eastern European workers has all but dried up.Many British farmsare lossmaking, while Lea Manor – Grosvenor’s only dairy farm – is profitable, after a big revamp starting in 2012 to improve efficiency using technology. The farming divisionmade a profit before tax of £2.6m in 2024, down from £3.6m the previous year, with turnover of £16.2m. By contrast, Grosvenormade an underlying profit of £88.7mfrom its UK properties last year, up 14% on 2024. The duke received dividends of £53.7m from the group in 2025.View image in fullscreenThe Duke of Westminster, Hugh Grosvenor, is one of the UK’s richest individuals, with an estimated fortune of £9.5bn.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA Wire/PA ImagesDespite the differing scale, Roach says that the farm is “not a hobby of the duke, it’s a commercial business”. Hugh Grosvenor is one of the UK’s richest individuals, withan estimated fortune of £9.5bn, who upon the sudden death of his father in 2016 inherited the vast estate his family has owned for centuries.The bequest waslargely shielded from 40% inheritance taxbecause the estate is held in a series of trusts rather than by the duke personally. Grosvenorsays that it pays inheritance taxthrough a recurring 6% payment on the value of its assets every 10 years, instead of a single payment of 40% upon death.At Lea Manor, the cows are led three times a day from their open-sided barns to an indoor carousel where they are milked using automated machinery. The milking unit is attached by a farm worker but comes off automatically once the udder has been emptied to prevent overmilking, which can lead to mastitis; two robots clean the teats before milking and disinfect them before the animals step off the carousel. Standing in 60 berths, 360 cows can be milked in an hour.Three tankers are filled every day, with 29,000 litres pouring into each tanker, plus another part-filled tanker, which then go to a Müller processing plant in Manchester, and the milk is for sale in a Tesco supermarket the following morning.Sensors in the floor measure how the cows walk, so if they show signs of having a sore foot, they will get a foot bath to prevent rot. Sometimes the cows do not want to get off the carousel and have to be guided out of the door back to their barn.Recurring bovine tuberculosis is another challenge for dairy farms, with testing often unreliable and no vaccine available. Meanwhile,sheep farmers struggle with bluetongue, an insect-borne virus, as changing weather patterns have led to warnings of new diseases.The rise in factory-style dairy farming has raised concerns over farms using intensive systems to increase productivity from“battery cows”.View image in fullscreenCows are milked using automated machinery in an indoor carousel.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianGrosvenor insists that overall its cows are healthy, pointing to its own statistics. “Unhealthy cows do not produce much milk,” Roach says. Though its milk is not classed as organic, the farm feeds cows grass and has no routine antibiotics use.The group says the barns are larger than industry standards and open on the sides, allowing plenty of natural light and airflow. However, the cows are not put out to pasture and stand on concrete floors (with anti-slip grooves). Only 8% of dairy herds in the UK are housed all year round,according to the RSPCA, which says cows should be allowed to graze some of the time.Grosvenor says: “The health of our herd, low incidence of disease and minimal antibiotic use gives us confidence that the system is working well. We have welcomed representatives from the RSPCA to the farm, who described it as one of the quietest and most content herds they had seen.”Grosvenor is building a biomethane plant on the estate to produce energy from cow manure, in an effort to broaden its revenue streams. The 2.4-hectare (six-acre) facility is expected to generate 72 gigawatts of renewable gas a year from up to 170,000 tonnes of manure, enough to heat about 6,000 homes, starting in 2027.View image in fullscreenManure is used as fertiliser in Grosvenor’s fields as part of its circular farming process.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIt is not the only such rural family estate to have a reactor. Apsley Farms in Hampshire, which has been owned by the Du Val de Beaulieu family since 1936, operates the UK’s third largest biomethane plant and has been supplying renewable gas to the grid since 2014. It generates 104GWh of green gas a year along with renewable electricity for the local network, supplying 10,000 households.Manure is also used in Grosvenor’s fields, which means more than 80% of the forage fed to the dairy herd is grown without artificial fertilisers. Grosvenor prides itself oncircular farming, a system designed to eliminate waste and reuse resources by turning crop waste into feed and animal waste into natural fertiliser, regenerating soil health. As a result, the group has not bought mined phosphate or potash fertilisers for about 15 years and only buys some nitrogen fertiliser.The near-total blockade of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran warhas led to global fertiliser shortages, a situation described as a “food security timebomb” by the head of the International Rescue Committee, David Miliband. Preston echoed those concerns, warning in May that theknock-on effects on food pricescould arrive next year.“The concerns we raised earlier this year remain very real,” Preston says. “Ongoing disruption to fertiliser supply chains continues to affect both availability and cost.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingClimate crisisBiomass and bioenergyAgriculturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stuff of nightmares? Meet the bootlace worm – super-long, super-elastic, and it fires toxic slime | Marine life | The Guardian
description: Its mucus, which can kill crabs and cockroaches, could be the basis of new insecticides
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Its mucus, which can kill crabs and cockroaches, could be the basis of new insecticides
Content: The bootlace worm can stretch out longer than an Olympic swimming pool, but usually measures 15 metres.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe bootlace worm can stretch out longer than an Olympic swimming pool, but usually measures 15 metres.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Marine lifeStuff of nightmares? Meet the bootlace worm – super-long, super-elastic, and it fires toxic slimeIts mucus, which can kill crabs and cockroaches, could be the basis of new insecticidesPatrick BarkhamMon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the shuddery stuff of nightmares for some, but for a select group who admire extending ladders, giraffes and the Odyssey, one of the longest animals in the world is bound to appeal.This creature is nneither the blue whale, nor a lion’s mane jellyfish but the humble bootlace worm,Lineus longissimus,one of the most remarkable marine invertebrates of them all.It can stretch out longer than an Olympic swimming pool. In fact, one worm, found washed ashore after a storm at St Andrews, was recorded at an incredible 55 metres in length. Worm-sceptics suggest it may have been stretched out, because the species is also very elastic. A more usual length is a mere 15 metres. Its width is just 5–10mm.View image in fullscreenWhen threatened, the bootlace worm discharges a poisonous mucus.Photograph: Nature Photographers Ltd/AlamyThis slender, super-long superworm has a second superpower: it can fire toxic slime. When threatened, the blackish-brown bootlace worm discharges a poisonous mucus which may remind you of the smell of sewage if you pick up a beached worm.Although the Swedish archbishop and naturalistOlaus Magnusfirst noted its toxic slime back in 1555, it wasn’t until 2018 that the worm’s toxins werefully describedby (Swedish) scientists. Its mucus was designed to paralyse and kill crabs.Researchers have discovered the toxins, known as alpha-nemertides, can also kill cockroaches but have little impact on mammals, leading to the possibility that they could be the basis for new insecticides. There are likely to bemany more useful chemicals and medicines still to be discoveredwithin the invertebrate world.The bootlace worm is one of many little-known nemerteans – ribbon or proboscis worms. The phylum contains more than 1,250 described species of worms which are found everywhere from intertidal zones to great ocean depths – a little-heralded but rich and vital branch of the tree of life.This record-breaking and yet rather overlooked worm is a voracious and extremely effective predator, enjoying nothing more than swallowing annelids (soft-bodied, segmented worms) whole. It was nominated by a reader who says it is “a neglected but quite amazing branch on the tree of life. The longest of all wormy creatures (up to 15m?!) and only a few mm wide.” He loves “a worm that can stretch and stretch and stretch” and argues that it is one of the “many amazing creatures contributing to Britain’s coastal heritage”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLong, slimy and lethal – what’s not to love? Vote bootlace worm!It’s invertebrate of the year again! From 3-12 August, every day we will profile one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated. And then, when you’ve heard about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. title: From M&S pants to fancy skincare: the celebrity shopping recommendations you loved the most | Celebrity | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s expensive regrets or brilliant bargains, we celebrate the stars’ shopping secrets – and the products that tempted you
Author: Lucy Pavia
Headline: Whether it’s expensive regrets or brilliant bargains, we celebrate the stars’ shopping secrets – and the products that tempted you
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterHow I shopCelebrityFrom M&S pants to fancy skincare: the celebrity shopping recommendations you loved the mostWhether it’s expensive regrets or brilliant bargains, we celebrate the stars’ shopping secrets – and the products that tempted youDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLucy PaviaMon 10 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Like snooping in someone else’s supermarket trolley, discovering other people’s shopping habits satisfies a certain nosiness. And never more so than when it comes to celebrities – there’s nothing more human than knowingKim Cattrallloves fish and chips, or thatHenry Hollandis a Skims guy.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.And as celebrities often have the inside track–or perhaps we just think they do – on everything from coffee machines to skincare, their recommendations in our biweeklyHow I Shopcolumn have inspired more than a few of your own retail habits. In some cases, however, such asDavid Gandy’s £2,500Cobra Fortis lawnmower, the price was a little too out of reach.View image in fullscreenLawnmower man … even David Gandy has shopping regrets – including a very expensive mower.Photograph: Raquel Lonas/GettyBeauty products have proved particularly inspiring, from author Nussaibah Younis’s favouriteChanel foundation, which she buys “on repeat”, to theMarvis whitening toothpastethat TV presenter Ben Fogle has been using “for decades”. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given her expertise as a beauty pro, Caroline Hirons’Vieve skin dewwas also popular (she likes to mix hers with Chanel primer for a glowy look).Even the £1,999 cost of Dawn O’Porter’sLyma laser kitdidn’t put some of you off: “The price tag is OUCH,” O’Porter agreed, noting she was given hers as a gift, but said it has dramatically cut down on the amount of Botox she gets around her eyes: “A device like this goes deep and definitely works,” she said.From beauty buys to kitchen gadgetsWe always ask our celebs about coffee. Their answers generally fall into two camps: obsessed and never-touch-it. Some of you were inspired by Patrick Grant’s favouriteBialetti coffee maker, while others decided to invest in other kitchen gadgets, such as Andi Oliver’sNinja food processor, perhaps due to her ringing endorsement about its durability: “[This is] the only one that doesn’t die on me.”View image in fullscreenFresh thinking: Jo Malone swears by a clothes steamer for smoothing bed sheets.Photograph: Suphansa Subruayying/Getty/iStockphotoBut your favourite celebrity-recommended product of all? Perhaps because wedding season is in full swing, or perhaps because you wanted to follow her tip about using it on bed sheets,Jo Malone’s£29.99 Philips clothes steamerproved a bestseller.And becausecelebs, they’re just like us, there were a few purchases our celebrities regret. David Gandy thinks that pricey Fortis lawnmower was a mistake – “I should have gone for one of Allett’s petrol mowers,” he said – whileDawn O’Portersays she’s bought “countless” pairs of jeans but never worn them because she “can’t quite [find something] right for my shape”.Nussaibah Younisalso regrets buying her Christian Louboutin Miss Z patent leather 100mm stilettos as she “can barely walk three steps in them”.Andi Oliveralso told us about her niche but dangerous habit of “sleep shopping”: “I’m pretty menopausal, so I take sleeping pills. When I’m half falling asleep and lying in bed on my phone, I scroll and shop. I don’t even remember I’ve done it. And then weird things turn up.” Her worst buy? “A weird Tory wife outfit.”View image in fullscreenBrief encounter … there was an overwhelming favourite when it came to celebrity underwear shopping.Photograph: Atitaya Pimpa/GettyMany of the celebrities we’ve spoken to enjoy finding bargain alternatives to everyday items. Gandy refills posh bottles of hand soap with cheaper versions (don’t we all?), andHironscounterintuitively drives miles to get cheap petrol. And we’re not afraid to ask personal questions: when we quiz our celebs on where they buy their underwear, there’s been one clear winner: Marks & Spencer, of course.We’ve found the gifts they buy their loved ones particularly touching, such as the hand-embroidered hankiesPatrick Grantgave his dad, the jewellery belonging to her late mother that Caroline Hirons saved for her granddaughter, orBanjo Beale’s DIY engagement ring.We’re occasionally reminded that these people really aren’t like us at all:Ben Foglegot his kids melted snow from the summit of Mount Everest, poured into vintage silver bottles he found on Etsy, engraved with his summit date. Slightly blows that Star Wars Lego set out of the water, doesn’t it?Explore more on these topicsCelebrityHow I shopEthical and green livingInteriorsHomesThe Filterbest ofShareReuse this content

title: Three-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave looms | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Four more regions given drought status, putting 27 million people under restrictions on water use
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Four more regions given drought status, putting 27 million people under restrictions on water use
Content: There has been an unprecedented period of hot, dry weather in the UK this year.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere has been an unprecedented period of hot, dry weather in the UK this year.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesUK weatherThree-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave loomsFour more regions given drought status, putting 27 million people under restrictions on water usePippa NeillEnvironment reporterMon 10 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 03.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost three-quarters ofEnglandis now in drought, as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.Four more regions of England have officially been declared to be in drought: the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs.They join seven regions already under drought status sincelast month: East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).Farmers have reported their earliest harvests in 20 years, with reduced yields, while reservoir levels have fallen to 69% – 11.6% lower than expected for this time of year.Yorkshire and the North East have joined Cumbria and Lancashire and Greater Manchester, Merseyside and Cheshire in prolonged dry weather status – the stage before drought – meaning nowhere in England is deemed to be in normal status.This flash drought, which developed quickly because of very low rainfall and higher temperatures, means 27 million people have restrictions on their water use.Prof Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said it was a “stark reminder that climate change isn’t just about rising temperatures – it’s making droughts develop faster and hit harder.“With three droughts in the past five years, we’re seeing the growing influence of a changing climate. We need to adapt to more frequent periods of extreme heat and drought while taking action to reduce the emissions driving these changes.”View image in fullscreenPeople using umbrellas as parasols in Hyde Park, London.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PASouthernWaterhas applied for two drought orders. The first is to maintain normal abstraction rates from the River Test even during low river flows and the second is for a non-essential use ban. These are both under consideration by the government. South East Water said last week supplies in its area were “critically low” and warned customers they might lose supply unless demand for water in the area dropped.The drought announcement comes as England braces for its fifth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures possibly exceeding 36C in some places. This year has so far seen 34 days where temperatures have reached 30C or above somewhere in England, including 13 consecutive days in July.central England temperatures graphicRivers, reservoirs and groundwaters are also continuing to decline, with 22% of rivers now classed as exceptionally low.Glenn Watts, director of water science at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, said river flows across England andWaleswere approaching or worse than previous records set in 1976.The record temperatures and extremely dry weather are having wide-ranging impacts: 245 wildfires have been recorded on the country’s most protected sites this year alone and the government said important wetland and sensitive peatland habitats were drying out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEurope’s dry riverbeds and scorched earth – in picturesRead morePaul Tompkins, the deputy president of the National Farmers’ Union, said that with no meaningful rain forecast in the coming weeks, the situation for farmers was increasingly concerning.“Many farmers have completed the earliest harvest on record, with poor yields in key crops reported in some areas of the country. Livestock and dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing, while growers are working hard to keep fruit and vegetables watered, but many are struggling to access the water they need,” he said.The government said it was considering ways to give more support to the farming sector. The water minister, Emma Hardy, said this would include making it easier to build on-farm reservoirs.River temperatures are rising, reaching 28C on the River Misbourne, a chalk stream in Buckinghamshire, 27C on the Hampshire Avon and 27C on the River Trent – around 2C higher than to be expected.England is on track to record its highest number ofheat-related deathsthis summer, after the UK Health Security Agency announced that an estimated 2,877 people died in the May and June heatwaves.View image in fullscreenPeople sit on a beach at Allhallows on the Thames estuary as a yellow heat-health alert remains in force.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersThe UKHSA has updated heat health alerts for nine regions in England, warning that rising temperatures this week may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.The NationalDroughtGroup, whose members include the government, water companies, the National Farmers’ Union, the Met Office and conservation experts, met on Monday to assess the situation across England.Many other parts of Europe are also bracing for another heatwave. The French national weather agency said on Monday that temperatures in the south-east could reach 35C, spreading further across the country, while Italy and coastal Croatia are already experiencing extreme heat. Countries including Slovakia, Austria and Hungary haveregistered record temperaturesin recent days.Additional reporting by Andrew GregoryExplore more on these topicsUK weatherDroughtExtreme heatEnglandWalesWaterClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ann Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incident | UK news | The Guardian
description: Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home
Content: Ann Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenAnn Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Lucy North/PAUK newsAnn Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incidentPolice looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then homeVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage.Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, was charged with the murder of Widdecombe, 78, who was killed at her Devon home in July, after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.On Friday, police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time, which they have said was an attempted burglary. Other sources describe it as an attempted arson.Police attended the incident, which they initially recorded primarily as a burglary. The Guardian understands detectives are studying fingerprints taken from the scene, as well as video from CCTV cameras in the area and from devices such as video doorbells. They examined the scene to see if an accelerant, such as lighter fluid, was used.On Friday, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said it had referred itself to the police watchdog over the initial investigation of the April 2025 incident.It said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.“In April 2025, the Metropolitan police received a report of an attempted burglary at an address in the Greater London area. Enquiries were carried out by the Metropolitan police, supported by Counter Terrorism Policing London. No arrests were made and the investigation was subsequently closed, pending any new lines of inquiry.“Following the reopening of the attempted burglary investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing London identified a line of enquiry which was not identified and pursued by them at the time, which may have been relevant. As a result, to ensure their support to the initial investigation is thoroughly reviewed, Counter Terrorism Policing London made a mandatory conduct referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct today.”On Monday, Farage said at a press conference: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.”He said he now had confidence in counter-terrorism police and said they were not trying to cover anything up.The Reform leader said of CTP’s decision to refer itself to the IOPC: “The fact they’ve done that shows you they’re not trying to cover up, they’re not trying to ignore, and I have to say I have met Laurence Taylor [the head of CTP] and I did feel a great, great confidence in it.”Widdecombe’s body was found with “serious injuries” by paramedics at her home in Haytor Vale, Devon, at 11.40am on Thursday 9 July.Kerry’s first court appearance in July heard that Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times in her home. Police have said they believed the 78-year-old former minister was attacked the day before her body was found.The attack on Widdecombe has not yet been declared a terrorist incident. CTP took the lead in the investigation because of the possibility there may have been a political motive behind her killing.CTP’s investigations continue.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths | Iran | The Guardian
description: US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled
Content: Donald Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making claims for the damages from the five-month war.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making claims for the damages from the five-month war.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APIranTrump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deathsUS president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalledAndrew Rothin WashingtonMon 10 Aug 2026 16.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse.The US president is trying to end conflicts inIran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza.In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response toIranian negotiators making similar claimsfor damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy.Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reachRead more“Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social.“Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.”The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised.The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls.On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace.Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreTrump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”.Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region.“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform backer Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalists | Arron Banks | The Guardian
description: Industry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after Banks apparently admitted doing so
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Industry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after Banks apparently admitted doing so
Content: Arron Banks, pictured in 2018, is reported to have previously hired operatives to surveil political opponents.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAView image in fullscreenArron Banks, pictured in 2018, is reported to have previously hired operatives to surveil political opponents.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAArron BanksReform backer Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalistsIndustry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after Banks apparently admitted doing soDaniel BoffeyChief reporterMon 10 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe businessman and Reform UK backerArron Banksis facing calls to lay out the extent of his surveillance of journalists, described by an industry body as an “attack on our democracy”.The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns after Banks appeared to admit over the weekend to hiring private investigators tospy on a Sunday Times journalist.The revelation, first reported in the New Statesman, has led to fears that other journalists examining the funding of Reform and Nigel Farage, including those at the Guardian, could have been targeted.When asked over the weekend whether he had commissioned investigators to surveil reporters at the Guardian, Banks, a Reform UK member andformer mayoral candidate, said he was “not really interested in the Guardian” but declined to comment further.The Guardian, along with the Sunday Times, hasbroken a series of storiesin recent months revealing how cash has been given to Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said aggressive attempts to deter journalistic inquiry were at risk of becoming normalised.He said: “Using private investigators to try to deter journalists from making legitimate inquiries about public figures is an attack on our democracy. Sadly, intimidation and abuse of local and national journalists is increasingly used as a weapon to limit scrutiny and deflect attention away from matters of public interest. This must not become normalised.“Ministers must wake up to this threat to our democracy and do much more to protect the independent journalism which underpins our democratic way of life.”According to theNew Statesman, Banks instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a private investigations company he once owned, to examine Gabriel Pogrund, the editor of the Sunday Times’ Insight investigations team.In response to inquiries, Banks told the magazine: “We believe theSunday Timesused hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”The Sunday Times has strongly rejected Banks’s suggestion.Banks, when asked directly by the New Statesman whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, responded: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of Index on Censorship, said Banks should be open and transparent about the extent of his surveillance of journalists.She said: “I really, really hope that it’s not happening to other journalists. But my fear is that it will be, because Gabriel is not the only one who’s asking the right questions about Reform.“These tactics are often used to just stop the questions, to stop accountability, and that can have hugely detrimental effects on our democratic structure.”Reform UK has denied any knowledge of Banks’s alleged use of investigators.Gawain Towler, a member of Reform’s board and a former head of press for Ukip, said he was uncomfortable with the development but there were legitimate questions as to where journalists were sourcing private information.“Personally I don’t like it,” he said. “Buttruly how in the light of the situation does one ask questions with a possibility of getting an answer …“I think the issue with Banks is that there was actually silence about this possible collusion with the [National Crime Agency and journalists] … It would be ridiculous of us not to ask questions. So how do you ask questions?”Nicky Morgan, a former Conservative secretary of state for culture, media and sport, said such intrusions in press freedom were “not compatible with an open democracy”. She said: “Investigating a journalist can only be intended to have a chilling effect on free speech.”Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrats’ Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “Hiring private investigators to target journalists who are simply doing their jobs is a desperate attempt to dodge accountability.“Anyone who uses or condones these tactics demonstrates complete contempt for a free press and should have no business in British public life.”Banks, who helped run the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave.EU, is reported to have previously hired what he described as “ex-MI5 and SAS” operatives to surveil political opponents in the run-up to the EU referendum.Included among those was Matthew Elliott, a Conservative peer who was the chief executive of the rival Vote Leave campaign. He has warned that such tactics will “drive out the decent people we need in public life”.Explore more on these topicsArron BanksPress freedomSunday TimesNewspapers & magazinesReform UKJournalist safetySurveillancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour peer urges Tories to sack former neo-Nazi who abused her | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Badenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana Berger
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Badenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana Berger
Content: Luciana Berger and Joshua Bonehill-Paine.Composite: Getty Images/C4/YoutubeView image in fullscreenLuciana Berger and Joshua Bonehill-Paine.Composite: Getty Images/C4/YoutubeConservativesLabour peer urges Tories to sack former neo-Nazi who abused herBadenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana BergerAletha AduPolitical correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Labour peerLuciana Bergerhas urged Kemi Badenoch to “listen to victims” and reverse her decision to give a national advisory role to a former neo-Nazi.Joshua Bonehill-Paine was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, an MP at the time. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.Berger said she was still affected by his crimes more than nine years later, and questioned what safeguarding checks Badenoch and the Conservative party had carried out in relation to his appointment to the party’s culture and integration commission.Berger, who is Jewish, asked whetherBonehill-Paine’s new rolecould bring him to Westminster. She wrote on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?”Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate.View image in fullscreenLuciana Berger said she was still affected by Bonehill-Paine’s crimes more than nine years later.Photograph: Parliament TV/PABerger’s intervention came after the Conservative party leader publisheda lengthy defenceof Bonehill-Paine in the Times, describing questions over his suitabilityto stand as a councillor in Somersetas a “pile-on”.Bonehill-Paine was set to stand as a Tory local councillor but announced last week that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections after Badenoch offered him the advisory role.Badenoch said: “People need to understand that the Conservative party under my leadership is now the party of personal responsibility and law and order. That means insisting on consequences by punishing wrongdoing and protecting the public, especially victims.“We need fewer double standards and instead higher standards in a system that is repeatedly failing to protect the public. We should be tough enough to stand by our beliefs even when politically inconvenient, wise enough to recognise rehabilitation and consistent enough to apply the same principles to friend and foe.”Berger said she had seen the piece late on Saturday night and “tried to ignore it” but after Badenoch shared the article on Monday, the former MP for Liverpool Wavertree accused her of giving insufficient consideration to Bonehill-Paine’s victims.“Badenoch makes one passing reference to the ‘victims’,” Berger wrote. “There were many. And I was one of them. Did Badenoch read the judge’s sentencing remarks? In court we heard the victim impact statements from people unable to testify, whose lives he had destroyed.“His appointment as an adviser to the Conservative party’s culture and integration commission could conceivably bring him to Westminster. Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?“It’s still not too late for Badenoch to listen to victims and reverse her decision.”View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch defended the decision to allow Bonehill-Paine to stand as a Conservative councillor as a ‘pile-on’.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAA spokesperson for Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine had served his time, completed Home Office Prevent (counter-terrorism) courses, and had gone into schools to teach about combatting antisemitism and extremism. But the party did not answer questions about what safeguarding checks it had carried out in relation to his appointment as an adviser, or why Badenoch had not contacted Berger.The abuse Bonehill-Paine directed at Berger included calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He also has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.Berger challenged Badenoch over what consideration had been given to safeguarding: “Badenoch’s article says she wants to safeguard the public and victims, but what safeguarding checks have she and the Conservative party carried out?”If Badenoch or her team had reached out to her, Berger said, “I would say, I don’t think it is ‘harder politics’ for this man to be part of Kemi’s operation. I think it’s the wrong politics.”She added: “I’m all for rehabilitation. But someone convicted of neo-Nazi misogynistic crimes is not suitable for public office less than a decade after his conviction. And neither should he be gifted a national advisory role, even closer to power.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesFar rightLuciana BergerKemi BadenochnewsShareReuse this content

title: Octopus Energy urges millions of households to use less electricity during solar eclipse | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Firm urges customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm on Wednesday
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Firm urges customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm on Wednesday
Content: The solar eclipse is expected to knock out the last of Great Britain’s solar power generation for the day.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe solar eclipse is expected to knock out the last of Great Britain’s solar power generation for the day.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesEnergy industryOctopus Energy urges millions of households to use less electricity during solar eclipseFirm urges customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm on WednesdayWhere in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?Jillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreat Britain’s biggest household energy supplier is calling on its customers to use less electricity this week during the deepest solar eclipse in almost 30 years.Octopus Energy has urged customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm this Wednesday as the moon is expected to blockup to 95% of the sunover parts of Britain.The eclipse is expected to knock out the last of Great Britain’s solar power generation for the day, at the same time as the country’s fifth heatwave of the year is likely to increase demand for electricity to run air conditioning, fans and refrigeration systems.Millions in Great Britain can now face emergency power cuts at short noticeRead moreIn return for avoiding unnecessary electricity use during the eclipse, the supplier is offering customers who are signed up to its rewards programme a free hour of electricity to use the next weekend. The offer is open to Octopus customers who are signed up to take part in the supplier’s “saving sessions”, when households can earn rewards for using more electricity at times when renewables are abundant or less electricity when wind and solar power are scarce.Octopus believes that if enough households delay using electricity for a short time during the eclipse, it could reduce the need for Great Britain’s electricity system operator to fire up extra gas-fired stations to replace the lost solar power.“Household flexibility is one of Britain’s biggest untapped energy resources,” the supplier said. “Octopus estimates homes could provide a whopping 13 gigawatts of flexible capacity to support the electricity system – particularly through smart appliances, EVs and home batteries – yet only a fraction of this potential is currently being used.”View image in fullscreenNeso expects the daily early evening peak in electricity demand to occur later than usual during the eclipse on Wednesday.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe NationalEnergySystem Operator (Neso), which is responsible for running Great Britain’s electricity system, said it had been “planning for over a year” to manage the effects of the eclipse, “one of the most unusual evenings our control room will manage this year”. In addition to a major fluctuation in solar power generation, Neso expects the daily early evening peak in electricity demand to occur later than usual as millions head outdoors to watch the eclipse before returning home to cook, clean and watch TV.The heatwave forced Neso to issue its first warning notice for electricity supplies during a summer period in late June. Soaring temperatures lifted demand while disrupting electricity supplies owing to low wind speeds and power plant outages across Europe.In total, the solar eclipse is expected to wipe out 9.7GW of power production across Europe between 7.15pm and 9.30pm during its strongest point. In the UK this could mean losing between 700 megawatts and 1.3GW of solar generation while in Spain, solar power could be reduced by up to 5GW, according to the country’s system operator.This would “pile pressure” on Europe’s already “tight” power system, according to analysts at RBC Capital Markets. The heatwaves have forced nuclear and coal plants to lower their output or shut down entirely across Europe because of reduced river water levels needed for cooling. The drought has also affected hydropower reservoirs in Norway, a leading exporter of electricity to continental Europe, which have reached their lowest levels in 30 years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Europe’s electricity supply is already tight amid the heatwave, with power plants forced to shut down or reduce production as high temperatures have reduced hydro levels as well as the need to cool nuclear and coal plants,” the analysts said.Rebecca Dibb-Simkin, the Octopus chief customer officer, said: “Many of us will be looking up at the sky on Wednesday evening to experience this once-in-a-generation event. But as the sun disappears, so will some of Britain’s solar generation, just as demand peaks.“By shifting everyday tasks like the washing machine or dishwasher until later, households can help reduce the need for gas power stations – and earn rewards for doing their bit.”Neso is also facing scrutiny over its management of the grid after control room whistleblowers accused senior executives ofcovering up instability in the energy systemfor political reasons.In late June it was forced toabruptly cut planned exports of electricity to the Netherlandsvia the high voltage BritNed power interconnector, and call in emergency imports from a large power cable to France, after the grid’s frequency fell to the edge of its operating limits.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryOctopus EnergySolar powerRenewable energyEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta drops open-source model | Mark Zuckerberg | The Guardian
description: Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation
Content: Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the company's Connect developer conference on 17 September 2025 in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Nic Coury/APView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg speaks during the company's Connect developer conference on 17 September 2025 in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Nic Coury/APMark ZuckerbergZuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta drops open-source modelMeta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulationNick Robins-EarlyMon 10 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerbergpublished a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views onartificial intelligenceand announced several plans for howMetawould develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-source AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer.Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled “The Future is for Everyone,” Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times.“Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote.Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kindMetadevelops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them.Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta saysRead moreZuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in aheated debate over how to regulate AIdevelopment, which has involved the creation of asecret White House frameworkfor testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. AsAnthropicandOpenAIhave surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives.Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs.“If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote.Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology.In addition to weighing in on open source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such asdatacenters. The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition andcalls from politicians to issue moratoriumson their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest more in local communities near datacenters, as well as cited an example from Louisiana where some teachers received a $50,000 bonus check as a result of increased sales tax revenue from the company’s infrastructure investment.On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern afterrogue models have hacked outside organizationsin recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanityRead more“Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg.Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’sAI-enabledsmart glasses.“Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.”On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI.
