Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities.“People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.”Explore more on these topicsMark ZuckerbergAI (artificial intelligence)MetaComputingDatacenters – USnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barack Obama launches podcast about books that ‘shaped his worldview’  | Books | The Guardian
description: The former US president will host six episodes of A Great Book for Audible, discussing work from Toni Morrison and John le Carré to James Baldwin
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The former US president will host six episodes of A Great Book for Audible, discussing work from Toni Morrison and John le Carré to James Baldwin
Content: Former president Barack Obama speaks to WNBA All-Stars during a practice at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Friday, July 24, 2026.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APView image in fullscreenFormer president Barack Obama speaks to WNBA All-Stars during a practice at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Friday, July 24, 2026.Photograph: Paul Beaty/APBooksBarack Obama launches podcast about books that ‘shaped his worldview’The former US president will host six episodes of A Great Book for Audible, discussing work from Toni Morrison and John le Carré to James BaldwinElla CreamerMon 10 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarack Obama is set to host a podcast about books that have “profoundly shaped his worldview and our society”, from Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy byJohn le Carré.The podcast, called A Great Book withBarack Obama, will launch on Audible on 24 September.In each of six episodes – produced by the Amazon-owned company in collaboration with the Obamas’s production company Higher Ground – the former US president will discuss one of his chosen titles with a guest.Along with the Morrison and le Carré, Obama has chosen The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, All the Pretty Horses by Cormac McCarthy, Gilead byMarilynne Robinson, and All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren.“Great books have always helped me figure out who I am and what I believe,” said Obama. “The six books featured in this series have stayed with me throughout my life, and each one has something to teach us about the human experience.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Audible and Higher Ground“For this podcast, I invited some friends to explore why they resonate, how they can shape our understanding of ourselves and each other, and why literature matters now more than ever,” he said. “I hope listeners will be inspired to discover or rediscover books that change the way they see themselves and the world”. The podcast’s guests are yet to be announced.Obama has publicly shared his favourite books for years, posting summer reading lists and end-of-year roundups. This summer’s list, which hepublishedin late July, includes Kin by Tayari Jones, Vigil by George Saunders, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, Transcription by Ben Lerner, and Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead.While his roundups are often made up of recently published books, all of his picks for his podcast were published in the 20th century, except for Robinson’s Gilead, released in 2004. Robinson and Obama struck up a correspondence after he invited her to dinner at the White House, and in 2012, he awarded her the National Humanities Medal.Explore more on these topicsBooksPodcastsBarack ObamaPodcastingToni MorrisonJohn le CarréJames BaldwinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his allies | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump
Content: Netanyahu’s comments blindsided IDF commanders and could alienate Trump, his main allyPhotograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersView image in fullscreenNetanyahu’s comments blindsided IDF commanders and could alienate Trump, his main allyPhotograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersBenjamin NetanyahuAnalysisFlip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his alliesEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemIsraeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald TrumpMon 10 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareBenjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks onGazaand establish settlements inside the territory.Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.On Sunday, herejecteda new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.He came to deliver in person the message that theTrump administrationwants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.Last week, Netanyahuscaled backIsraeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”.Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October.Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspapernoted.It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”.Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security expertshave warned.Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpTrump administrationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: From Dubai luxury to an Irish jail cell: Daniel Kinahan’s drastic lifestyle shift | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Only spending outlet for man accused of helping to control a third of Europe’s cocaine supply will be prison tuck shop
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Only spending outlet for man accused of helping to control a third of Europe’s cocaine supply will be prison tuck shop
Content: Daniel Kinahan (back, right) leaving the criminal courts of justice in Dublin after being remanded in custody.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAView image in fullscreenDaniel Kinahan (back, right) leaving the criminal courts of justice in Dublin after being remanded in custody.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAIrelandFrom Dubai luxury to an Irish jail cell: Daniel Kinahan’s drastic lifestyle shiftOnly spending outlet for man accused of helping to control a third of Europe’s cocaine supply will be prison tuck shopRory CarrollIreland correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sounds like the penal equivalent of five stars: a private gym and library, daily outings to the exercise yard and a landing cleared of other prisoners.Daniel Kinahan’s first full day inside the walls of Portlaoise prison on Monday, however, marked a drastic change from hisluxury lifestylein the United Arab Emirates.The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group is confined to a cell for about 20 hours a day, and instead of presiding over an empire said to be worth hundreds of millions of euros his only outlet for expenditure is the tuck shop.The facilities, it turns out, are meagre consolation – a treadmill, some free weights and limited reading material. “The so-called gym and library are nothing much,” one sourcetold the Irish Times. “The gym is probably slightly bigger than a box room in a house.”View image in fullscreenPortlaoise prison, which will be Daniel Kinahan’s home at least until his trial in October.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThat is the reality facing Kinahan, 49, for months until his trial – and possibly decades if convicted.The Dubliner has not been convicted of any crime and remains innocent before the law, but hisextradition on Sundayrepresents a victory for the Irish state and law enforcement agencies across the world.Kinahan was named a leader of a cartel said to control about a third of Europe’s cocaine supply, along with running criminal sidelines in firearms and racketeering. From his base in Dubai he had appeared impervious to such allegations for almost a decade, while becoming aninfluential figure in sportthrough his boxing management company MTK Global, which arranged championship bouts.View image in fullscreenWanted posters at Dublin city hall after the US government announced it was offering $5m for information on the Kinahans.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThat changed after the US offered a reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) for information that led to his arrest or conviction. The US treasury department said the Kinahan group had engaged in a gang war with another group inIrelandand Spain, “resulting in numerous murders”.The US bounty helped Ireland to secure an extradition treaty with the UAE last year, paving the way forKinahan’s arrestin Dubai in April on foot of an Irish warrant.After failing to block extradition, Kinahan was flown in an Irish government jet to Casement aerodrome on Sunday and taken to the criminal courts of justice in central Dublin where he was charged with directing organised crime.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA sketch of Daniel Kinahan at the criminal courts of justice in Dublin.Photograph: Mike O’DonnellTold by one of the three judges that a bail application would have to be made to the high court, the prisoner was phlegmatic. “I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you,” he said.Observers at the hearing noted that Kinahan, wearing a black hoodie, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers, looked older than the photographs that show a smiling, more youthful figure. He was pale, reflecting his incarceration since April.Crowds lined part of the route to watch as he was driven in a Garda car – not a blast-proof prison van, as originally expected – to Portlaoise, a high-security prison 50 miles (80km) outside Dublin that used to house republican paramilitaries and is now home to drug gang members and others convicted of serious crimes.View image in fullscreenOnlookers take photos as the car carrying Daniel Kinahan passes on route to court.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAKinahan is the sole prisoner on a landing in A block that usually hosts eight inmates. During visits to the yard, which has wire netting to prevent contraband being dropped in, he will be alone. He will be served breakfast at 8am, lunch at 12.30pm and supper at 4.30pm and have a tuck shop account to buy personal items from the prison shop.Video calls will afford contact with his wife and children inDubai. A glass pane will separate him from in-person visitors. Kinahan is scheduled to return to the non-jury court on 5 October.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeDubainewsShareReuse this content

title: Amanda Knox in Cartwheel review – rookie standup acquitted of murder tells her story | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show
Content: Knox brings off some adroit jokes while staying respectful to the memory of Meredith Kercher, who was murdered in 2007.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKnox brings off some adroit jokes while staying respectful to the memory of Meredith Kercher, who was murdered in 2007.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAmanda Knox in Cartwheel review – rookie standup acquitted of murder tells her storyGilded Balloon TeviotPerformer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy showBrian LoganMon 10 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Welcome to themost controversial show on the fringe!” Some audiences will diagnose self-regard in that intro by rookie standup Amanda Knox. For others, as for Knox herself, it merely acknowledges the continuing efforts to silence her. But then, Knox is “the human version of the blue/gold dress”, a canvas on to which we all project guilty, innocent – or weird. Her innocence now proved, it’s the last of these charges she takes on in this fringe outing, retelling her oft-told tale through the lens of new motherhood.Is it a disgrace that she’s telling it at all – and profiting from it, some would say. (Although they’ve presumably never taken a show to the Edinburgh fringe.) Classifying Cartwheel as comedy may be a misstep; it risks looking insensitive and inaccurately describes the show. But, judging by the evidence, Knox would be damned whatever she did. Now at least she can tell her story in her own way, articulating a growing anger at her treatment and a determination to raise her daughter, not to be silenced and scared but “to be the exact girl I was punished for being”.View image in fullscreenAmanda Knox in Cartwheel at The Wine Bar at Gilded Balloon.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf we’re here for an insight into what it’s like to beAmanda Knox, we get it, as episodes from the 39-year-old’s “extremely prolonged and public trauma” are recounted while folding children’s clothes and maintaining a dialogue with the voice of her four-year-old daughter. How can she tell her kids about her wrongful imprisonment? As a Dr Seuss story: “Knox the fox in a box with locks”? How to react when her baby’s birth is greeted with hateful online abuse? Becoming a mum has refined Knox’s understanding and sharpened her fury at everything she, and her own mother, have been put through.More power to her for peppering this account with several adroit jokes – even if they elicit more rueful smiles than laughs. She’s an inexperienced comedian, this isn’t a “show” – but she shapes and performs this umpteenth telling of her story well. I found its spirit of defiance stirring, I found it respectful to the memory of her murdered roommate, and as well judged an effort by Knox to reclaim her awful story as we have any right to expect.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Amanda KnoxComedyEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Makes Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey seem understated’ – critics weigh up Game of Thrones: The Mad King | Theatre | The Guardian
description: ‘Spectacular’ or ‘stolid’? The reviews are in for the Royal Shakespeare Company’s prequel to George RR Martin’s fantasy blockbuster
Author: Guardian stage
Headline: ‘Spectacular’ or ‘stolid’? The reviews are in for the Royal Shakespeare Company’s prequel to George RR Martin’s fantasy blockbuster
Content: Callum Woodhouse in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenCallum Woodhouse in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatre‘Makes Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey seem understated’ – critics weigh up Game of Thrones: The Mad King‘Spectacular’ or ‘stolid’? The reviews are in for the Royal Shakespeare Company’s prequel to George RR Martin’s fantasy blockbusterGuardian stageMon 10 Aug 2026 06.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Googledouble quotation markYou don’t need to read the entrails of a raven to guess the target of the subtitle The Mad King: the various Brutuses plotting his fall conclude that the “paranoid and delusional” monarch will destroy their civilisation. The focus, though, is not just Trumpian. Macmillan references two wider international crises – the instability of heads of state and the weather – and a UK national concern: the endurance of a royal bloodline. The RSC’s patron, King Charles III, might skip this one.Mark Lawson, the Guardiandouble quotation markThe main auditorium has been reconfigured so that the audience presses in on all sides with the action predominantly confined to a cruciform stage with mighty gates at the far end and a coronet-style arch at its centre. The opening wordless sequence, featuring an inordinate procession of arrivals (there’s a cast of 36), conjures a due aura of wonder and clanging foreboding. Most strikingly, a number of characters enter on horseback; these magnificent metallic steeds are operated, as in War Horse, by an obliging trio of handlers.Dominic Cavendish, the Telegraphdouble quotation markThe great achievement of this reimagining of George RR Martin’s universe by writer Duncan Macmillan and director Dominic Cooke is that it ties up plot points from the Song of Ice and Fire franchise in ways likely to satisfy avid fans of the novels and the subsequent TV series but simultaneously creates a narrative clear and engaging enough to entrance the only partially affiliated or the complete newbie.Sarah Crompton, WhatsOnStageView image in fullscreenAuthor George RR Martin arrives at the gala evening for Game of Thrones: The Mad King at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty Imagesdouble quotation markDesigner Chloe Lamford creates a visionary space, where dragon puppets and vast stomping horses stalk in shadowy slo mo like they’re embedded deep in this world’s collective memory. Silk-skirted courtly dances and unwieldy but spectacular joust scenes show how these dynasties enjoy themselves, before the noble blood starts to fall.Alice Saville, the Independentdouble quotation markThis prequel to a blood-soaked dynastic saga wanders on for so long that it makes Christopher Nolan’s journey into Greek mythology seem a model of understatement. There’s no reason why the RSC shouldn’t bring Martin’s epic books to the stage in Game of Thrones: The Mad King, but if this stolid production gives hardcore GoT fans a chance to hunt for “Easter eggs”, it seldom comes close to matching the grim aura of the TV series.Clive Davis, the Timesdouble quotation markThe first half of Cooke’s superbly staged, spectacular production has the feel of a dynamic Bayeux Tapestry: a stunning pageant of medieval stop-motion animation. But after the interval, the plot takes off. Sparks fly romantically and dramatically, which is just as well because, at three hours 45 minutes, it’s almost as long as Hamlet.Georgina Brown, Daily Mail‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingRead moredouble quotation markMacmillan’s adaptation takes pains to explain. Some of the exposition clanks, but I understand the necessity. More problematic is too many actors portentously declaiming everything with Shakespearean affectation, not helped by the jarring excess of ofts, betwixts and mayhapses, when Martin’s success lies in making (fictional) history feel viscerally immediate. In that, all the actresses dazzle, notably Elizabeth Ayodele’s vivid Princess Elia and Mariah Gale’s monstrous yet magnificent Queen Rhaella.Stefan Kyriazis,ExpressExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGame of ThronesGeorge RR MartinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t watch it without sobbing’: your happiest TV endings | Television | The Guardian
description: From poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joy
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joy
Content: A fitting testament to love, endurance, and above all, friendship … The final episode of Superstore.Photograph: NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fitting testament to love, endurance, and above all, friendship … The final episode of Superstore.Photograph: NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty ImagesTelevision‘I can’t watch it without sobbing’: your happiest TV endingsFrom poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joyGuardian readersandJoe PinnerMon 10 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA missing monkey, a token tennis bracelet, and the end of the Korean war! These are the most uplifting and moving finales in TV history, according to Guardian readers. Warning, spoilers lie ahead.Friday Night Dinner‘The magnificent, the magical, the marvellous!’ It’s TV’s happiest endingsRead moreAfter nine years of following the Goodman family, the boys – Adam and Jonny – finally bring home “females” to meet parents Jackie and Martin. The dinner is absolute chaos, Martin has ruined all of the food, he’s thrown a piece of bread at Adam’s girlfriend, their neighbour Jim keeps running in with bags of dog vomit, Jackie is having a total meltdown, and then everything stops in a beautiful moment when both girls announce they’re pregnant.The family boogie to the theme song would be a moment of sheer joy on its own, but it’s made even more so since this turned out to be the final episode. The sad and untimely death of Paul Ritter, who played Martin, the year after the broadcast makes this scene all the more poignant. The image of the family celebration is a reminder to embrace the family dance, whether it’s happy times or times when you say: “Sh*t on it.”Amy, Tampa, FloridaSuperstoreThe US sitcom Superstore spends several seasons gently pointing out the flaws of capitalism, US employment and immigration law, and the general folly of humanity, while making you fall in love with (most of) the flawed and horrifying characters you meet. Has there ever been a greater villain than Sandra’s arch-nemesis Carol?Set in a fictional supermarket, it takes you through increasing digitalisation of the industry and the Covid pandemic with a feather-light touch, and absolutely hilarious vignettes of the worst behaviour you can imagine in retail. The arc of its central pairing, Amy and Jonah, is compromised through the final series as lead actress (and producer) America Ferrera briefly left the programme, but she returns to wrap things up with a beautiful and deeply satisfying peek into the future. The finale is a fitting testament to love, endurance and, above all, friendship.Jill, 43, DerbyshireHeated RivalryView image in fullscreenMagic … Connor Storrie (left) and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry.Heated Rivalry, season one. I hope they don’t make any more seasons because they’ll never be able to capture the magic of the first. The ending was a perfect wrap-up of the short six-episode series. As a gay guy of a certain age, I’ve found that the vast majority of movies and TV shows about gay men I’ve had to sit through have been tragic or whitewashed. In the US, we drag shows out until all the fun has been completely drained out and at the end they’re unrecognisable from where they began.Danny, 57, New YorkstateThe Good PlaceThe Good Place is an extraordinarily rare gem. It’s a comedy that’s actually funny, with characters that you really care about despite their varied faults. However, the end of the first series immediately sent up the red flag for other series with such a strong opening – where can you go from here?However, it remained a gem for all four seasons, until the four principal protagonists finally create the heaven they’d always wanted and, one by one, each at their own time, they decide they’ve had enough of everything, are as happy as they could ever be, have experienced everything they’d ever wanted to experience, and that it’s finally the right time to just … go. It’s beautiful and uplifting, and makes me feel happy whenever I think about it.Andy, JapanScrubsScrubs is an amazing show with some genuine character development. We follow a trio of budding medical interns – JD, Elliot and Turk – as they grow and become well-rounded doctors and human beings.View image in fullscreenPitch perfect … Scrubs.Photograph: PRIn a final two-parter, (for season eight, that is, and not the “should-have-been-a-spin-off” season nine, or the recent reboot), JD accepts a job at a new hospital to be closer to his son. And then, on his last day, he goes to painstaking lengths to have the perfect swan song – the constant farewells with his best friend, Turk, finally learning the name of the janitor who tormented him the entire series, and having the perfect final moment with his gruff but ultimately caring mentor, Dr Cox (even if it did take some coaxing).And then the grand finale: JD realises through a patient that you need to accept the future and all the uncertainties it holds. JD walks through the hospital’s halls, filled with all the people he interacted with right back to the first season, as he stops to watch a giant screen projecting a moving montage of the future, set to Peter Gabriel’s The Book of Love. A pitch-perfect ending.Arjun, 26, LondonGhostsThe ending of Ghosts is moving and life-affirming, and a perfect example of what this show does brilliantly, which is to land its moments (sad and funny) without lingering on them for too long. It might be because I binged it, but it felt like the ending was really made up of the season’s last three episodes. The fifth one has the heartbreaking reveal of the Captain’s backstory, followed by that joyous line dancing scene. Then there’s episode six, which has a well-crafted throwback to the beginning, with Alison finding out that Julian pushed her out of the window. He’s the one who has to persuade her to stay, via a beautiful monologue made all the lovelier coming from him.And then, just when you think it’s settled and they’re staying – the Christmas special. It’s happy and satisfying and sad. I love Pat teaching the Captain how to do baby talk and the way they all run to the answering machine to hear Mike’s message. The episode gives all of the characters a moment to be truly themselves. You get a sense of how much Alison loves the ghosts and vice versa; it’s incredibly sweet without being saccharine.Emily, HampshireView image in fullscreenIncredibly sweet without being saccharine … BBC’s Ghosts.Photograph: PRSleepersDoes anyone else remember Sleepers? A post-glasnost spy comedy in which Warren Clarke and Nigel Havers are Soviet agents sent to infiltrate Britain in 1965, and build lives they’re very happy with, thank you, and don’t want to go back to shabby apartments in the Nevsky Prospect. By the end of the series, both have been captured by the hardline KGB officer sent to recover them, and are drugged and shipped out to a waiting submarine. They wake up, and the KGB is returning them to their homes. But while the lead characters are safe, Clarke’s daughter’s cuddly monkey Maurice is missing! Weeks later he appears, wearing a Russian fur hat, having been on an adventure of his own. A perfect show.Nick, 58, YorkshireM*A*S*HThe show I grew up with in the 70s. Beautifully anti-war with top-drawer writing and brilliant characters. The ending is a tear-fest. After the ceasefire is announced, the members of the 4077th throw a party before taking down the camp for the very last time. So many great moments: Hawkeye and BJ saluting Colonel Potter, upper-class Charles leaving in a garbage truck, the death of Henry, and Hawkeye saluting Radar. And the final scene where Hawkeye, who spent the last episode unable to say goodbye, spells it out in rocks that BJ can only view from the air as he lifts off in a chopper. No, you’re crying.Cameron, LedburyView image in fullscreenTear-fest … M*A*S*H.Six Feet UnderEverybody dies! But that’s also what makes it such a special ending, because we get to see how every character’s life plays out in vignettes as the weight of the show’s themes are lifted from them. Claire finally escapes her mother’s overbearing influence, without having to destroy their relationship to do so. Rico gets to run his own funeral home, without the Fishers’ influence. David slays his demons and lives happily ever after with Keith when it looked as if they would destroy him. Brenda realises she can be a good mother after all. Then – yes, as everybody dies! – we get surely the greatest closing montage sequence on TV, with an exceptional soundtrack (Sia’s Breathe Me) to accompany it. I think someone’s started chopping onions in here again …Stephen, 47, SolihullSchitt’s CreekNot only does the finale offer the sheer joy of David and Patrick’s wedding (Moira in her papal mitre and gloves, sobbing her way through the ceremony, the Jazzagals singing Simply the Best, Alexis accidentally dressed as a bride), but the beautiful denouement of the show, as they quietly move on with their lives, back to success but so differently than they imagined in the beginning.View image in fullscreenThe happiest of endings … Schitt’s Creek.I can’t watch it without sobbing. It is to me the happiest of endings: the guy gets the guy, the girl gets the career, Johnny finally makes it back to business, and Moira? Exactly where she belongs, back to Sunrise Bay, along with a token tennis bracelet. It is a sublime moment that takes such good care of the fans and how invested we are in each of Rose’s (and Stevie’s) journeys. It is so refreshing to give everyone a simple happy ending without compromise or drama.Casey, 34, BrightonExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedySchitt's CreekThe Good PlaceFriday Night DinnerHeated RivalryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kissing in public: will it make your relationship stronger? | Relationships | The Guardian
description: Public displays of affection are widely mocked online and off, but they have a positive side – and now science has proved it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Public displays of affection are widely mocked online and off, but they have a positive side – and now science has proved it
Content: Love is in the hair.Photograph: Posed by models; Flashpop/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLove is in the hair.Photograph: Posed by models; Flashpop/Getty ImagesPass notesRelationshipsKissing in public: will it make your relationship stronger?Public displays of affection are widely mocked online and off, but they have a positive side – and now science has proved itMon 10 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Kissing in public.Age:Kissing is 17m-21m years old– probably older than the notion of privacy.Appearance:Romantic, uninhibited.Sounds horrible.Actually, I think attitudes tend to vary from person to person.Well, they shouldn’t. When I go to the cinema, I want the orgy to be on the screen.In fact, public kissing is very big right now among celebrity couples.I think we have amassed enough evidence over the years to establish that celebrities simply don’t know how to behave.Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Kylie Jenner and TimothéeChalamet, Brooklyn Beckham and Nicola Peltz – they’re all at it, kissing and cuddling for the cameras.No good will come of this.That’s where you’re wrong: new research suggests that public displays of affection, or PDAs, are strongly linked to higher-quality romantic relationships.I prefer theprivatedisplay ofaffection.Also good for your relationship, according to the research.What sort of research is this?The study, published in the journalPlos One, looked at 461 people in three countries: Poland, Nepal and Indonesia.Quite a random selection.These societies all have different, though generally negative, attitudes towards PDAs. Yet subjects who engaged in more PDAs consistently reported higher relationship satisfaction across the three cultures.Why would that be?“Because affectionate behaviour is one of the ways people communicate closeness, love and emotional connection,” said the leader of the study, Dagna Kocur.I still think it’s just showing off.And icky.You don’t think it’s ever appropriate to kiss in public?During a wedding ceremony, maybe, or at the end of a major world war, but otherwise it should remain behind closed doors. Fewer PDAsand moreprivate displays of affection, please!You’re right, in a way: Kocur went on to point out that private displays of affection are even more strongly linked to relationship satisfaction, “so it may be worth making the time to hold hands and kiss at home, too”.At home, on the bus, in the bread aisle atMorrisons– don’t these people ever get tired of pawing one another?A further study is now planned to include 1,000 people across nine countries.Good!We’ll finally get proofthat a persistent lack of affection builds character.Actually, it can lead to mental health problems.What sort of mental health problems?A condition commonly known asskin hunger, which may cause anxiety, depression and alexithymia – an impairment of your ability to interpret emotion.Relax, Casanova – you’re not my type.A case, I think, in point.Do say:“Physical affection, wherever it occurs, is essential to our wellbeing as humans.”Don’t say:“Get a room!”Explore more on these topicsRelationshipsPass notesSocial etiquetteDatingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sam Neill on making Hunt for the Wilderpeople: ‘We were attacked by a puppet pig!’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatised
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatised
Content: ‘It felt like both of us were 12’ … Julian Dennison and Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Piki Films/AllstarView image in fullscreen‘It felt like both of us were 12’ … Julian Dennison and Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Piki Films/AllstarHow we madeMoviesSam Neill on making Hunt for the Wilderpeople: ‘We were attacked by a puppet pig!’Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatisedWarning: contains spoilersInterviews byChris BroughtonMon 10 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Neill, played Hector FaulknerTaika Waititi’s filmBoyis one of my favourites ever, so when I got the Wilderpeople script I was already well disposed to it. Hec is sort of a New Zealand archetype. When I was at university, during the holidays I’d work at cutting hay and shifting sheep and fertiliser. There was always a Hec driving the truck. They were men of very few words, but when they did say something it meant a lot. It was clear I was never going to have many lines in the film.Hunt for the Wilderpeople is based on Wild Pork and Watercress, a novel by Barry Crump, a legendary figure when I was growing up. A lot of his stuff is very amusing, but not this one – it took Taika to make it funny. Just about every comedian inNew Zealandis in the film. I was probably the only non-comedian, but the film has a complexity beyond the humour. A lot of that comes, I think, from Rima Te Wiata. She plays Hec’s wife Bella with such warmth, compassion and empathy that when she dies both Hec and Ricky are suffused with grief. That grief gives a powerful dimension to the remainder of the film.View image in fullscreen‘When Bella dies both Hec and Ricky are suffused with grief’ … Sam Neill, Rima Te Wiata and Julian Dennisonin Hunt for the WilderpeopleThe Ricky Baker birthday songseems to have become a sort of informal national anthem, but it’s only in the film because the traditional Happy Birthday song wasn’t then in the public domain. The scene was all set up with Rima about to play the conventional version on her little keyboard when the producer came running in and said: “We can’t use that, we don’t have copyright!” Rima, Taika and I had to write something new in 10 minutes, but it was mostly Rima. Sometimes, working under pressure produces the best things.I didn’t have the best relationship with the canine actor that played Hec’s hunting dog, Zag. I’m a dog guy, but he wasn’t the pal you would expect a dog to be – he had other things on his mind. The wild boar that wounds Zag was realised on screen in a mixture of ways. But on location we were reacting to a couple of guys operating a kind of puppet pig! The finished scene is pretty full-on. A lot of people have to comfort their children after it.People often stop me and say it’s their favourite film. They remember it with affection, and when something is taken to heart, that’s a wonderful thing to have in your CV. The only thing that irritated me after its release was some people saying Julian stole the film from me. I don’t think there was any theft involved – the film was always his in the first place.Sam Neill gave this interview in June, a monthbefore his death on13 July.Julian Dennison, played Ricky BakerI’d worked with Taika before on an anti-drugs advert and didn’t have to audition. Ricky is this broken kid stuck in a system of foster care that’s failing him. I come from a community where that happens a lot with young people – I had cousins who acted like Ricky Baker, I had friends who dressed like him and my brother listened to Tupac.I knew Sam Neill was big and lots of people liked him, but I didn’t really know who he was. Knowing there were going to be all these scenes of just him and me in the bush, I thought: “Man, I hope he’s not lame …” He turned out to be very young at heart, like an older cousin. I had the best time and loved hanging out with Sam – sometimes it felt like both of us were 12 years old.I grew up in a religious home and went to Sunday school, and I wasn’t a big swearer like Ricky. When it came to lines like: “Shit just got real!” I was like: “Am I allowed to say this?”double quotation markI said: ‘Wouldn’t it be funny if Sam opened the door and realised he hadn’t dug the tunnel yet?’Rachel House, who played the child welfare officer leading the hunt for Hec and Ricky, was also my acting coach. She taught me tricks like recording my lines and listening back to them the night before we shot a scene. I still do that today. The movie is full of pop-culture references from way before I was born which I didn’t get while I was making it, but I see the bigger picture now.Taika was open to ideas, which often arrived while we were all practising our lines in a hot tub. In the scene where Ricky and Hec are trying to come up with an escape plan with Rhys Darby’s character, Psycho Sam, there was a line in the script about an underground bunker. I said: “Wouldn’t it be funny if Sam opened the door and realised he hadn’t dug the tunnel yet?” That ended up in the movie.The big car chaseat the end was shot on the ancestral land of the Ngāti Rangi tribe, who were really welcoming and helpful, as were the army, who use some of their territory as a training ground. We had to travel in a truck with army people when we went from the filming base to the location. I guess they’d lost some of their mines or something – they’d be like: “If you see metal things sticking out of the ground, just let us know.” If anything was spotted, someone would come over with bright pink spray paint and draw a circle around it, like some people do to draw attention to dog poo.The 10th anniversary release of Hunt for the Wilderpeople in 4k is in cinemas and on digital platforms now, with UHD and Blu-ray editions on 17 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeSam NeillTaika WaititiNew ZealandComedy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: Working at a toy store was my teen feminist awakening  | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: I loved the business of selling toys – it felt like I was selling joy. But my least favourite part was the gendered language
Author: Maggie Zhou
Headline: I loved the business of selling toys – it felt like I was selling joy. But my least favourite part was the gendered language
Content: ‘Despite the lows, my memories of Toys R Us are extremely fond.’Composite: Maggie Zhou/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘Despite the lows, my memories of Toys R Us are extremely fond.’Composite: Maggie Zhou/Guardian DesignA job that changed meAustralian lifestyleA job that changed me: Working at a toy store was my teen feminist awakeningI loved the business of selling toys – it felt like I was selling joy. But my least favourite part was the gendered languageMaggie ZhouMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas 15 when I landed my job atToysR Us. Before that, my first job was a one-month stint at the local fish and chip shop, where I was paid in $20 bills slotted into Chiko roll packets. After a burn on my forearm (I still have it), I left the gig. That was the end of my hospitality career.This was 2014. I knew my strengths and weaknesses; I was no good with deep-fry baskets or carrying more than one thing in each hand. I wanted to work in the hallowed halls of retail.Lucky for me, there was an excess of Christmas casual jobs specifically looking for the youngest workers they could legally pay the least. So I became one of Toys R Us’s checkout chicks, dressed in a blue polo shirt, black pants, a lanyard and my school shoes. I processed transactions, pointed customers in the right direction, counted the end-of-day tills and cleaned up the store once the doors shut. To decompress, I’d play a few rounds of Bop It! in the board games aisle.I loved being in the business of selling toys. It felt like I was selling joy. As with any job involving children, there were ugly bits. Vomit and urine in aisles weren’t uncommon sights – though it was the floor staff’s job to deal with the clean-up. We also had its subsidiary, Babies R Us, in the store. I found it amusing that 17-year-olds were allowed to advise expectant parents on breast pumps.A job that changed me: At the Titanic theatre restaurant we always hit an iceberg, but were often hit by bread rolls tooRead moreAs a burgeoning feminist, my least favourite part of the job was the gendered language entrenched in the industry. I took great pleasure in playing dumb – head cocked to one side, brows furrowed – when customers asked where the “girls” or “boys” toys were. If forced to adopt such language, I’d pair it with exaggerated air quotes.A woman once called to place an order for balloons for her grandson’s birthday. We took down the typical details – how many balloons? When could she pick them up? – but when it came down to the colour, we touched a nerve. “Theboycolour!,” she insisted. She arrived and we handed her a bunch of blue balloons. She recoiled. She wanted red. Obviously.I saw hyper-consumerism on overdrive. I worked an overnight shift during Chadstone Shopping Centre’s34-hour Christmas trade period, watching on as frantic shoppers raced to purchase plastic that would end up in landfills by the next festive season. I came to understand that retailers employ harsh lighting in windowless stores so shoppers are unaware of the time.I met dozens of adults hardcore into collectibles, getting us to bring out boxes of Hot Wheels from the backrooms so they could rifle through stock before it hit the shelves. I learned that we’d play Justin Timberlake’s Can’t Stop The Feeling! on the hour, every hour, the year the Trolls movie came out. I knew which toy was hot one month, and which would be the next big thing the month after. It was a short course in capitalism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite the lows, my memories of Toys R Us are extremely fond. I ended up leaving to work in fashion retail around the time I started university. Soon after, Toys R Us Australia entered administration andall stores closed the same year.When I applied to Toys R Us as a teenager looking for some pocket money, I didn’t realise that – to this day – I’d be entering my longest place of employment. I also didn’t realise a fluorescently garish 78-year-old US toy company would be the one to radicalise me.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleA job that changed meBusinessToysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is Andy Burnham seriously about to tour Britain like some medieval monarch? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The ‘King of the North’ is on the march – or rather, on a bus. But maybe he’d be better off staying at home and thinking than heading out to press the flesh, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The ‘King of the North’ is on the march – or rather, on a bus. But maybe he’d be better off staying at home and thinking than heading out to press the flesh, writes Zoe Williams
Content: It’s good to talk, but … Burnham on a visit to a family centre in Sheffield last month.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersView image in fullscreenIt’s good to talk, but … Burnham on a visit to a family centre in Sheffield last month.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersOpinionAndy BurnhamIs Andy Burnham seriously about to tour Britain like some medieval monarch?Zoe WilliamsThe ‘King of the North’ is on the march – or rather, on a bus. But maybe he’d be better off staying at home and thinking than heading out to press the fleshMon 10 Aug 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareAndy Burnham is going on a “listening tour”, travelling the country on a bus to find out what real people are concerned about. I’ve heard commentators rationalise the idea in various ways: apparently it underscores the difference between him and his predecessor, who only ever relaxed when he was out of the country; what else is Burnham going to do in recess, with his cabinet already chosen – organise his Post-it notes?; he’s been out of politics a long time, and many people will be only dimly aware of who he is; his speeches to date have had a very urban focus, and particularly with farming being this season’s crisis sector, he needs to broaden his sphere of interest to take in rural areas. Truly, the prime ministerial honeymoon period is like a one-year-old’s birthday party – all you have to do is stand up and smile, for everyone to clap.None of the rationalisations are in any way true: an in-person focus group, where you journey to discover a range of concerns you could figure out for yourself with one report from the Institute for Public Policy Research and half a brain, is exactly the kind of thing Starmer would have done, if he’d thought of it. There’s quite a bit to be getting on with, between now and September, since autumn’s looming crises – food shortages, energy price hikes due to the ongoing war in Iran – are plain, and there’s no better time to plan than when you don’t have the leader of the opposition yanking your chain. Burnham actually has tremendous household-level recognition, thanks to a combination of hinterland and eyelashes, as evidenced by the fact thateven when contesting Makerfieldhe got mobbed every time he got out of a car. Now,the conditions devastating farmers, being the direct result of climate crisis, would be better addressed by a long-range strategy on the transition to renewables, not a chinwag.I’ll meet the road show halfway, though, and accept that the thinking behind it is buried deeper in the squishy collective subconscious than the “marketing strategy for mid-sized building society” strata. This is the living definition of “peripatetic”, an adjective usually attached to kings. Medieval kings travelled around the country in order to collect their taxes by literallyeating them from one noble estate to the next. Tax hikes could be exacted by simply adding to your entourage and eating more. King John’s train stretched two miles, bulked up by the mercenaries required to protect the pampered non-warrior class from rebel barons who were sick of having their food eaten. In a pesky feedback loop, the larger your entourage, the more you all ate, the more annoyed the aristocracy became, the more mercenaries you needed and the larger your entourage.The Manchester years: how Burnham’s rebirth as ‘king of the north’ set him on road to No 10Read moreBurnham could be forgiven for thinking he’s more than a match for this death spiral, having the lessons of history right there, but can we forgive him for the emotional leap that put him on his tour bus? His first question seems to have been not “What would the leader of a mature democracy in an embattled period do?” but “What would be the first move ofthe King of the North?” His kingly role models must all come from the dawn of monarchy, since by the time you get to Henry VIII, he’s only really travelling to escape sewage overflow from his last great palace. But then “King of the North” has always had a very medieval overtone. A sign of the early modern period’s growing governmental sophistication was its ability to distinguish one bit of the north from another.It is endearing, if also nerve-racking and painful, to consider the faith underpinning this self-fashioning – that leadership is an innate quality more important than sequential thought and planning, and that if the stars light upon a leader who can connect with his people, the nation will come together, good decisions will be made, and the rest is detail. One can but hope that’s the limit of the wishful thinking, and he’s not also banking on some dragons.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament
Content: The flaw in the Water (Special Measures) Act was always obvious.Photograph: AKP Photos/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe flaw in the Water (Special Measures) Act was always obvious.Photograph: AKP Photos/AlamyNils Pratley on financeWater industryWater companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect?Nils PratleyDoor was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliamentThames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government departmentMon 10 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAnybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up.Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not guaranteed) bonus and getting a smaller (but still hefty) increase in fixed pay instead. Some even preferred greater certainty over what they would take home.In water-land, the Labour government arrived in 2024 promising to “ban the payment of bonuses to polluting water bosses until they have cleaned up their filth”, which generated a few pleasing headlines. But theflaw in the resulting Water (Special Measures) Act 2025was obvious. While the regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, was given powers to block performance-related bonuses at the worst environmental and financial miscreants, it could do nothing formally about other payments.Thus – surprise, surprise – salary increases, allowance awards and, most of all, retention payments have proliferated. After the English and Welsh companies published their annual reports last month,this newspaper foundthat overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers for the year. It was thesecond year in a rowthat a bonus ban had resulted in higher overall pay across the sector.One can usually rely onThames Waterto muddy things further, and its post-annual report contribution was the news that the chief financial officer, Steve Buck, who was paid £591,000 in the financial year to March,got a delayed £1m signing feeat the end of July. As for retention payments for other executives that were “paused” after a political kerfuffle a year ago, the company has “entered into 14 agreements” to “resolve its liability for any potential claims”.The government is shocked, or pretends to be. “It is unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust,” a spokesperson for the environment department said.Again, though, one must ask: what did ministers think would happen? It’s easy to agree that executives of underperforming monopolies are grossly overpaid but it was fantastically naive on the part of politicians to think a ban on bonuses would not result in alternative wheezes. Itwas predictable.Water companies in general have deployed the retention manoeuvre in less-than-transparent – or just shameless – ways, it should be added. Helen Campbell, the interim executive director of Ofwat, was clearly correct last month whenshe complainedthat customers’ trust is harmed when remuneration committees make decisions that “give the appearance of circumventing the rule” or aren’t explained.The point, though, is that the government left the door wide open to such behaviour. If ministers were relying on remuneration committees to obey the “spirit” of their reforms, they were born yesterday. Restricting bonuses is not the same as restricting overall pay. And Ofwat can use only the powers it was given by parliament.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe dance now moves to the regulator’s review, due in the autumn, of whether the rules should be strengthened. Maybe it will yield something different in the prime minister Andy Burnham’s undefined era of “greater public control”. On past experience, however, believe it when you see it.Explore more on these topicsWater industryNils Pratley on financeExecutive pay and bonusesThames WaterUtilitiesWatercommentShareReuse this content

title: The media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why? | Mehdi Hasan | The Guardian
description: The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear
Author: Mehdi Hasan
Headline: The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear
Content: ‘Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press.’Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press.’Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionMediaThe media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why?Mehdi HasanThe challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clearMon 10 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTShareWestern media outlets cannot seem to get enough of Gadi Eisenkot.Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press as he and his party take the lead in the polls in the run-up to October’s elections.“Will Israel embrace the ‘anti-Netanyahu’ who lost a son in Gaza?”askedthe Times of London.“He lost his son in Gaza. Now he’s coming for Netanyahu,”declaredthe Daily Telegraph.“How Netanyahu’s Top General Became His Strongest Challenger,”ranthe headline on a lengthy David Remnick profile of Eisenkot in the New Yorker.“Does Gadi Eisenkot offer Israel a new chance?”wonderedthe Economist.It’s a fair question. But perhaps British and American commentators aren’t the right people to answer it.Why not ask the Palestinians of Gaza?At the height of the genocide, between October 2023 and June 2024, Eisenkot sat in Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet while Israel waged its barbaric military campaign in Gaza. During that period, Israeli airstrikes leveledentire apartment buildings, hitschools,hospitalsandrefugee camps, and killedmore than 30,000Palestinians.Eisenkot eventually resigned from the war cabinet in 2024. But not over the horrific death toll. He left over what he regarded as the government’sstrategic failures. Even the New Yorker’s Remnick, in hissympathetic profile piece, noted how the general, who lost his own soldier son Gal in the fighting, “remains reluctant to condemn Netanyahu in any detail for the extraordinary severity and duration of the war in Gaza”.And Eisenkot has form when it comes to killing Gaza’s Palestinians. As Israel’s chief of staff during the“Great March of Return” in 2018 and 2019, he oversaw the armed response to mass Palestinian demonstrations against the siege of Gaza.Israeli soldiers, mostly snipers,killedmore than 200 Palestinians, including dozens of children. “The Israeli security forces killed and maimed Palestinian demonstrators who did not pose an imminent threat,” concluded aUN commission of inquiry, adding that it “found reasonable grounds to believe that demonstrators were shot in violation of their right to life”.If the Economist wants to know whether Eisenkot represents “a new chance”, perhaps it should also ask Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.Yes, Eisenkot may be opposed to the far-right Netanyahu government’s annexation plan, but he is also opposed to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. “I have never said two states for two peoples,” he proudlydeclaimedin an interview in June, “because I understand the depth of this religious-national-social conflict, and anyone who talks about ‘peace now’ and two states doesn’t understand the conflict.“I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria,” he continued, using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank.So much for Eisenkot’s supposed pragmatism and liberalism. He openly rejects a two-state solution and proudly supports Israeli settlements – settlements that theinternational court of justiceand multipleUN resolutionsconsider illegal under international law.Or perhaps journalists should ask the residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of men, women and children were killed in the2006 Israeli assault on Lebanon, whether Eisenkot represents a fresh start.As head of Israel’s Northern Command, he became closely associated with what came to be known as the“Dahiya Doctrine”: an Israeli military strategy of deterrence premised on the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure.“What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on,” Eisenkotexplainedto an interviewer in 2008. “We will apply disproportionate force on it [village] and cause great damage and destruction there.”The use ofdisproportionate forceagainst civilian targets is, of course, an undeniablewar crime.Netanyahu may be a clear villain – but he can also be acartoon villain. The danger with Eisenkot is that he is a villain who projects the image of a “moderate”. While Netanyahu has become a lightning rod, thanks to his arrogance and belligerence, and hisindictmentat the international criminal court (ICC) has made Israel an international pariah, Eisenkot cuts a more sober and reasonable figure; a “humble soldier”, toquoteRemnick.By simply not being Netanyahu, a Prime Minister Eisenkot would neutralize a lot of western liberal critics of Israel and restore the country’s standing in western capitals, while allowing the Israeli military and settlers to pursue the same policies of expansion and destruction in both the West Bank and Gaza.Nor is Eisenkot unique. The Israeli political scene is filled with wolves in sheep’s clothing. There are Eisenkot’s fellow retired “moderate” generals in the Israeli opposition: Benny Gantz, who oncebraggedabout sending parts of Gaza “back to the stone age”, and Yair Golan, whosaidafter 7 October that Israel should prevent humanitarian aid from entering Gaza and the people there could “starve to death – it’s completely legitimate”.Then there is Naftali Bennett, who has a long history ofvile anti-Arab racism, oversaw thedeadliest yearon record for West Bank Palestinians when he was last prime minister of Israel in 2022, and is currently threatening bothTurkeyandQatar.Those who championed free speech in the UK and US now wage war on it. And here’s why: Palestine | Mehdi HasanRead moreThe point is not that these Israeli politicians are all identical. They are not. They do differ in terms of tactics, personalities and political coalitions.The point is that replacing Netanyahu with Eisenkot or any other Israeli opposition leader would not be a fundamental change in direction on the key issues of genocide, apartheid and occupation; it would only be a change in branding and messaging. For Palestinians and Lebanese, among many others in the Middle East, the result would be the same.So come October, Israel’s most notorious prime minister may finally be voted out of office. If that happens, we can and should all celebrate the end of the Netanyahu era – and hope the ICC gets its man.But then we’ll meet the new boss of Israel, same as the old boss of Israel.Mehdi Hasan is Guardian US columnist and the editor-in-chief and CEO ofZeteo.Explore more on these topicsMediaOpinionIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliens | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Content: A ‘die-in’ organised by Extinction Rebellion in Toulouse, France, with a placard that reads ‘Do our children have a future?’, 26 March 2022.Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA ‘die-in’ organised by Extinction Rebellion in Toulouse, France, with a placard that reads ‘Do our children have a future?’, 26 March 2022.Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockOpinionChildren's fantasy books (children's and teens)How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliensAlexander HurstThe Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than everMon 10 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.31 EDTShareRecently I found myself thinking about slug-like aliens that crawl through people’s ears and into their brains, with the ultimate purpose of global domination. It would explain a lot about what has gone so wrong with the world, wouldn’t it? And it was why I immediately flashed back to the children’s fantasy series Animorphs when Donald Trump’s health secretary andconspiracy theorist, Robert F Kennedy Jr, admitted to having had aworm in his brain.While visiting my parents in Cleveland, Ohio recently, I realised that a few books from the children’s fantasy series were still sitting on the shelves in my old bedroom. No fewer than 54 Animorphs titles were published between 1996 and 2001, and a total of 35m copies have been sold. “I may have just landed a job thanks to Animorphs,” my childhood friend Clifton texted me with excitement in the mid-2010s, when we were fresh out of college. “It was an interview for a vegan food cart and the last question they asked me was what Animorph I would morph into. I said an orangutan.”The premise sees five adolescent friends encounter a crashed alien spaceship and then face an intergalactic war against the Yeerks, genocidal slug-adjacent beings that slither into the brains of the host species. The young humans are given the ability to transform into any animals they’ve touched, along with the simple task of defending humanity. My generation were told we could grow up to do anything, that life was a continual arc of progress towards better lives, and that the old ideological battles of the past had been laid to rest. We were empowered by what we found in the pages of Animorphs: that Jake, Cassie, Rachel, Marco and Tobias had been endowed with the power ofnature itselfto help Earth fend off the existential threat of alien conquest.View image in fullscreenThe cover of a novel in the Animorphs series.Photograph: Scholastic PublishingDespite the optimism of the 90s, Animorphs was surprisingly dark and morally nuanced for millennial children’s fiction. Foreshadowing the real-world future, the teenagers watch parents and other family members fall under the cognitive control of the Yeerks. Looking back at the series now – and the era that produced it – the Animorphs’ baddies had to be an alien species, because it would have stretched credulity that humanity might destroy the Earth by itself, of its own volition. Now, instead of the Yeerks, we have megalomaniac billionaires and fossil fuel interests that have instilled climate denialism and defeatism into our minds – aided by media they so often control – and stripped us of the ability to even conceptualise our collective agency.The concept of discrete “generations” might be dubious, but where it holds most firmly is in shared cultural references. What millennials share is the distinct feeling of being a bridge: between the analogue and the digital; between a shared informational reality and the post-truth world; between an optimistic world and a pessimistic one. (This latter point shows up even in scientific analysis of pop music: studies have concluded thatpop has become sadder.)It’s the reflex towards a hopeful worldview, and the subsequent shattering of this optimism, that lie at the heart of millennial nostalgia for the less fraught times of our youth. On social media, it’s been dubbed the “millennial optimism era”. You don’t have to search hard to find the sources of that nostalgia: Akon and Britney Spears coming out of the speakers at my gym, Sum 41 playing at the bougiebrasserie around the corner. Meanwhile one huge comeback tour collides into the next. Onscreen, too, everything seems to be getting a remake or a reboot: Toy Story, Scary Movie, Air Bud and, if things go well, Animorphs too, which had a brief, two-season run on TV just before the turn of the millennium. Ryan Coogler, who directed Sinners, is developing a new Animorphs TV series for Disney+.Across the generational line, millennials and gen Z share the same eco-anxiety: in France, it has been found to be significantlymore pronouncedamong those aged 15-34 than among those over 50. Researchers in India founda similar pattern, just as they did in the US. Hannah Ritchie from Our World In Data writes in her personal newsletter that older generations are actually more likely to say that we’re already feeling the impacts of the climate crisis, because they can compare today’s heatwaves and snowless winters with the climate of their childhoods. But the emotional response is different,she writes: millennials and gen Z are more likely to feel fear, guilt and outrage about it.There is a cruel irony to the fatalism of the young: those who will most suffer the consequences of the climate emergency are those most resigned to that fate. Similarly, I think there is something that doesn’t show up in data yet, but is there in gen Z’s nostalgia for the “millennial optimism era”. It’s the difference between millennials believing that all of this can and should be fought, and gen Z having no nostalgic point of reference for the plausibility of fighting it at all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSinners was an intensely literate movie about history, racism and trauma, forces that sap us of our vitality, and our ability to fight back. So I’m not surprised my fellow millennial Coogler might be turning to Animorphs next. In the end, I suspect that he might circle the following: the threat to all of us is not solely alien, but an alien version of ourselves. That fighting back successfully will mean remembering who we really are. That nature is our ally, and we have to remember how indeliblyourfuture is tied toitsstate of wellbeing. I can’t think of a more urgent millennial-optimist metaphor to splash on to the big screen.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoirGeneration Desperationis out nowDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
