title: It’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaos | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: Matt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APView image in fullscreenMatt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APOpinionPoetryIt’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaosCharlotte HigginsFrom Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enoughMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe biggest sales of poetry since records began are expected this year. The reason? The movies, of course. UK print sales ofThe Odysseyincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period last year. In the US, year-to-date sales of The Odyssey areup 76% so far. Christopher Nolan is doing miracles for Homer – whatever problems one might have with the movie (and Emily Wilson, who made the most popular recent translation,has a few).Strip out the Odyssey factor, though, and poetry is still doing exceptionally well, driven by writers whose work is often mildly denigrated as “Instapoetry”, such asLucas Jones. His is a kind of versifying that delivers immediate uplifting aphorisms rather than either the kind of dense, allusive play with language that might reward repeated reading; or the sort of limpid, performable music that propels a well-translated Homeric epic. But even so, the poets of Instagram reach for something that can’t quite be expressed through everyday speech. And readers respond to it.Sales figures are a rough and insubstantial metric, though. They don’t tell us how someone feels when they read a good poem, what it expands for them, what memories it brings, what connections to other times and places. What shiver of alienation it offers; what moment (often) of puzzlement.Poetrycan be baffling; it can refuse to unfurl all of itself to the reader. Better, I think, to sink into the sensations that a poem creates than always to worry at it like a puzzle. By its nature, poetry expresses what can’t be said in prose; it can be resistant, you can snag on it. Poetry is needed in an emergency, when ordinary ways of writing or speaking can’t get at the moment, or the feeling, or the thought.What poetry is not, however, is peripheral to human life. What I have learned by reporting from Ukraine is that when catastrophe hovers overhead rather than looms from a distance, poetry seems more, rather than less, vital. The mostrapt poetry readingI have ever attended was in the frontline city of Kharkiv, the border with Russia only 30km away, when one poet described scratching poems into the wall of her Russian prison cell and audience members silently mouthed the learned-by-heart words of writer Serhii Zhadan’s poems as he performed them.The foreign correspondent Lindsey Hilsum, who has covered wars and humanitarian crises for decades, has long understood this, which is whyI Brought the War with Me, her anthology of work by poets across time and geographies, accompanied by her stories, is such a treasure. The poetry emerging from Gaza, and from Palestinian poets scattered across the world – figures such as the young writerHaia Mohammed, or the Palestinian-American poetFady Joudah– collectively provides the most arresting document of lives lived amid cataclysm: such poetry is composed with an urgency, vividness and compression that no other art form can quite achieve.It is true, as the Ukrainian poet Halyna Kruk said in 2022, that “no metaphors work against a man with a machine gun … no poetry can save you from a tank”. It is true, as her fellow Ukrainian writer Kateryna Iakovlenko has put it, that the poetry created most obviously by war is asemic, ugly and inscribed into the very land: “Ruins and abandoned houses, devastated forests, burnt land and roads carved up by tanks and armoured personnel carriers began to resemble letters and unwritten sentences.”View image in fullscreenSerhii Zhadan reads a debut book by Yulia Paevska, call-sign ‘Taira’, at a poetry festival in Kharkiv last year. They are both serving in the Khartia brigade.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAnd yet, with remarkable speed, and despite its failure either to deflect bullets, or keep its writers and readers physically safe, poetry quickly began to be written inUkraineafter the full-scale invasion. Poetry was the form that could grapple most effectively with the collapse in meaning brought about by the shock of violence, the feeling that time had ceased to carry significance, the future ripped away. Poems could be written relatively quickly, with limited means, and even in inhospitable places (the shelter, the trench).The novelist Victoria Amelina, who was later killed by a Russian bomb that targeted the restaurant where she was eating, stopped writing novels (which both take time to write and contain time as an ingredient) and started writing poetry. Some of it denied its own status as poetry, as if it were just the shrapnel-hit remnants of language. One poem, Not Poetry, translated by Uilleam Blacker, contains the lines, “But the reality of war / devours punctuation / plot structure / structure …”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘After the reading, the poets hold each other’: what happens when Ukraine’s largest literary festival comes under Russian attackRead morePoems were written at the front. The young writer Artur Dron’, who served in the Ukrainian armed forces for more than three years,did not writeabout bravado or heroism, but made small, delicate memorials for fellow soldiers who had been killed. Or sometimes he built encapsulations of seemingly insignificant moments.One of his poems is about a child in some unnamed village near the frontline, who becomes the unofficial mascot of the soldiers posted there. At Christmas, they leave the young boy “a bag with our crushed Snickers bars / and tangerines. / The ones with seeds, / but oh so sweet.” It was a fleeting incident: not newsworthy, not impressive, nothing for the history books – but it was material for a poem. Yaryna Chornohuztold methat her work as asoldier poetwas the “documentation of feelings”.In the midst of a cataclysm, poems survive, often stripped back to their most essential forms, which are surely universal and primordial human forms of expression: the lament for the dead, the lullaby for the child, the curse. In the end, humans need those things: those songs, those poems. They are proof of life. They may not be remembered; but poetry has a better chance at survival than much else that humans do or make. They may become memorials more lasting than bronze.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, is published on 20 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOn Wednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. title: Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not? | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Americans want someone on their side in the fight against sordid interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Americans want someone on their side in the fight against sordid interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters in Detroit, Michigan, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed greets supporters in Detroit, Michigan, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDemocratsCentrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not?Nesrine MalikAmericans want someone on their side in the fight against vested interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran MamdaniMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.48 EDTShareAbdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary was a historic breakthrough. Not only because he is a Muslim son of immigrants who broke with almost every single tenet of establishment Democratic party politics. But because he has wiped that complacent sneer at progressive wins off the faces of centrist gatekeepers. Zohran Mamdani? Relax, he’s just a mayor. And it’s New York City. Outside urban and liberal corridors, there is nothing to worry about. Now El-Sayed has won the Democratic party’s nomination in a swing state that is also on thelist of presidential nomination states.There is a lot to be excited about. Not only within the US, but for observers abroad hopeful for the emergence of a truly revolutionary left that is able to weather powerful and well-funded adversaries and prevail. The money raised to defeat El-Sayed was staggering. He was outspent by more than nine to one. It was the mostexpensive Democratic congressional primary ever. A roll call of cartoon bad guys, such as Chevron and Philip Morris, funded his opponent, Haley Stevens, to the tune of over $60m. Of that funding,nearly halfcame from a Super Pac backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).The symbolism of the win is heavy, that of a politics snapping the chains of corporate power and special interest groups whose agendas run counter to voters’. It suggests two things. One, an electorate waking up to the fact that its democracy is captured. Two, features in the past that would have been disqualifying – lack of experience, lack of establishment endorsement – now render a candidate a “clean skin”. Someone untainted by the sordid game that keeps in play expensive healthcare, cruelty to immigrants and the hoovering of tax dollars out of the country.‘Voters are fed up’: Michigan primary forces Democratic party to accept leftwing shiftRead moreIsrael took up a large role in the campaign, both on the part of El-Sayed and his opponent. But it’s striking how both were talking about different things. El-Sayed’s detractors stuck to repetitivetalking pointsabout “Israel having the right to exist”, a question that is not relevant to the average voter. El-Sayed framed Israel as simply a place that has taken too much of Americans’ money. “The question is quite secondary to whether they have a right to our tax dollars.” It was a clear and salient approach.What El-Sayed’s win isn’t, yet, is a promise that this success can be replicated not only outside primary contests and against Republicans, but across the board among progressive candidates. The Democratic establishment has been hapless in the face of Donald Trump, and new fiery candidates can appear to have the answers that their party so far has not.But they are up against huge challenges. First, what the Republican party will throw at them: accusations that,as Trump said, “full of shit” candidates like El-Sayed are radical commies who will bring nothing but “death, squalor, poverty” and “a life of hell”. Then there is what the centrist wing of the Democrats can mobilise against them.3:45Three key takeaways from Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary – video explainerA leading centrist group called Third Way has alreadyraised millionsto discredit democratic socialists by investing in social media and mobilising activists against candidates like El-Sayed. “We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” said the group’s leader. Their fear, they say, is that the momentum behind democratic socialists will go all the way to the presidential nomination, and then produce a candidate who would be crushed by Republicans. Because, of course, that has never happened before to a centrist Democratic presidential candidate running against Trump.Still, the portrayals of progressive candidates as radical can go a long way in a country where people think that Trump is moremoderatethan Kamala Harris or Hillary Clinton. Fighting on a national level, the left can get away with far less in the political imaginary than the right. That is because the very promise of change that gives progressive candidates the edge in certain contests becomes easily framed as a race into the unknown. This becomes an even more resonant threat as progressive candidates do not have the depth and breadth of a long party record behind them, or the familiarity that comes with ubiquity on the political landscape.It doesn’t have to be this way. Politicians like Mamdani and El-Sayed are modelling something truly unique. They signify a new US in which the politics of outsiders and their cultural and ideological features is fused powerfully with and against the features of their adopted countries. They have opted not for meek total assimilation for mobility, nor have they recused themselves from contests for a country in which they have claimed a stake.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut they and the rest of the US are carrying too much on their shoulders at a time of domestic and global upheaval. Their movement battles with the stubborn entrenchment of a bankrupt Democratic party establishment, the savage culture wars of the right, and, even though some have thus far prevailed, a gargantuan machine of lobbyists and corporate interest groups.Progressive voters are not simply found, they aremade.And constantly remade into coalitions. If theDemocratswould rather lose on their own terms than win on the progressive left’s, then fighting these new candidates will establish the impression that they are freak radicals destined to fizzle out. But these candidates have alighted on what seems like the most viable politics right now. Refuse to embrace them wholeheartedly, and you guarantee that Trumpism wins again and again. Back them all the way to 2028. What, after all, do you have to lose that you haven’t lost already?Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decades | Gene Marks | The Guardian
description: The practice of openly proclaiming to the world what you can’t afford can lead to lower fees, reduced prices and better deals
Author: Gene Marks
Headline: The practice of openly proclaiming to the world what you can’t afford can lead to lower fees, reduced prices and better deals
Content: Loud budgeting ‘makes oversharing cool – and effective’.Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenLoud budgeting ‘makes oversharing cool – and effective’.Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoUS small businessGen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decadesGene MarksThe practice of openly proclaiming to the world what you can’t afford can lead to lower fees, reduced prices and better dealsMon 10 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTShareAsk any small business owner what has challenged them the most over the past couple of years and you’ll frequently hear about cashflow. It’s no secret that costs have risen dramatically and finding places to save money isn’t easy.If this describes your situation then I’ve got a solution to your problem. Ever hear of “loud budgeting”? Of course you have! You’ve probably been doing it for years.Loud budgeting is considered to be a relatively new trend. According to onerecent surveyfrom Bank of America, as many as 42% of gen Zers “swear by it”. The concept isn’t hard. It’s basically the practice of openly proclaiming to the world that you can’t afford to do stuff instead of just quietly going along with the crowd and paying for something that you can’t afford. Financial services firm Charles Schwab & Cosaysit “makes oversharing cool – and effective”. The Economic Timessays“it’s the smartest way to build wealth in 2026”.“Loud budgeting is effectively being upfront about your financial situation and when something doesn’t align with your financial goals, values or capacity,”saysEmma Edwards, founder of the Broke Generation who offers millennials financial advice on social media. “We have this belief that our financial situation shouldn’t have to be an inconvenience to others, or we shouldn’t reveal ourselves as being on a budget.”How does one practice loud budgeting? That’s easy. Just complain a lot about money. Make it clear that you can’t afford to do stuff. Or, to save face among your friends, say that you probably could afford to go to that great restaurant or concert or trip to the lake, but choose not to because you simply don’t want to spend the money. Don’t blame yourself. Blame the economy. Blame the president. Point to the high cost of living and your paltry raise. Just be vocal and transparent about your finances. People like honesty. And they’ll understand. If they don’t – well, that’s their problem not yours.All of the reports I’ve read about loud budgeting have focused on individuals, particularly younger people grappling with a challenging economic environment. But this strategy certainly isn’t new. In fact, I’ve seen a number of my clients – older, boomer, well-seasoned business owners – practice this behavior for literally decades.“What? You want$0.02 more per pound for that poly-laminate? I can’t afford that!”“A 4% price increase? Believe me, I hate doing it, but have you seen what my insurance company is charging me?”“A 5%raise? Is he crazy? We’re barely able to stay in business and this guy wants a 5% raise. Sheesh!”“I am certainly not going to pay $200 an hour for your accounting services. You of all people should know we can’t afford that.”“A holiday party for the staff? Bah. Humbug!”See what I mean? It’s loud budgeting, but from a business owner’s perspective. For many, this is not easy, because it goes against what we’re taught in business school.The business gurus want us to be confident. And bold. We’re encouraged to take risks, work hard and relentlessly pursue our goals. “Fail greatly!” they say. “Reach for the stars!” “Push yourself to the limits!” “Be positive!” No one ever says to complain about your costs, gripe about your margins or whine about your money problems.Loud budgeting turns all that positive-thinking advice on its head. Instead, it’s telling everyone around you – your customers, your employees, your suppliers – that you’re barely holding it together and that the $0.02 increase in poly-laminates is going to put you out of business.You don’t have to reveal the truth. My clients who complain the most are the ones who are generally sitting on the biggest piles of cash. They’re driving 10-year-old cars, fly economy and eat at Outback Steakhouse. They don’t actually tell anyone that they’ve got enough money to afford more expensive things. That would destroy their ruse. They’re not broke. They just consider paying full price a character defect.Loud budgeting is part of that ruse. Go ahead, try it. You’ll find that it’s a strategy to constantly remind anyone within earshot of your constrained budget and inevitably people start believing it. You’d be surprised at how many of them offer concessions – lower fees, reduced prices, better deals – out of sympathy or empathy or simply just to stop you from complaining.You don’t need to be a young adult to understand this. Most successful small business owners do.And it’s never too late to start. Go ahead: complain about your company’s terrible cashflow. Grumble. Grouse. Moan. Bellyache. Do this in public and do it loud. Make it so anyone will think twice before coming to you with something that’s going to cost more than what you’re already paying. People don’t want to get into fights. More than a few will be forced to come up with better ideas, rather than suffer your protests. Others may abandon their price increases altogether just to keep the peace. The ones that pursue their course of action will learn to really think through their case before presenting it to you.“Loud budgeting helps take an element of shame away from feeling like you don’t have enough money,”saidone financial educator.Shame? I think shrewd is the better word.Explore more on these topicsUS small businesscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted
Content: ‘Much of the population is repeatedly displaced amid the rubble, as different areas are targeted and bombed.’Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Much of the population is repeatedly displaced amid the rubble, as different areas are targeted and bombed.’Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/GettyOpinionIsrael-Gaza warThe Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in JerusalemEditorialIsrael’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exertedMon 10 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAt the end of July, Donald Trumpannouncedthat a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it wasreportedthat another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe.Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitlyrejectedthe sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.”In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazenviolationof the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersFormal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largelydestroyedand the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first buildingcontractissued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted  to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievousmiscalculationin which Israel’s prime minister also played his part.In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue ascorched earthproject of revenge following the Hamasmassacreof October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruptionchargesfirst laid more than five years ago.Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point.Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recentpollingsuggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Privacy needs defending against invasive wearable gadgets. So far, businesses are ahead of the government
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Privacy needs defending against invasive wearable gadgets. So far, businesses are ahead of the government
Content: Mark Zuckerberg in a pair of Meta Oakley Vanguard AI glasses, 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg in a pair of Meta Oakley Vanguard AI glasses, 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionTechnologyThe Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front footEditorialPrivacy needs defending against invasive wearable gadgets. So far, businesses are ahead of the governmentMon 10 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt is not yet clear to what extentMeta’s new smart glasseswill live up to the nickname of “pervert glasses” – bestowed in recognition of the obvious appeal of wearable cameras to voyeurs. The past week has seen rising criticism of the devices, which in the UK havebeen bannedby the pub chain Wetherspoons and the theatre group ATG, as well as restaurants, schools and members’ clubs. These organisations deserve praise for standing up for privacy. By contrast, regulators appear once again to be on the back foot.There have, inevitably, already been reports of women being mistreated. Earlier this year the BBC spoke to several who had been filmedwithout their consent, with footage subsequently uploaded to social media. In one case, the content creator demanded a fee to remove it. In the year to March 2025,image-based sexual abuse and cyberflashingwere responsible for more than half of an 11% increase in reported sexual offences in England and Wales. Normalisation of smart glasses would, clearly, make such offences easier to commit.Worrying as this is, it is not the only reason to be concerned. Privacy has much wider significance and most people, as the businesses banning smart glasses from their premises have recognised, do not want to be filmed as they go about their lives. While videoing in public is not illegal, this does not give smart glasses wearers the right to place others under involuntary surveillance. An LED light that blinks when the camera is in use, and cannot be disabled, is not an adequate safeguard, whateverMetamight think. Pubs, parks, beaches and workplaces are not film sets.View image in fullscreenRay-Ban Meta smart glasses.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesHaving invested $80bnin its latest product, Mark Zuckerberg’s company is unlikely to give up easily on its ambition to make the glasses, which have been likened to face-mounted smartphones, as ubiquitous as the handheld kind. More than a decade after the first smart glasses, made by Google, flopped, Meta has bet heavily on making its latest version more stylish, functional and affordable – with UK prices starting at £269. The choice of Kylie Jenner to front this summer’s advertising campaign, and the slogan“Never miss a moment”, aimed at parents of young children, appear calculated to dispel fears about how the glasses will be used by sexually predatory men.Like most digital devices, these ones can be helpful as well as harmful. Asaids for people who are blindor visually impaired, smart glasses that can read text or describe images have been described as life-changing. Any restrictions, in the UK or elsewhere, should be crafted so as to enable such uses to continue – just as guide dogs are exempted from rules about pets. But while the benefits that smart glasses offer to groups of people with specific needs should be recognised, this must not be allowed to distract from their potential to cause harm.Tech regulation is difficult. But given the UK government’s recent moves towards restricting smartphone use among young people, and thepublic outcryregarding sexualised AI imagery, it is disappointing that ministers have so far had almost nothing to say about the rollout of wearable hidden cameras. While the tech companies market their products as tools to be used, one of thekey lessonsof the last two decades is that users are rarely, if ever, as in control as they would like to be. Ministers and regulators should be active, not passive, as Meta intentionally blurs the line between looking and filming.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Mental health: one step forward and two steps back? | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Kate Martin is encouraged by the new network of community clinics, while Prof Dr John R Ashton says the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, while Marjorie Wallace expresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHS
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Kate Martin is encouraged by the new network of community clinics, while Prof Dr John R Ashton says the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, while Marjorie Wallace expresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHS
Content: ‘Successive governments have insisted that mental health should be given the same priority as physical health.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘Successive governments have insisted that mental health should be given the same priority as physical health.’Photograph: GettyMental healthLettersMental health: one step forward and two steps back?Dr Kate Martinis encouraged by the new network of community clinics, whileProf Dr John R Ashtonsays the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, whileMarjorie Wallaceexpresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHSMon 10 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareIt’s very encouraging to hear the announcement about the new network of community mental health clinics in England (Editorial, 6 August). The focus on early intervention is crucial, as it means that people can access treatment as early as possible, rather than waiting for their mental health to reach a crisis point. The centres should improve access, reaching people where they are. The government should make sure that they meaningfully involve people with lived experience of mental health problems to ensure the centres are co-designed and co-led with them.As your editorial says, parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011.Mental healthis an issue that unites us. According to new research, which we commissioned from More in Common, nearly three-quarters of the public believe that mental health is as important as physical health, most people are comfortable talking about it, and support for early intervention is high across the political spectrum. Three-quarters also say the government should do more to improve services.The centres are an important step forward, but the government needs to make sure that people can access the many new and improved mental health interventions that have the potential to transform lives. New evidence-based mental health treatments must be rigorously evaluated, adopted and made available across the NHS. This will help people get the right treatment at the right time, and lead fulfilling lives.Dr Kate MartinHead of field building and lived experience, Wellcome TrustWhile the announcement of a new initiative on early access to mental health care must be welcomed, there is a danger that without a parallel programme on mental health promotion, it could compound an already disastrous situation by uncovering massive further unmet need.A public health approach to mental health is long overdue. I refer to one which takes its cues from the history of tuberculosis, the “captain of the men of death” that was brought under control not by pharmaceuticals alone, but by paying attention to the environmental conditions that predisposed to transmission.The initial prescription for action was written 60 years ago by the Manchester psychiatrist Gerald Caplan, who identified how those with psychiatric training might best be deployed to build population-level mental health resilience through their support in the community, school, places of work and recreation; in Caplan’s blueprint, clinical work was only one aspect of the daily round of the psychiatrist and their team.The forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp this nettle; for too long these opportunities have been missed.Prof Dr John R AshtonFormer president, Faculty of Public HealthYour report (NHS mental health trust plans £25m in cuts to jobs and services, 3 August) is concerning. As the NHS faces yet another reconfiguration, patients and staff can only look forward to an uncertain future as not only this trust but other mental health trusts are expected to make savings to already impoverished levels of care. This is in stark contrast to the recent announcement of a major expansion of community mental health support in England.Successive governments have insisted that mental health should be given the same priority as physical health, yet each year psychiatric services undergo ever more cuts to funding, services and beds. This has left people with minimal help and nowhere to go in times of loneliness or crisis.Marjorie WallaceChief executive, SaneHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Katriona O’Sullivan’s story of growing up in poverty is one that we can all learn from | Poverty | The Guardian
description: Letters: Reading the memoir Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty – an issue that still blights the lives of countless young people today, says Sarah Schofield
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Reading the memoir Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty – an issue that still blights the lives of countless young people today, says Sarah Schofield
Content: Katriona O'Sullivan. ‘It was heart-warming and affirming to read about the lasting, positive impact certain school staff had on her,’ writes Sarah Schofield.Photograph: Johnny Savage/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKatriona O'Sullivan. ‘It was heart-warming and affirming to read about the lasting, positive impact certain school staff had on her,’ writes Sarah Schofield.Photograph: Johnny Savage/The GuardianPovertyLettersKatriona O’Sullivan’s story of growing up in poverty is one that we can all learn fromReading the memoir Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty – an issue that still blights the lives of countless young people today, saysSarah SchofieldMon 10 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareAdrian Chiles’s emotional response to Poor by Katriona O’Sullivan really resonated with me (I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing, 30 July). I read it and my heart both sobbed and cheered for Katriona’s younger self and the woman she has become.With its linear narrative, rich cultural references and “rags-to-riches” form, it might be taken for a tale of “that was then but this is now”. However, the defining part of the book is the epilogue, making clear that Katriona’s account of growing up in grinding, abject poverty is a story of thenandnow. Every day, countless Katrionas enter schools with “pissy pants” and empty bellies, their nervous systems on high alert, in fight, flight or freeze.School is a place to survive, not thrive. I know, because I have worked in a primary school for over 20 years. I provide mental health support to vulnerable children and their equally vulnerable and disadvantaged families.My job is not to educate, but to help make children feel seen, heard, cared for and valued – to try to reduce the stigma attached to being poor ie, the misconception that having less means being less.Reading Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty as an issue – it can feel “too big”. But that doesn’t prevent each of us from treating others with dignity, respect and kindness, noticing when someone is struggling, is hungry, dirty or alone, and offering a supportive hand.Pollyanna-ish? I don’t think so. It was heart-warming and affirming to read about the lasting, positive impact certain school staff had on Katriona. When school reopens in September, my copy of Poor will be available in the staffroom – anyone who works in a school (or indeed anyone at all) should read it.Sarah SchofieldWhitefield, Greater ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The cricket fiction of Sassoon and De Sélincourt isn’t in a ‘bucolic dreamworld’ | Sport and leisure books | The Guardian
description: Letter: There are serious political and societal messages to be found in some of the best-known fictional accounts of village cricket, argues Rod Edmond
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: There are serious political and societal messages to be found in some of the best-known fictional accounts of village cricket, argues Rod Edmond
Content: A batsman plays a stroke in a friendly match between teams from Sidmouth and Exeter in July 2020.Photograph: Harry Trump/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA batsman plays a stroke in a friendly match between teams from Sidmouth and Exeter in July 2020.Photograph: Harry Trump/Getty ImagesSport and leisure booksLettersThe cricket fiction of Sassoon and De Sélincourt isn’t in a ‘bucolic dreamworld’There are serious political and societal messages to be found in some of the best-known fictional accounts of village cricket, arguesRod EdmondMon 10 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareYour leader (The Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricket, 30 July) recycles the persistent caricature of Siegfried Sassoon’s, Hugh de Sélincourt’s and AG Macdonell’s cricket fiction as existing in a “bucolic dreamworld”.Sassoon’s The Flower Show Match is set against the background of the Boer war, with recurring references to the relief of Ladysmith. The home umpire is also suspected of using his wooden leg to make dents in the pitch.In De Sélincourt’s TheCricketMatch, a war profiteer has felled the fir trees surrounding the Tillingford ground to have them sawn into pit props. The club is struggling to recover from the war, and there’s a feeling of “melancholy certainty that each season must surely be the last”. There are passing references to the Russian Revolution, and the hope expressed by the lady of the manor that village cricket will ease class antagonism is contradicted by the contempt the team’s fast bowler, a labourer, feels for her public-school son who also plays for Tillingford.Macdonell’s England, Their England is pervaded with the after-effects of the first world war. Its Scottish protagonist who is inquiring into the vaunted English principle of “team spirit” said to characterise the national game is none the wiser after a day spent with a motley team of metropolitan writers and publishers playing away in a Kent village.Rod EdmondAuthor of Cricket, Fiction and NationHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Breast cancer screening guidelines discriminate against families like mine | Breast cancer | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Health concerns | Rubbish decisions | In sympathy | Funeral songs | Short illnesses
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Health concerns | Rubbish decisions | In sympathy | Funeral songs | Short illnesses
Content: ‘If your grandmother and mother have both had breast cancer, you are still not added to the intensified screening list unless an aunt or great-aunt or sister has also had breast cancer’Photograph: Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If your grandmother and mother have both had breast cancer, you are still not added to the intensified screening list unless an aunt or great-aunt or sister has also had breast cancer’Photograph: Ian Miles-Flashpoint Pictures/AlamyBrief lettersBreast cancerLettersBreast cancer screening guidelines discriminate against families like mineHealth concerns | Rubbish decisions | In sympathy | Funeral songs | Short illnessesMon 10 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareCalls for changes to breast cancer guidelines for GPs are welcome (Report, 4 August). The existing guidelines are irrational. If your grandmother and mother have both had breast cancer, you are still not added to the intensified screening list unless an aunt or great-aunt or sister has also had breast cancer. Hence the system discriminates against families – like mine – with only one woman in a generation.Helen HillsYorkIt seems that Anna Tims’s correspondent committed the wrong environmental crime (I was fined £500 after putting a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a full bin, 3 August). Instead of unwittingly littering, they should have dumped thousands of tonnes of sewage into a river andbagged a multimillion-pound reward.Matt SheardTayport, FifeAs a interested follower of the regular letters from the owner of the Gordon Bennett, I offer my sympathies for the loss of his wife and share his frustration at the uncooperative stance of the Canal and River Trust (Letters, 9 July). I write this on the anniversary of my own wife’s death.JK MitchellDinton, BuckinghamshireCommiserations to Ian Grieve on board the Gordon Bennett. He could add to the Nick Cave/Neil Young playlist celebrating his wife’s life.Cave’s The Ship SongandYoung’s Birdsare sad but also uplifting, like his letter.Jim HatleyBrighton, East SussexMy mother used to say people with short or long illnesses (Letters, 7 August) “enjoyed ill health”.Rory MurphyLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter secured the 100m European title in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter secured the 100m European title in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze
Content: Amy Hunt shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 100m final.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 100m final.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsBritain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd24-year-old secures title in 11.00sec in BirminghamNorway win 4x400m mixed relay, Britain secondSean Ingleat Alexander StadiumMon 10 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a display of icy resolve and sustained power had secured Amy Hunt a European 100m gold medal, Britain’s new sprint queen reached for a Freddie Mercury lyric. “I want it all,” she said, before peering into a golden future.The Cambridge graduate, 24, now plans to leave the European Championships with four gold medals, adding the 200m and 4x100m women’s and mixed relays to her 100m title. On this evidence, would you dare bet against her?Jakob Ingebrigtsen returns from injury woe to win European Championships 5,000m goldRead moreHunt is never the quickest starter. In truth, she reacted to the gun like a woman whose spikes had been superglued to her blocks and she was still behind with 30m to go before coming through to take her first major title in 11.00sec.“I’ve probably had much worse starts than that,” Hunt said. “The biggest thing is not panicking, trusting in my very, very long legs, long femurs, and just staying calm and pulling through at the end.“‘Trash’ is probably going to be his [her coach, Marco Airale] words about my start,” she said. “And maybe a little bit of Italian blasphemy, but we came through at the end. One of my biggest skills in terms of championships is I know I’m so strong in the end and I always have that kind of extra magic in the last 40, 50m.”Ewa Swoboda of Poland secured silver in 11.02, while Delphine Nkansa took bronze for Belgium in 11.06.“Honestly, it’s just euphoria,” said Hunt. “My first gold. I think it was definitely time to upgrade. This was definitely a coming of age for me. I’m someone that thrives under that pressure, so the stage for the final isn’t intimidating to me. I just knew I had to stay calm and not overthink myself into the gold before I had it in my grasp.”It was also sweet vindication after being beaten into silver at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow a fortnight ago. “It really came in handy for me,” she said. “I wanted to have that experience of being in front of a home crowd and having that meta-expectation, because I’ve never had that before. I took a lot of learnings from Glasgow into today and it really helped me.View image in fullscreenBritain’s Amy Hunt reacts after crossing the finish line to win gold.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APHunt’s story loses little in its retelling. She was the world’s fastest woman over 200m at 18, then had a series of injuries that got so bad some questioned whether she would ever fulfil her potential. A few years ago she ruptured one of her quadriceps so badly that her mum needed to lift her out of the shower.When she won a 200m silver medal in Tokyo last year, she called herself a “track goddess and an academic badass”. “I don’t know if I have any more one-liners in me,” she said. Then came the Freddie Mercury line.Hunt later revealed she had a premonition that she was going to win gold. “I just had such a magical feeling,” she said. “I’ve won English Schools here. I’ve raced here as 13-14-year-old. So, this is really my track. I’m a girl from Newark, I’m a Midlands girl. So I just had a feeling that this was going to be my night.”Hunt insisted that this could be just the start as she now chases an historic four gold medals. “I want to be the best,” she said. “I don’t shy away from that. I train incredibly hard, and I back myself so incredibly hard because I do want to be the best. “I’m not saying that I’m the best right now, but that’s something I aspire to be.”Hunt said she was so nervous before the race that she was unable to nap. Instead, she was just lay awake in bed with her eyes closed. “But I as soon as I get to the track, my nerves disappear,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I love doing what I do. My coach keeps me really chilled. Megan Thee Stallion [American rapper] kept me kind of nice and upbeat, and you can’t be nervous when you listen to that.”View image in fullscreenHenriette Jæger shows her delight after sealing gold for Norway in the 4x400m mixed relay.Photograph: Alex Livesey/British Athletics/Getty ImagesShe also relaxed by playing puzzle games such as Connections, Spelling Bee, Pips and Wordle. “It wakes my brain up without having to overthink.“Even at training, we’re all competitive every single day about Wordle and how many kind of words we got on Spelling Bee, so it just keeps my brain ticking over, listening to Megan Thee Stallion, house music, a bit of Mamma Mia in there, so just not getting too overly serious.”Moments before Hunt’s victory there was also a plucky silver for Great Britain’s mixed 4x400m relay team behind the gold medallists Norway.Britain’s team of Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich, Toby Harries and Yemi Mary John all ran well. But a Norway team spearheaded by the 400m hurdles world record-holder, Karsten Warholm, and the fastest woman in Europe this year, Henriette Jæger, proved too strong as they set a Championship record of 3:09.62, nearly a second clear of Britain.The only disappointment was that more people were not here to witness it given that the Alexander Stadium, which seats about 20,000, looked barely half full.However, organisers said 13,623 tickets had been sold for the Monday night – along with 170,000 tickets for the week – and that from Thursday night onwards the event was pretty much a sellout.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 3: Bournemouth | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: New head coach Marco Rose has a lot to live up after last season’s sixth-placed finish while fans have a first year in Europe to look forward to
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: New head coach Marco Rose has a lot to live up after last season’s sixth-placed finish while fans have a first year in Europe to look forward to
Content: Bournemouth’s new manager, Marco Rose, speaks with his players during a pre-season training camp in Saalfelden, Austria. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty ImagesNew head coach Marco Rose has a lot to live up to after last season’s sixth-placed finish while fans have a first year in Europe to look forward toByBen FisherMon 10 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:12th (NB: this is not necessarily Ben Fisher’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:6thProspectsIt was the day after the final game of last season at Bournemouth’s secluded, swish training base and, before clearing his belongings on his last day in the building, the departing head coach, Andoni Iraola, spent a couple of hours in his office chewing the fat with his successor, Marco Rose, talking players, pubs and tactics. The story goes that, with time moving on, Tiago Pinto, the club’s sporting director, knocked on the door to advise them there were other things to tackle.It was an interesting scenario that speaks volumes of the respect between the pair. Long before joining Bournemouth, Iraola cited Rose’s Borussia Mönchengladbach side as one of his favourite teams to watch, the German’s “vertical football” helping them qualify for the Champions League in Rose’s first season in charge.Rose accepts that Iraola, in absorbing the sales of key players totalling more than £250m last season and qualifying for Europe for the first time, has set a high bar. Remarkably, Bournemouth did not lose a game after the sale of Antoine Semenyo in the second week of January. Rose put it succinctly during pre-season in Austria. “Andoni didn’t leave a lot of space to improve,” he said. “Pressure’s on.”In his first session, Rose told the players he loved the way they attacked the Premier League last season. Playing in the Europa League, however, represents uncharted territory for a team in the second tier as recently as four years ago. It is why Bournemouth’s hierarchy contacted peers at Crystal Palace and Nottingham Forest to understand the realities of juggling the Thursday-Sunday rhythm the competition will bring. Rose is close friends with Oliver Glasner, who is now at Forest, but won theConference League last season with Palace. “We are not going to Europe just to enjoy, we want to be competitive,” Rose said. “We are not there just to watch.”Unlike last summer, so far they have retained all key players, chiefly Alex Scott, Rayan andEli Junior Kroupi, the 20-year-old forward who breezed into double figures in his debut Premier League season and the club consider a generational talent. Kroupi attracted serious interest from Paris Saint-Germain, among other European superpowers, but a freak foot injury during a pre-season drill means he is sidelined for at least three months.At the end of the season, Bournemouth earmarked a centre-back to replace Marcos Senesi and a striker to compete with Evanilson as key priorities and by the start of August the club had recruited Álvaro Rodríguez, whom Rose wanted to sign at Leipzig, and António Silva from Elche and Benfica respectively. Juanlu Sánchez joined from Sevilla to provide competition for Adam Smith, the evergreen 35-year-old into his 14th season at the club, and will also fill the void left by Álex Jiménez, who has joined Fiorentina on loan with an option to sign permanently because he remainssuspended in England while under investigationby the Football Association.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureThe smallest stadium in thePremier Leaguehas been a building site this summer, with the club working to ensure their 11,357-seater ground complies with Uefa regulations. There has been a wider facelift, too, with every seat being replaced, while they are filling in two corners to increase the capacity by 800 this season. Playing in Europe brings the challenge of meeting Uefa’s squad-cost ratio (SCR) rules, which caps on-pitch spending at 70% of a club’s revenue. Bournemouth finished the 2025-26 season at 82% and they continue to work towards meeting the threshold. Last month the academy was awarded category one status, four years after being category three.Owner-fan relationshipThe American billionaire Bill Foley described himself as a dictator uponbuying the club approaching four years ago, but supporters are grateful for his naked ambition. Foley, who made his fortune in insurance, is forthright and somewhat prophetic. In 2023, he said the club would play in Europe within five years – and achieved it in three. It was a similar story with Vegas Golden Knights, whom he vowed would win the Stanley Cup within six years of him launching the ice hockey franchise in 2017 – they won it in their sixth season. Foley recently added rugby union’sExeter Chiefs to his sporting stable, which extends to Lorient, Auckland FC and Moreirense. Not every decision is universally popular but Foley, who turns 82 in December and predominantly splits his time between California and Vegas,puts his money where his mouth is.The managerAs a defender, Marco Rose was schooled by Jürgen Klopp and Thomas Tuchel at Mainz, and Ralf Rangnick at Hannover, so had quite the education before beginning his coaching career at home town club Lokomotive Leipzig. Klopp told Rose, after promotion to the Bundesliga in 2004, that he would excel in the dugout and he has since managed some of the biggest names: Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham at Borussia Dortmund, Dominik Szoboszlai and Dani Olmo at RB Leipzig. Rose has been compared to Klopp and, naturally, Iraola, given his appetite for high-energy tactics. Bournemouth routed Genoa 10-1 in pre-season so, could his style be even more aggressive than Iraola’s? “I would say [to be] even more aggressive than Andoni is quite difficult,” came the reply. His grandfather, Walter Rose, represented Germany in 1937.Star signingView image in fullscreenAntónio Silva has all the attributes to be a bargain buy for Bournemouth.Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty ImagesThese days, £50m is about the going rate for an elite defender. Tottenham paid £52m to sign Jan Paul van Hecke. Chelsea paid the same fee to take Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace. Bournemouth pocketed £50m when Dean Huijsen joined Real Madrid last year, though that price was set by a release clause. They are deals that make Bournemouth’s £25.7m purchase of António Silva, a 22-year-old who has been a regular at Benfica since breaking into the team and has experience in the Champions League, Europa League and 20 caps for Portugal, appear a snip. Silva, who is right-footed but prefers to play as a left-centre back, is a direct replacement for Senesi.Stat attackBournemouth scored nine goals from Opta-defined counterattacks last season, the joint most in the Premier League. But their threat was varied; in only two of their preceding eight top-flight campaigns did they score more set-piece goals than the 14 they managed in 2025-26. It is very rare for a team to be so productive on both fronts.Stat attackSet for a breakthroughIt was a November night of ecstasy when Scotland qualified for the World Cup for the first time in 28 years, but for Ben Gannon-Doak it was a bittersweet evening and one that curtailed his club season. The 20-year-old was forced off after 21 minutes, replaced by Kenny McLean who capped the scoring in style. A £25m arrival from Liverpool last August, Gannon-Doak featured in all three of Scotland’s World Cup matches, starting the first and last, and has impressed in pre-season. After being limited to 113 minutes in eight league appearances as a substitute last campaign, there is optimism Gannon-Doak will make his mark.World Cup impactRayan became the first Brazilian teenager to start a World Cup match since Marco Antônio in 1970 when he was named in Carlo Ancelotti’s starting XI for their Group C game against Scotland. The then 19-year-old, signed from Vasco de Gama in January, set up Vinícius Júnior for Brazil’s openerin the 3-0 winand afterwards swapped shirts with Gannon-Doak. Tyler Adams enhanced his reputation, impressing for the USA en route to the last 16. Two new members of Bournemouth’s coaching staff, the set-piece coach, Nicolas Gagnon, and goalkeeping coach, Frederic de Boever, worked with Canada and Belgium respectively.Alex Scott’s inclusion in Tuchel’s pre-World Cup training camp in Florida spoke volumes of the Guernsey-born midfielder’s wider standing.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27BournemouthPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Uefa, Concacaf and AFC push for Infantino to quit and discuss rival competitions | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf will push for Gianni Infantino to resign after writing an open letter calling for ‘leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it’
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf will push for Gianni Infantino to resign after writing an open letter calling for ‘leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it’
Content: The confederations said of Infantino: ‘When an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.’Photograph: Gabriel Aponte/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe confederations said of Infantino: ‘When an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.’Photograph: Gabriel Aponte/Getty ImagesFifaUefa, Concacaf and AFC push for Infantino to quit and discuss rival competitionsConfederations write open letter damning Fifa presidentConcacaf president Montagliani seen as top contenderNick AmesandMatt HughesMon 10 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf will push forGianni Infantinoto resign after writing an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.In a dramatic escalation of the war that has threatened to tear football apart since details emerged of theFifapresident’s failed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, the three governing bodies accused Infantino of “trust broken through deception” and condemned his failure to acknowledge that the proposal should not have been unilaterally launched.Somali referee Omar Artan grateful for Super Cup chance after ‘tough’ World Cup exclusionRead moreThe three confederations have started preliminary discussions about the organisation of new competitions along with Uefa’srepeated threats to boycott Fifa events. As things stand, the under-20 women’s World Cup next month could take place without European teams and alternative options are being sought.The letter is signed by theUefapresident, Aleksander Ceferin, his AFC counterpart, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, and the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani. Efforts to unite around a suitable candidate to replace Infantino have stepped up since his privately backed plan was revealed and Montagliani is believed to be among the contenders.“Leadership in football is not a possession,” the letter reads. “It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.”It strongly criticises Fifa’sresponse to the crisis, when a meeting between a small number of senior staff in Rabat was followed by an apology from Infantino that appeared not to show remorse for the scheme.“It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgment,” the letter says. “It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong. There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the Fifa World Cup was a profound failure of judgment – not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions Fifa exists to serve.”View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after the World Cup final. He is believed to be interested in running for the Fifa presidency.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAThe three presidents also call for an independent review, conducted by a body outside football, into the affair. Fifa had committed previously to presenting a full report to the Fifa Council at its next scheduled meeting.The letter directly addresses concerns that countries may lose out on financial aid under a different leadership, saying it is “[not] about any member association losing the support it has earned, despite the fearmongering directed at our leadership to suggest otherwise”.The letter concludes: “There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness … Football’s strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now, with leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it.”51:14Infantino hangs on by a thread and the overhaul at Newcastle | Football Weekly – videoAny candidates for the Fifa election must announce their bid by 18 November. The confederations are understood to consider all options in their push for Infantino to be replaced, provided they fit within Fifa’s statutes and governance framework.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile the letter outlines the stances of the three confederations, and particularly their leaderships, the story is more complicated within individual member associations. Few outside Europe have been willing to come out publicly against Infantino and only a small minority have been tempted to recall the letters of support they had sent backing his re‑election next March. The influential African and South American confederations, Caf and Conmebol, have come out backing Infantino in recent days.A number of larger member associations have written to Infantino asking for a meeting where he would be required to explain his actions around the FFE scheme. No response has been received. Nor has Infantino been in touch with federations to address his leading role in the turmoil.The confederations’ tripartite statement was followed by another joint release headed by the World Cup hosts US Soccer and Canada Soccer, who along with the Caribbean Football Union and Central American Football Union also called for governance change at Fifa.The four bodies comprise 40 of the 41 Concacaf members, with the outliers being the third World Cup hosts Mexico,who went publiclast Friday with their continued support for Infantino.US Soccer had previously been silent and its willingness to condemn Fifa is significant, particularly as it is bidding to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup and also wants to stage games at the 2029 Club World Cup.“US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU [Caribbean Football Union] and UNCAF [Central American Football Union] stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens Fifa’s governance, transparency and accountability,” the statement read.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool owners close to £1.35bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool
Content: Fenway Sports Group has owned Liverpool since 2010.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenFenway Sports Group has owned Liverpool since 2010.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersLiverpoolLiverpool owners close to £1.35bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff BezosGroup including Amazon founder has held talks with FSGBhatia and Facebook co-founder Saverin also involvedWill UnwinMon 10 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks withFenway Sports Group. The investors are led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal and who previously was a shareholder and director at Queens Park Rangers.The Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is another member of the group who will pay in the region of £1.35bn. The deal is effectively agreed, but may take up to a month to complete.Van Dijk looks forward to more quality arriving at Liverpool before new seasonRead moreBezos has a personal fortune of around $257bn (£190bn), according to Forbes, making him the fourth-richest person in the world, while Saverin is reportedly worth $32bn. This will be Bezos’s first investment in football, but he has previously looked into bidding for NFL franchises. The 62-year-old will receive equity as part of the deal, which Deloitte has advised on.Bezos is the executive chair ofAmazonhaving relinquished day-to-day control when he stepped down as chief executive five years ago. Under his leadership, the online retailer has diversified into being an entertainment provider and has bought numerous sports rights for its streaming service.Amazon had live UK rights for 20 Premier League games each season for six seasons until the end of last year and broadcasts the Champions League in several European countries, as well as some NFL games in the US.FSG bought Liverpool in 2010and have overseen two Premier League titles. FSG sold 3% of the club tothe US private equity firm Dynasty Equityin 2023.It has been a summer of change at Anfield, withAndoni IraolareplacingArne Slot as head coach, Mohamed Salah left on a free transfer and hasjoined Trabzonsporand Michael Edwards departed his role as chief executive officer at FSG.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFSG has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolJeff BezosFenway Sports GroupAmazonFootball politicsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

Content: Premier League sides enter the fray in round two as clubs aim to make next March’s showpiece for the trophy.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenPremier League sides enter the fray in round two as clubs aim to make next March’s showpiece for the trophy.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PACarabao CupCarabao Cup second-round draw: Chelsea host Luton, Forest at home to LeedsSpurs will play Charlton, Preston v EvertonBrentford away at Birmingham; Ipswich v LeicesterPA MediaMon 10 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive-time winners Chelsea have been handed a home draw against League One Luton in the second round of theCarabao Cup. Chelsea’s new manager, Xabi Alonso, will begin the club’s attempt to win the competition for the first time since 2015 later this month.Fellow Premier League side Tottenham have also benefited from a home draw, against Championship opponents Charlton. title: Vondrousova’s antics put tennis doping tests in spotlight – a far cry from football’s view | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The former Wimbledon champion’s suspension comes as Mykhailo Mudryk returns for Chelsea, exposing a stark contrast in processes
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The former Wimbledon champion’s suspension comes as Mykhailo Mudryk returns for Chelsea, exposing a stark contrast in processes
Content: Marketa Vondrousova was given a four-year ban after refusing a doping test in December.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarketa Vondrousova was given a four-year ban after refusing a doping test in December.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesTennisVondrousova’s antics put tennis doping tests in spotlight – a far cry from football’s viewTumaini CarayolFormer Wimbledon champion’s suspension comes as Mykhailo Mudryk returns for Chelsea, exposing stark contrast in processesMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 04.04 EDTShareIn the months between the first announcement of Marketa Vondrousova’s doping test refusal and the release of the full reasoned decision after her four‑year ban, the 2023 Wimbledon champion did her best to grab hold of the narrative. Between her social media posts and later interviews, Vondrousova explained that she had serious concerns about her safety during the encounter, that the doping control officer at her door had acted improperly, and that her mental health problems had affected her judgment.Then came the 58-page document, a summary of the court tribunal process, which was finally released a little over a week ago. Among the ample questionable decisions it showed Vondrousova to have made that evening, the text to her boyfriend shortly after the doping control officer arrived was particularly revealing, an indication that she felt disdain towards the tester rather than fear: “So like here is ringing some cunt from the doping,” she wrote.Game, set, Chat: how tennis players use AI to scout opponents and run their livesRead moreOn 22 June, the InternationalTennisIntegrity Agency announced that Vondrousova had been suspended for four years after refusing an anti-doping test last December. The 27-year-old had been approached by an anti-doping officer at around 8pm at her flat at a time that fell outside the one‑hour slot players provide to the anti-doping authorities as part of the whereabouts programme for doping control officers to reach her.The full reasoned decision makes for excruciating reading from Vondrousova’s perspective. The most compelling conclusion is that she was ignorant of basic anti-doping rules, that she acted arrogantly due to her irritation at the 8pm anti-doping call and her decision to sign a document refusing a doping test, despite being told there could be severe consequences, will go down as one of the most ill-advised, self‑sabotaging decisions from any tennis player in history.Vondrousova seemed to believe that testers should arrive only in her designated whereabouts slot, and her agent was also painfully clueless about the anti-doping rules, and she acted on those incorrect assertions. Aside from this, the only other compelling theory would be that she knew what was in her system and deliberately did not want to be tested.Once the seriousness of her situation became clear after the refused test, Vondrousova even distastefully invoked the horrific stabbing of Petra Kvitova by a home intruder in Czechia when explaining her apparent fearfulness on social media. Despite that, Vondrousova still felt safe enough to walk out of the apartment building to take her dog for a walk, while the doping control officer was still at her door.View image in fullscreenMarketa Vondrousova became the first unseeded Wimbledon women’s singles champion after her 2023 success.Photograph: Rob Newell/CameraSport/Getty ImagesEven a large part of Vondrousova’s defence was centred on her dire decision making. She argued that she had been suffering from generalised anxiety disorder and acute stress reaction, which impaired her cognitive functions and led to her questionable actions. One point of interest ahead of the reasoned decision was how compelling her evidence would be to support this argument. Of the four written testimonies she put forward from experts, however, two doctors did not attend the hearing for cross‑examination and one confirmed at the hearing that he did not actually diagnose her. The tribunal concluded that, even if they accepted all of Vondrousova’s evidence, her excuse did not meet the high threshold to justify refusing to take a test.The World Anti-Doping Agency code is gruelling and stressful for athletes, and most are critical of parts of the system, but it is still part of an athlete’s job to understand the rules and ensure, to the best of their ability, that they comply. An appeal to the court of arbitration for sport may follow in the future, but for now the consequences of Vondrousova’s errors are catastrophic. She is suspended until she is 31, a potentially career-ending absence for one of the most talented players of her generation.On the same day that Vondrousova’s full decision was released, another high-profile sports doping case was resolved with the announcement from the Football Association that Mykhailo Mudryk, the Ukrainian winger who plays for Chelsea, was free to return to competition after his initial four-year suspension following a positive test for the banned substance meldonium had been shortened.View image in fullscreenMykhailo Mudryk returned to the Chelsea squad this month after his four-year suspension was shortened.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesIn contrast to the lengthy, detailed document that accompanied Vondrousova’s case and most doping cases in prominent Olympic sports, the Mudryk case, like the few public doping cases in football, has been defined by how little information is available due to the FA’s confidentiality rules. Forget a 58‑page document, the FA never even announced that Mudryk had received a four-year suspension; this information was revealed by Cas in April when Mudryk appealed against the suspension.The FA then announced on 31 July that it had, along with Wada, come to a case resolution agreement with Mudryk, reducing the length of suspension. The Ukrainian accepted the anti-doping rule violation but was allowed to return to competition. According to the FA’s press release, the low concentration of meldonium in Mudryk’s sample would not have been reported under Wada’s new technical document, which comes into force in January, and there were apparently “other circumstances of the case”, none of which were specified, that led to the resolution. There are no further details.After this announcement, the swiftness with which the narrative shifted from the doping suspension to how Mudryk could possibly reintegrate in the Chelsea team, to football matters, was fascinating. Little was made of the secrecy that football’s governing bodies operate with when it comes to anti-doping. This is merely one example – the circumstances around Paul Pogba’s doping ban in 2024, for example, were also murky until Cas became involved after his appeal.Considering the confidentiality with which the FA operates in anti‑doping matters, it is hard not to wonder which other players might have quietly failed doping tests over the years and how other potential cases might have been resolved. Most other sporting governing bodies, including cycling, athletics and more recently tennis have been forced to become more transparent due to the damage inflicted on their reputation by high-profile doping cases.Football, however, is eternally popular and there have been relatively few significant doping cases despite how high the competitive stakes are in the sport, meaning there is far less pressure on its governing bodies to be more transparent. As a result, the FA continues to manage its anti-doping programme in relative silence.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTennisWadaDrugs in sportThe FAcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes steps out of Pogacar’s shadow to showcase truly compelling racing | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Overall winner of Tour de France Femmes was uncertain until final climb – a world away from Tadej Pogacar’s dominance of men’s event
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Overall winner of Tour de France Femmes was uncertain until final climb – a world away from Tadej Pogacar’s dominance of men’s event
