Content: Demi Vollering’s superior climbing and descending secured the final stage – her third of the nine-day Tour de France Femmes – and a decisive general classification victory in Nice on Sunday.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering’s superior climbing and descending secured the final stage – her third of the nine-day Tour de France Femmes – and a decisive general classification victory in Nice on Sunday.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersTour de France FemmesAnalysisTour de France Femmes steps out of Pogacar’s shadow to showcase truly compelling racingJeremy Whittlein NiceOverall winner was uncertain until final climb – a world away from Slovenian’s dominance of men’s eventMon 10 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareDemi Vollering’ssecond overall win in the Tour de France Femmesin Nice on Sunday was achieved after a heated dispute with Kasia Niewiadoma, but by the time the sun was setting on the Promenade des Anglais, the sisterhood that has always characterised this race had kicked back in.On a final stage of high drama, the Dutchwoman erased the lingering controversy with an attacking win of the highest quality, further boosting the prestige of the long-dormant native cycling scene in a gutsy performance from her French‑sponsored FDJ United-Suez team.Dogs, descents and dehydration: Tour de France Femmes 2026 – in picturesRead moreNiewiadoma’s uncharacteristicoutburst on the finish lineat Vollering’s teammate Célia Gery on Saturday fuelled the controversy that dominated the final stage, but did not diminish the scale of her achievement.The former florist has had a golden 2026, winning theGiro d’Italia Women, in addition to Liège‑Bastogne‑Liège, the Tour of Flanders and Flèche Wallonne. Her achievements this season compare with, and arguably outstrip, those of her men’sTour de France‑winning counterpart, Tadej Pogacar.Vollering has long been outspoken about the wellbeing of young people and reacted angrily to Niewiadoma’s public criticism of Gery, her 20-year-old teammate. “She got a lot of nasty messages,” Vollering said on Sunday. “It makes me very angry, especially because she’s such a young girl. We should always protect young people from these kinds of stupid actions. She had a really rough time.”Vollering and Niewiadoma had a clear-the-air conversation on their bikes during the early kilometres of the final stage on Sunday. “I wanted to have a chat with Kasia because I was a bit disappointed she let all the emotions out like that,” she said. “It was good that we had a talk together. It was all good in the end.”The Polish rider, who wonthe spectacular stage on Mont Ventouxon Friday and finished in the Tour’s top three for the fifth time, was equally conciliatory. “We’ve been competing together for years. None of us ever wants to have any sort of beef.”It was a different story for the unfortunate Marlen Reusser,another key protagonist in the nine-day drama. The Swiss rider, who began the final stage in third place, crashed at speed on the second descent of Col d’Èze. She remounted, in tears, all hopes of the podium lost, but finished the stage.The men’s Tour de France was effectively over as a contest as soon as stage six, whenPogacar won over the Col du Tourmalet, but there was uncertainty about the outcome of the women’s race until the final narrow climb of the Chemin de Vinaigrier, a little-known lane in suburban Nice. Pogacar will go toEdinburgh for the Grand Départon 2 July next year seeking a sixth win, but it is uncertain if Jonas Vingegaard will remain his greatest rival. While Pogacar has confirmedhe will race in the Vuelta a España, starting in Monaco on 22 August, Vingegaard’s future remains unclear.Mattias Skjelmose, a fellow Dane, has revealed Vingegaard, whocrashed out of the Tour with a broken collarbone, has become disheartened by Pogacar’s domination. “Jonas says: ‘I can’t do any more. What am I supposed to do? I produce the best I’ve ever done and he just rides away from me,’” Skjelmosetold a Danish podcast.Vingegaard’s crash came hours after he was subjected to a 2am visit by drug testers from the International Testing Agency. The debate over the appropriateness of such extreme anti-doping measures – and the consequences for the riders – dominated the rest of the Tour. Pogacar rode on to Paris, apparently untroubled by his own 5am wake-up call, but the UCI’s president, David Lappartient, said: “There will always be suspicion in cycling.”The men’s Tour throws up the biggest stars and biggest controversies, but in the era of Pogacar it is theTour de France Femmesthat offers the most compelling racing. “When you have a Tadej Pogacar, at such a high level, you’re talking more about second place,” the Tour de France Femmes director, Marion Rousse, said. “It’s not like that in the women’s race. Women’s cycling at the moment creates more suspense than you see in men’s cycling, because Pogacar is so dominant.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTour de France Femmes: Vollering wins second title but tactics row rumbles onRead moreThe refreshing nature of theTour de FranceFemmes remains intact even as it grows at a rapid pace. Pogacar, a constant advocate of the women’s peloton, seems enthralled. He was spotted at the roadside, in beanie hat and shades, during the stage to Mont Ventoux on Friday, running alongside and cheering on his partner, Urska Zigart, and was present again at the weekend in Nice.Rousse believes the women’s race, which will hold its Grand Départ in Leeds on 30 July next year before stage finishes in Manchester, Sheffield and London, has not lost its innocence. “There’s a freshness, which you don’t get in men’s racing because the men are more used to it,” she said. “Women’s sport is more accessible. I think it’s because before, during the years before women’s cycling had profile, there was little ‘mediatisation’of women’s racing. Now they see the media coverage, they see so many people come to watch and it’s powerful for them. They’re moved and every time, up on the podium, there’s lots of emotion. That’s a new experience.”Rousse said the sceptics who doubted the quality of the women’s peloton have been silenced. “Back then it was all: ‘Are the women good enough? Can they do the big climbs?’ Now it’s: ‘Why don’t you have more stages? Why isn’t it every stage shown live on TV?’ Nobody asks if the women are good enough any more. They have proved themselves, they’re champions who have shown on the road and on their bikes that they deserve their place.”View image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma accepts theprix de la combativité(most attacking rider) for stage nine after finishing second to Demi Vollering overall.Photograph: Silvina Brodersohn/CameraSport/GettyExplore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingTour de FranceTadej PogacaranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates | India | The Guardian
description: Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
Content: Students march towards Jharkhand’s state assembly in protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudents march towards Jharkhand’s state assembly in protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaPolice use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalatesDemonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobsPenelope MacRaein DelhiMon 10 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.The unrest comes just weeks after theCockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.How gen Z exposed India’s prime-time propaganda machineRead moreThe demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.View image in fullscreenPolice use water cannon to disperse demonstrators during a protest.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar/AFP/Getty ImagesThe state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsiaYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy
Content: Smoke appears to rise from an oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles from the border.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke appears to rise from an oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles from the border.Photograph: ReutersUkraineUkraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economyLuke Hardingand agenciesMon 10 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep insideRussiahas killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline.Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery.Ukraine’s general staff said the raid waspart of a campaignto reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”.Russian investigators claimed civilian and industrial sites in the city had been hit. The head of the Tatarstan region, Rustam Minnikhanov, said a Ukrainian drone hit a hostel, killing nine people. He posted images showing a badly damaged building.If the death toll is confirmed, the strike would be among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the growing reach of Kyiv’s strikes deep inside Russia.Map showing location of Nizhnekamsk in RussiaThe Uzbek consulatesaid in a Telegram postthat seven of the victims were Uzbek citizens. Minnikhanov declared a day of mourning and Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case into alleged terrorism.Local video footageshowed Ukrainian drones buzzing above the city’s skyline, flying low over grey and box-like Soviet-era apartment blocks. Two plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above an industrial zone on the wooded outskirts of Nizhnekamsk.View image in fullscreenUkraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk on Sunday night.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe site is home to Taneco, one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, owned by Tatneft. It also houses a plant that produces rubber and petrochemical products.Ukrainealso bombed the area in June.In an address on Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “long-range sanctions” against the Kremlin and its war machine would continue. In recent months Ukrainian drones have wreaked havoc on Russia’s oil export industry, even hitting refineries in Siberia, 1,500 miles from the frontline.The governor of the Tyumen region in western Siberia said on Monday that several Ukrainian drones had fallen on an industrial facility and that emergency services were dealing with a fire.There have been several strikes on warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, as well as on oil tankers in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. Ukraine’s long-term goal is to slowly strangle the Russian economy so Moscow can no longer fund its war.3:41Who has the momentum in the Russia-Ukraine war? – video explainerZelenskyy described his country’s remote bombing campaign as “entirely justified”. “Every Russian strike [on Ukrainian towns and cities] will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia,” he said on social media. “The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.”Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones flying above Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Ukraine says it isknocking out its opponent’s air defence systemsmore quickly than they can be replaced, creating air corridors or “doors” it can exploit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFour people, including a child, were injured in Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOvernight, Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk parts of eastern Ukraine, while ⁠Russian-appointed local authorities said the ⁠Zaporizhzhia region in south-east Ukraine was largely without ⁠electricity on Monday ⁠after ​Ukrainian attacks destroyed key power facilities.On Russia’s Black Sea ⁠coast, power outages were ​reported in ‌parts of ‌Novorossiysk, a major export ‌port, and in the holiday resort of Gelendzhik, regional authorities said on Telegram.Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essayRead moreThere were unconfirmed reports that Russian ballistic missile launcher systems were destroyed inside Russia, not far from the border.According to Telegram channels citing Ukrainian military sources, the targeted high-value military assets were in Russia’s western Kursk and Bryansk regions. Both were used to launch Iskander and hypersonic Zircon missiles towards Kyiv.Ukrainian prosecutors said five people were killed on Sunday in a Russian artillery strike on a village outside Kharkiv. Several houses were flattened as a result of an “enemy strike” on Buhaivka in the Chuhuiv district, they said.Sweden’s security service, Säpo, said on Monday it ⁠had shut down a Russian spying operation that had tried to ⁠influence decision making ⁠there ​and discredit the Nordic country as well as its EU and ⁠Nato allies.Säpo said the operation had been planned and directed by Russia’s SVR foreign ⁠intelligence service and involved three people working under ​the cover of ‌diplomatic immunity.“This is ‌consistent with the threat we see Russia posing,” a Säpo spokesperson said. “We have been able to monitor ​what happened at these meetings between the individuals involved, what was said and what assignments were given. They are ⁠no longer in Sweden and we ​have ​been able to break up ​this operation.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDrones (military)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Record 230 people cross Channel to UK as smugglers turn to ‘mega-dinghies’ | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Crossing in larger vessel highlights changing tactics despite increased enforcement on French coast
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Crossing in larger vessel highlights changing tactics despite increased enforcement on French coast
Content: The use of mega-dinghies poses an even greater risk to life than the smaller vessels.Photograph: Facebook/Station SNSM Berck sur MerView image in fullscreenThe use of mega-dinghies poses an even greater risk to life than the smaller vessels.Photograph: Facebook/Station SNSM Berck sur MerImmigration and asylumRecord 230 people cross Channel to UK as smugglers turn to ‘mega-dinghies’Crossing in larger vessel highlights changing tactics despite increased enforcement on French coastDiane TaylorMon 10 Aug 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday.It is the clearest indication yet that people smugglers in northernFranceare adapting their business model and escalating their so-called taxi boat strategy to evade enforcement by UK and French authorities.The development is likely to be a blow to the prime minister and home secretary. Andy Burnham hasvowed to be “relentless”and “bring back control”, while Shabana Mahmood has said the government is “bearing down” on small boat crossings.French authorities told the Guardian that beforean incidentlast week, in which a mega-dinghy carrying 173 people capsized after its engine caught fire, there had been nine mega-dinghy crossings of the Channel so far this year.View image in fullscreenA Home Office spokesperson said the latest incident ‘demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings’.Photograph: Facebook/Station SNSM Berck sur MerAlthough the number crossing the Channel this year has fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year, the increasing use of larger vessels demonstrates how quickly people smugglers have adapted to stronger enforcement by French police on beaches in northern France.The UK government has struck a deal with Germany to increase seizures of traditional dinghies and engines “upstream”.Last year, 106 people were reported to have crossed the Channel in a single dinghy in August and 125 in September. The emergence of mega-dinghies coincided with the announcement in July 2025 of the UK-France“one in, one out” deal, under which a person arriving in the UK from France by small boat can be returned in exchange for another person being brought legally to the UK to claim asylum.On 12 July this year, a mega-dinghy carrying 128 people arrived in the UK, followed by another carrying 165 people on 23 July. On 4 August, a dinghy carrying 173 peoplecapsized after the engine caught fire. All those onboard are believed to have been rescued, with 11 sustaining minor injuries and three taken to hospital in Boulogne.The use of mega-dinghies poses an even greater risk to life than smaller vessels, which have recently carried an average of between 50 and 60 passengers, according to NGOs working with asylum seekers crossing the Channel. When small-boat crossings began in 2018, only a handful of people typically travelled in each dinghy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTwo children in foil blankets and two women walk along the beach in Gravelines, France, after failing to board a dinghy attempting to sail into the Channel in April.Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Getty ImagesWhile there have been “green days” this year, when adverse weather has made conditions too dangerous for smugglers to launch dinghies, NGOs say many continue to wait in northern France for an opportunity to cross the Channel. They include some who have been returned to France under the one-in, one-out scheme and hope to reach the UK for a second time.Hannah Marwood, the head of legal access at Care4Calais, which delivers emergency aid to refugees, said: “Deterrence doesn’t stop people seeking safety, it just pushes them towards greater danger and greater exploitation. We’ve worked with people who were returned to France only to face violence, exploitation and unsafe conditions, leaving them with no option but to risk another dangerous journey.“Politicians keep promising that another tough policy will solve this but the evidence keeps proving them wrong. If the government is serious about stopping dangerous journeys, it needs to stop recycling failed gimmicks and create safe routes to claim asylum. When people have a safe way to reach protection, they don’t have to risk their lives to find it.”AHome Officespokesperson said: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people on to unseaworthy vessels.“We are making progress, with the number of small-boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeLabourAndy BurnhamShabana MahmoodFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Discovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Discovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’
Content: 0:28Ancient Roman pottery discovered in shipwreck off Sicilian coast – videoArchaeologyRoman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of SicilyDiscovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’Lorenzo Tondoin Palermo and agenciesMon 10 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck carrying about 500 amphorae has been discovered 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in Sicily.Italy’s Carabinieri cultural heritage protection squad investigated the wreck with the help of divers and underwater cameras after receiving a tip-off from fishers. The vessel was found at a depth of about 46 metres (151ft) and was carryinghundreds of amphorae– ancient two-handled ceramic jars with a narrow neck – thought to have been used mainly to transport wine.The wreck, measuring about 21 metres long and 6 metres wide, was described by Italy’s culture minister, Alessandro Giuli, as “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years”.Giuli said the wreck offered “precious fragments of our history” and provided further evidence of the trade routes and exchanges that made the Mediterranean “a crossroads of civilisations”.The divers Giacomo De Mola and Igor Bisulli described how they came across the wreck.“Visibility wasn’t the best … I got closer. And my heart stopped. Below me was a vast expanse of amphorae,” De Mola said in an Instagram post accompanying video footage of the discovery.“This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life,” he said. “It’s hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again.”Most of the ship’s cargo consisted of Dressel 1A amphorae, widely used to transport wine and particularly valuable to archaeologists because they can help reconstruct the commercial networks that linked Italy with other parts of the Mediterranean between the second and first centuries BC.Over the coming months, Sicily’s superintendency of the sea is expected to carry out a new phase of scientific documentation and research at the site. Archaeologists will seek to establish more precisely the date of the wreck, the origin and intended destination of its cargo, and the condition of the surviving material, while also drawing up measures to protect what officials have described as a site of exceptional archaeological significance.The discovery is the latest in a series of important Roman wrecks found in Italian waters.In 2021,another Roman vessel dating from the second century BCwas discovered off the coast of Palermo. The wreck lay 92 metres beneath the sea near Isola delle Femmine and images taken by an underwater robot showed it carrying a large cargo of wine amphorae.Before that, an almost intact Roman vessel dating from the second century BC was discovered in 2013 off the coast of Liguria. The ship, carrying about 50 valuable amphorae, was located by police divers about a mile off Alassio at a depth of about 50 metres.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn that case, police were alerted to the wreck during a year-long investigation into archaeological artefacts believed to have been looted and sold on the black market in northern Italy.Italian police recover hundredsof illegally removed ancient Roman amphoraeeach year, many of them found in the homes or warehouses of collectors and art dealers.The waters surrounding Sicily are regarded as one of the Mediterranean’s richest areas for underwater archaeology. The island’s strategic position along the ancient maritime routes linking Greece, the Middle East, north Africa andEuropemeans its seabed is believed to contain some of the most significant surviving wrecks from the ancient world.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsArchaeologyItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggest | Animals | The Guardian
description: Researchers analysed activity in regions of brain when dogs were shown images of different facial expressions
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Researchers analysed activity in regions of brain when dogs were shown images of different facial expressions
Content: The researchers worked with pet dogs, mostly border collies, that had been trained to lie still in an MRI scanner.Photograph: Laura V CuayaView image in fullscreenThe researchers worked with pet dogs, mostly border collies, that had been trained to lie still in an MRI scanner.Photograph: Laura V CuayaAnimalsDogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggestResearchers analysed activity in regions of brain when dogs were shown images of different facial expressionsNicola DavisScience correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile dogs are known to turn thepuppy eyes on their owners, it seems our pets are keeping a close eye on us too: research has revealed dog brains can distinguish different types of unhappy human faces.Dr Laura Cuaya, a co-author of the study from the University of Vienna, said previous behavioural studies had shown dogs could tell apart some human facial expressions, but such studies tended to only test two at a time, one positive and one negative. As a result, it was not clear if dogs could distinguish different types of happy or unhappy faces.Now Cuaya and colleagues have revealed dog brains can not only distinguish happy faces from other expressions, but can tell apart different negative expressions, distinguishing fearful faces from those that are angry or sad.“This is the first demonstration that the dog brain can distinguish between emotions from the same valence,” she said.While the team’s previous research has suggested dogsdo not have a particular region of the brain devoted to processing faces, Cuaya noted that did not mean the brain activity pattern was the same for the front and back of the head.View image in fullscreenThe scans revealed increased activity in certain parts of the brain when the dogs were shown happy faces compared with neutral ones.Photograph: Laura V CuayaWriting in the journal iScience, Cuaya and colleagues report how they worked with pet dogs that had been trained to voluntarily lie still, awake and unrestrained, within an MRI scanner.In the first experiment, eight dogs were shown five sets of happy faces and five sets of neutral faces. Each set contained four photos of humans that were unfamiliar to the dog but were of the same gender as their primary caregiver. This was repeated five times for each dog.The results revealed increased activity in certain parts of the brain when the dogs were shown happy faces compared with neutral ones.Cuaya said these areas were associated with higher visual processing, social processing and reward processing – suggesting the dog was processing something positive.Dr Raúl Hernández Pérez, the first author of the study, said the results raised another question, however: “We don’t know if these regions are related just to happy faces or to emotional faces in general.”The team then carried out a second MRI experiment involving 12 dogs. Each was shown new sets of unfamiliar male and female human faces, this time bearing four different expressions: happiness, sadness, fear and anger.The researchers used machine learning to analyse activity in the same brain regions identified in the first experiment, revealing such activity could distinguish happy faces from each negative expression – but could not distinguish between different types of unhappy face.However, when the team analysed activity in the whole dog brain, they found it was possible to distinguish between sad v fearful faces, and angry v fearful faces – with differences in activity in different parts of the brain – but not angry and sad faces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHernández said different negative expressions might trigger different responses as they represented a different type of threat.The authors said it might be harder for dogs to tell apart two human facial expressions if they were both negative or both positive, and dogs might also need additional information – such as body language – to distinguish anger from sadness.The research has limitations, including small sample size; most of the dogs being border collies, and all were healthy and without behavioural problems.View image in fullscreenDogs may need additional information, such as body language, to distinguish anger from sadness.Photograph: Laura V CuayaCuaya said the study could have practical implications: for example, expressing happiness when training a dog could aid the learning process.Bridget Waller, a professor of evolution and social behaviour at Nottingham Trent University, who was not involved in the study, described the work as fascinating, saying it showed how dogs have been shaped through domestication to understand human behaviour.“Smiling is the most commonly used human facial expression, vital to our social interactions, and so it makes sense that dogs have developed a particular ability to distinguish this from other facial movements,” she said. “It seems less clear that they can distinguish between the other facial expressions, and again this would make sense as these are much less commonly produced in human social interaction.”Explore more on these topicsAnimalsDogsNeuroscienceAustriaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unprecedented, dangerous territory’: US north-west reckons with a summer of historic wildfires | Washington state | The Guardian
description: Extreme conditions in Washington and Oregon have fueled fast-moving fires, leaving the region draped in toxic plumes – and the danger isn’t over
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Extreme conditions in Washington and Oregon have fueled fast-moving fires, leaving the region draped in toxic plumes – and the danger isn’t over
Content: The aftermath of the Old Trails wildfire in Spokane, Washington, on 4 August. Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersExtreme conditions in Washington and Oregon have fueled fast-moving fires, leaving the region draped in toxic plumes – and the danger isn’t overByGabrielle CanonMon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePiles of twisted metal and ashen debris line the cul-de-sacs where the tranquil suburbs of Spokane,Washington, once stood.The scale of devastation from a historicwildfireseason in the Pacific north-west has come into sharper focus as firefighters wrangle a trio of blazes that consumed at least 846 structures on the eastern side of the state.More than 2.9m acres (1.1m hectares) have already burned across Washington and Oregon this year, as extreme conditions fuel fast-moving fires that have draped theregionintoxicplumes for weeks on end. Oregon has alreadylogged more burned acreage this yearthan any in recorded history. Washington, meanwhile, is in themidst of its most destructivefire season.And the dangers are far from over.Firefighting resources are already being pushed to their limits, but there are months left before the highest risks on desperately dry landscapes might begin to subside.In the US and around the world, the climate crisis has pushed temperatures higher and extended the seasons when infernos are more able to erupt. With the threat of another warm winter looming large, experts say there will probably be even more time for calamitous conditions to align.Active wildfires in Pacific north-west as of 7 August 2026On Friday, firefighters were battling 95 large blazes across the US, with reports of extreme fire behavior across multiple regions. More than6.3m acres have burnedacross the US since the start of the year, according to the US National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC).The number of fires ignited has also been exceedingly high. Firefighters have had to battle more than 45,800 blazes across the country since the year began. A hundred new fires erupted in a single day last week.Aerial perspective of two matching views with a slider, showing before and after images of a residential neighborhood. The after image shows blackened areas.A satellite image shows damage from the Old Trails fire to the Balboa neighborhood of Spokane. Credit: Vantor/Reuters“We are living through climate change and it’s accelerating,” said Dr Susan Prichard,a fire ecologist at the University of Washington. “There’s a longer window where if we get the dreaded ignitions – whether they’re accidental, or purposeful, or lightning – the forests become really receptive to burning.”A landscape primed to burnThe stage was set for an intense summer of fire long before the flames ignited.Vegetation across the region cured during anexceptionally hot, dry, July, according to an outlook from the NIFC, as swathes of Oregon and Washington received only half or a quarter of the rainfall typically seen in the month.With the thirsty terrain primed to burn, more than 600 fires exploded to life in a 10-day periodin July, started by rounds of lightning and fueled by strong winds. Some ignited and spread through areas thatshould have still been covered by snowin mid-July . The so-called Old Trails fire, one of at least three fires that converged around Spokane,may have been ignited by an arsonist, and a man has been taken into custody.Thousands of people rushed from their homes as the fires closed in on Washington’s second-largest city. Whole neighborhoods were wiped from the map as flames bellowed through communities, sweeping from structure to structure.View image in fullscreenTim Hansen retrieves a statuette of an angel from the remains of a home burned in the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington, on 3 August.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersThe resulting urban conflagrationfollowed a devastating pattern of destructionseen in other cities hammered by wildfire in recent years, including Los Angeles in 2025; Lahaina, Hawaii, in 2023; and the suburbs of Boulder, Colorado, in 2021.“Spokane has joined the rapidly growing list of our communities that have been devastated by these climate-exaggerated fires,” said Jay Inslee, the former Washington governor.Wildfires rage across Washington as drought and heat fuel painful summer: ‘It’s not normal’Read moreWhile most of the fire activity has been concentrated on the eastern side of the Cascade mountains, an area that’s hotter and drier than the landscapes known for their lush rainforests and dense coastal fog to the west, Prichard expressed concerns about the risks that still lay ahead.Large fires are more rare in the moisture-rich areas closer to the Pacific, but not unheard of. Prichard pointed to the deadly and devastating Labor Day fires of 2020, when flames howled through communities on the western side of the Cascades inOregon, fueled by dry winds. More than a million acres were scorched, thousands of homes were destroyed and 11 people died.“I hope I’m wrong,” Prichard said. “But western Washington and western Oregon are ready to burn.”Conditions across the region aren’t expected to ease any time soon. Increasedsignificant fire potential will extend through September, according to the NIFC. Precipitation that might otherwise provide relief across the parched landscapes is forecast to be below normal into November.Aerial perspective of two matching views with a slider, showing before and after images of a residential neighborhood. The after image shows blackened areas.Damage to the Balboa neighborhood in Spokane. Credit: Vantor/ReutersThe climate phenomenon known as El Niño, characterized by warming surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific, could also punch fire risks higher through the end of the year, especially in the Pacific north-west. Models show there’s now a 95% chanceof a very strong El Niñodeveloping by September, and scientists have warned it could become the strongest ever recorded.El Niño has the power to affect weather around the world, but outcomes vary. In Oregon and Washington, however, the pattern trends hotter and drier through the winter.“It’s unprecedented, dangerous territory –Washington statehas never been so exposed to multiple losses,” Inslee said. “You layer El Niño on top of that, and there could be additional catastrophes even this summer.”Across the Atlantic, Europe is also having a historic season,fueled by deadly heatwaves that baked moistureout of desiccating landscapes across the continent. More than 1.3m acres have burned so far this year, on pace with last year, when new records were set.Much like in the western US, extreme heat and drought globally aren’t expected to soften in the months ahead, and risks will remain high through autumn. Infernosripped across France and Spain in July, leaving widespread destruction in their wake and cloaking millions of people in toxic air.Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfiresRead moreResearchers found the extreme weather driving the fires in several countries was made more likely by human-caused climate change. The fires in south-western Francewere twice as likely, and in central Spain 20 timesmore likely, because of greenhouse gas emissions, mostly caused by the burning of oil, coal and gas that has increased global temperatures, according to a study released at the end of July.“This is a new beast that is attacking our communities across the western United States and across the world,” Inslee said. “We’ve got the way to fight this beast right at its heart, which is climate change induced by pollution.”Firefighters under pressureThe explosion in fire activity in the Pacific north-west in July made the region the focus of firefighting efforts over the last month, but across the US, crews are already spread thin.As of 18 July, the country has been classified at “preparedness level 5” – the highest level, and one that indicates resources are fully deployed.“PL5 means triage – it means some fires aren’t going to get firefighters,” a federal fire captain said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press. “A well-staffed and well-functioning fire service should mean that there’s never a PL5, or that it’s very, very rare.”The fire captain described the emotional and physical strain inflicted on first responders who are taking on longer, harder and increasingly more dangerous assignments as the wildfire crisis outpaces resources provided.“We are trying to save what we can, but we’re just watching houses burn,” the fire captain said. “As a wildland firefighter, no matter how much you give, your presence is never enough.”View image in fullscreenA Cal Fire firefighter hoses down the remains of a home destroyed in the Old Trails fire in Spokane, on 6 August.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesInjuries are common among the men and women who spend seasons away from friends and family on the frontline in the harshest environments. Seven wildland firefightershave reportedly died in the line of dutyso far this summer.“We need to have a more realistic expectation about what our firefighters can do when we’re experiencing fire seasons like this one,” said Bobbie Scopa, a retired fire chief who now serves as a vice-president for the firefighter advocacy group Grassroots Wildland Firefighters.Along with the harrowing conditions firefighters face on the biggest blazes, she emphasized the thousands of fires that are quickly extinguished before they become infernos, which rarely reach public perception. Anestimated 98% of fires are suppressedbefore they spread across 100 acres, according to federal statistics.“We live in a fire environment and it’s getting worse,” Scopa said. “If we really expect to put out every single fire before it gets big, we would need double the workforce and probably triple the budget. Otherwise, we’re going to kill people trying to put out those last couple per cent and we’re going to spend a lot of money doing it.”Explore more on these topicsWashington stateOregonWildfiresClimate crisisWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland
Content: 1:12Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – videoExtreme weatherTyphoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on ShanghaiAuthorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inlandYu-chen Liin TaipeiMon 10 Aug 2026 00.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 23.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening aspowerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfallamid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas.Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwaveRead moreIn Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening, substantially higher than an earlier figure of 30,300.A weather station in central Shanghai recorded nearly 313mm of rain in the 24 hours to 7am on Monday, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records. Another station in the city recorded nearly 400mm. The hashtag “Shanghai turns into the sea” began trending on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, as videos circulated showing streets flooded around the Wukang Mansion, one of the city’s best-known tourist landmarks.The average rainfall recorded across Zhejiang from Friday evening to Monday morning reached 173mm, reportedly surpassing the levels seen during previous major typhoons including Lekima and Bavi.Dolphin weakened rapidly to a tropical storm by 5am on Monday. But as the storm continued to move northwards and farther inland, heavy rain was forecast across large parts of eastern and centralChina, extending north into Shandong and affecting Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai.Authorities maintained an orange alert for heavy rain and warned that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides through Wednesday, urging people to stay indoors during the heavy downpours. Forecasters in China predicted some areas could see 200-400mm (7.9–15.7 inches) of rainfall over the coming days.View image in fullscreenA temporary shelter in Hangzhou, where thousands of people were evacuated because of Typhoon Dolphin.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesThe storm forced Shanghai’s two airports to cancel more than 1,300 flights. Public transport services, including many local trains, have been suspended in the financial hub.Zhejiang’s Ningbo international airport, about 150km south of Shanghai, will resume flight operations from midday (0400 GMT) on Monday. But the airport warned some journeys may yet be delayed or cancelled.Provincial capital Hangzhou resumed subway services on Monday morning, after halting some train operations on Sunday.Elsewhere, Dolphin fuelled intense heat over Hong Kong on Sunday, pushing the city toits highest ever temperature of 36.9C. The extremely hot weather was expected to continue into Tuesday, officials said.In Taiwan, ferry services were suspended and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought downpours and strong winds on Sunday.Dolphin earlier swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and ⁠cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.In the Philippines, the typhoon did not make landfall in the country’s north but intensified the seasonal monsoon rains, which flooded many areas of the main northern Luzon region, including around Manila.Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherChinaHong KongAsia PacificFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: PM urged not to change scheme to stop PC Andrew Harper killers’ early release | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Manslaughter exemption would mean more releases would be needed within 18 months, Prison Service officials say
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Manslaughter exemption would mean more releases would be needed within 18 months, Prison Service officials say
Content: Jessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAView image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAUK criminal justicePM urged not to change scheme to stop PC Andrew Harper killers’ early releaseManslaughter exemption would mean more releases would be needed within 18 months, Prison Service officials sayWhat could Andy Burnham do to block early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers?Rajeev SyalHome affairs editorMon 10 Aug 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been warned that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so PC Andrew Harper’s killers are kept behind bars would force another spate of early releases before the next general election.Prison Service officials have told No 10 that adding an exemption so that those convicted of manslaughter, such as Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, remain in jail would mean further early releases would be needed within 18 months.Governors told the Guardian the prime minister’s decision last week to exempt rapists and serious child sex offenders would force thousands of sentences to be recalculated in haste and could lead to the mistaken early release of some prisoners.On Monday, Downing Street said the prime minister had “pushed hard on what more we could do” but it was not possible to exempt “one or two offenders” from early release, as manslaughter of an emergency worker was not a stand-alone offence. Instead, if they wanted to block the release of Cole and Bowers then every offender with a manslaughter conviction would be affected.The government plans to release 5,000 prisoners early over a period of 10 months from October to free up places. Harper’s killers are due to be released in January.Burnham is facing demands to exclude Cole and Bowers from the early release scheme. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.Despite the concerns from the Prison Service and a lack of obvious options, a No 10 source said the prime minister was “still pushing” for a way of keeping Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars.The prime minister said last week he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do” by exempting 1,000 rapists, child sexual abuse offenders and groomers from early release, which reduced the number of spaces to be freed up in the next 10 months from 6,000.Blocking the early release of Cole and Bowers could mean delaying the release of at least 500 other offenders also convicted of manslaughter, a Whitehall source said. “People in the Prison Service are terrified by the prospect of another exemption,” they said. “They have told the PM that if they carve out manslaughter cases there will have to be another early release scheme before the general election.”Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said ministers have been warned that delays to the early release scheme mean some prisoners could be released at the wrong time.“We have expressed concerns to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) officials about increased ‘releases in error’ and ‘unlawful detention’ risk because of the government’s last-minute changes to the Sentencing Act’s implementation. Officials have assured us that ministers have been briefed on the increased risk environment,” he said.Each prison will be expected to re-evaluate the sentences of every prisoner affected by Burnham’s changes. This could mean recalculating many thousands of prison sentences in a short period of time when staff are on holiday, Wheatley said.“These late changes come at a time when many staff who specialise in calculating sentences and met the original deadline are off work, on a well-earned break. Because this is a time-pressured and manual process, involving paper files that can be inches thick, it carries an increased risk of error,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMinisters have been advised that they are at risk of a legal challenge if they try to carve out exclusions for Cole and Bowers but not others convicted of manslaughter. Nick Hardwick, who was the chief inspector of prisons for six years until 2016, said he felt “uneasy” at the suggestion the government could draw up exemptions from the scheme to satisfy a public outcry.“I am appalled by what happened to PC Harper,” he said. “But we have to be careful about the principle here. We should be uneasy about politicians deciding what happens to particular offenders. It is something that needs careful debate. It should not be up to politicians to choose how long individuals spend in prison.“If the government did change the legal framework to exclude these two men from early release, it could well be an example of ‘hard cases making bad law’.”MoJ officials said prisons could run out of places in November if the scheme was abandoned.Asked on Monday whether ministers were accepting the situation as it stood, Burnham’s spokesperson said: “I think you’ve seen from the prime minister’s words that he’s far from accepting the situation and, as he wrote last week, he wants to go even further. He’s pushed hard on what more we could do and his focus now is on fixing the prison system long-term to avoid a repeat of this prison crisis so that it never happens again.”Pressed on whether the prime minister was admitting there was nothing more he could do, the official said: “He understands the public wants him to go further, and he wanted to go further, but on the wider issue … prisons would have run out of space, police would stop making arrests, it would be impossible to lock up convicted offenders and that would put public safety at untold risk.”Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceAndy BurnhamPrisons and probationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds | Civil service | The Guardian
description: Chloe Moffat, 26, killed herself after disciplinary proceedings that coroner in Surrey found be to be flawed
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Chloe Moffat, 26, killed herself after disciplinary proceedings that coroner in Surrey found be to be flawed
Content: Chloe Moffat’s mother said ‘she was left frightened, isolated and convinced that her career and reputation had been destroyed’.Photograph: Anne MoffatView image in fullscreenChloe Moffat’s mother said ‘she was left frightened, isolated and convinced that her career and reputation had been destroyed’.Photograph: Anne MoffatCivil serviceTreasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner findsChloe Moffat, 26, killed herself after disciplinary proceedings that coroner in Surrey found be to be flawedHelena HortonMon 10 Aug 2026 07.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Treasury “materially contributed” to the death of Chloe Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant who took her own life after facing disciplinary proceedings, a coroner has found.Anna Crawford also found there was a risk of future deaths within the civil service from flawed handling of disciplinary proceedings. She said she would send a prevention of future deaths report to the head of the civil service, the Treasury, and the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service (Acas).Moffat had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years. She “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard during the three-day hearing.However, she was driven to “distress” by an informal meeting about an anonymous complaint at work. It alleged she had informally shared information about colleagues which she had been privy to during her job. Moffat had denied the allegation.During the disciplinary process,the Surrey coroners court heard, she was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, and she was not allowed to have a third party of her choice in the meeting. She had her job responsibilities temporarily changed and her access to the diary of her manager removed. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”.The process left her “devastated” and convinced she had lost her job. The morning after the meeting, Moffat killed herself.The coroner found Moffat “appeared well and happy” before the meeting on 19 May last year and that there were no previous concerns about her mental health. She said: “I am satisfied that the shock and distress of the allegations and thinking she was going to lose her job contributed to her state of mind.”View image in fullscreenChloe Moffat’s mother described her as ‘a bright, caring and talented young woman’.Photograph: Anne MoffatThe Treasury’s human resources policy, which is in line with Acas guidelines, says that serious misconduct allegations have to be dealt with formally. This is so the person involved is “not deprived of their rights”, such as having a third party present during meetings, being given five days’ notice and being informed of the likely outcome if the allegations are found to be true, the coroner said.She found that because decisions had already been made to limit Moffat’s role and responsibilities, the allegations “needed a formal process”. Crawford said: “I find the meeting was not in accordance with [Treasury] policy”, which “makes no provision” for such informal meetings. “The reason for this seems abundantly clear,” she added. “It is necessary to put safeguards in place, including informing about the likely penalty and the right to be accompanied.”The head of global issues at the Treasury, who was running the investigation into Moffat, said during the coroner’s hearing that she did not give Moffat prior notice of the meeting because “she did not want Chloe to worry about it”. She had also told the court that when Moffat asked in tears whether she would lose her job, she had replied that she could not predict the outcome of any potential investigation.Earlier in the hearing, when asked if she would have done anything differently, Moffat’s line manager told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.”But the coroner found: “By handling the matter in the way they did, Chloe was denied safeguards.“The concern that she would lose her job did materially contribute to her state of mind and the decision to take her own life,” Crawford said. She found the Treasury played a part in Moffat’s death by not informing her that the likely outcome would be a written warning and not dismissal.Crawford was issuing a prevention of future deaths notice because the Treasury claimed these informal meetings were “standard practice”. “That is a matter of concern,” she said. “It runs the risk of serious and/or gross misconduct allegations being put to colleagues without safeguards in place.”The Treasury previously said it was reviewing its disciplinary process. “This does not set my mind at rest,” the coroner said. “I consider there remains a risk of future death.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnne Moffat, Chloe’s mother, said: “Chloe was a bright, caring and talented young woman who loved her family, her friends and her work. The evidence heard during the inquest has reinforced our belief that the allegations made against Chloe were nothing more than workplace gossip.“She was treated with a complete lack of empathy with regard to allegations made by colleagues who chose to remain anonymous. We continue to believe that HM Treasury failed in its duty of care towards Chloe. At a time when she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced that her career and reputation had been destroyed.”Anne Moffat suggested the family may take further action: “We will continue to honour her memory and seek the changes needed to ensure that no other family suffers a similar loss.”A Treasury spokesperson said: “We continue to mourn Chloe’s passing as a colleague and friend. Our thoughts remain with her family and friends. We take the coroner’s concerns extremely seriously and recognise it is important to act quickly. We are now considering the findings carefully.“We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”An Acas spokesperson said: “This is an extremely distressing and upsetting case and our thoughts are with Chloe’s family. Acas has a disciplinary and grievance code of practice that sets out good practice advice for employers on how to handle disciplinary cases.“Revisions to this code are currently being consulted on with a deadline for responses of 23 September. Our proposed revisions to the code includes a new advice section for employers on how to handle concerns informally. We welcome any feedback on the revised code and will consider any recommendations for Acas from the coroner’s report.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsCivil serviceEnglandWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ofcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarks | GB News | The Guardian
description: Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia
Content: Caroline Farrow describes herself as a Catholic commentator.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCaroline Farrow describes herself as a Catholic commentator.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockGB NewsOfcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarksRegulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophiliaMichael SavageMedia editorMon 10 Aug 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia.The remarks are thought to have set a new record for individual complaints about a GB News programme, with more than 12,000 people raising concerns about comments made by the guest Caroline Farrow.Those to speak out included the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, andBimini, the star of RuPaul’s Drag Race UK.Farrow, who describes herself as a Catholic commentator and is a campaigns manager for theultra-conservative advocacy group CitizenGO, made the remarks during a discussion after the Pride in London march in July.Speaking on the Alex Armstrong Tonight show, Farrow said the march was “not about gay rights” and had instead “become about celebrating every single sexuality that isn’t heterosexuality”.She said this included “some very bizarre and unhealthy kinks and quirks, you know, like furries and bestiality and even minor-attracted, they call themselves minor-attracted people, you know, paedophiles”.The remarks prompted an open letter signed by Polanski and Bimini calling onOfcomto deal with the “dangerous” disinformation.Ofcom confirmed to the Guardian that it was investigating the show over potential breaches of broadcasting standards. The rules dictate that “material which may cause offence is justified by the context”.The edition of the show containing the remarks has since been removed from YouTube.Armstrong, the show’s presenter, challenged the comments at the time, saying “the overwhelming amount of people at pride were there for good reasons”.He added: “I don’t think it was full of paedophiles and everything, I’m sure there are nefarious people.”He went further on a later show, saying: “Comments made by guests last weekend conflated gay pride with the celebration of paedophilia. This is an age-old gay trope that’s been used over a number of years to demonise and slander gay people. Those comments by guests had no place in that discussion.”TheGreen partydeputy leader welcomed Ofcom’s latest decision to investigate Farrow’s comments.“Zack was right to complain about it at the time,” Rachel Millward said. “The suggestion that gay people are somehow a particular threat to children is baseless, irresponsible and deeply harmful.“GB News is a regulated broadcaster, and broadcasters are supposed to meet basic professional standards. That should include not using their platform to spread hateful lies about a marginalised group.”GB News has been approached for comment. At the time, it said: “These comments were expressed within a live debate by a contributor. They were her own views, and do not reflect the views or editorial position of GB News.“Anyone watching the debate would have noted the comments were robustly and repeatedly challenged by two other contributors.”GB News has previously been criticised by Ofcom for similar remarks on another programme. Last year, the regulator concluded that the channel breached the broadcasting code after a presenter, Josh Howie, said the “full inclusion of LGBTQ+ persons” at a church would “include paedos”.On that occasion, sanctions were not imposed on GB News because it had already broadcast an apology and a fuller discussion about the context of the comment within weeks of the original broadcast.The investigation comes amid increased pressure on Ofcom to enforce broadcasting rules.While the regulator is also investigating a GB News repeat of itsinterview with Donald Trump, it declined to investigate a claim by a GB News presenter that there had been noriot in Belfastin June, despite cars and houses being set alight, attacks on police and families fleeing their homes.The previous Ofcom chair, the Conservative peer Michael Grade, who left the post in April, accused GB News’s critics of seeking to restrict free speech to a“liberal, Islington consensus”.Explore more on these topicsGB NewsPrideOfcomLGBTQ+ rightsTelevision industryTelevisionZack PolanskinewsShareReuse this content

title: Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Utility firm’s payment criticised by Defra and campaign groups, with some urging Andy Burnham to nationalise it
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Utility firm’s payment criticised by Defra and campaign groups, with some urging Andy Burnham to nationalise it
Content: Thames Water is one of at least eight water companies banned from paying performance-related bonuses.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenThames Water is one of at least eight water companies banned from paying performance-related bonuses.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThames WaterThames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government departmentUtility firm’s payment criticised by Defra and campaign groups, with some urging Andy Burnham to nationalise itNils Pratley: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect?Jasper JollyMon 10 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 04.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThames Water has paid its finance chief a £1m signing fee despite teetering on the brink of a government-handled administration – a decision the environment department labelled “unacceptable”.The utility company revealed that it made the payment last month, in a letter sent last week by Adrian Montague, its chair, to MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs select committee.Thames is one of at least eight water companiesbanned from paying performance-related bonusesbecause of continued environmental failings from its creaking infrastructure. The company, which provides water and sewage services to 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley, has been on the verge of collapse for more than two years.Turn failing water firms into not-for-profit cooperatives, MPs and mayors tell PMRead moreAndy Burnham has previously indicated thegovernment should take control of Thamesin order to write off debts worth billions of pounds. However, the creditors who in effect control Thames have spent months negotiating to take formal ownership, if regulators will give leniency on future fines. The creditors haveoffered the government a “golden share”in the business in a last-ditch attempt to avoid having their debts written down.Yet the continued payments of millions of pounds to executives will probably strengthen calls for the government to step in and take formal control via a special administration regime.A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “It is unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust.“We’ve banned bonuses for polluting water bosses and expect companies to follow both the letter and the spirit of the rules. We look forward to the outcome of [industry regulator] Ofwat’s review, which will assess if and how these rules should be strengthened.”The payment to Steve Buck was made at the end of last month, after Thames took legal advice over its obligations.The payment wasdrawn from a £3bn emergency debt packageagreed last year with creditors. That money is designed to keep Thames running while it tries to negotiate a longer-term takeover by its creditors, more than two years after its shareholders effectively walked away from the business.The River Action head of campaigns, Amy Fairman, said: “Thames Water is on the brink of financial collapse with a debt pile of £20bn, rivers in their region are drowning in sewage and 571m litres of water are lost every day. Yet there’s still £1m for a finance chief’s signing-on payment when over a quarter of Thames Water customer bills go to servicing debt.“Meanwhile, frontline staff are out around the clock holding this failing company together. It’s indefensible. Put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it to serve its customers, and clean up our rivers, not reward failure.”Cat Hobbs, the director of We Own It, a campaign group calling for nationalisation of the water industry, said: “The Thames Water saga is beyond a joke a this point – they are completely taking the mickey.“Andy Burnham must step in immediately and take back the company … the shareholders have walked away, and the debt can be drastically cut and refinanced more cheaply in public hands. It’s criminal to let this rip-off continue with 16 million households paying the price.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe payment to Buck, first reported by Sky News, was deferred from April 2025, when he joined Thames Water from Pennon Group, the owner of South West Water. Buck had worked at Anglian Water before that.The payment would come on top of total pay for Buck of £591,000 in the financial year to 31 March. That included a £491,000 base salary, as well as a £25,000 discretionary payment to “support his appointment and facilitate his timely onboarding, recognising costs incurred in connection with his recruitment”. However, the extra £1m payment was not detailed in Thames Water’s annual report, released last month.Buck’s base salary was also increased to £630,000 in April. The total pay of the chief executive, Chris Weston, for the year to 31 March rose to £1.2m.Thames last month disclosed it hadpaid £4.1m in bonuses for senior managers.Although retention payments paid to executives come from the emergency funding, from creditors rather than customer bills, executive pay is still understood to be a matter controlled directly by Thames Water’s remuneration committee.Thames Water and the creditor group declined to comment. The environment committee was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterExecutive pay and bonusesWater industryUtilitiesAndy BurnhamPublic services policyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: US intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’ | Germany | The Guardian
description: German government talks of a ‘new level of danger’ but declines to say who it thinks was responsible for device
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: German government talks of a ‘new level of danger’ but declines to say who it thinks was responsible for device
Content: A police officer in protective clothing in front of an explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig/Halle airport in Schkeuditz, Germany on 5 August.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersView image in fullscreenA police officer in protective clothing in front of an explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig/Halle airport in Schkeuditz, Germany on 5 August.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersGermanyUS intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’German government talks of a ‘new level of danger’ but declines to say who it thinks was responsible for deviceDeborah Colein BerlinMon 10 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican intelligence experts believe Russia was behind an attack on a German airport last week witha drone laden with explosives, US media have reported, as Berlin remained silent on the likely culprit.Last week’s security emergency prompted the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, to break off his summer holiday in Italy and rush to the scene in the eastern city of Leipzig, as he spoke of a“new level of danger”for Germany.Dobrindt called the incident, in which a quadcopter with semtex plastic explosives attached was found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at the major shipping and military hub, part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” by a well-equipped foreign actor.As the German investigators raced to identify the perpetrators, the tabloidBild reportedthat authorities had found DNA traces at the scene that matched a sample from a firebomb, posted via DHL, that exploded at Leipzig airport in July 2024.Five men suspected in a related series of mailed incendiary devices are on trial in Lithuania, where it emerged in court last weekthat the plane that was the target of the firebomb only avoided being set on fire in mid-flightbecause it was delayed. The suspects are alleged by Lithuanian prosecutors to have beenemployed by Russian intelligence.Even as MPs and security analystspointed the finger at the Kremlinover the latest incident in Leipzig, German government officials have not levelled a specific accusation against Moscow.The Wall Street Journal, however, hasquoted US officialsfamiliar with intelligence reports about the incident as saying that the drone probably belongs to the Russian government.CNN reported that Washington had concluded the drone came from a Russian secret service, citing a US defence official inEuropenoting the explosive material found on the drone suggested a military manufacturer.German officials said the drone managed to fly past Leipzig airport’s defences.It was only immobilised when an alert airport bus driver ferrying a group of late-night passengers spotted and reported it, an estimated four hours after it breached the facility’s security, averting what authorities have said could have been amultiple casualty event.The same night, a DHL cargo plane, which had been forced to abort its landing at the airport due to the discovery of the drone, then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere, with minor damage.Investigators now believe it hit a second hostile drone being flown that night.A day later, drones were detected above an army installation in western Germany housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems, whichUkrainehas often requested to help fend off Russia’s aerial bombardments.In response to the increased threat, the German interior ministry said on Monday it plans to double its federal team of anti-drone experts to 300, with the number of operational bases for the unit to rise to eight from four.Germany and other European countries have long reported suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies, and accused Russian agents of spying as well as atargeted campaign of sabotage, disruption and intimidation.Moscow has denied this, and late last week its embassy in Berlin called any suggestion it had a hand in the Leipzig case a “rashly contrived provocation” that “serves only the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political establishment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBerlin is Ukraine’s biggest national supplier of military aid in its defence against the Russian onslaught.Next month,Germanywill hold three pivotal elections in eastern states, where support for defence assistance for Kyiv is
