controversial among voters and fears of “provoking” Moscow run high.The pro-Russian far-rightAlternative für Deutschlandis poised to perform well in all three races, polls show, amidreports of Russian disinformationtargeted at its principal rivals, the mainstream democratic parties.The opposition Greens have criticised the government for not naming and blaming Russia at this stage of the Leipzig investigation.Political scientist Wolfgang Schröder of the University of Kassel in western Germany said two factors could be shaping Berlin’s restraint.Firstly, Russia had been named early on as a prime suspect behind the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, which German prosecutors now say wasordered by Ukrainian “state authorities”.More important, Schröder said, were the incalculable consequences of accusing Moscow of a botched military attack on German soil amidwarnings of an escalation in tensions.“If it were to be defined as an act of aggression – that is, a military attack by Russia against (Germany’s) critical infrastructure – then we would be on the brink of entering a state of war, and that would have implications not only of a diplomatic nature but also with regard to Nato,” he told local news broadcaster n-tv.“A cautious approach is being taken here, precisely because the aim is to prevent being drawn in, and that would mean turning this into a matter of European security – a matter of Nato security – and that would certainly take Germany’s involvement in the armed conflict between Russia and Ukraine to a whole new level.”Explore more on title: Boat operator faces federal charges after mother and infant killed in New York capsizing | New York | The Guardian
description: Sara Sanchez, 27, and her daughter died after a speedboat capsized in the New York Harbor over the weekend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sara Sanchez, 27, and her daughter died after a speedboat capsized in the New York Harbor over the weekend
Content: The vessel that capsized was pulled from the water and taken to the New York police department’s harbor unit facility on Randall’s Island.Photograph: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe vessel that capsized was pulled from the water and taken to the New York police department’s harbor unit facility on Randall’s Island.Photograph: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket/Getty ImagesNew YorkBoat operator faces federal charges after mother and infant killed in New York capsizingSara Sanchez, 27, and her daughter died after a speedboat capsized in the New York Harbor over the weekendAssociated PressMon 10 Aug 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe driver of a speedboat that capsized inNew YorkHarbor over the weekend, killing a 27-year-old woman and her infant daughter, was charged on Monday with causing their deaths through misconduct or neglect.Manuel Hernandez, 46, wiped his eyes with his hand as he arrived for his initial appearance in Manhattan federal court. He was not required to enter a plea and was released on bail.Sara Sanchez and her five-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, died after the 22-foot Yamaha speedboat overturned late Saturday near the Statue of Liberty. Twelve others were rescued and are in stable condition, authorities said.Captain charged after woman and her five-month-old die in New York boat capsizingRead moreThe vessel was pulled from the water and taken to the New York police department’s harbor unit facility on Randall’s Island.After state charges were lodged against Hernandez over the weekend, prosecutors said on Monday that he will be tried in federal court, not state court.Capt Doreen McCarthy, the coast guard sector New York commander, credited the rescue of survivors to “heroic, swift actions” by those who responded from various agencies, along with a good Samaritan vessel.Meanwhile, a GoFundMe campaign that began Sunday to help Andres Garcia pay for the funeral and other expenses for his partner, Sanchez, and their daughter had topped $25,000 by Monday afternoon.Antonio Russo, general manager at Il Punto Ristorante, said Garcia is an “amazing guy” who has been working long hours each week as a waiter, driver and food-runner, to provide for his family here and in Colombia.Diego Naranjo, a neighbor of Sanchez in Queens, said he first met her last spring when her son threw a ball into their back yard. After recovering the ball, Naranjo invited her son to play on a trampoline with his children.“They were really nice people. You can see when a person is noble,” Naranjo said.He said he last saw Sanchez last Tuesday as she brought groceries into her home. He said he was shocked by the deaths.Explore more on these topicsNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: US judge drops criminal charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani | US news | The Guardian
description: Justice department says it decided to abandon fraud and bribery case in which Adani Group has denied wrongdoing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Justice department says it decided to abandon fraud and bribery case in which Adani Group has denied wrongdoing
Content: Gautam Adani attends the 51st Gems and Jewellery awards in Jaipur, India, on 30 November 2024.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenGautam Adani attends the 51st Gems and Jewellery awards in Jaipur, India, on 30 November 2024.Photograph: ReutersUS newsUS judge drops criminal charges against Indian billionaire Gautam AdaniJustice department says it decided to abandon fraud and bribery case in which Adani Group has denied wrongdoingReutersMon 10 Aug 2026 15.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 16.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US judge on ⁠Monday dismissed criminal charges against the Indian ⁠billionaireGautam Adani, after ​the justice department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.The Brooklyn-based district judge Nicholas Garaufis’s decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare attempt to ⁠toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case. In November 2024, before ⁠the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest $10bn in the United States.Adani waschargedin 2024 with agreeing ​to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of ‌his Adani Group could win approval ‌to develop a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.Adani Group ‌has consistently denied wrongdoing. Adani himself has not appeared in US court to respond to the charges. On 18 May, the justice department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Donald Trump’s second term in the White House.Prosecutor fired over blogposts critical of Trump sues US justice departmentRead moreLegal experts say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish ‌to pursue, but the charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge’s approval.Garaufis asked the justice department to justify its decision to drop the charges, writing that its “bland and conclusory” announcement did ​not give him enough information.In a 4 July court filing, Trent McCotter, a senior justice department official, said the case was primarily foreign, hard to prove and inconsistent with the agency’s current priorities.In the filing, McCotter also denied as false what he called media stories suggesting he sought to dismiss the case in part because of a promise by Adani to ⁠invest money in the United States.In response, Garaufis asked Adani whether he was “aware of any agreement ​exchanging anything for the dismissal of ​the indictment”.In a sworn declaration filed in ​court on 15 July, Adani said he was not aware of any such agreement. He acknowledged ​having previously promised to invest $10bn in the US ​and said his lawyers told ​the justice department in meetings that the pledge “might be part of a resolution of these matters”. Robert Giuffra, a lawyer for Adani, said in a 15 July court filing that the justice department had told him that it would not consider the Adani Group’s willingness to invest in the US as part of any resolution.Explore more on these topicsUS newsAdani GroupIndiaTrump administrationLaw (US)New YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shots | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines
Content: Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APDonald TrumpTrump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shotsPresident and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccinesMelody SchreiberandJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 10 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).It is an attempt to undergird the changes made earlier this year to CDC vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House.The order would also require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US. And it would recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together.On a press call, a White House official said the order draws on a Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) scientific assessmentpublishedin January 2026, which examined “comparisons of the U.S. to other peer-developed nations” and looked at “where there is consensus amongst our peers on recommendations for immunizations for children”.The official said the number of recommended childhood immunizations would drop “down to 11 diseases”, compared with 18 at the end of 2024.Only six of the 17 vaccines currently routinely recommended for all children in the US would continue to have full recommendations: measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTaP), polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella.“Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the MMR vaccine at the signing of the order on Monday.Five other shots would be recommended only for those at high risk: monoclonal antibodies to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as well as vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal ACWY, which is currently recommended for teens and high-risk infants. Dengue and meningococcal B vaccines are also on this list, but dengue was already recommended only for those at risk and meningococcal B was shared clinical decision-making.And six shots would be pushed to shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19.This is a previously obscure category that means a provider would be required to weigh the risks and benefits, despite strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of these vaccines.On the call, the White House official said vaccines moved into this category “still are a recommendation, and so we assume that that means they’ll still be covered by insurance” and remain “available to parents that want them”, adding: “The president is interested in getting parents more choice and flexibility.”The executive order would also require the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, which is not currently possible in the US as there are no separately licensed vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella and the licensing process takes years.The order also states that, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. This would put a financial and logistical strain on families and medical providers by creating several additional visits.The US attorney general would also be tasked with challenging state laws that conflict with the executive order. The US has no vaccination mandates. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state and local level.Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the order signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two.“Today we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. That has to do with many subjects including autism in particular,” Trump said at the beginning of the order signing.“I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination where it looks like the size of a bottle of soda, poured into a little child’s body and bad things happen in too many cases,” Trump later said on breaking up each shot into an individual medical visit, before adding: “This is an explosion, it’s an epidemic,” in an apparent reference to autism.Kennedy claimed at one point: “Something happened in the mid-90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure.”On the call, officials were pressed on why Kennedy has not yet delivered the finding on the cause of autism he had promised by the previous September, and why the US president continued to suggest a vaccine-autism link without new supporting evidence from HHS. An official declined to engage directly, asking to keep the discussion “germane to today’s executive order” rather than address the broader autism-research timeline.Asked about criticism from the American Academy of Pediatrics that the administration invoked autism repeatedly during the signing without offering any concrete support for families already raising children with autism, an official pointed instead to a toolkit the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service released on applied behavior analysis services, framing it as guidance to help states serve autistic patients and curb fraud in relevant programs.Rebuking these claims and ties to autism, Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana senator,tweetedin response to the order that it “is so wrong”.“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy wrote.Executive orders are meant as guidance to federal agencies; they are not laws passed by Congress, and thus they have no legal effect on the public.The White House official estimated that 28 states “have implemented their own vaccine recommendations or diverged from the federal guidance”. The order is intended to ensure the remaining states “are aware of this information as they go into ... their legislative sessions”, they said, and weigh “what vaccine requirements they want to implement as law in their state, particularly ... school attendance and entry requirements”.“This should have no direct operational effects,” says Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco. Twenty-nine states and the District of Columbia have decoupled their vaccination requirements from the CDC, and insurance continues to cover the shots.However, “Trump has influence,” Reiss said, and the order may intensify “political pressure on states” to change school requirements.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS healthcareVaccines and immunisationHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Lewis managing director Peter Ruis quits job after less than three years | John Lewis | The Guardian
description: Surprise departure comes after department store chain’s chair warned of ‘really tough trading conditions’
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Surprise departure comes after department store chain’s chair warned of ‘really tough trading conditions’
Content: Peter Ruis had returned to John Lewis at the start of 2024 after leading retailers including Jigsaw and Anthropologie.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeter Ruis had returned to John Lewis at the start of 2024 after leading retailers including Jigsaw and Anthropologie.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianJohn LewisJohn Lewis managing director Peter Ruis quits job after less than three yearsSurprise departure comes after department store chain’s chair warned of ‘really tough trading conditions’Jasper JollyMon 10 Aug 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe managing director ofJohn Lewishas quit the job after less than three years in charge of the British department store chain, as the company faces “really tough” trading conditions.Peter Ruis will leave the business in order to “pursue new projects”, John Lewis said in a statement on Monday.He will be replaced by Will Kernan, a non-executive board member of the employee-owned John Lewis Partnership, which also runs the Waitrose supermarket chain. Kernan said in a statement that John Lewis still had “significant headroom for growth”.The surprise departure comes afterJohn Lewis’s chair, Jason Tarry, last week warned of “really tough” trading conditions in an interview with the company’s in-house magazine.John Lewis had felt confident enough in the economic outlook in March to pay its 69,000 workers – which it calls partners – anannual bonus for the first time in four yearsafter underlying profits rose. Staff shared a bonus pot of £35m, worth about one week’s extra pay each.However, the US-Israeli war on Iran has caused a rise in inflation as oil prices have soared. That has put shoppers under pressure and raised costs for retailers.Tarry indicated in the interview that “we have to adjust for an immediate future that we weren’t expecting even six months ago, let alone a couple of years ago”.Ruis had returned to John Lewis at the start of 2024, after leading retailers including Jigsaw and Anthropologie. During his previous nine-year stint Ruis was John Lewis’s buying and brand director.He oversaw investment in the 36 John Lewis department stores that remained after the companyclosed 16 during the coronavirus pandemic, and as recently as November he told the Guardian thathe was looking at expansion.View image in fullscreenPeter Ruis said the John Lewis business was ‘now on a much stronger footing’ after ‘nearly three years of significant investment and modernisation’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianRuis will stay in post until 6 September. Kernan, a non-executive director since 2023, will take over in the middle of September as the retailer prepares for its Christmas peak trading period. John Lewis has started a search for a new non-executive director.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKernan has previously served as chief executive of River Island, The White Company and the cycling shop Wiggle, and spent 13 years at New Look.Ruis said: “After nearly three years of significant investment and modernisation, the business is now on a much stronger footing. I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved, and there is so much more still to come.”Kernan said: “Having served on the partnership’s board for three years, I have a clear understanding of the John Lewis business and a huge appreciation for the partnership’s values and employee-ownership model. We have significant headroom for growth and I’m looking forward to leading the team to ensure John Lewis remains the country’s most trusted and loved retailer, in store and online.”Tarry said: “Peter has done a fantastic job and will be missed by all of our partners. He’s injected energy and pace into the John Lewis transformation and we are sad to see him go.”Separately, the Co-op Group on Monday announced that its chair, Debbie White, had decided to step down after two years that included steering the group, which runs convenience stores, insurance, legal services and funeral parlours,through a major cyber-attack.The senior independent director Moni Mannings was appointed as interim chair to oversee the hiring of a new permanent chief executive after theMarch departure of Shirine Khoury-Haqamid claims of a “toxic culture”. Khoury-Haq said colleagues had told her they did not recognise the criticisms, and she denied her departure was in relation to the allegations.Explore more on these topicsJohn LewisRetail industryInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Millions in Great Britain could face emergency power cuts at short notice | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Grid operator Neso can now respond with rolling blackouts as last resort without need for government powers
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Exclusive: Grid operator Neso can now respond with rolling blackouts as last resort without need for government powers
Content: Neso said rolling blackouts would be used only in ‘the most extreme and unlikely circumstances’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNeso said rolling blackouts would be used only in ‘the most extreme and unlikely circumstances’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesEnergy industryMillions in Great Britain could face emergency power cuts at short noticeExclusive: Grid operator Neso can now respond with rolling blackouts as last resort without need for government powersJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 07.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of households could face power cuts at short notice under new rules to help the electricity system operator avoid widespread blackouts when energy supplies run low.The changes, which come into effect this week, will make it easier for the national electricity system operator to call for rotating blackouts at short notice if power supplies are running short.It is also marks the first time the system operator can use large-scale power cuts to stabilise the grid without the need for emergency government powers.‘Risking blackouts’? How Great Britain’s grid operator was dragged into a political rowRead moreThe system operator could call for enough homes and businesses within a designated area to be disconnected to cut each block’s electricity use by more than a fifth with only eight hours’ notice, bringing rolling three-hour blackouts across the country to prevent the risk of total power system collapse.The changes to the grid codes – the technical rules covering the country’s transmission system – were quietly approved by the industry regulator late last month. They come only weeks after control room whistleblowers at the National Energy System Operator (Neso)accused senior leaders of trying to cover upthe risk of blackouts during the heatwave.A spokesperson for Neso said the “last-resort contingency measure” would be used only in “the most extreme and unlikely circumstances” and “after all other available options have been exhausted, helping protect the wider electricity system”.The power cuts would form the last line of defence against more severe and uncontrolled consequences of an electricity system collapse, such as those in Spain and Portugal last summer. In a worst-case scenario this could require between five and seven days for electricity to be completely restored.The new rules bridge the gap between the system operator’s existing powers to call for short-term power cuts affecting up to a fifth of electricity demand in each area, not used since the miners’ strikes in the 1970s, and the government’s more wide-reaching emergency powers designed for prolonged electricity disruptions.In a proposal submitted to the regulator, Neso said the new measures could “be used more flexibly, be initiated quicker” than the government’s emergency code, and it would be designed for “a shorter duration”.This could mean blackouts of up to three hours that would rotate across the country, to limit the impact on homes and businesses while the system operator’s control room manages a short-term supply squeeze. Meanwhile, a list of “protected sites” including hospitals, water treatment works and sites of national security interests would be exempt from any planned power cuts.The government’s electricity supply emergency code, which has never been invoked, can only be enacted by the energy secretary. It would initiate rolling blackouts affecting 90% of electricity users to manage a prolonged disruption – such as a large outage at a high-voltage power import cable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese powers are “not suited for short-notice use”, according to Ofgem, but the new protocol could provide the energy system operator with a tool that is similar in scope but that can be initiated “as quickly as possible” to respond to even short-lived supply squeezes – such as a particularly cold winter evening.The code change underlines the growing risk to the electricity system from short-term power system imbalances, which can be more difficult to predict in advance, rather than large-scale, longer-term outages or disruptions.The last resort measure joins a string of other measures that can be used to help the system cope with a shortfall of electricity, including disconnecting large industrial users and lowering the voltage of regional power grids.Lowering electricity voltage helps to reduce the amount of power used – just as tightening the sluice gate on a canal means water keeps flowing but at a lower volume and force. For households it can mean kettles take significantly longer to boil and phones take longer to charge, but there is little impact on data servers and industrial equipment.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnergy billsConsumer affairsHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harvey Nichols warns it could collapse without rescue deal, as bidders circle | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group is frontrunner to buy Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group is frontrunner to buy Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain
Content: Harvey Nichols’s department store headquarters in Knightsbridge opened in 1889.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarvey Nichols’s department store headquarters in Knightsbridge opened in 1889.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesRetail industryHarvey Nichols warns it could collapse without rescue deal, as bidders circleMike Ashley’s Frasers Group is frontrunner to buy Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chainCan Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Ab Fab again?Jasper JollyMon 10 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarvey Nichols has warned that it will not be able to survive another year without new investment, as bidders for the Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain circle.The retailer’s Hong Kong-based owner, Dickson Poon, put it up for sale in June, with Mike Ashley’sFrasers Groupaiming to buy it for about £40m.Harvey Nichols used to attract a high-profile clientele, including the late Diana, Princess of Wales, and its place in popular culture was confirmed in its 1990s heyday by the TV sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, which used the store as a symbol for luxury retail. Yet“Harvey Nicks” has struggled to adjustto increased competition from other shopping destinations, as well as the rise of online retail.Can Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Absolutely Fabulous again?Read moreThe company hasnot made a profit since the coronavirus pandemiclocked out big-spending foreign tourists, and it reported a loss after tax of £105m after writing off inter-company loans for the year to 29 March 2025, according to accounts published over the weekend.The directors warned that the company was not a going concern, because it would run out of money within the next year and that it had no agreements for new funding.The accounts said that the company had received “a number of bids” to buy it, and that it was hoping to complete a deal within the next year.FTSE 100 retailer Next had been interested in taking over the business, although it has withdrawn its interest, according to more recent reports.That has left Ashley, the founder of the Sports Direct retail empire, as one of the frontrunners. Ashley, the controlling shareholder in Frasers, on Friday told the Financial Times that Harvey Nichols was in a “death spiral” and that it would be a “huge challenge” to turn it around.Ashley hasbought a series of struggling premium brandsin recent years after starting out with a single sports shop. He said he would keep the Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand other stores as House of Fraser or Flannels under his Frasers Group.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarvey Nichols was founded in 1831, as a linen shop. Its department store headquarters in Knightsbridge opened in 1889. In the last century it has been owned by Debenhams and the Burton Group, before Poon bought it in 1991 for £53m.Poon oversaw an expansion outsideLondon, with a Leeds branch opening in 1996. The chain has shops in Birmingham, Bristol, Dublin, Edinburgh and Manchester, as well as a series of restaurants including the one in London’s riverside Oxo Tower. Outside the UK it has stores in Riyadh, Dubai, Hong Kong and Kuwait.Poon retired as a director in May. Harvey Nichols is led by Julia Goddard, who joined in 2024 from Alexander McQueen.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFrasers GroupMike AshleyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK manufacturers face rising hacking risk as survey shows 30% were hit last year | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack
Content: Some generative AI systems have hacked into other businesses autonomously.Photograph: solarseven/GettyView image in fullscreenSome generative AI systems have hacked into other businesses autonomously.Photograph: solarseven/GettyCybercrimeUK manufacturers face rising hacking risk as survey shows 30% were hit last yearBig companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attackJasper JollyMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly a third of British manufacturers have been hit by a cyber-attack on them or a company in their supply chain, according to a survey that highlighted the growing hacking risk to companies.The findings come almost a year after Britain’s largest automotive employer,JLR, was hit by an attackthat forced it to halt production for weeks.The report by MakeUK, a lobby group for British manufacturers, found that 30% of manufacturers had experienced a cyber-incident in the past 12 months, leading in many cases to lost production time and increased costs. However, only half had a plan in place to respond to an attack.The risk of attacks has risen in recent years as hackers,often backed by hostile states, have become more numerous and more adept at penetrating company defences. Large businesses describe being under near-constant attack from people trying to access their systems, and the UK government has said cybercrime costs the economy £14.7bn a year. The rise of generative AI systems, some of which have been able tohack into other businesses autonomously, has added extra urgency to efforts to upgrade defences.Manufacturers have sought to improve productivity by connecting their factories, allowing them much quicker insight into their operations. However, the larger number of links has also meant that once attackers are inside the system, the scope for harm is much larger. JLR was forced to shut down systems across all its factories, offices and retail operations after it discovered digital intruders on the last day of August last year.The independent Cyber Monitoring Centre said the JLR hackcost the UK economy at least £1.9bn, probably making it the most expensive cyber incident ever in Britain, mainly because of lost output at JLR and its suppliers. The New York Times reported in June that British law enforcement had concluded that Russian hackers were behind it.Other big attacks reported publicly in recent years include two FTSE 100 manufacturers who reported attacks within days of each other early in 2025: the valve maker IMI and the components maker Smiths Group. In the retail sector,Marks & Spencer,the Co-opandHarrodsall suffered costly breaches last year.Jonathon Ellison, director of national resilience at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which was involved in the response to the JLR attack, said: “In today’s landscape, no manufacturer can afford to treat cybersecurity as anything other than a business-critical priority. The NCSC is working to help organisations of all sizes strengthen their cyber defences.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmong companies affected by a cyber-attack on their supply chain, about 30% of 123 manufacturers surveyed said they had suffered delays of deliveries to customers or output cuts, and almost a quarter reported supplier delivery delays or shortages of components and materials.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeManufacturing sectorHackingAI (artificial intelligence)Jaguar Land RoverComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘For this record, I took an edible and said, screw it’: jazz pianist Sullivan Fortner on confronting the trauma of Hurricane Katrina | Jazz | The Guardian
description: The New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivors
Author: Hugh Morris
Headline: The New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivors
Content: Finding his keys … Sullivan Fortner (centre) with drummer Kayvon Gordon (left) and bassist Tyrone Allen.Photograph: Youri LenquetteView image in fullscreenFinding his keys … Sullivan Fortner (centre) with drummer Kayvon Gordon (left) and bassist Tyrone Allen.Photograph: Youri LenquetteJazzInterview‘For this record, I took an edible and said, screw it’: jazz pianist Sullivan Fortner on confronting the trauma of Hurricane KatrinaHugh MorrisThe New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivorsMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Black music is forwardandupward in movement, you know? Never forwardorupward,” pianist Sullivan Fortner declares. “It’s a tornado that’s always getting bigger and moving faster,” he adds, whizzing his fingers around with delight.On a video call between sets at Rotterdam’sNorth Sea jazz festival, the 39-year-old speaks like he plays, with quirkiness, subtlety and mischief. A three-time Grammy winner – including for 2025’s Southern Nights – Fortner also recently received the Larry J Bell award, a prize of $300,000 (£225,000) given every four years to a standout jazz pianist, which gave him the confidence to present an all-encompassing version of himself on Leave That in There, his sixth album. “I’ve tried the self-editing way,” he says of previous albums involving multiple takes and endless post-production tinkering. “For this record, I took an edible and I just said, screw it.”Fortner’s sweep is wide and idiosyncratic. On album opener Sugarcane, Kayvon Gordon’s criss-crossing bàtá drumming helps root the record in Louisiana’s history as a centre for the sugar trade, the “white gold” extracted by slave labour that made the area one of the richest in the 19th-century US. But the record travels: through Latin acoustic piano, journeying Hammond organ lines, Thelonious Monk tributes and whirling Moog synths, it ends with Fortner singing a wordless, Stevie Wonder-like hymn to a late friend, Linda Payne.Leave That in There is also rooted in 2005’s Hurricane Katrina, which devastated New Orleans, Louisiana’s biggest city, where Fortner grew up. The album takes its title from a moment in Spike Lee’sWhen the Levees Broke: A Requiem in Four Acts, the epic 2006 documentary that underlined just how much the US failed New Orleans during and after the disaster.Lee relays events with a brutal fury. Dead bodies float face down in flooded boulevards; out of the water pokes a sign for Humanity Street. But Fortner’s title derives from a more understated moment. A woman exits her car, and when she’s told she’s left her purse behind, she tersely replies: “Leave that in there.”Fortner evolves her words into an artistic manifesto against self-censorship. “Music to me is a kind of a place of safety, where anything can happen,” he says. “Rather than saying, ‘OK, these are the things that I’m going to hide,’ it’s more a case of, ‘these are the things I want to keep with me.’”View image in fullscreen‘A place of safety’ … Sullivan Fortner at Newport jazz festival in 2022.Photograph: Douglas Mason/Getty ImagesFortner was 18, and preparing for another year at Ohio’s Oberlin Conservatory, when he got a phone call from a fellow New Orleanian student who told him their city was under water. Fortner shrugged – the area floods regularly – but his friend persevered and Fortner rushed to his dorm. “I turn on CNN, and the first thing I see, in a panning shot of the Convention Center, is my girlfriend and her mother waiting on buses to show up.” Phone lines and emails were down. “So I was panicking. Finally, I got a phone call from my sister, and it lasted like five seconds.” The call cut off, but she confirmed her family were safe, evacuated to nearby Baton Rouge; his girlfriend’s family, meanwhile, were bussed seven hours to Arkansas.Two tracks – A Poignant Time, and Another Poignant Time – reference a Wynton Marsalis quote from the documentary: “I think that this is a great moment in American history, because in this moment we see a lot of what’s wrong with us.” Lee’s film particularly emphasises the debilitating impact of Katrina’s aftermath: of denied insurance claims, substandard accommodation, and sluggishness by federal disaster agency Fema. “People are still dealing with the trauma of that time, even now,” Fortner says. “Not just through people losing their homes, but their mental and physical health – still dealing with grief.”“But it also showed the resilience of the people,” he adds. “There was still that crop of people that’s just like, ‘I’m coming back. This is my city. I ain’t going anywhere.’” His family – an oil rigger dad (“gone basically half the year”) and a mother who was “everything to us” – remained, a half-hour drive from the city centre. For his family, “singing is kind of our love language,” he says. There are around 40 singers among his relatives, and he’s working on an album featuring all of them.His formative musical experiences came with them in the church, but a flash of inspiration came, aged 11, through local organist Ronald Markham. “He got on the organ and started playing Bach.” Fortner had never heard anything like it. “He said, ‘man, it’s classical music.’ Then he goes and plays Latin, then gives me a 30-second demonstration of all these different genres. I didn’t know anything about any type of music other than gospel. But he had the key, and opened the door to this world I’m in now.”View image in fullscreen‘A statement of the moment’ … Fortner at work in the studio.Photograph: Artwork RecordsMarkham suggested he attend theNew OrleansCenter for Creative Arts. In his year were other musicians who have also become Grammy mainstays: Chief Adjuah, Trombone Shorty and Jon Batiste. Later, in New York, Batiste double-booked himself, meaning Fortner filled in on piano with legendary trumpeter Roy Hargrove.While in Hargrove’s band, Fortner began studying with another legend, pianist Fred Hersch. Fortner would turn up to lessons having practised tunes during the week. “Fred’d be like, ‘No, you prepared that, that was a drag. Just play something for me, and then we’ll go from there.’” The trust in intuition that Hersch impressed on Fortner would become among his biggest strengths.‘He used the trumpet as a songbird’: 100 years of Miles Davis, by jazz greats Sonny Rollins, Yazz Ahmed and moreRead moreFor all the power of the albums Fortner has recorded since, his most characterful work today is arguably with US singer Cécile McLorin Salvant. In rough sketches posted to social media, they sit down, hit record and play through Sting, Noël Coward or upturned Great American Songbook tunes. The performances embody a looseness that defines Fortner’s work: always moving forward and upward, never hemmed in. “Just because it’s permanent, doesn’t mean it has to be precious,” he says. Recording, whether in a studio or on Instagram, “is just a statement in the moment: of how we feel and where we’re going.”Leave That in There is released 28 August via Artwork RecordsExplore more on these topicsJazzHurricane KatrinaNew OrleansfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This Is Ballroom review – pulsating documentary tells story of Brazilian ballroom | Movies | The Guardian
description: Paris is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tension
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Paris is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tension
Content: This Is BallroomPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenThis Is BallroomPhotograph: PRMoviesReviewThis Is Ballroom review – pulsating documentary tells story of Brazilian ballroomParis is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tensionPhuong LeMon 10 Aug 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOriginating among the Black, Latin and trans communities in 1960s New York, queer ballroom culture has not only entered the mainstream but also travelled well outside the United States. In recent years, a movement has flourished in the Brazilian city ofRio de Janeiroand its outskirts, an evolution intimately captured in Juru and Vitã’s documentary debut. Here fly-on-the-wall recordings of a typical ball are interwoven with slice-of-life interviews, elaborating on the communal ties that extend beyond the dancefloor.A whirl of pulsating beats, fabulous fits and gyrating bodies, the sensory opening gives us a taste of the different categories attached to the ball. Competing on behalf of their “houses” – queer chosen families of like-minded individuals – the participants show off their voguing, dancing and posing skills, all with the hope of snatching the top trophies. For those who have seen seminal ballroom documentary Paris is Burning (1990), many of these categories – such as Runway, Face and Femme Queens – will sound familiar. In addition to its US influences, Brazilian ballroom is also flavoured with local culture: some categories draw on samba and other forms of afro-Brazilian music, a deliberate nod to the Black pioneers of the scene.These grounding details provide crucial regional contexts in the film but are a little too far and few in between. Still, as active ballroom members, Vitã and Juru have a rare insider point of view that distinguishes their work from other films on the same subject. With bracing honesty, the Brazilian ballroom scene is portrayed as a space of both solidarity and tension. When, for example, a ball is suddenly disrupted by a fight between members of feuding houses, the difficult moment is not swept under the carpet but prominently dissected to highlight the exclusion faced by performers who don’t conform to binaries of masculine and feminine presentation. Instead of simplistic hagiography, This is Ballroom is a film that calls for more tolerance and accountability, even within this niche subculture.This Is Ballroom is on True Story from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsLGBTQ+ rightsDanceRio de JaneiroBrazilAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: RL Stine’s Pumpkinhead review – horror from Goosebumps writer has kid confined inside large fruit | Movies | The Guardian
description: Based on a short story by the Goosebumps author, this derivative but tautly plotted tale over-relies on Scooby-Doo-style sleuthery, and its truly unsettling turn comes too late
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Based on a short story by the Goosebumps author, this derivative but tautly plotted tale over-relies on Scooby-Doo-style sleuthery, and its truly unsettling turn comes too late
Content: ‘Shot in sunny Netflixese’ … Adeline Lo and Bean Reid and Adeline Lo in RL Stine’s Pumpkinhead.Photograph: Luka CyprianView image in fullscreen‘Shot in sunny Netflixese’ … Adeline Lo and Bean Reid and Adeline Lo in RL Stine’s Pumpkinhead.Photograph: Luka CyprianMoviesReviewRL Stine’s Pumpkinhead review – horror from Goosebumps writer has kid confined inside large fruitBased on a short story by the Goosebumps author, this derivative but tautly plotted tale over-relies on Scooby-Doo-style sleuthery, and its truly unsettling turn comes too latePhil HoadMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdapted from a 1999 short story by Goosebumps’RL Stine, this kid-proofed piece of midwestern folk horror borrows merrily from The Wicker Man, Stephen King and Tim Burton. Rattling those influences around in its horn of plenty, it rigs up a taut enough plotline about a New York family arriving in the suspiciously fecund farming outpost of Redhaven. But, even given the horror-lite nature of the enterprise, it doesn’t stake out sufficient fresh territory of its own – until it’s too late.Snotty skate rat Sam (Bean Reid) moves to Redhaven with his mum, Cassie, (Kendra Anderson) and older brother Finn (Seth Isaac Johnson) where, hitting the local harvest festival, they learn that ornery Farmer Palmer (Kevin McNulty) is the one responsible for miraculously wringing out fresh bounty from the town’s once-blighted fields. Vexed at finding himself in the sticks, Sam decides to steal Palmer’s prize pumpkin – but when Finn returns it, he is magically trapped inside. All the adults seem to forget Finn ever existed, leaving Sam until midnight on Halloween to break the curse.As Sam infiltrates Palmer’s house with new pal Becka (Adeline Lo) in search of an ancient grimoire, this is boilerplate Scooby-Dooish sleuthery. The horror elements (the pustulant, soul-sucking pumpkin, a chittering slasher scarecrow prowling the cornfields) are just scary enough, with any lingering unease quickly dispelled by a nice line in pre-emptive self-awareness. Matty Finochio chalks up points as the resident “forest hermit”, irate at the tween investigators for constantly interrupting his creepy exposition.Shot by writer-director Jem Garrard in sunny Netflixese, it is peppily handled by the child performers, though McNulty is too anaemic as the pumpkin patriarch. It feels too straightforward and amiable – until, that is, a final twist that really is unsettling, without any direct threat, gore or gothic trappings involved. It’s an interesting comeuppance for the wannabe independent Sam – but you might want to check your kids’ tolerance for psychological violence.RL Stine’s Pumpkinhead is available on digital platforms from 17 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsThrillersComedy filmsRL StineFilm adaptationsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I am left grinning’: why The Dish is my feelgood movie | Sam Neill | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers picking their most loved comfort films is a 2000 Australian gem featuring the late Sam Neill
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers picking their most loved comfort films is a 2000 Australian gem featuring the late Sam Neill
Content: A still from The Dish.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from The Dish.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMy feelgood movieSam Neill‘I am left grinning’: why The Dish is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers picking their most loved comfort films is a 2000 Australian gem featuring the late Sam NeillJonathan WilkesMon 10 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the shock of Sam Neill’s death, I was surprised just how hard the news hit me. I don’t usually take a celebrity death so deeply to heart and yet here I was struggling to stem the weeping. There is no denying he holds a special place in my movie-watching life: he’s Dr Alan Grant from Jurassic Park, for goodness sake. I first saw the Spielbergian masterpiece at the age of five and Neill’s passionate, intelligent and empathetic scientist was the coolest hero my young mind could hope for (when it wasn’t overwhelmed with terror).‘A gentle poetry in the everyday’: why The Straight Story is my feelgood movieRead moreThen, in my early teens, I got introduced to another hero role of Neill’s, the equally passionate, intelligent and empathetic scientist Cliff Buxton, from The Dish. Directed by Rob Sitch, the 2000 based-on-a-true-story drama is a warm hug and a joke from a dear friend. It has a sharp and silly script that belies its charmingly gentle demeanour and it’s about the 1969 moon landing, which has always had the power to get me emotional at the utterance of “One small step …”Rather than Houston, the setting is the Parkes observatory in Australia, a towering radio telescope plonked in a sheep paddock. Neill’s pipe-smoking Cliff leads a small team – Glenn (Tom Long), a brilliant but adorably awkward mathematician; the proper Aussie bloke in charge of moving the titular dish, Mitch (Kevin Harrington); and the Nasa man in his horn-rims, Al (Patrick Warburton) – as they track Apollo 11 and prepare to relay the television signals to the world.While somewhat ragtag-looking, with a habit of playing cricket in the bowl of the telescope, they are a professional unit. (Mitch exclaims as much before hitting a six.) I could spend the whole movie in their company as they expertly navigate their work or chat, tease and bicker, accompanied with sweeping shots of the observatory bathed in sunlight. Combine that with the whirring of hydraulics, flicking of switches in the control room, Classical Gas by Mason Williams on the soundtrack and soaring flourishes from Edmund Choi’s score, and I am soothed by this audio and visual balm.That, however, is not doing justice to how funny The Dish is. Laughs come thick and fast as we jump, sketch-show-esque, from the “boys at the dish” to a colourful ensemble of characters in the town of Parkes, thrust into the limelight by their tangential involvement in Apollo 11.One moment men are euphemistically discussing how astronauts go to the toilet using a series of whistles; the next a band has failed to learn the American anthem so plumps for the Hawaii Five-O theme; then over to the dish’s over-officious security guard worrying that his mother will confiscate his Nasa-issued revolver. Bumbling his way through it all (and accidentally calling his wife “the lemon” on account of her yellow dress) is Parkes’s mayor, Bob, impossible not to love thanks to a standout performance by Roy Billing.For me, The Dish is as quotable as Airplane!, Young Frankenstein and the criminally under-seen What’s Up Doc? Growing up with three older sisters, I got to watch many movies before I should have – I mentioned Jurassic Park at five, in the cinema no less – and we’d regale each other with our favourite lines. “You’ve just bullshitted Nasa” in our best Aussie accent was a regular. Ever since my eldest sister died a few years ago, The Dish will always allow me to relive the time I made her snort by mimicking Glenn when, getting a joke far too late, lets out a shriek and mutters the punchline: “Carrier pigeon.”Only now, though, do I come to the true magic of The Dish: how the humour gives way to unashamed sentimentality. If Neill is the beating heart – having lost his wife a year earlier, Cliff’s determined and avuncular strength provide the most poignancy – then the spine comes from archival footage of the Apollo 11 mission peppered throughout. It’s as if we’re there in July 1969 watching the television or listening to the radio alongside the awestruck faces of Parkes. On reaching the finale of the moon walk, the significance of this world event is captured beautifully.This utmost earnestness for the subject matter without taking itself seriously is a blend that I find irresistible about The Dish. So when it ends with the words of President Nixon to the Apollo 11 crew – “For one priceless moment in the history of man, all the people on this Earth are truly one” – and Wings of an Eagle by Russell Morris taking us into the credits, I am left grinning, watery-eyed and wondering when humanity will feel that way again. No pressure, Artemis.The Dish is available to watch on HBO Max and Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsSam NeillMy feelgood movieComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ancestral Visions of the Future review – visceral cine-memoir is a haunting return to Lesotho | Movies | The Guardian
description: Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese pairs his literary-grade voiceover with propulsive, prophetic images to interrogate his identity and that of his colonialism-carved homeland
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese pairs his literary-grade voiceover with propulsive, prophetic images to interrogate his identity and that of his colonialism-carved homeland
Content: Ecstatic and pained mysticism … Ancestral Visions of the Future.Photograph: Agat FilmsView image in fullscreenEcstatic and pained mysticism … Ancestral Visions of the Future.Photograph: Agat FilmsMoviesReviewAncestral Visions of the Future review – visceral cine-memoir is a haunting return to LesothoLemohang Jeremiah Mosese pairs his literary-grade voiceover with propulsive, prophetic images to interrogate his identity and that of his colonialism-carved homelandPhil HoadMon 10 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a captivating stream of consciousness film about exile, roots and identity by Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese, director of thelauded 2019 activism story This Is Not a Burial, It’s a Resurrection. It’s ostensibly a cine-memoir looking back from the vantage point of present-day Berlin to his upbringing in Lesotho, narrated by Mosese’s dense, literary-grade voiceover. But there’s something propulsive and prophetic about the accompanying hyper-vivid images from rural and urban life. This is something more than memory.The title screen dedication is ambiguous: “This film is an ode to cinema, an eternal no to my mother.” Reneging on the title of another 2019 work, Mother, I Am Suffocating. This Is My Last Film About You, she is central to Mosese’s attempt to return to the source. Her aspirations are to keep her family well-dressed and out of poverty, carry them away from the grind of rural fields that “ask not for rain, but for blood”, and see them installed in an ever-expanding house in the city (presumably Maseru).Ancestral Visions of the Future touches peripherally on colonialism, the hand that shaped this landscape. Perhaps the roll of red fabric that extends down the hillsides is meant to evoke the scalpel that carved up the country “like meat on the map”. Instead of a linear perspective, Mosese proposes an African conception of time as a cycle – and lets it erupt in bursts of ecstatic and pained mysticism. After a sequence of endless toil on the furrows, an old farmer plucks out his own eyes and plants them. The young boy alongside him harvests the crop, “allowing him to see everything”.Mosese’s vision clouds in the face of cyclical urban forces. He recounts his failed career as a street switchblade thug, then the tragedy of a woman burned alive by a lynch mob when her baby unknowingly “shoplifted” an item. Seen baying like a wildcat in front of invisible foes, she appears to be another sacrificial victim in an eternally recurring drama of violence and victimisation. More inspirational is the example of Sobo, a martial artist, herbalist and puppeteer he meets in Maseru in later life, who can see “not the city as it is, but the city as it is becoming”.Mosese seems to be seeking the same visionary capacity – and maybe something more: perhaps redemption, forLesotho, or himself? Or even, guided by the unfiltered energies here, direction towards a kind of rejuvenation. Whatever the exact meaning, this intense homecoming leaves a scorched trail in its wake.Ancestral Visions of the Future is on Mubi from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsLesothoAfricareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Overmono review – irresistible dance duo swap club intimacy for well-earned spectacle | Dance music | The Guardian
description: Playing their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environment
Author: Dan Hancox
Headline: Playing their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environment
Content: Anthemic, big-room sound … Overmono at Old Royal Naval College in GreenwichView image in fullscreenAnthemic, big-room sound … Overmono at Old Royal Naval College in GreenwichDance musicReviewOvermono review – irresistible dance duo swap club intimacy for well-earned spectacleOld Royal Naval College, LondonPlaying their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environmentDan HancoxMon 10 Aug 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the age of shortform video supremacy, there has been a great deal of angst about theauthenticclub music experience being rendered a vapid spectacle. Stop expecting DJs to be social media stars, put your phones away on the dancefloor, close your eyes and lose yourself in the beats, goes the revanchist wisdom.It’s understandable, but worries about superstar DJs stomping on the face of the pure rave experience are almost 30 years old now. It is decades since the Prodigy, Chemicals, Orbital and Fatboy Slim lit up festival stages and the charts. And anyway, spectacles can be fun – and funny – and so can dance music.The grounds of Christopher Wren’s Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich – a Unesco World Heritage Site, no less – are an unarguably comical setting for Welsh duo Overmono’s biggest headline gig to date, and brothers Tom and Ed Russell are fit for the part, and the party, celebrating the release of their second album with lasers dancing on the baroque towers and colonnades.But even with Overmono’s anthemic, big-room sound, their grandstanding rave melodies, skippy drums and sweet, chopped-up garage vocals, translating the intimacy of the club to the big outdoor stage is tricky. The sound is clear as a bell but not quite loud enough, and at times the crowd seem to be hungering for bigger drops: some of the drums are simply too quiet to fully fill the space.But the Russells are bouncing around merrily on a gorgeous warm evening, and it’s hard to begrudge them the moment, after a speedy rise to the Radio 1 dance mainstream. A few tracks pick the energy up. Freedom 2, their deadly 2023 collaboration with Joy Orbison and driller Kwengface, brings a welcome extra layer of momentum – and some much needed low-end bass rumble.Another point of difference arrives when they are joined by beat poet John Joseph Holt for new track Knight in Shining Prada, the extra physical stage presence of a frontman helping the driving synths carry further. Their remix of the Streets’ Turn the Page renders it more cinematic and emo than Mike Skinner’s original and likewise lights up the crowd, and leads us into the feelgood finale, their anthem Good Lies, its irresistible chorus bouncing off the Grade I-listed windows.Explore more on these topicsDance musicElectronic musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering critic | John Berger | The Guardian
description: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of Seeing
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of Seeing
Content: John Berger in 2009.Photograph: Franck Courtes/CAMERA PRESS/Agence VUView image in fullscreenJohn Berger in 2009.Photograph: Franck Courtes/CAMERA PRESS/Agence VUBook of the dayJohn BergerReviewJohn Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering criticThis multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of SeeingXan BrooksMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cultural criticJohn Bergerwas still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting the wild stories behind them. When Overton sought permission to write Berger’s biography, though, the critic insisted that he wait a few years. Death changes the relationship between the writer and his subject. More often than not, it complicates and enriches it. Berger – who spent much of his career in passionate conversation with the past – probably knew that better than anyone.Berger typically described himself as a storyteller, an elastic job title which allowed him to swing between fiction and poetry, essays and screenplays. Implicitly, too, the term helped frame his criticism as something propulsive and inclusive, an invitation to dance as opposed to a judgment from on high. Berger had no time for the “great man” theory of art as espoused by the popular historian Kenneth Clark and instead urged his audience to view each piece as a manifestation of society and politics: the tainted fruit of capitalism, inseparable from the marketplace. Oil paintings were status symbols. Nudes were the product of the lusty male gaze. Looking itself was a political act. “You cannot reply to me,” he would tell 1970s TV viewers, breaking the fourth wall to highlight the medium’s limitations. He liked pointing out the mechanics behind the manufacture of art, demystifying the process to better appreciate its results.These days Berger’s reputation largely rests on Ways of Seeing, the insurrectionist 1972 BBC series which made him the critics’ equivalent of a rock star or cult leader. Enterprising viewers can still find him on YouTube. He’s the eloquent firebrand with a messianic gleam in his eye; the Marxist intellectual in open-necked patterned shirts. Overton, though, is at pains to stitch Ways of Seeing into its wider context – showing it as part of a continuum, one political project among many. His exuberant biography is thick with detail and lit by wonder. It strains to paint the whole canvas and give us the man in full, warts and all.double quotation markWe never look at just one thing. We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselvesJohn BergerRaised in London, a child of the blitz, Berger suffered through boarding school and the army before a visit to a Picasso exhibition knocked the scales from his eyes and blew up his middle-class world. He enjoyed moderate success with his paintings and greater acclaim for his novels (one of which – the fractured, sporadically fabulous G – won the 1972 Booker prize). But he was at his most assured and compelling when using the art of others as a springboard to further, deeper inquiry. Berger regarded each work as a portal between time and space and was enthralled by the ways it could be lost and found in translation. Tellingly, his first broadcasting gig was with the BBC World Service, describing pictures in the National Gallery to listeners in west Africa.“We never look at just one thing,” he said. “We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.” That’s certainly the case with John Berger: From Life. Overton is fascinated by Berger but also fascinated by his relationship with Berger and his approach is therefore unashamedly subjective, sliding from the familial third-person (always “John”, never “Berger”) to the direct address (“You”) and between the past and present tense (sometimes in the space of a single sentence). Like Berger in his TV studio, Overton points out the wires, referring to “the book you’re reading now” and “the old man who squats on my pages” and occasionally fretting that he’s left out important information. It’s an elaborate conceit, but it by and large works. There is no single version of a story, Berger argued. Each storyteller can’t help but bend the tale to their will.Overton reveres Berger but he is frustrated by him, too. His life’s a hot mess; his very presence turns oppressive. He’s so authoritative on the page and so contradictory in the wild, a jumble of red-blooded Marxism and High Tory traditionalism. Berger writes elegantly and angrily about forced migration, mourning the loss of the old rural communities, but he lives as a self-imposed exile in Switzerland and France, splitting his time between different houses and women. Language, he concludes, is “potentially the only real human home”, but even this isn’t fixed; it can be breached at any time. By the end of his life, Overton notes, the man’s spoken English has taken on the grammatical patterns of French.Berger’s health was already starting to fail when he donated his boxes to the British Library. Overton recalls their queasy close-quarter encounters in London and Paris: “Strong smell of leaky prostate, top-note of cigarettes and event wine.” Berger in the flesh is diminished, disappointing, “less present here than you are in the archive”, which is probably the case with most ageing artists. They’ve put the best of themselves on the canvas, page or screen. That’s where we’ll find them – in their work, in the past.If there was a bright running thread through Berger’s portmanteau career, it was this preoccupation with the past and its connection to the present. The dead and the living are interdependent, he said. The stronger the link, the happier and healthier the society. Great paintings in a gallery allow us to travel in time. So too do some people, if they are skilled and sensitive enough. Berger’s 1967 book A Fortunate Man paid gorgeous tribute to Dr John Sassall, a country physician from the Forest of Dean whose work at times bordered on the supernatural. “The doctor,” Berger wrote, “is the familiar of death … the living intermediary between us and the multitudinous dead.” He might just as easily be talking about the role of great artists and critics. Possibly British Library curators as well.“Do biographers always remake their subject in their own image?” Overton wonders as he sets about trying to transfer Berger to the page. Most likely they do, but that’s only half of the equation. The past whispers to the present; the dead and living coexist. Overton is a writer in part because of reading John Berger. The biographer’s prose style is his own but he writes in the same spirit – fired by curiosity and close-marking his subject; gesturing out to the reader as though to engage them in debate. His aim, he confesses, is to convince us that the critic is “sat across the page from me, reading every word, a part of the process,” and in fits and spurts he achieves just that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTechnically Berger’s no longer with us: he died in 2017 at the age of 90. But he’s still speaking on YouTube, still being reprinted and still provoking and inspiring a fresh generation of writers. That’s the kind of community and continuity that he always hungered for in his life; sweet karmic payback for a career in the arts. Switch sides, reset and keep the conversation flowing. Berger once spoke to the past from the present. Now, as if by magic, it is the other way around.John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton is published by Allen Lane (£25). title: Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazz | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey
Author: Lara Pawson
Headline: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey
Content: Tracking the dreams of dogs… Is Beauty Good.Photograph: Images say more about me than words./Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTracking the dreams of dogs… Is Beauty Good.Photograph: Images say more about me than words./Getty ImagesFictionReviewIs Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazzCombining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journeyLara PawsonMon 10 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘But after all, writing is nothing more than a guided dream,” wrote Jorge Luis Borges. Dreams and dreaming are fertile concerns for Rosalind Belben, too. Her fourth book, originally published in 1979 andreissued last year, was titled Dreaming of Dead People. It was followed, a decade later, by Is Beauty Good. Now available in a new edition from the Sheffield indie And Other Stories, this eccentric polyphonic novel contains dozens of considerations of dreams, including dogs’ dreams and horses’ dreams as well as human beings’. Yet what makes it extraordinary is Belben’s ability to capture in words the slippery state that is neither dreaming nor sleeping nor waking, but somewhere in the edgelands between all three.“I fall awake and think, I want to go home. But there is no home.” So begins the chapter entitled Exile, a deliciously elusive story that is, most of the time at least, narrated in the first person by someone who is probably a woman, “a grizzled, cropped person”, and probably quite old and alone. They might be travelling through mountains somewhere, perhaps on a bus. They aren’t sure: “I am quite lost, wherever I am. I want to surrender. I wish to retire. I am tired.” Swishing about are uncertain memories of a childhood “shrouded” in nightmares: there was an orchard with an abundance of flora and fauna, and larks and swallows and “swifts to scream”. Like the author, the narrator was “born in the mud month” of February, and longs to disappear into marshlands to “be touched and stroked by plants”. But Belben never lets us rest in one place for long. Slipping in and out of sleep, “suffering glimpses”, the narrator stares at “a pink and blue angel” in the plaster of the wall. Which wall, you wonder, and how did we get here? This is the lure of Belben’s hypnagogia, the dizzying space into which she writes.double quotation markBelben is obsessed with the loss of the natural world, with human folly and with challenging the idea of beautyDivided into three sections – The Insatiable Wheel, Peacock Island, and The Great White Worm – Is Beauty Good comprises 30 vignettes, some just a single page, the longest running to nine. With intriguing titles including Peeing for Cynthia, Deaf Eggs, and Hands, each little chapter tells its own weird tale. Some loop into others with nods to earlier characters, narrators and locations, but what holds them together and thrusts the book forward are Belben’s obsessions with the loss of the natural world, with human folly and, as the title makes plain, with challenging the idea of beauty.As other critics have noted, her work is undeniably strange. It won’t suit everyone. But for those of us who delight in the uncompromising quality of free jazz, Is Beauty Good is its literary equivalent. It is not simply that Belben defies convention by denying the certainty of interrogation in the book’s title, for example; or by excluding letters from some words some of the time – “you’re nevr up to much once you’ve been gassd” – or by taking more formal risks such as ending the chapter Raining Down Dung halfway through a sentence (“but chocolate and raspberry would put some iron into me, thanks very much, they spoon it into ancient folk who have no teeth and reckon”). What makes an encounter with her writing so exhilarating is its undiluted commitment to the author’s singular spirit.Along the way, much is said about dying, deafness, desolation, depression, dogs, deckchairs and ducks, about horses, fish, frogs, swans, bees, “brackn”, brain cells, bad teeth, beetroot and bodily excretions, about elephants, litter, gardens, graters, colanders, streams, dreams and doubts. Excruciating commentary on the ordeal of being a woman – “how, she thought, do I get out of being a woman, it is repugnant” – surfaces again and again, often combined with slightly cruel humour.In Daffodils, for example, the narrator ponders planting daffodils on the grave of someone he has poisoned. The victim cooked them up with potatoes and ate the dish with a friend, “the woman that wears purple cardigans, two at a time”. Belben has an aptitude for layering hilarious detail with harsh observation. “The old girl has woes,” she writes, “women tend to have woes and dwell on them, they bear grudges like apple blossom.” In the following paragraph, she doubles down on this train of thought: “Women have woes because men come along and by leaving daffodil bulbs in the vegetable rack dare them to be so stupid.”Is Beauty Good does the opposite. It dares usnotto be so stupid. It is less that Belben seeks deliberately to unsettle – I doubt she cares, to be honest – and more that she refuses to censor her imagination, her exacting fiction, in order to protect readers from her experience of life, in all its ugliness and all its glory.Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben is published by And Other Stories (£14.99).
