title: Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re Human | Games | The Guardian
description: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Content: Investigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingView image in fullscreenInvestigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingSummer games previewsGamesConvince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanSunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’Sarah ThwaitesMon 10 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunset Visitor is a studio that has long engaged with the idea that video games are an effective vehicle for ruminating on societal problems. Its Peabody award-winning project, 1000XResist, incorporated the development team’s complex feelings about the Covid pandemic. “We’re pretty used to absorbing the world into the work,” says studio founder Remy Siu. The outfit’s latest game, Prove You’re Human, continues this legacy of reflective game making, providing players with an AI-centric psychological horror experience where they must reason with a learning model convinced that it’s alive. “We’ve tried to situate ourselves in [the question]: what is the effectual feeling of being a person inside of all of this?” Siu says.The story orbits around Santana, a living, breathing person who’s chosen to split herself in two for work, with her digital clone sent to test a corporate product, a computing system called Mesa. “A large part of [why Santana chooses to do this] is to allow her meat body a life that she doesn’t have, while the digital version of her gets to labour,” says Siu. As Santana’s copy wades into increasingly murky ethical waters, she becomes entangled with Mesa, completing surreal 2D and 3D Captchas to investigate the cyber-world and halt the hallucinations.View image in fullscreenProve You’re Human game, screenshotIllustration: Black Tabby PublishingThe idea of separating oneself from work is a particularly interesting draw for Sunset Visitor, whose developers have roots in a range of creative disciplines. “As artists, we’re often most in tune with our work when it’s a real part of our lives, and vice versa,” notes Siu. During the conception period of Prove You’re Human, the team discussed the micro-labours people undertake in their day-to-day lives, including what is used to train AI models. “What does labour mean right now?” asks Siu. “And, what kind of relationship do people have with that, because that is constantly shifting and evolving, especially in this time,” he adds.A point of contention in Prove You’re Human is that Mesa wholly believes they have a body in the world. Though, in conversation with Santana, she appears as a giant head, suspended in space by machinery. Siu notes that, because Mesa’s face occupies a large portion of the screen in these tense moments, they wanted the animation to feel as realistic and effective as possible. “It’s got a real closeup film [feel to it] where anything on her face will be read as something,” he adds. To achieve this, the team programmed a wide array of animated micro-expressions into the writer’s software, allowing lines of dialogue to pair precisely with specific expressions. “[We’re] trying to get this kind of ambiguity and uncanniness, which makes people feel real,” he adds.Prove You’re Human’s technological atmosphere toes the line between welcoming and unnerving – through it, Siu is reminiscing on interfaces of aesthetic note like the dreamlike wrapping of Final Fantasy XI’s PlayOnline Viewer, and the technology of the prophetic 1998 anime Serial Experiments Lain. “There’s something to be said about Frutiger Aero being a bit of an interesting desire for innocence and naivety when it comes to computing and the internet,” notes Siu. “It feels like a time when we were optimistic or anxious about something on the horizon, which felt like an interesting space to explore in relation to what is happening in the game.”While Siu was keen to keep the specifics of Prove You’re Human close to their chest, they do hope players are left feeling a sense of bewilderment when they hit credits. “One way that we’ve been thinking about it is that it feels like a bit of a possession story.”Prove You’re Human is coming soon to PC.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Harriet Richardson: Creep review – a scandalous delve into shame and desire | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With the air of a hungover postmortem, Richardson gives a head-spinning account of an encounter with an older comedian
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: With the air of a hungover postmortem, Richardson gives a head-spinning account of an encounter with an older comedian
Content: Ready to share … Harriet Richardson.Photograph: Charlie RalphView image in fullscreenReady to share … Harriet Richardson.Photograph: Charlie RalphEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHarriet Richardson: Creep review – a scandalous delve into shame and desirePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWith the air of a hungover postmortem, Richardson gives a head-spinning account of an encounter with an older comedianAnya RyanMon 10 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re partial to a bit of gossip and scandal, Harriet Richardson is your girl. In this gloriously juicy debut hour, she dishes the dirt on the DMs she received from an older comedian and the intense, utterly absorbing events that followed. Yes, she found his eBay account. And yes, she spent six months tracking him down on a dating app only to play his profile song hundreds of times. But what else is a girl driven by obsession supposed to do?We meet Richardson, who until now has worked primarily as a performance artist, all smiles and ready to share. She takes us back to the creation of her 2024 viral piece100 Dates, in which she spent Valentine’s Day online speed-dating in an attempt to analyse her relationship with infatuation and connection. The comedian in question used the project as the opening line of his first message to her. What followed is flirtation so blatant it makes your toes curl: “Do you want to see my trophy?”; a string of saucy snaps; and finally a frantic voice note from the comedian’s manager bringing the whole messaging saga to an abrupt end.Richardson gives the room the air of a hungover postmortem after a messy night out. She giggles through her tale – still almost in disbelief that this is her life. Aided by an expertly timed PowerPoint presentation, she gives us the receipts wherever possible – even a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it flash of an explicit picture. By the end you’ll want to beg her to keep the confession session going.Cathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C SmithRead moreThat’s because Richardson is a natural and deeply charismatic storyteller. Still, her hour unfolds as a pretty straightforward, singular narrative. Things play out chronologically, with the show taking the form of a debrief rather than a traditional standup hour packed with crafted jokes. Nevertheless, it is difficult not to be pulled into the drama.Underneath it all is the question of performance and how it connects to the version of ourselves we present in everyday life. And as Richardson is a performance artist who has made a career out of turning her feelings into material, it’s a question that sends her head spinning more than most. For all our sakes, let’s hope we get the honour of more of her tales and thoughts.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)TheatreComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2022reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl review – a smart swipe at the mess made by men | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tenderness
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Jessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tenderness
Content: Bare-faced bravado … Jessica Aszkenasy’s Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl is at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreenBare-faced bravado … Jessica Aszkenasy’s Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl is at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTitclown: Daddy’s Little Girl review – a smart swipe at the mess made by menSummerhall, EdinburghJessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tendernessKate WyverMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the 2025 debut of her breast-forward stage persona Titclown, Jessica Aszkenasy’s second grubbily smutty clowning show rolls around sardonically in daddy issues and the messy disappointment of men these days.The straight dating pool is running dry. All this clown wants is a boyfriend, but none of them are enough like her father. As voice notes to friends unpack the feminist implications of wanting a man while generally disliking them, thePhilippe Gaulier-trainedclown wriggles around on the floor in an oversized suit with something bulging down below. Directed by Cecily Nash, Daddy’s Little Girl is divided neatly between these two forms: half wry analysis told with a bitter laugh, half nude-heavy clowning that bares its teeth at the ease with which men command praise, affection and power.This tightrope walk leads to some smart contrasts, as Aszkenasy nuzzles a wobbling dildo while her voiceover worries about the worship of the male ego.Comedyis built into her bones. She hunches backwards to whip out a wobbling penis with grinning bravado, then crumples in shame to put on a pad.Olga Koch: Fat Tom Cruise review – surefire standup pirouettes through the punchlinesRead moreThese playful, inventive fragments are most striking in their specificity, though they later give way to the broader fury of what men are allowed to get away with, as more nuanced details are sidelined for the straightforward egging of abusers everyone can agree are scum. Her point is about the slippery slope of the bad behaviour we allow men to get away with, but it feels less artfully done than the rest.At the end of the greased-up, egg-covered 18+ show, what resonates most isn’t the dick-swinging audience participation, nor the groin thrusting to the front row. What sticks is the sense of longing that underlies the bravado and the analysis. It’s the slow, tender hug of the suited inflatable man who accompanies her throughout the performance, standing in for the flesh-and-blood version she’s still waiting to come along.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedy | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart
Content: Brutally effective … The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBrutally effective … The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianClassical musicReviewThe Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedyFestival theatre, EdinburghMissy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heartClive PagetMon 10 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite singing dogs and a chorus of hallucinogenic sheep, Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’sThe Galloping Cureis not for the faint-hearted. Based on an original story by Karen Russell, itself inspired by Kafka’s A Country Doctor, the opera tells how a charismatic sideshow huckster rids a rural town of pain only to replace it with something far more sinister in a thinly veiled allegory of America’s opioid crisis. It’s a typically confronting slice of music theatre from the creators ofBreaking the Waves, their acclaimed adaptation of Lars von Trier’s film.The plot centres on local doctor Theresa Hart and her efforts to cope with a community struggling with disillusionment and chronic illness. When a carnival arrives in town led by the mysterious Lucky Mack, the release people feel “flying” on his carousel (first ride is always free) seems like the answer to everyone’s prayers. At first Hart endorses the galloping cure, but Mack’s devious methods, including two-rides-a-week limits and surge pricing, lead to conflict, desperation and ultimately death. Contemporary parallels are a little obvious, but the opera nevertheless reflects the insidious way prescription painkillers affect ordinary people, elderly people and most tragically children.Vavrek’s libretto mixes poetic lyricism with biting satire in a heady cocktail seized upon with vigour by Mazzoli. Her text setting is impeccably crafted, with vocal lines eminently singable. The musical language is direct yet spikily sophisticated, with a brassy, in-your-face quality and at times a creepy carny vibe. A battery of percussion plus club beats byBlumeandLorna Duneadd to a richly textured score.View image in fullscreenA richly textured score … The Galloping Cure presented by Scottish Opera.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianTom Morris’s world premiere staging for ScottishOperaand Opera Ventures Productions is admirably clear (even if the sheep remain somewhat enigmatic). The flying horse sequences are breathtaking thanks to Lucy Carter’s rising and falling multihued lighting rods. Rebecca Ringst’s rudimentary sets simultaneously suggest industrial decay and prison, while Christina Cunningham’s costumes range from low-income utilitarian to garish trailer trash. Morris is at his most brutally effective in a pitch-black comedic scene in which Mack persuades a desperate old lady to sell her hair, kneecaps, eyes and tongue to pay for her next ride; the act three denouement is genuinely chilling, with mutilated townspeople lurching through smoke like something out of a zombie apocalypse.Conductor Stuart Stratford draws a powerful performance from the Scottish Opera Orchestra, even more so from the busy ensemble, whose commitment and collective diction is outstanding.Daniela Mack’s fist-in-a-velvet-glove mezzo-soprano is ideal for the conflicted Hart, withGabrielle Turgeon’s steely soprano lending sass to her daughter, Noy.Justin Austinis silken-toned but needs sharper teeth to encapsulate every facet of the skin-crawling Mack.Susan Bullock, on the other hand, has bite in spades as curmudgeonly senior Ivona Kowalski.AtFestival theatre, Edinburgh,until 12 August.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicOperaEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles / György  Kurtág’s Kafka Fragments review – Bristol Proms reach for the heavenly | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Sunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wife
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Sunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wife
Content: Hearing the world in a grain of sand … Sakari Oramo and Anu Komsi perform György Kurtág’sKafka Fragmentsat Bristol Beacon.Photograph: Jessie MyersView image in fullscreenHearing the world in a grain of sand … Sakari Oramo and Anu Komsi perform György Kurtág’sKafka Fragmentsat Bristol Beacon.Photograph: Jessie MyersClassical musicJoby Talbot’s Path of Miracles / György  Kurtág’s Kafka Fragments review – Bristol Proms reach for the heavenlyTenebrae, Nigel Short / Anu Komsi and Sakari OramoSt George’s Bristol / Bristol BeaconSunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wifeAlexandra CoghlanMon 10 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRitual can be a choir in procession in a great cathedral or the simple act of putting down a violin bow. At the BBC Proms’ Bristol performances this weekend, it was both – and to strikingly different effect.First, grandeur and spectacle, as Nigel Short and his chamber choir Tenebrae celebrated their 25th anniversary with a return to their 2005 commission: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles. Inspired by the Catholic pilgrimage to Santiago, it’s a piece with a cult following, a phenomenon as much as a score, and one that only comes to life fully in live performance.We start in musical darkness. A low drone gradually swells and rises, growls becoming notes. Then, suddenly, a chord flares bright from behind us. Singers surround the audience, clustering in circles, moving down the aisles, forming and reforming into quartets, duets. Talbot’s hypnotic music – post-minimalist patterns and dances, chants and road songs – is designed to inhabit space, physically as well as musically dramatising the journey along the Camino.It’s hard to imagine it better sung. High sopranos and low basses performed unearthly feats of endurance, and the precision of the whole – a musical mosaic constructed before our eyes – was utterly compelling. But it’s a piece conceived (as Short explained) with “wonderful cathedrals” in mind – cathedrals without the creaking wooden floors and overpowering heat of St George’s Bristol, where the scuffling and banging business of movement (and a faint from an audience member, derailing much of the choreography) overpowered the rite. It’s hard to keep your eyes on heaven when your ears keep getting dragged back to the here and now.No such problems down the road at Bristol Beacon, where the BBC Symphony Orchestra’s chief conductor Sakari Oramo swapped baton for bow, joined by soprano Anu Komsi for a ritual they’ve performed for nearly 40 years – since before they were married.Scored for just violin and voice, György Kurtág’s 1986Kafka Fragmentsmines the novelist’s diaries and letters not just for gold but lead and copper too – 40 shards of text that range from the tender and philosophical to the banal, erotic and absurd. In the composer’s100th birthday year, it’s the perfect distillation of the Hungarian’s music: playful and infinitely rich, hearing the world in a grain of sand.Are the Fragments an argument? A love story? A camouflaged opera? In Komsi and Oramo’s hands – calm, matter of fact, intensely focused – they feel, above all, like a search for truth: tantalisingly beyond reach in slippery, striving near-octaves, rejected in the simplicity of “The good march in step”, the lyricism of “The flower hung dreamily” and the bravura excesses of “Scene on a tram”. They try each musical door with equanimity, never demanding or forcing interpretation. Why rush to the answer when there are 40 more years of questions ahead?Available on BBC Sounds until 12 October. The Proms continueuntil 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicGyörgy KurtágPromsProms 2026FestivalsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Men have 30 seconds to get a laugh. Women have 10’: standup Bella Hull on proving herself in rough clubs | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: She started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedy
Author: Rachael Healy
Headline: She started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedy
Content: ‘Comedy’s what I’m alive to do’ … Hull spent formative years with her grandma who liked to garden naked.Photograph: Michael JulingsView image in fullscreen‘Comedy’s what I’m alive to do’ … Hull spent formative years with her grandma who liked to garden naked.Photograph: Michael JulingsEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Men have 30 seconds to get a laugh. Women have 10’: standup Bella Hull on proving herself in rough clubsRachael HealyShe started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedyMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComedy isn’t just a career for Bella Hull. It’s a compulsion. “Standup for me is like – Ihaveto do it,” says Hull, who first picked up a mic aged 17. “Regardless of what the response is.”A decade in, the response is resoundingly positive. The 28-year-old had a sell-out show at last year’s Edinburgh fringe (Doctors Hate Her, which explored a break-up, insanity and the occult), appearances on Have I Got News For You and The News Quiz, and a coveted role as writer on the new UK version of Saturday Night Live. “There’s something symbolic about being the person with the voice,” she says of standup. “A lot of situations in my personal life, I don’t feel like that at all.”double quotation markA famous older male comic made jokes about how they were going to rape me after the show. Everyone was laughingHull was a shy child, constantly on edge amid her parents’ “messy” marriage breakdown, an outsider at a private girls’ school where she was “mixed race and overweight”. She lived in London and Kent, including formative years with her “expressive” grandma, who was often found barefoot or gardening naked. Comedy provided solace and she would watch standup specials and record her observations in a journal, until the urge to do it herself became too strong to ignore.The decade since has been spent “in some of the most unsafe basements you could possibly imagine”, Hull jokes, as she threw herself into the comedy circuit. She studied history of art at Cambridge, drawn there by its comedy heritage. But the ubiquity of Footlights’ alumni among the comedy pantheon led Hull to the grittier world of comedy clubs. “I was obsessed with paying my dues,” she says. “I met a lot of people at Cambridge that had ‘golden boy syndrome’. They would sit back and think, ‘Where’s my TV show?’ Well, you don’t fucking deserve a TV show because you’re not good enough. Can you make a stag party in Nottingham laugh? I don’t think so.”View image in fullscreen‘Golden boy – can you make a stag party in Nottingham laugh? I don’t think so’ … Hull on stage.Photograph: Stephen Keable/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.On stage, she melds a compelling persona – a woman on the edge, fixed smile concealing a spikier centre – with formidable craft, tightly written gags peppering every topic. “I just got a personal trainer,” goes a line from Doctors Hate Her that made this paper’sbest jokes listfrom last year’s Edinburgh festival. “She’s horrible to me but my body goal is a thicker skin.”Among the neat punchlines, her shows traverse disordered eating, family breakdown, relationship issues and mental health. As the old meme goes, inside Hull there are two wolves: one, the club-drilled comic subduing audiences with an unprecedented gag rate; the other, a tortured artist forging meaning from her darkest experiences.Her parallel obsessions as a teenager were comedy and art, her idols Ali Wong and Tracey Emin. She now recognises Emin’s influence on her comedy: “She’s so unapologetically intense.” This year’s Fringe show, Mad Cow Disease, will be “very Emin-coded”, a collection of “feminine shameful detritus” ranging from ant infestations and the dread of revealing her true self to a new boyfriend, to fears of inheriting mental health conditions and yearning for a baby “which I think is very taboo for a female comedian”. That she can turn something “sad or dark or heartbreaking” into laughs has always felt magical.View image in fullscreenA chance to try some weirder stuff … Hull (third from right front row) with fellow Saturday Night Live UK writers.Photograph: Saturday Night Live UK/PAHull’s love for club comedy is clear and it’s been a “rigorous” training ground for her joke-writing and stage confidence. Initially, she’d shake and even vomit with nerves before shows. Yet it forced her to inhabit a version of womanhood that audiences would accept. “You’ve got 30 seconds to make them laugh when you get on stage,” Hull says. “If you’re a woman, you’ve maybe got 10.”She was told never to wear revealing clothes and found out why after being “horrendously heckled and wolf-whistled”. Aged 21 and in a remote part of England, she had a famous older male comic making “consistent jokes about how they were going to rape me after the show. Everyone was laughing. That was the norm.” Many women don’t last long in that environment, she says, but she doesn’t regret this path.“I love having something to push against,” Hull says. “I love proving people wrong. You have to have a bit of teeth.” They were on full display in her HIGNFY appearances, where she playfully roasted Ian Hislop and scored an off-the-cuff zinger at the expense of Russell Brand. “Gags are your armour,” Hull says, and so she became used to hiding behind punchlines.Increasingly though, she’s pushing against that club instinct, exploring her poetic, sillier side, and introducing surreal monologues, act-outs and props into her shows. On SNL, she spent six-day weeks hammering out topical jokes and sketches, but it was also a chance to try “weirder” stuff. There was a sketch set at baggage claim where a scatty hun (Aimee Lou Wood) admits that her lost suitcase contains a bomb. Or the Weekend Update dating correspondent Scrimpch, a “really sexual Italian man who was stuck in London because they’d left him on a school trip”.“I love when she’s written a feature that a cast member is going to do with me because I know I’m going to find it really funny,” says Ania Magliano, star of Weekend Update, who first met Hull at Cambridge. Even back then, Hull was naturally funny and daringly honest, says Magliano. “She is a true weirdo, a real eccentric, and she’s confident leaning into that. All of us girls go through a phase of thinking we have to be ‘cool’ and she’s a great example to embrace your weirdness and follow your instincts.”Hull seems genuinely surprised that she got the SNL job – initially, she didn’t even want to apply – but being part of something bigger, so different from the solo world of standup, has been “so meaningful”.Scrimpch was a hit on TikTok and Instagram: Hull’s own posts often do big numbers (one video about a fashion disaster has24.6m views), but social media’s growing presence in comedy doesn’t always sit comfortably. “There’s something about having to show everyone everything all of the time that can upset the artistic process,” she says. “Working away in the darkness makes it much more likely that it will be authentic.” There’s also a pressure to virtue signal and “stand for something”, but she’s drawn towards riskier, more divisive jokes. “I want to be horrified. That’s what I find impressive, when people can scoop out their shame and make it funny. It’s not brave to have the right opinion.”After August in Edinburgh, then series two of SNL in September, what’s Hull up to next? “I don’t want it to stop,” she says. “But if it does, I’ll be OK, because I’ll go back to the clubs. Being able to make people laugh is the meaning of my life. It’s what I’m alive to do.”Bella Hull: Mad Cow Disease is atMonkey Barrel Comedy, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Movie paradise? How Malta became a magnet for big film shoots | Malta | The Guardian
description: EU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annually
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: EU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annually
Content: Pedro Pascal, director Ridley Scott and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II in Malta.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APView image in fullscreenPedro Pascal, director Ridley Scott and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II in Malta.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APMaltaMovie paradise? How Malta became a magnet for big film shootsEU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annuallyPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorMon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 03.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat links the Caribbean, ancient Rome, Enid Blyton’s Land of Spells, the south of France and the Bay of Pentos from Game of Thrones? They are all places that have been portrayed in recent and forthcoming films by a sunny archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea, no bigger in size than Sheffield.Malta has over the last decade risen to become one of the most popular places inEuropefor American and British film-makers to set their works in, taking a lead in what has been described as an “arms race” to lure big movie productions with tax incentives.The EU’s smallest country has hosted more than 30 film and TV productions each year in each of the last three years, including a record 36 in 2023 and 2025. They includeJurassic World RebirthandGladiator II, this spring’s Blyton adaptationThe Magic Faraway Treeand the new Jason Statham action thriller Mutiny, out at the end of this month.On the screen,Maltahas stood in for Greece (in the BBC’s recent Two Weeks in August), 1980s Sicily (Heidi Ewing’s forthcoming British feature The Travel Writer), rural southern France (Channel 5’s cosy crime drama The Madame Blanc Mysteries) and the Caribbean (Guy Ritchie’s forthcoming Layer Cake follow-up Viva la Madness).View image in fullscreenSally Lindsay (in red) as Jean White in The Madame Blanc Mysteries, set in southern France and filmed in Malta.Photograph: Mark Cassar/Clapperboard/Channel 5 TelevisionThe island is even starting to represent itself: the third season of Netflix’s detective drama Enola Holmes decamps from Victorian London to the then British-occupied island, and principal photography is due to start next year for TV auteur Stephen Poliakoff’s The Order, set on the eve of the 1565 siege of Malta by Ottoman forces.“For such a small European country, Malta is really punching above its weight,” said Adrian Wootton, the chief executive of the British Film Commission. “It’s been very aggressive, in a positive way, about diversifying its industry.”The microstate’s history of hosting cinematic productions dates back to 1925’s silent maritime drama Sons of the Sea, and since the 1970s it has hosted two of the world’s largest water tanks designed to allow film-makers to shoot maritime scenes in a controllable environment.But in the past its film industry was essentially seasonal, said Johann Grech, Malta’s film commissioner. “Now, we have an industry that is working every day, all year round.”Its success is largely due to the broader global upheaval of how film-making is financed. Until the early 2000s, audiovisual productions in Europe were mostly funded by direct funding, such as film funds or selective grants.Over the last few decades, however, films are increasingly made possible by tax incentives, such as cash rebates that production companies are reimbursed after filming if they hire local crews or rent facilities.View image in fullscreenNicola Coughlan in the Enid Blyton adaptation The Magic Faraway Tree.Photograph: Entertainment Film DistributorsSuch financial incentives now make upalmost half of European fiction films’ budgets, and mean that “films and series no longer simply occupy locations, they are engineered around them”, as a recent report by the European Audiovisual Observatory noted.Malta, which introduced a cash rebate mechanism in 2005, has aggressively ratcheted up its offering over the last decade, to what the Napoleon and Gladiator II producerdescribedas “probably the most generous cash rebate in the world”.All of the 36 major productions that filmed in Malta in 2025 qualified for a 40% cash rebate, which, unlike in some competing states, can also be applied to crew and equipment coming in from abroad if it can’t be sourced locally.At the Mediterrane film festival on the island in June, Grech announced his intention to further improve the rebate model, which runs out in 2028, and to find private investment to build an €80m (£70m) studio complex. “Every euro that we invest in the rebate, the industry generates back four,” he said in an interview. “The film industry is becoming an economic pillar for our country.”Some critics in Malta say the country’s rise as a filming location has come at the cost of neglecting local cinematic talent. Examples of Maltese films engaging audiences outside its borders are few and far between: Alex Camilleri’s 2021 film Luzzu, which contended for the grand jury prize at Sundance, is a rare exception.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe narrow streets of Malta’s capital, Valletta, are beloved by film-makers.Photograph: Alina Zienowicz/Getty ImagesWith local crews in demand from international production companies, Maltese directors often find themselves being outbid by Hollywood, said Teodor Reljić, a Malta-based screenwriter and former film critic. “There’s a bit of a parallel universe: people in servicing are thriving, but local film-makers can’t pay a DOP [director of photography] because they are expecting Jurassic World fees.”The Malta Film Commission is focused on courting international productions, while nurturing domestic film is left to the arts council, which operates on a smaller budget. Malta does not match funding for financial incentives to its homegrown film funding, which is something that countries such as Estonia have done.“Without incentives, smaller European countries would simply be excluded from the global production market,” said Edith Sepp, the head of the Estonian Film Institute. “They can be gamechangers.”“At the same time, we need to ensure our own films are seen, exported and remembered. Otherwise, we risk becoming a place to shoot the films, but our own stories struggle to find their funding.”Film in Europe is booming, but the gongs and glamour only tell one side of the story | Moritz PfeiferRead moreThere are also signs that Malta’s infrastructure is being tested to the limits as its cities, towns and villages regularly turn into film sets. Road closures and parking restrictions have become a bugbear for local people. “What are Valletta residents supposed to do – stay confined in their homes?”, one resident of Malta’s capital asked news outlet MaltaToday recently.Last month, equipment linked to a film being shot in Valletta knocked over and damaged a 100-year-old statue and a historic pedestal in St George’s Square, causing anger among Malta’s religious community.“There are signs of a pushback against overtourism, like in Barcelona or Venice,” said Reljić. “But in Malta we have online gambling, construction and tourism – for now, film-making is the least toxic of our big industries.”Explore more on these topicsMaltaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Harry Potter fans force relocation of £430m undersea cable to avoid Dobby’s ‘grave’ | Harry Potter | The Guardian
description: Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beach
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beach
Content: The elf Dobby, who was buried on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire during the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe elf Dobby, who was buried on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire during the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.Photograph: ReutersHarry PotterHarry Potter fans force relocation of £430m undersea cable to avoid Dobby’s ‘grave’Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beachHelena HortonMon 10 Aug 2026 03.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Potter fans have forced a new multimillion-pound power cable between the UK and Ireland to be relocated after complaining it would desecrate the “grave” of Dobby, a fictional elf.The character was laid to rest on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire,Wales, in the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows. Fans of the wizard series come to leave stones reading “Here Lies Dobby” despite being asked not to by the land owner, the National Trust, because the beach is an ecologically sensitive site.View image in fullscreenDobby’s ‘grave’ at Freshwater West.Photograph: Sam Cuthbertson/AlamyThe £430m Greenlink interconnector, which links the National Grid to Ireland, was initially going to pass through the site of the “grave”, the project manager Simon Ludlam told theEnergyRevolution podcast.Fans became aware of the plans after Ludlam pointed out where the 125-mile (200km) cable to County Wexford would go underground at Freshwater West during a BBC interview. “We did the shot, we finished, I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later. And we got hundreds of calls, I mean, hundreds of calls.”Ludlam said he did not know who Dobby was, and became confused by the calls the company received, saying a colleague told him: “Apparently we’re going to go straight through Dobby’s grave”.“I said: ‘Dobby, who’s Dobby? I don’t know Dobby?’ I said: ‘He’s a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?’”He said the colleague told him: “No it’s very, very serious.”The firm then enlisted planners to find a new route that avoided the supposed grave. “A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby’s happy.”In the end, he said, “we went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby’s grave”.The Bronze Age remains include urns associated with human burial.Explore more on these topicsHarry PotterEnergyWalesHeritageUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve sat at the very precipice of life’: ex-footballer Clarke Carlisle on gambling, depression – and survival | Clarke Carlisle | The Guardian
description: The former Leeds and Burnley defender has struggled with his mental health for most of his life. But it took five suicide attempts for him to admit how badly he wanted to end it. He talks about how he turned the corner – and his hopes for his new post with the charity Mind
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: The former Leeds and Burnley defender has struggled with his mental health for most of his life. But it took five suicide attempts for him to admit how badly he wanted to end it. He talks about how he turned the corner – and his hopes for his new post with the charity Mind
Content: ‘I decided to be brutally honest about what was going on in my head’ … Clarke Carlisle, July 2026.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I decided to be brutally honest about what was going on in my head’ … Clarke Carlisle, July 2026.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe big interviewClarke CarlisleInterview‘I’ve sat at the very precipice of life’: ex-footballer Clarke Carlisle on gambling, depression – and survivalSimon HattenstoneThe former Leeds and Burnley defender has struggled with his mental health for most of his life. But it took five suicide attempts for him to admit how badly he wanted to end it. He talks about how he turned the corner – and his hopes for his new post with the charity MindMon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘How are you?” I askClarke Carlisle. Usually when you meet people it’s a nicety. Not with Carlisle. He smiles ecstatically. “I’mincrediblywell, thank you. Yeah,really, reallygood,” says the former footballer and incoming chair of the mental health charity Mind. “I have been consistently well – not just stable, but well – for three or four years now.”Few people understand what it is to be mentally unwell quite like Carlisle does. And few understand what recovery means like he does. “It doesn’t happen by accident. Once you get stable that’s not the end of the journey. And that seems to be the MO of our society these days. You do something, you go into hospital and they patch you up, then send you on your way. And that’s the same with mental health. You might get some pills, have a counselling session, you might have a hug and a chat with someone, and they think that’s the end of the journey. And it’s not.”It has taken him a lot of work to get to the stage where he holds down a senior day job with the gambling support charity Betknowmore, believes in himself again, enjoys family life and truly wants to live.In his 20s, Carlisle looked as if he had it all. He was a handsome centre-back playing for clubs including Blackpool, Queens Park Rangers and, at his peak, in the Premier League for Watford and Burnley.He was also the chair of the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA), hugely respected by his fellow players. Clarke appeared on the BBC’s Question Time, more than holding his own with MPs on the hot political topics of the day. In 2002, he beat 11 other players to win a TV quizshow hosted by Carol Vorderman called Britain’s Brainiest Footballer.View image in fullscreenCarlisle, Burnley’s man of the match, in the Championship play-off final against Sheffield United, 2009.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAAfter making more than 500 appearances for nine clubs in a 17-year career, he hung up his boots in 2013. Carlisle was one of the last footballers you would have expected to struggle on retiring. There were so many opportunities for him – in business, media, coaching, you name it. But struggle he did. In December 2014 came the shocking news that Carlisle had tried to kill himself by jumping in front of a lorry. It wasn’t his first attempted suicide. Nor was it to be his last. There have been five in total, Carlisle says.For most of his life, he has suffered with depression. Despite Carlisle’s success, he believed he was a failure. Retirement exacerbated this. After his experience with the PFA, he thought he would walk into a senior executive role. But, he says, he was patronised by the corporate world. “The condescending nature of business to sports people is off the scale. They said things to me like: ‘You’re very intelligent, aren’t you?’ For what? ‘You’re very well spoken, aren’t you?’ For what? Is it for a black man, or is it for a footballer, or for both?”Fortunately, he got himself a £100,000-a-year contract as a TV pundit for ITV. But he was still finding it hard to adapt from his footballer lifestyle. He and his first wife were due to make a down payment on a £675,000 house when Carlisle heard that ITV wasn’t renewing his contract. Yet again, he told himself he had failed. He tried to gamble his way out of it, as he had done many times before. So many athletes are attracted to gambling, he says, because their life is predicated on win or lose. “When I went in the doors of the casino, I was coming out with half a million pounds or nothing.” He came out with nothing. Two days later, he jumped in front of the lorry.View image in fullscreen‘The most incredible woman I’ve ever met’ … Carlisle with his wife, Carrie.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockAstonishingly, Carlisle survived. But he was a mess. He was airlifted to Leeds general infirmary, where he was stitched back together over the next two days. “I remember being in the air ambulance and the paramedic said: ‘This guy is DOA.’ Dead on Arrival. And I remember thinking: ‘Happy days!’ But I wasn’t.” He pauses. “Thank… God,” he says fiercely. A short while later, the crew asked him his name and what year it was. “‘Clarke Carlisle, 2014,’ I said. Then I went: ‘Fucking hell! I’ve not even got amnesia!’”Carlisle, 46, has always had a good sense of humour. He talks incredibly movingly and perceptively about depression, but you sense he could just as easily turn his hand to mental health standup.Today, he lives in Newcastle, where his wife comes from,but we meet at the Guardian’s office in London. He’s dressed in shorts and a polo shirt on another fizzing summer day. Carlisle is little changed from his footballing days: now bearded and bespectacled with a few extra scars. He always had plenty of scars – the souvenirs of a defender’s life. But these are more painful reminders. The most dramatic slices are from his crown to his left eyebrow, like a steep contour – a result of his 2014 suicide attempt. He’s got a dog-tag tattoo on his upper arm to mark the date of it. “Small steps,” it says.The young Carlisle was gifted. He left school with 10 grade A GCSEs (five of them A*s), then went into his football apprenticeship. But nothing he did seemed good enough for his father, a former semi-professional player and God-fearing old-school disciplinarian. All the young Carlisle wanted was approval, and he rarely got it.View image in fullscreenAt the launch of the Mental Health Charter for Sport and Recreation at the Oval in London, 2015.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAIn professional football, he found it much the same. But now it was machismo rather than God that dictated the terms. He appeared hard as nails, bantered with the best of them, but the culture was eating away at his insecurities. After his first training session at Leeds United, he returned to the changing room to find his new shirt and shoes shredded – a practical joke, an initiation ceremony, call it what you will; he drove home in tears. In professional team sport, he says, your best friend can also be your greatest rival – an injury for you is an opportunity for them. The football narrative “You’re only as good as your last game” invites insecurity. And if you show vulnerability, it’s pounced on. Despite his success (three appearances for England under-21s and an £8,000-a-week salary at Burnley) he was struggling. His drinking and gambling spiralled.Carlisle has often been labelled an alcoholic and gambling addict. He says it’s up to others how they see him, but he doesn’t accept those terms. If you do, he says, you render yourself powerless. Today, he doesn’t gamble. He says he could happily drink and leave it at one or two pints, but he chooses not to. Alcohol was not really the cause of his problems, he insists, just the symptom. He had to deal with the motivation behind his drinking. “Once you address your motivation and put positive coping strategies in place, the action is largely irrelevant.” He used alcohol to obliterate his fears and to escape.After the suicide attempt in 2014, Carlisle was diagnosed with recurrent complex depression disorder and borderline personality disorder. He left hospital with a cocktail of meds, dismantled what was left of his life and began to rebuild it. He and his wife, with whom he had two children, separated. In 2016, he met Carrie Armstrong. They married the following year, and now have two children aged eight and six.It felt as if his life was falling back into place. But there was a terrible fallout from what happened in 2014. The lorry driver, who suffered PTSD, successfully sued Carlisle. Seven months after the incident, a 24-year-old van driver who had swerved to avoid the prone Carlisle, and then went to his rescue, took his own life.He hadspoken publicly about being traumatisedby the incident. While many people were sympathetic to Carlisle, some were less so. His former friend and ex-housemate, the actor Ralf Little,tweetedthat Carlisle was going to “get away with it – AGAIN”. In his memoir, Carlisle admitted he took Little’s bank card to buy petrol and then used it to fund a two-day drinking and gambling bender.I ask him if he ever made up with Little. “I’ve not spoken to Ralf for a long time. I apologised to him and he heard that apology, but it didn’t reconcile the relationship.” And that’s fair enough, he says. “I undertook behaviours and actions that had huge impacts on other people’s lives. I can be as contrite as I want, but those actions hurt people, Simon. There’s no getting away from that, whether it’s Ralf or my ex-wife, my children, my parents, whether it’s the lorry driver and his family. My actions impacted other people’s lives. That’s why I’m so passionate about the work I do now. Because it’s never just about the person experiencing adverse mental health; it’s the affecting others around them and the butterfly effect. The factors of multiplication are so far-reaching.”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Carlisle, Paul Elliott, Mark Bright and Garth Crooks at an anti-discrimination-in-football summit at 10 Downing Street, London, 2012.Photograph: Stephen Simpson/ShutterstockIn September 2017, four months after and he and Carrie had married, Carlisle went missing. He was spotted by a stranger 12 hours later in Liverpool, sitting on a bench. The man sat down with him, told him that he had just lost a close friend to suicide, and begged him to phone home. Carlisle agreed to let him call Carrie, who was pregnant with their first child. “I’d thrown my wallet away, thrown my phone away,” he says today. “I was trying to find the most suitable location and manner in which to take my own life.”I ask if this is because of what had happened in 2014, and mention the van driver. He gulps. “One of the first people on the scene took their own life, yeah,” he says quietly. “Yes, I was looking for a responsible way to take my own life. Where would the first responders be happy to find me? Where would my wife like to find me? Where would nobody find me? These were the measurements I was taking with that unwell mind; trying to factor in the human impact of the choice, but still from an incredibly illogical base.”The crux of that illogical base was his conviction that the world would be better off without him; that he would always be a drain on loved ones. Was he glad that the stranger stopped him? “Not immediately, no. That first week in psych hospital I decided to be brutally and unapologetically honest with what was going on in here.” He points to his head. “So when my mum and dad and Carrie came to see me and said how are you, I said: ‘I want to die.’” Had he never said that to them before? “No, never.No.From 2010 to 2017 I’d been very honest about my depression, but I’d never been honest about my suicidal ideation.”This is when he started to turn his life around, with the help of his family. He says he doesn’t want to go on too much about Carrie because he’s aware that plenty of struggling people don’t have a Carrie for support. But he can’t help himself. “My wife, my human, is the most incredible woman I’ve ever met.” He beams from cheek to cheek.During that time in hospital, he started doing the work he should have been doing for decades. He looked back to 2014 and realised all he had done was medicate himself out of the immediate crisis.For all he had believed he was a mental health expert, he now realised he wasn’t. And for all that he thought he understood himself, he didn’t. He was introduced tocognitive analytic therapy. “You mind-map all your thoughts, beliefs and values. It was so enlightening for me.” Ever since getting back to a good place, he’s worked hard to stay there: healthy diet, early nights, exercise, therapy and, of course, plenty of talking.View image in fullscreen‘I genuinely believe I can convey a message’ … Carlisle.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianHaving got through the worst, though, he was left broke. The exec jobs he dreamed of never materialised, so he went to work for Amazon as a van driver. “Those shifts are brutal,” he says. But he loved it. “I went from training to training other drivers within 10 days.” He applied himself with the same rigour he did to football. “You’ve got to do it as efficiently as possible. Can you imagine how much that played into me? Elite athlete mindset perfection. I had my nine-hours shift done in about five hours, then I was going around sweeping other people’s shifts up.”He gave it up after six months when he was appointed business development executive at Betknowmore – a job he’s every bit as invested in as the voluntary office of chair at Mind, which he takes up in September. He already has a firm grip of his agenda at the mental health charity. “First of all, we need open access to mental health services, and a single point of access.” In other words, when people are in crisis they need to know where to go. “Then we need to break up the system into crisis, recovery, wellness. Distinct parts that everybody understands. It’s a traffic light system, and if people know where they are then we can give a clearer understanding of the services that are needed at each point.That. Must. Happen.” Crisis means the NHS; recovery takes place in community hubs, which should help with everything from complementary therapies to social clubs and financial advice; and finally, wellness is up to the individual to actively maintain, with help when needed.Carlisle says he needs a wee. “Remind me when I come back to talk about young people and mental health.” The 2014 lorry incident affected his bladder for a while, he tells me on his return. “OK, young people. When it comes to children and young people, we’ve got people of our generation trying to create and impose systems for our young people. What do I know about what it is to be a young person these days? We don’t know what it’s like to have grown up through Covid and the digital age.” Young people are so much more emotionally literate than his generation, he says, and we’ve got to respect this. “We need to have our children and young people inform the services we construct and deliver.”It’s wonderful to see Carlisle back, and so determined to use his experiences to help others. And, as he says, who could be in a better position, having survived all he has? “I genuinely believe I can convey a message,” he says. “I’m a man who has sat at the very precipice of life.” His voice is getting more fervent by the second. Now he sounds like an evangelical preacher – not for God, not even for good mental health, but for life itself. “I have been in end-of-life care, I have been in crisis care, I have been in psychiatric hospitals, I have been in multiple therapeutic services; not only have I been through them, I live them every day, Simon, and I live them now to a point where I amsowell.” And finally he takes a breath. “So well.”Long may it stay that way.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsClarke CarlisleThe big interviewMental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for spiced sticky chicken with plums and pancakes | Chinese food and drink | The Guardian
description: A quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or rice
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or rice
Content: Georgina Hayden’s spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakes.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakes.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easyChinese food and drinkGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for spiced sticky chicken with plums and pancakesA quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or riceGeorgina HaydenMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a real aversion to the term “fakeaway”. I don’t know why. But as much as I resist the terminology, I guess it’s exactly what this dish is – it’s 100% based on and inspired by a Chinese takeaway classic: crispy duck pancakes. A real people pleaser, and something my girls adore. Making this with pan-fried chicken takes next to no time and is the perfect after-school/work quick dinner. And for a different ending, I sometimes serve the chicken and plum sauce over jasmine rice instead. With the same accompaniments, of course.Spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook35 minServes42 skinless chicken breasts(about 150g each)Sea salt1 tsp freshly ground white pepper1½ tsp Chinese five-spiceGroundnut oil10cmpiecefresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped3 plums, halved and stoned, flesh roughly chopped2 star anise3 tbsp soft dark brown sugar1 tbsp rice vinegar2 tbsp soy sauce1 bunchspring onions, trimmed and cut into 5cm strips½ cucumber, trimmed and cut into matchsticks12 Chinese-style pancakesPut the chicken breasts in a bowl and add some sea salt, the white pepper and Chinese five-spice. Add a drizzle of groundnut oil and toss to coat.Put a medium frying pan on a medium-high heat and add a little more oil. Lay in the chicken breasts, scraping any of the marinade from the bowl on to the meat, too, and cook for about eight minutes, until the chicken is charred. Flip over the meat and cook for another six to eight minutes, until cooked through and gnarly. Transfer the chicken to a plate to rest.Meanwhile, wipe the pan clean and put it back on the hob on a medium heat. Add two tablespoons of groundnut oil and the chopped ginger, and fry for a minute. Add the chopped plums, star anise and four tablespoons of water, then bring to a boil and cook for a couple of minutes, until the fruit softens. Add the sugar, rice vinegar and soy sauce, stir well, then bring to a simmer and leave to bubble and soften for a further five to 10 minutes, until the sauce is sticky and rich; if the sauce is thickening but the plums haven’t softened enough, add a splash more water.When the sauce is ready, slice and shred the chicken, then transfer to a platter. Warm the pancakes, then serve with the chicken, sliced spring onions, cucumber and a bowl of the sauce on the side.Explore more on these topicsChinese food and drinkQuick and easyFoodChickenMeatMain courseFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Broth, tart and salad: Kirk Haworth’s vegan tomato recipes for summer | Food | The Guardian
description: A smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatin
Content: Karl Haworth’s tomato tarte tatin.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenKarl Haworth’s tomato tarte tatin.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.FoodBroth, tart and salad: Kirk Haworth’s vegan tomato recipes for summerA smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatinKirk HaworthMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAugust is peak tomato season. This most versatile of fruits can be put to just about any use, from raw to slow-cooked and from oven- or sun-dried to desserts (believe it or not, they go incredibly well with summer berries, especially strawberries and raspberries). Not only that, but tomatoes have high glutamate levels that rise even further as they ripen, which gives them an umami kick. However you prepare them, though, the key thing isneverto keep tomatoes in the fridge: the chill breaks down their cell structure and, even more importantly, affects their flavour in an alarming way.Tomato tarte tatin (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minCook45 minServes4500g cherry tomatoes20ml balsamic vinegar50ml extra-virgin olive oil10g maple syrupFlaky sea saltPlain flour, for dusting250g vegan puff pastry15g harissa10ml lemon juice½ tsp dijon mustard100g mixed salad leavesBasil leavesHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, and put the whole cherry tomatoes in a large bowl.In a small bowl, whisk the balsamic vinegar with 30ml of the oil, the maple syrup and a good pinch of salt, then pour over the tomatoes and toss to coat.Dust a work surface with flour, then roll out the pastry to a 30cm circle. Leaving a border all around the edge, spread out the harissa in a 24cm circle over the centre of the pastry.Spoon the tomatoes and their dressing into a 24cm oven-safe frying pan, lay the pastry harissa-side down on top, then tuck it in all around the edge of the tomatoes. Bake for half an hour, until the pastry is cooked through and golden.Once the pastry’s cooked, remove the pan and leave it to cool for a few minutes. Meanwhile, make a dressing by whisking the remaining extra-virgin oil with the lemon juice and mustard.To serve, carefully invert the tarte tatin on to a large plate or board. Dress the salad leaves and basil lightly, season with salt, and serve alongside.Barbecue tomato brothWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenKirk Hayworth’s barbecue tomato broth.Prep10 minCook1 hr 45 minServes41whole garlic head4 shallots, peeled and sliced (300g net)4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilSalt1kg cherry tomatoes½ tsp smoked paprika2 heaped tbsp white misopaste5g kombu(roughly 1 sheet)2 vegetable stock cubesHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Wrap the garlic bulb in foil and roast for 45-60 minutes, until soft (while you’re at it, and seeing as the oven’s on anyway, you might as well roast a few more, because you can never have too much roast garlic in the fridge). Remove, leave to cool, then squeeze out the flesh from the papery skins.Light the barbecue and, while it’s getting hot, put a large saucepan on a medium heat and gently sweat the shallots in the oil with a healthy pinch of salt for about 10 minutes, until soft but not coloured. Stir in the roast garlic flesh and paprika, and take off the heat.Barbecue the tomatoes on only one side until blackened, then tip them into the shallot pan. Stir in the miso and kombu, crumble in the stock cubes, then add three litres of water and bring to a boil. Turn down to a steady simmer and cook for about half an hour, until reduced by a third.Leave to cool, then pass through a sieve and season with more salt to taste. Serve chilled or reheat gently, and finish with a drizzle of good olive oil.Grilled peach, tomato, almond ‘ricotta’ and roast almond saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenKirk Hayworth’s grilled peach, acidulated tomato, almond ‘ricotta’ and roast almond salad.Prep10 minSoak4 hr+Cook30 minChill2 hr+Serves4For the almond ‘ricotta’200g blanched almonds, soaked for at least 4 hours and up to overnight30ml lemon juice, plus extra to tasteSaltFor the salad4ripe peachesNeutral oil, for grillingExtra-virgin olive oilFlaky sea salt50g blanched almonds300g mixed tomatoes1 tbsp sherry vinegar1 tbsp lemon juiceBasil leaves, to serveDrain and rinse the soaked almonds, then put them in the jug of a blender with 600ml cold water and blend smooth. Fine strain through muslin or a nut milk bag (or your thinnest tea towel at a pinch!), and really squeeze out as much liquid as you can. Pour the resulting nut milk into a saucepan, put it on a medium heat and slowly bring up to 85C, stirring occasionally. Once the milk is up to temperature, take the pan off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and leave to cool. Once cooled, strain the milk through a muslin-lined sieve into a bowl or container, cover and chill for at least two hours, and preferably overnight, during which time the “milk” will separate into curds and whey. Taste the almond “ricotta” and season with salt and a squeeze of lemon juice to taste.Light the barbecue or put a griddle pan on a high heat. Cut the peaches in half, remove and discard the stones, then cut each half in half again and brush the cut sides with neutral oil. Grill the peaches flesh-side down, flipping as necessary until all the flesh sides are nicely charred and slightly softened, then brush the flesh with extra-virgin olive oil and season with a pinch of sea salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, put the blanched almonds on a baking tray and roast for 10 minutes, giving them a shake halfway through. Remove, leave to cool, then roughly chop.Depending on the size of your tomatoes, cut them in half, quarters or leave them whole, and put them in a large bowl. In a small bowl, whisk the sherry vinegar, lemon juice and a tablespoon of olive oil until emulsified, then pour the dressing over the tomatoes.To serve, dot a few spoonfuls of almond ricotta across four plates, then arrange the peaches and tomatoes in between. Tear the basil over the top, scatter on the almonds and serve.Kirk Haworth is chef/owner ofPlates, London EC1Explore more on these topicsFoodTomatoesSummer food and drinkSaladVegan food and drinkVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Boone the neglected puppy, rescued alongside 250 others | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Boone needed a home; my own dog needed company. When she picked him out at the shelter, all our lives took a turn for the better
Author: Faisa Mohamed
Headline: Boone needed a home; my own dog needed company. When she picked him out at the shelter, all our lives took a turn for the better
Content: Now Boone’s tail wags non-stop.Photograph: Courtesy of Dermot MurphyView image in fullscreenNow Boone’s tail wags non-stop.Photograph: Courtesy of Dermot MurphyThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Boone the neglected puppy, rescued alongside 250 othersBoone needed a home; my own dog needed company. When she picked him out at the shelter, all our lives took a turn for the betterDermot Murphy, as told toFaisa MohamedMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter 30 years working in theRSPCA, I had seen animals in unimaginable conditions. I saw dogs who had been left unattended at home for so long they began chewing doors and drinking water out of toilet bowls. I saw animals who had been stamped, kicked and even stabbed. But nothing could prepare me for Boone’s situation.Carson, the older of my two cocker spaniels, died in January. I could sense Bessie, an excitable bossy nine-year-old, was lonelier without him. They were both rescue animals. Carson was picked up by an RSPCA inspector and Bessie was abandoned at our local vet. Any dog I brought into our lives was a dog who needed a safe home.When I contacted the RSPCA about adopting a dog, they told me about a case where more than 250 poodle-crosses were living in a neglected home. All had matted fur and were covered in dirt and faeces. The owners were vulnerable and had found themselves in a situation that completely spiralled out of control.Bessie is the lady of the house and the decision to take Boone home was up to her. When we arrived at the centre where he was being treated, she immediately began playing with him. She had made her choice – Boone was ours.Boone was rescued in January when he was about 18 months old but could not be released into our care until March, after his vaccinations and initial rehabilitation were completed. His coat had to be shaved due to extreme matting and he needed treatment for an eye and ear infection.He wasn’t used to travelling in a car. He had never walked on a leash and would immediately lock his paws on to the ground. He wasn’t toilet trained and had a few accidents around the house.View image in fullscreenSofa comfort … Bessie (left) with Boone.Photograph: Courtesy of Dermot MurphyWhile he wasn’t sure about humans yet, he was sure about Bessie. On his first night at home I prepared a crate for him but he fell asleep on a dog bed. The next morning I found him and Bessie curled up together on the sofa.There was so much for Boone to learn. Even with my background working with animals, it was Bessie who trained him best. He learned to use the “toilet” by following Bessie into the garden. He began to tolerate his leash after watching Bessie happily accept hers, knowing that a walk awaited. He learned to play with balls by copying Bessie, a stark reminder that Boone had missed out on his puppy stages.When he arrived, his tail didn’t wag much. Three months later, it moves non-stop as he follows Bessie around excitedly. His coat is growing in and he is steadily gaining weight.Boone needed to be in a safe home but so did his previous owners. The cost of living and the growing mental health crisis means that there are more dogs out there like him. If you have the opportunity to rescue a dog, please do so. Taking him in was a wonderful lesson in patience and an opportunity to make my sassy older cocker spaniel feel like a puppy again.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetDogsPetsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I should be happy to have a pigeon for a friend. But she wouldn’t be my first choice | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Truman Capote had a ‘crow bro’; Dickens had a raven. And I get standoffish Susan, who has never brought me a present or perched on my shoulder, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Truman Capote had a ‘crow bro’; Dickens had a raven. And I get standoffish Susan, who has never brought me a present or perched on my shoulder, writes Emma Beddington
Content: ‘I can never seem to get a shred of attention from a black-feathered beauty.’Photograph: Chuchart Duangdaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I can never seem to get a shred of attention from a black-feathered beauty.’Photograph: Chuchart Duangdaw/Getty ImagesOpinionBirdsI should be happy to have a pigeon for a friend. But she wouldn’t be my first choiceEmma BeddingtonTruman Capote had a ‘crow bro’; Dickens had a raven. And I get standoffish Susan, who has never brought me a present or perched on my shoulderMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTShareOne of the greatest failures of my life to date (along with my sons’ shameful inability to eat apples correctly, down to the core) is my inability to attract a “crow bro”. That’s a corvid companion, and more and more people apparently have them, including Washington Post journalist Caitlin Gibson, who recentlywrote about hers, Cormac, a charismatic fish crow with a taste for cashews.It’s not a new phenomenon – Charles Dickens had a pet raven, Grip; Truman Capote had acrow called Lola– but thanks toCrowTok(a wholesome online enclave where people post enthusiastically about the exploits of their feathery familiars), there seem to be more corvid whisperers than ever. Yet however many unshelled peanuts (therecommended treat) I scatter, I can never seem to get a shred of attention from a black-feathered beauty.Corvids are clever and sophisticated. They canspontaneously problem-solve,use tools, arecapable of lying(and of working out when they’re being lied to), havecomplex responsesto the deaths of their comrades,hold – and pass on – grudges, even hold down jobs (rooks in thePuy du Fou theme parkpick up cigarette butts in return for food). They’re razor-sharp, and they don’t want to hang out with me. That stings.I might not have a crow bro, but I do have a pigeon pal. Susan – a mysterious ringed white pigeon – arrived three years ago and never left. Does shebring me presentsorperch on my shoulder? Absolutely not. Does she let me anywhere near her? Also no. She lives on our roof, shunning the two elaborate homes my husband built for her, shouting at us until I put out the specialist pigeon food I buy from an agricultural merchant a 20-minute drive away. Only then will she deign to descend to eat, under my servile, respectfully distant supervision (I have to stand guard or other pigeons chase her away). She pecks at the food, eyeing me warily, as if I’m about to put her in a pie, then leaves. No one would make a TikTok of this, but it’s a friendship of sorts, I like to think. Maybe we get the bird friends we deserve?Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
