title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: your passport to a folding phone future | Samsung | The Guardian
description: Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life
Content: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 ditches the skinny candy bar profile of its forebears in favour of a retro passport-like shape.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 ditches the skinny candy bar profile of its forebears in favour of a retro passport-like shape.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsungReviewSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: your passport to a folding phone futureNovel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery lifeSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Samsung’s latest folding phone breaks the mould with a squat, passport-like shape reminiscent of the Blackberry, which opens up to become a tablet similar to an iPad mini. It is certainly a better shape for a tablet than other designs, but is a short and wide phone when closed a compromise too far?The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is an entirely new variant in Samsung’s foldable family for this year launched alongside the Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more familiar candy bar shape. Both folders are extremely expensive, with the Fold 8 starting at £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699) and the Fold 8 Ultra at £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), withRAMageddondriving up prices even at the top of the market.While Samsung’sfirst folding phoneadopted a candy bar shape that opened up like a book to a square tablet, others began with more squat and wide forms including the originalGoogle Pixel FoldandMicrosoft Surface Duo. But as the technology matured most folders adopted the narrower closed form, which proved a better shape for performing phone-type duties such as messaging.View image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 in its closed form is almost the same size as a passport, feeling more like a small notepad than a phone.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 is 9.7mm thick when closed, which is about the same as a regular phone in a case, but its short and wide design looks more like a mini tablet or notepad in your hand. Its width also makes it hard to reach the other side of the screen one-handed, making it a two-handed affair most of the time, similar to huge superphonessuch as the Galaxy S26 Ultra.Photos, apps, games and websites look and work great on the crisp and super-bright outside screen. That is until you open the keyboard, which then takes up just over half the screen, leaving you very little space to see the content you are trying to type into. Apps that include a bar at the top, such as WhatsApp, shrink that space even further.View image in fullscreenWith the keyboard open you only have a narrow window to see the content of messages when typing on the Fold 8 (left) compared with a regular phone or the taller Fold 8 Ultra (right)Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOpen the Fold 8 like a book to reveal a beautiful 7.6in OLED display, which is crisp, smooth and super-bright, making it easy to see in direct sunlight. Like all folders the necessarily softer screen material is fragile and a fingerprint magnet, so needs regular gentle cleaning.The tablet screen’s 4:3 ratio matches that ofApple’s iPadsorMicrosoft’s Surfaces, which makes it a better fit for video with smaller black bars top and bottom when held in landscape compared to squarer foldables.View image in fullscreenWebsites, comics, books and apps look great on the inside screen when held in portrait orientation.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianPortrait orientation is great for websites and the keyboard only takes up about two-fifths of the screen giving you plenty of space with which to work. Most apps will present a dual-pane tablet interface in either orientation.But when you directly compare the Fold 8’s internal screen with last year’sFold 7or the new Fold 8 Ultra’s squarer display, you realise that landscape video is almost the same size on both tablets; only the thickness of the letterboxing black bars differs significantly.The speakers of the Fold 8 are pretty good for a phone, but they are only stereo when the tablet is held in portrait, not landscape when watching video which is unfortunate.View image in fullscreenWith both folders held in landscape, standard 16:9 ratio YouTube videos are 151 x 85mm on the Fold 8 Ultra (left) and 154mm x 86mm on the Fold 8 (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsMain screen:7.6in QXGA+ 120Hz (403ppi) AMOLED flexible displayCover screen:5.5in WUXGA+ 120Hz (428ppi) AMOLEDProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for GalaxyRAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:One UI 9 based onAndroid17Camera:50+50MP rear; 10MP+10MP selfie camerasConnectivity:5G, dual sim, e-sim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSSWater resistance:IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:123.9 x 81.9 x 9.7mmDimensions unfolded:123.9 x 161.4 x 4.5mmWeight:201gPlenty of power for multitaskingView image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 fully charges in 65 minutes hitting 70% in about half an hour using a 45W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included). It also supports 20W wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 has the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and memory asSamsung’s top S26 Ultraand performs very similarly, making it one of the fastest Android phones available with plenty of power for multitasking, gaming or anything else.The battery lasts a solid 40 hours between charge, using an even split of both screens for a total of eight hours on a mix of 5G and wifi for browsing, messaging, shooting photos and making notes. Gaming and other more intensive tasks drained the battery faster, but the Fold 8 should comfortably see out even the heaviest of days without needing a top up.One UI 9 softwareView image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 can have up to three apps on screen in a multiple different grid layouts with more running as small floating windows.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsung has the best, most adaptable software for making the most of folding phones, allowing multiple split-windowing configurations with up to three apps in a grid on screen and more in floating windows. One UI 9 is based on the latest Android 17 with Samsung providing Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.The great Now Bar remains from last year’s version for live sports scores, music, timers and other ongoing tasks at the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The improved Now Nudge, Samsung’s AI suggestion toolfrom the S26, can surface information from a greater number of sources in a wider range of apps. The Now Brief AI box remains a weak point, however, rarely suggesting anything useful beyond the weather or your calendar events.Google’s Gemini is baked in along with plenty of other AI tools that can occasionally be useful. One oddity is that if you choose not to have the same home screen on the outside and inside displays, the tablet screen ends up with two separate home screen layouts, one for portrait and one for landscape orientation. That means you have three separate home screens to customise with their own configuration of apps and widgets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has plenty of modes and can be used open or folded for different shooting methods.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 has two 10-megapixel selfie cameras but only two 50MP cameras on the back with no telephoto camera.The main 50MP camera is the best of the bunch and similar in performance to the main camera of thestandard S26, shooting good photos across a range of conditions. The 50MP ultrawide is also solid, with consistent colour across both cameras. The 2x crop zoom on the main camera works fairly well, but magnifying beyond to 4x or 10x digital zoom rapidly becomes poor.The Fold 8’s selfie cameras are decent and handy for video calls, but you get better results using the main camera for selfies with the outside screen as a viewfinder, even if it is a bit ungainly.The camera app has plenty of modes and shoots decent video, with some fancy auto-tracking features that make it easy to set the camera up partly folded and keep a subject in frame.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe crease in the middle where the screen folds is still evident when the display is off or you run your finger over it.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery has expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone isgenerally repairable. Inside screenrepairs cost about £600. Samsung offers aself-repair programme, as well as Care+accidental damage insurancethat reduces the cost of repairs to £50.The Fold 8 is made from 14.9% recycled material by weight, which Samsung breaks down inits environmental report. The company offerstrade-inandrecycling schemesfor old devices.PriceThe Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs from£1,699(€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699).For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs£1,899, theS26 Ultracosts£1,279, theHonor Magic V6costs£1,999.99and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,299.VerdictThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a bit of a curio from Samsung. Having forged the way with narrower book-style foldables, suddenly offering a squat, passport-shaped version seems like an odd step.On paper, the inside screen’s more conventional iPad-like shape makes it better suited to websites, video and apps. But because the Fold 8’s internal screen isn’t any wider than that of theFold 7or Fold 8 Ultra, apps have less screen space to work with while landscape videos are practically the same size, just with slimmer black bars at the top and bottom on the Fold 8.Meanwhile, the short and fat form of the closed Fold 8 makes for a worse phone experience. It is much harder to use one-handed and the keyboard takes up far too much of the screen. I didn’t find it any easier to fit in a pocket than narrower rivals, either.Shape aside, the Fold 8 is another stunning piece of technology from Samsung with excellent software to make the best of its folding form, plenty of processing power and surprisingly good battery life. But it only has two cameras on the back with no telephoto option, which is poor for this kind of money.The Fold 8 is better than some of the original attempts at the passport folder shapes, but there are many good a reasons book-style folding phones evolved into candy bar shapes over the last eight years.Pros:a phone and tablet in one, thin and light, powerful multitasking abilities, great tablet screen, top performance, solid battery life, water resistance.Cons:extremely expensive, passport-shape not ideal for phone duties, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, no telephoto camera.View image in fullscreenWith the Fold 8 Ultra (left) and Fold 8 (right), Samsung offers a choice of shapes for its book-style folding phones.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsSamsungAndroidSmartphonesTablet computersMobile phonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hastings Direct’s failures forced my family out of our home | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: A leak beneath our fridge-freezer last winter caused extensive damage but there’s still no functioning kitchen
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: A leak beneath our fridge-freezer last winter caused extensive damage but there’s still no functioning kitchen
Content: Hastings Direct insurance admitted its service had ‘fallen short’ after months of delay.Photograph: Nicholas Jermy/AlamyView image in fullscreenHastings Direct insurance admitted its service had ‘fallen short’ after months of delay.Photograph: Nicholas Jermy/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer affairsHastings Direct’s failures forced my family out of our homeA leak beneath our fridge-freezer last winter caused extensive damage but there’s still no functioning kitchenAnna TimsMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight months after reporting a leak to our home insurer, Hastings Direct, my husband and I and our two-year-old are still effectively homeless.Last winter, we discovered that an unnoticedleak beneath ourfittedfridge-freezer had caused extensive damage to the floorboards of our kitchen/living room.Since then we have experienced significant delays, poor communication and conflicting information, and what I believe is a failure by the insurer and itsappointedcontractors to properly manage the claim.A promised call-back never materialised because call staff failed to log the claim. Workfinally commencedmore than five months later.The contractors removed all the kitchen units, despite the fact that most were undamaged andwere not included in the schedule of works, and Hastings now wants us to contribute £8,000 to replacethem.There is still no functioning kitchen in the property, which means we cannot return home.We initially agreed to move into temporary accommodation for what we were told would be approximately two weeks. It’s now been nearly three months.The insurer only authorises accommodation in two-week increments, creating uncertainty about where we will stay next. We have had to pay for extra nursery sessions for our daughter since we both have to work from home, and the latest temporary flat is too small to accommodate all of us.We have also had to keep our two cats in a cattery at our expense and, because the kitchen is ill-equipped, we have to rely on takeaways and ready meals.We still have no clear timeline for when the workwill be finished.JS, CroydonHastings Direct readily admitted to me that on this occasion its service has fallen short. You will be delighted to hear that it is “taking forward learning” to improve things in the light of your ordeal.It attributes some of the delays to the unexpected extent of the damage, and some to “issues” with the contractors who are managing the claim. The kitchen units and appliances should never have been removed, it acknowledges.So why were you charged for their reinstatement? It was a “statement” that was issued “prematurely”, it says, adding that it would shoulder the cost of the blunder as a “goodwill gesture”.You contacted me in mid-June. Under pressure from me, the company has now agreed a programme of repairs and an estimated timescale. It simultaneously extended your accommodation for a month to give you some security.You hope to be back home in a week’s time, and Hastings has agreed to offer an as-yet-unspecified amount of compensation to reflect the distress caused and to refund your nursery, cattery and other expenses.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: A new start after 60: I took up slalom skateboarding – and I’m off to the world championships! | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Darren Miles had skateboarded all his life. But in his 50s, he realised he was losing his skills and flexibility. So he took it in a new direction
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Darren Miles had skateboarded all his life. But in his 50s, he realised he was losing his skills and flexibility. So he took it in a new direction
Content: ‘It’s amazing what humans can learn to do’ … Miles.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s amazing what humans can learn to do’ … Miles.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianA new start after 60Life and styleA new start after 60: I took up slalom skateboarding – and I’m off to the world championships!Darren Miles had skateboarded all his life. But in his 50s, he realised he was losing his skills and flexibility. So he took it in a new directionPaula CocozzaMon 10 Aug 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDarren Miles never thought he would compete in any sport for Britain. But in October, he will represent Great Britain in slalom skateboarding – a form of downhill racing – at theWorld Skate Gamesin Paraguay. Last week, he completed his World Anti-Doping Agency awareness training. He had to tick a box confirming: “I’m aninternational athlete.”“Justification” is the word that comes to mind, he says. “A feeling that I haven’t wasted my life skateboarding, that diverging into something new” – he took up slalom in his late 50s – “and working hard at it has yielded a result of which I am very proud.”“It’s now a personal ambition,” he adds, “to do my best. See who I can be.” A new feeling for someone who has lived with “all my light under a hundred bushels”.What he doesn’t often hear, he’s pleased to say, is: “Aren’t you too old?”Milesis 60 now, but he used to get asked that all the time when he was a teenager, skating to the shops or on the ramps where he lived in Colchester, Essex. His mum gave him a skateboard when he was 10; his aunt worked in the manufacturing factory. “We were the first generation of British skateboarders. And we didn’t know how long you could skateboard for. We just did it because we could do it,” he says.Darren Miles demonstrates his slalom skills on Plymouth promenadeHe pulls the little orange board his mother gave him out from beside his desk; it’s one of seven boards he keeps at home in Plymouth, south-west England.Miles has used a skateboard for almost his whole life – in his 20s, he skateboarded alongside his job repairing cameras, and in his 30s, while he went to university to study ocean science. He could ollie (a jumping technique) on to a handrail and slide down it, and he once skateboarded the legendary pipeline under the Mount Baldy reservoir in California. In his 40s, he continued to skateboard while working as a consultant specialising in flooding. He now manages flood risk for the local council.But a few years ago, he began to sense his world diminishing. “The amount of people I knew was shrinking.” And his flexibility was deteriorating.During Covid, taking his skateboard to the local park, he realised: “I would slowly be unable to do these tricks, one by one.” He completed a “quite basic” trick – a 180-degree turn – and a stranger voiced an appreciative “Yeah!”“‘Oh, no!’” Miles thought. “‘This is a grim glimpse into the future’ … They were impressed that I was an old person doing an easy trick. That didn’t sit comfortably with me.”Having sat a while with “the pain of my lost youth”, he made a conscious decision to take up slalom. He has had to learn new ways to move his body, and how to build momentum while changing direction between the cones on the racecourse. “You have to pump through. It’s unexpectedly physical … You’re always judging, relearning what you’re capable of.”View image in fullscreen‘We were the first generation of British skateboarders’ … Miles.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianManaging speed and sharp redirections – the course sounds like a lifetime in miniature. “It’s a surprising amount that happens in 15 seconds,” he says.Slalom appealed because Miles believed “there must be an element of learning at the beginning”. An upward curve, “where you get better”. For anyone who enjoys skateboarding, it’s “a surprising way to extend your skateboarding life”. He mentionsTony Alva, the American skateboarder who will turn 70 next year.Slalom has also enlarged Miles’s circle of friends. “Racing has a habit of forging close friendships in a short time,” he says. He’s raced in Cambridge, London, France, Germany, and trains at anannual slalom camp in Czechia.Occasionally he still dreams of skateboarding the ramps, as he used to, “when you carve up and you float – weightless, that’s a very seductive sensation”. Slalom carries the risk of banging his head or breaking a collarbone; competitors move so fast, they don’t know they’re falling until they land.But it’s the “upbeat and positive” attitude of slalom that appeals to him. “You can’t imagine not making it. You have to visualise yourself rolling out of the course.“I find it amazing what humans can learn to do with enough time and commitment.”Tell us: has your life taken a new direction after the age of 60?Explore more on these topicsLife and styleA new start after 60SkateboardingFitnessHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Safe, quick and painless’: what is a DXA scan, and do you need one for bone health? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: The imaging test is most often used to help determine a person’s risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: The imaging test is most often used to help determine a person’s risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures
Content: Photograph: Kalinovskiy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kalinovskiy/Getty ImagesWell actually‘Safe, quick and painless’: what is a DXA scan, and do you need one for bone health?The imaging test is most often used to help determine a person’s risk of osteoporosis and bone fracturesMadeleine AggelerMon 10 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDXA – or sometimes DEXA – scans are important for people in their 60s and above. They are also increasingly used by younger people interested in body composition.A DXA – dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry – scan is an imaging test that uses low-dose X-rays to evaluate a person’s bone health, explains Dr Michael Perry, associate professor of radiology and medical imaging at the University of Virginia’s school of medicine. Most often, DXA scans are used to measure the strength and mineral content of an individual’s bones. This in turn helps determine that person’s risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures.This is valuable information, as broken bones in older adults can be “the start of more serious health problems and can lead to long-term disability”, according to theNational Institute on Aging.DXA scans can also help estimate body composition including “fat percentage, muscle mass, and where fat is distributed throughout the body”, explains Dr Ann Malbas, an endocrinologist at the Mayo Clinic who specializes in bone diseases.How exactly do DXA scans work and who needs one? We asked experts.How do DXA scans work?DXA scans are “safe, quick and painless”, says Malbas. During a scan, a person lies on a padded table while a scanning arm passes over their body. Two low-dose X-ray beams measure the amount of minerals in the bones, specifically in the hip and spine. It usually takes 10-20 minutes to complete.At 58, I have the spine of an 80-year-old. Navigating osteoporosis has been difficult and expensiveRead moreThe process is the same for measuring body composition, but instead of bone mineral density, itmeasures other elements, like total body fat percentage, fat distribution and lean mass.Who should get a DXA scan?“DXA is recommended for women aged 65 and older and men ages 70 years and older, as well as younger adults who have important risk factors,” says Dr Shadpour Demehri, professor of radiology and radiological science at Johns Hopkins University’s school of medicine.Risk factors for low bone density, which may make a DXA scan advisable, include a previous broken bone from a minor fall or injury, long-term use of steroid medications like prednisone, a family history of osteoporosis or hip fractures, and certain medical conditions like COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).Getting regular scans is important for high-risk populations, because osteoporosis is known as a “silent disease” – a condition most people don’t know they have until they experience a fracture. It’s also common, Malbas says, with osteoporotic fractures affecting one in three women and one in five men over age 50.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, 'Well Actually', then 'Read more on living a good life in a complex world,' then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say 'More from this section'Because it is easy and uses relatively low levels of radiation, a DXA scan is considered safe for most populations, though Demehri says that “pregnancy is generally considered a reason to postpone the examination, because it involves ionizing radiation”.People who have recently had imaging tests that include contrast material, like barium studies, may also have to delay their scans, as these materials can interfere with the accuracy of results, explains Malbas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs for those curious to know more about their body composition, DXA scans can provide a more accurate snapshot of one’s health.“Often, people associate body weight with health, but body weight measurements only account for the total amount of someone’s tissue, and not what type of tissue,” says Perry. This matters because studies have shown that body composition may have a better correlation with health than overall weight.“Someone may fall into the overweight category but may have large amounts of muscle but very little fat,” he says. “Conversely, a person with very low muscle mass may be at higher risk for falls and illness despite being ‘normal’ weight.”Lift, rest, recover: how to start weightliftingRead moreStill, routine DXA scans are not essential for most young people, as they are “unlikely to provide information that changes medical care”, says Demehri. Regardless of whether one has high or low body fat, he explains, medical recommendations remain the same: “Regular physical activity, strength training, an optimally balanced diet and maintaining a proper weight remain the most important recommendations regardless of the exact body fat percentage,” he says.What do you do if you have low bone density?If a DXA scan reveals low bone density, several effective strategies can help reduce one’s risk of future fractures, says Demehri. These include:regular weight-bearing and resistance exerciseadequate calcium and vitamin D intakeavoiding smoking and excessive alcohol consumptionprescription medications to strengthen bones“Bone health and muscle health are closely connected,” Demehri adds. “Strong muscles help support the skeleton, improve balance and reduce the risk of falls, while healthy bones provide the structural framework for movement.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHealthAgeingMedicinefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … you need to detox your scalp? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A good scalp cleanse can be useful, but it partly depends where you live
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: A good scalp cleanse can be useful, but it partly depends where you live
Content: Illustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … you need to detox your scalp?A good scalp cleanse can be useful, but it partly depends where you liveKate LloydMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe’re experiencing the “skinification” of the scalp, says Desmond Tobin, professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin. After decades of consumer obsession with improving the quality of facial skin, attention is now being turned to our heads.A wave of products have launched – from scalp scrubs and acid exfoliants to deep-cleaning shampoos – claiming to “detox” the scalp and promising everything from shinier hair to boosted growth.“It’s obviously a business opportunity,” says Tobin. “If brands have something that works on skin, they might be able to roll it over. It goes quickly and cheaply into another product range.”double quotation markPeople who live in highly polluted areas could also have deposits of traffic-associated chemicals on their scalpsTobin says he’d never use the word “detox”, because the process these products are helping does not remove anything toxic in the dangerous sense. But an occasional scalp cleanse can be useful for some of us, he says.Is it true that … a cold shower is the best way to cool down on a hot night?Read more“Some people throw so much product on their hair that some of it is likely to build up, not only on the hair, but also on the scalp. This could clog the hair follicle openings and interfere with optimal hair growth. It’s quite possible that a quick shower in the morning might not remove everything.”This is especially possible in hard water areas where minerals in the water can react with products to form a sticky residue. Tobin adds that people who live in highly polluted urban areas could also have deposits of traffic-associated chemicals on their scalps.Tobin says you may not need to buy an expensive product to deep clean your scalp. He advises people in hard water areas to use “a sulfate-free high-lather shampoo or to double-shampoo to break down mineral and product buildup”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …Hair careMen's hairBeautyWomen's hairfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A slow, boozy bus tour of Hungary’s secret vineyards | Travel | The Guardian
description: The spa town of Balatonfüred is a bucolic gem for sailors, hikers … and wine lovers. A new hop-on, hop-off bus tour offers a chance to get a taste of its little-known wineries
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The spa town of Balatonfüred is a bucolic gem for sailors, hikers … and wine lovers. A new hop-on, hop-off bus tour offers a chance to get a taste of its little-known wineries
Content: The wine tours are conducted on a vintage bus brought over from the Netherlands.Photograph: Buruzs PetraView image in fullscreenThe wine tours are conducted on a vintage bus brought over from the Netherlands.Photograph: Buruzs PetraTravelA slow, boozy bus tour of Hungary’s secret vineyardsThe spa town of Balatonfüred is a bucolic gem for sailors, hikers … and wine lovers. A new hop-on, hop-off bus tour offers a chance to get a taste of its little-known wineriesSarah RodriguesMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 90-minute train journey south-west from Budapest to the spa town of Balatonfüred unveils a landscape that segues from gritty industrial compounds to long sweeps of golden sunflowers and fields of pale grain. The carriage is pleasingly retro, with thick velour upholstery; windows that open, awkwardly, with a stiff metal lever; and a bushy eyebrowed conductor replete with ticket machine slung over his shoulder.But the real retromania is yet to come. Arriving at Balatonfüred station, I board a 1984 DAF bus, painted an almost audacious shade of green. From the open-air rear, I take in the view over Lake Balaton, central Europe’s largest freshwater lake, often referred to as the “Hungarian Sea”.A spa resort town since the late 18th century, Balatonfüred is a popular place for sailing and swimming, while the hilly countryside to the north is great for mountain bikers and hikers. It’s also home to hundreds of wineries, many of which have traditionally been difficult to access – especially without a car. The bus I’m on – the hop-on, hop-off46° Balaton Borbuszthat launched this summer – has changed all this, by taking visitors on day trips to local vineyards.It’s the brainchild of Virág Szabó, who has spent summers in the region since childhood. “The idea first came to me when I was travelling in South Africa, on the vintage wine tram that runs between Stellenbosch and Franschhoek,” she says. “I couldn’t believe that nobody had thought to do something similar here.” The 46° moniker is a reference to the fact that this area occupies the same latitude as Bordeaux, Burgundy and the Rhône.She found the bus in the Netherlands and, by May this year, had signed up 22 wineries along two distinct routes – one focused on better-known growers and the other on more remote ones. Since then, seven more have joined and many more are eager to get involved. “I have three criteria. Is the wine good? Are there nice views? And is the winery able to offer some form of hospitality?” she says. Many of the wineries are family-owned and run, with no previous thought of opening up to visitors. Very little of Hungary’s wine is marketed, and only around one-third is exported. Less still has it ever been the stuff of tourism.View image in fullscreenVineyards on the shore of Lake Balaton.Photograph: Bernadett Pogacsas-Simon/AlamyThe bus departs Balatonfüred about every two hours from 11am, with the final drop-off at 9pm and the option to visit four wineries. Guests can either choose these in advance or pick en route – and, if the bus returns for you and two hours have flashed by before you’re ready, you can simply ask to be collected two hours later. While tourism in Hungary is booming, with Budapest the country’s primary draw, the Borbusz hopes to lure visitors further afield, offering an alternative insight into the country – and the chance to meet local people. Originally, it was planned to run only until September – but will now operate until mid-October, thanks to its early popularity.Our first stop is Mórocz Pince (“pince” is the Hungarian for “cellar”), reached via a moderately steep, rocky path from the main road. Founded by former musician Tamás Mórocz, it produces between 4,000 and 5,000 bottles each year, with traminer and merlot rosé among its specialities. “During Soviet times, the emphasis was on quantity, for exporting to eastern bloc countries, rather than quality,” he says. “Fortunately, that’s no longer the case.”double quotation markMany of the wineries are family-owned and run, with no previous thought of opening up to visitorsAlthough just 38, Mórocz has been making wine for 15 years. “I wanted to approach it differently,” he says. “In a way that was lighthearted, irreverent and down to earth.” One way he’s achieved this is through his labels, with each vintage given a different theme. The 2025 bottles show photos, taken from family albums, of his grandfather, who introduced him to wine. “He died in 2012, so he doesn’t know he’s famous,” says Mórocz, with a smile. Over charcuterie platters on the terrace, with rows of vines and the expanse of the lake as a backdrop, it feels less like a tasting, and more like we’re drinking and chatting with friends – and the wine is delicious.We continue on, and some of the group jump off at another winery, Balogh, just down the hill from Mórocz. But Szabó has told me about the charismatic owner of Gazdag Pince, and I’m keen to meet him, so I remain on the bus for another 15 minutes as we pass neatly combed vineyards and pretty villages. “We only make wines that we want to drink,” says Gábor Gazdag, welcoming us to his winery. “I used to play badminton, but then I got too fat, and I started worrying about being bored in retirement. I wasn’t interested in hunting, fishing or collecting stamps – but I like wine, so I bought this land. It’s a hobby for me.”View image in fullscreenWine tasting at the Mórocz Pince vineyard.Photograph: Sarah RodriguesFor Gazdag, this may be a way to stave off lethargy in older age; for János Fogl, at next door’s Madaras Pince, “it’s my life”. Szabó tells me that Fogl – who has been making wine since 1994 – is a genius, cross-breeding grapes to create unique varieties that shouldn’t work in this region. Shaded under a vine-tangled trellis, we start with a cherry liqueur before moving on to a dizzying selection of wines. Each time I think we’re finished, Fogl shuffles off to his cellar and produces another bottle.Music spills from the Borbusz speakers as we travel back, picking up passengers – couples and groups of friends – from other wineries along the way. Everyone is in an unmistakably ebullient mood; this will almost certainly turn to somnolence later.The next day, floating in the warm, shallow waters of the lake, I watch families playing ballgames and the slow glide of sailboats. Novices wobble uncertainly on paddleboards; the more experienced strike confidently away from the shore. It’s hard to imagine that this was once undesirable marshland, and that the older buildings in Balatonfüred were constructed to face away from it. Thanks to large-scale civil engineering, the lake reinvented itself; now, the area’s wineries, with the help of the 46° Balaton Borbusz, seem poised to do the same – opening up their terraces, and their stories, to new generations of visitors.The trip was provided byVisit Balaton 365and46°Balaton Borbusz. A full day ticket on the 46°Balaton Borbusz is €42Explore more on these topicsTravelWine holidaysHungaryFood and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon | Hospitals | The Guardian
description: Concerns about feeling pressure to have caesarean section, or paying for hotel in Exeter after hospital in Barnstaple suspends birthing services
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Concerns about feeling pressure to have caesarean section, or paying for hotel in Exeter after hospital in Barnstaple suspends birthing services
Content: Expectant mothers in the region face having to travel for at least an hour and a half to give birth in a maternity unit.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenExpectant mothers in the region face having to travel for at least an hour and a half to give birth in a maternity unit.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianHospitals‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in DevonConcerns about feeling pressure to have caesarean section, or paying for hotel in Exeter after hospital in Barnstaple suspends birthing servicesSteven MorrisMon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 04.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor mother-to-be Harriet Knight, the suspension of maternity services at one of England’s most remote hospitals means having to face horribly stark choices.“The next closest maternity unit is a full two hours away and we have a family history of labour taking under two hours from start to finish,” said Knight.“So we have the option of potentially giving birth in a layby on the northDevonlink road as we try to get there or opting for free-birthing at home with no access to maternity care.”Sunday was the last day that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple accepted women in spontaneous labour. From Tuesday,births at the hospital will be suspendedbecause of “unsafe levels of medical staffing”.Mothers in labour will have to trek to Exeter or Taunton, at least an hour and a half away, but usually more, especially at this time of year when the roads are thick with holiday traffic.“It feels there is no safe option at the moment,” said Knight, who is 34 weeks pregnant. “We live in one of the most rural places in the country and this has left pregnant mothers in north Devon in a really scary situation. It feels like a complete failure by the hospital trust.”One option she and her partner are considering is spending all their savings on temporary accommodation in Exeter as her due day approaches. “Moving out may be the only thing we can do to keep us safe,” Knight said.View image in fullscreenHarriet Knight said pregnant women in the area had been left in a ‘really scary situation’.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianHannah Rulton, who is expecting her third baby in November, is to undergo a caesarean section because during her second labour she and her child suffered severe shoulder dystocia, an obstetric emergency in which the baby’s head is delivered, but the shoulder gets stuck behind the mother’s pubic bone.“He was stuck for 11 minutes. Both my son and I very nearly died. The trauma of that birth has never left us. Every appointment during this pregnancy has brought back memories,” she said.“I have been told there is a significant chance of shoulder dystocia occurring again and what now keeps me awake at night is the fear of going into labour before my planned surgery. The thought of making that journey knowing I have a history of one of the most time-critical obstetric emergencies imaginable is absolutely terrifying.“Instead of looking forward to meeting our baby, I am worrying about whether I will go into labour early, whether I will make it to another hospital in time and whether I could be forced to relive the worst day of my life.”View image in fullscreenHealth officials said that temporarily suspending birth services at the site was the ‘only safe course of action’.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianCarolyn Mills, the chief nursing officer at Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, said suspending services had been an “exceptionally difficult” decision.She said: “Unfortunately, we have now reached the point where we cannot safely provide the level of medical cover required to continue births at North Devon district hospital.Factors leading to failures in NHS maternity care | LettersRead more“While we recognise the additional travel this will mean for some families, we believe that concentrating services where safe medical staffing can be guaranteed is the safest option.”The trust said its projected consultant maternity rotas were at times 50% short, and tier 2 (registrar) doctors 40% short because of staff departures, maternity leave, absences through sickness and a scarcity of locums on short notice. It said it was continuing to work to recruit more staff.Births and face-to-face triage will be suspended. Other services including community midwifery, scans and antenatal outpatient clinics are continuing. The trust said it would restart birthing services when it was safe but could not estimate a timeframe.Almost 15,000 people have signeda petition started by Ian Roome, the local Liberal Democrat MP, expressing concern.He said he felt the trust had taken its eye off the ball on recruitment. “Babies are going to be born in laybys,” he said. “There may be deaths.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLouise Pamment, a local resident who mentors women, has set upa campaign on Instagramcalling for medical staff to apply for positions in north Devon. “I’ve seen genuine fear and distress in the women in my life who are pregnant,” she said.Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said: “Maternity services are currently under huge pressure, and we are aware of staffing gaps on almost every obstetric rota in the country. The RCOG is calling for urgent investment in the maternity workforce – to ensure safe staffing levels, so that we can provide the compassionate care that women and families deserve.”Chloe Ross, who is due to have her second child in October, described the situation as “utterly dangerous”. She said she had a previous bad birthing experience in Exeter and only decided to have another baby having moved to north Devon, thinking she would be able to give birth locally.“The idea of Exeter dealing with the additional pressures of women coming from our catchment is terrifying. Any way you look at it, women will have to labour in cars on overcrowded roads for nearly two hours,” Ross said.“The loss of triage will prevent women seeking support for things such as low movement, HG [extreme sickness] and much more.”View image in fullscreenChloe Ross, pictured with her son Milo, said she had only decided to have another baby after moving to north Devon because of her previous bad experience in Exeter.Photograph: Family handoutHannah, another expectant mother, is due to have her baby in January. “But I’ve already been told to prepare for travelling to Exeter to give birth,” she said.“As a first-time mum, it’s inevitable that questions are running through my mind. Will I make it to the hospital in time, or could I end up giving birth on the A361? At the moment, I’m feeling positive about labour and birth, but having to factor in such a long journey adds an extra source of anxiety that shouldn’t have to be there.What does the Amos report reveal about maternity and neonatal care in England?Read more“Many expectant parents are already talking about booking Airbnbs or hotels near their due dates to reduce the risk of not reaching Exeter in time. My partner and I are fortunate: we have access to cars, can afford temporary accommodation if necessary and have a strong support network around us.“But the closure of the unit will have the greatest impact on those who don’t have those advantages. How will people without reliable transport, financial flexibility or family support get to Exeter, particularly if an ambulance isn’t available?”She is also concerned some women may feel pressure to have planned caesarean sections, “simply because it offers certainty about when and where they will give birth. A caesarean is major surgery and should be a clinical choice, not something women feel forced to consider because local maternity services are unavailable.”Explore more on these topicsHospitalsHealthDevonNHSWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content
