He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.He came to deliver in person the message that theTrump administrationwants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.Last week, Netanyahuscaled backIsraeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”.Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October.Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspapernoted.It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”.Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security expertshave warned.Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpTrump administrationanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Monday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quo | Israel | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity
Author: Hettie O'Brien
Headline: In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity
Content: The religious right stormed the restricted area in July, apparently with the support of Benjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe religious right stormed the restricted area in July, apparently with the support of Benjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesFirst Edition newsletterIsraelMonday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quoIn today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicityHettie O'BrienMon 10 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 01.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover.With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahurejected a US-backed 15 point planfor peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in theWest Bankand East Jerusalem before its mandate expires.For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent,Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem. That’s after the weekend roundup.Weekend roundupUK politics| Sadiq Khanhas called on the governmentto commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves.US politics| The US Senate voted toconfirm Todd Blanche as attorney generalin a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.US-Israel war on Iran| Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterwayremained out of reachon Saturday.Russia-Ukraine| Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia,Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Seaafter a series of strikeson civilian ships thereWorld news| The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group wasextradited from Dubai on Sundayand met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.In depth: ‘To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull’View image in fullscreenOne of the most contentious places on earth.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesThe al-Haram al-Sharif site in Jerusalem’s old city, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is one of the most contentious places on earth. It’s governed by a fragile agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to pray and worship there, while Jews pray at the Western Wall below. But Israel’s messianic right, which has gained a powerful foothold in Netanyahu’scoalition government, is fixated on the site as a symbol of its political project. Their vision of building a new Jewish temple on one of Islam’s holiest sites – once a fringe idea – has become increasingly widespread.Since 2023, Jewish religious extremists have made numerous visits to the 35-acre compound which is home to both al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, the holiest sites for Muslims in Jerusalem and one of holiest sites for Muslims in the world. “At first, you had groups of perhaps 20 Jews, mostly settlers, who were escorted by the police to the far wall of the compound to pray discreetly,” Julian tells me. “If you were just a casual visitor, you wouldn’t necessarily see them”. Over the last two years, however, the groups have grown bigger and more audacious. On 23 July, they sang the national anthem, and prayed and performed rituals in the centre of the compound, while Israeli police – who report to Ben-Gvir, who was in attendance – set up tents to provide shade to the worshippers.“To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull,” Julian says. “The longstanding fear is that Israelis would knock down the Dome of the Rock or the mosque, or rebuild a [Jewish] temple on the site. And these tents were part of a gradual attempt to push the boundaries.” Eight Arab nations swiftly issued a joint statement condemning “mass incursions by settlers led by extremist Israeli ministers”. Last Wednesday, the Jordanian authorities, who administer the site, held anemergency meetingof Arab and Islamic nations to discuss these risks, and afterwards, the Jordanian authorities condemned Israeli violations and warned that they constituted a “blatant provocation” to Muslims worldwide.“All they can do is issue strong statements, saying, ‘don’t do this’,” says Julian. The Waqf, the Jordanian-appointed foundation that manages the site, is “defenceless”, he explains. In the run-up to Ramadan this year, Waqf sourcestold the Guardianthat five of its staff had been detained by the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service. Meanwhile, Israeli police have begunactively recruitingextremist activists to serve in the Temple Mount Unit, the force responsible for policing the compound. Accordingto Haaretz, the deputy commander of the police’s Temple Mount Unit published a callout to officers on social media and in WhatsApp groups associated with West Bank settlers. “Anyone who wants to take part in implementing sovereignty is welcome to contact me,” he wrote.Why is the site so significant?The site’s history is constantly enlisted in attempts to justify the present. Muslims know the raised compound in the south-east of Jerusalem as al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary), or simply al-Aqsa, after the mosque located at its southern edge. Next to the mosque, at the centre of the compound, is the Dome of the Rock, one of the oldest surviving Islamic places of worship. It’s on this site the prophet Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven.At the base of the compound is the Western Wall, a section of retaining wall that survived the destruction of the second Jewish temple in 70CE. The Temple Mount is also the holiest site inJudaism, the site of two temples which were built and then destroyed by invaders in ancient times.Access to the site has been delicately managed for centuries. After the six-day war in 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Israeli government agreed that Jordan would continue to be the site’s custodian. Since then, the “status quo”, as it is known, has sought to prevent violent conflict by circumscribing the rights of Muslims and Jews to access the compound. While Jews are permitted to visit the site at specific times, they cannot pray there. Many Jews opt not to visit the site, out of fear of treading on holy ground while ritually impure.“The status quo represented a historic compromise. Jews got the Western Wall. Muslims got Haram al-Sharif,” Julian says. “But the site has always been a detonator, sitting right there in the centre of the old city, with strong religious beliefs crammed together in a small area.”How has this erupted in the past?It’s not uncommon in the region for holy sites to be carefully managed with intricate arrangements. Elsewhere in the Old City, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is divided up between six Christian denominations, with its keys held by two Muslim families. At the Cave of the Patriarchs in the occupied city of Hebron, a mosque and synagogue share one building.Past Israeli moves to challenge the status quo at al-Haram al-Sharif have been incendiary, sparking deadly violence. In 2000, then Israeli opposition leader and future prime minister Ariel Sharon made a visit to the site in an attempt to demonstrate Israeli sovereignty, sparking a chain of events that helped ignitethe second intifada. More recently, Hamas gave the name “al-Aqsa flood” to its attack on Israel in October 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and triggered the war on Gaza, claiming it was provoked by Israeli violations at the Jerusalem mosque.What’s the end goal of these incursions?Some Jewish extremists have begun marching under the temple flag – a star of David overlaid with a picture of the (as yet nonexistent) third temple they hope to build. “You see these flags on the bulldozers that are flattening neighbourhoods in Gaza, and soldiers wearing patches with a picture of the third temple on them,” Julian says.The rise of the third temple movement comes at a time of surging attacks on Palestinians in the occupiedWest Bank, with the scale of violence prompting urgent calls for intervention from the heart of the Israeli establishment.Earlier this year,dozens of Israelis, including two former prime ministers, former heads of its security services and former judges, signed a “final warning” threatening legal action against their government over its support for “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank. They argued the actions of the government had isolated Israel internationally and put its security at risk.“There’s a feeling that the far-right side of Netanyahu’s government is now creating unnecessary, long-term security problems for Israel,” Julian says. That extends to attempts to change the status quo at al-Aqsa.Netanyahu has publicly backed Jewish prayer at the site, claiming that changes pushed by Ben-Gvir werecoordinated with him. “This isn’t the stuff of radicals any more,” Julian says. “It has government approval.”The week to comeWednesday| A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the whole of the UK, with the south-west of England getting the best of British views. Parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain will experience a total eclipse.Thursday| Clacton-on-sea residents will vote in the byelection Nigel Farage triggered last month, with the Reform leader taking on 33 mostly novelty candidates. Results are expected early Friday.Thursday| The Office for National Statistics will publish UK GDP figures for the second quarter of 2026.What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenYorleny Weigel holds a photograph of Gerson Turcios.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianSo many horror stories have emerged fromICE raidsand arrests in the US. Alex Hannafordreports expertlyon the ongoing nightmare for one young man snatched in upstate New York.MichaelYoung people – particularly those who came of age during the pandemic – have had a pretty raw deal. I enjoyedthis pieceon what “Neets” need, by William Davies (£).HettieI was already looking forward to readingSymeon Brown’s new book, andthis interviewhas confirmed it’ll be on my holiday reading list.Michaelskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering celebrates at the finish line.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesCycling| Demi Volleringwon the final stageto seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage.Football| London City Lionesses’ headline signing,Alexia Putellas, talks expectations, the lure of playing in England and the prospect of being kicked by her former teammates.Football| Fifa last night issueda thinly veiled attackon Uefa and other leading figures in European football in a statement which alleged there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president”.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Labour wants ‘deeper’ ties to EU under Burnham, says minister”, is theGuardian’s front page today. TheTimeswrites “PM’s adviser ‘concerned’ over Labour wealth taxes”,Metrohas “Andy wants a cancel culture” and theMailsays “Labour jail plan to spark 89,000 more crimes”.TheTelegraphhas “Chinese spy cameras found on Navy drones”, while theExpressleads on “You must keep our Fenella’s killer in jail”. On the heatwave, theMirrorsays “Days of danger”, and thei Paper’s headline is “Car washes and swimming pools could face water bans in UK’s next heatwave”.Today in FocusView image in fullscreenSocial media influencer James Beckett explains how he got into the world of finance and his aim to be ‘financially free’ by 45.Photograph: Rehan Khan/EPAThe Gen Z investorsAre Gen Z the most financially savvy generation of them all? Economics correspondent,Richard Partington,charts the rise of investors like social media influencer James Beckett and those even younger,and explores why Gen Z are differentfrom those who came before them when it comes to personal finance.Cartoon of the day | Tom GauldView image in fullscreenIllustration: Tom GauldThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenJo Moseley paddleboarding on the Esk in North Yorkshire.Photograph: Mary DaviesFrom paddleboarding the River Esk where you can experience tranquil wildlife and views of Whitby, to wild camping along the River Dart, a place which offers pristine moorland, oak-lined valleys and solitary swims in deep pools. There are many places to mess about on the river andfind some peace and joy.For more solo adventures you can relax with some fly‑fishing along the River Dove, a place which blends tricky casts, and pastoral beauty, where wild brown trout rise in crystalline, fast‑flowing pools. Something more strenuous might be a hike to find the sources of the Severn and Wye, a journey which blends scorching moorland with the wildlife‑rich upper Wye valley.Or take it all in by canoe along the River Tay in Perthshire, and enjoy kingfisher spotting and the view of beaver lodges.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsIsraelFirst Edition newsletterWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuIslamJudaismnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates | India | The Guardian
description: Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
Content: Students march towards Jharkhand’s state assembly in protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudents march towards Jharkhand’s state assembly in protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaPolice use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalatesDemonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobsPenelope MacRaein DelhiMon 10 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.The unrest comes just weeks after theCockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.How gen Z exposed India’s prime-time propaganda machineRead moreThe demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.View image in fullscreenPolice use water cannon to disperse demonstrators during a protest.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar/AFP/Getty ImagesThe state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsiaYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: British national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forces | Kashmir | The Guardian
description: Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters
Content: Protesters gather to support the Joint Awami Action Committee in Kotli, Kashmir on 30 July.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenProtesters gather to support the Joint Awami Action Committee in Kotli, Kashmir on 30 July.Photograph: ReutersKashmirBritish national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forcesMohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protestersShivam PatelMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security forces and protesters, the Guardian can reveal.Another Briton has been held in a regional prison for more than two months despite his family’s efforts to secure his release through the Foreign Office.The details, which have not been previously reported, shed light on how Britons with familial ties to the region have been affected by the clashes, which have killed dozens in the Himalayan territory and posed the biggest challenge for Pakistani authorities in recent years.Mohammad Akhtar, 50, a resident of Peterborough, was killed on 9 June after his family said Pakistani security forces opened fire on a gathering where protesters were demanding economic and electoral reforms in the disputed region that is also claimed by India.View image in fullscreenMohammad Akhtar, from Peterborough, was killed in Kashmir.Photograph: SuppliedAkhtar was staying in the city of Kotli, close to the area where the clashes occurred, and his family said he was hit by a stray bullet.“He wasn’t taking part in protests but the demonstrations were happening close to his house,” said Mohammad Saad, Akhtar’s cousin.“There was firing by the forces that day and he was hit by a stray bullet. There was a bullet wound on the side of his chest,” said Saad, adding that Akhtar’s children decided not to pursue the matter with British authorities.They could not get a police complaint registered inKashmirand feared that the family could be targeted if the case was highlighted, said Saad.The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: “The UK is deeply concerned by the situation in parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.“FCDO ministers and the UK high commissioner in Islamabad are in touch with their counterparts, and UK travel advice was updated on 7 August and continues to advise against all but essential travel to affected areas.”It is understood that MP Hamish Falconer, during his previous role as a Foreign Office minister, raised the situation in Kashmir in talks with his counterparts during a 16-17 June visit to Islamabad. Stephen Doughty, who currently holds the role in the Foreign Office, has also been in touch with his counterparts.Pakistan’s foreign ministry and its high commission in London did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment.Islamabad has been accused of launching aviolent crackdown on supporters of the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a civil society group that launched protests in Kashmir months ahead of a three-phase vote in the region that began on 27 July and which have been repeatedly disrupted by the unrest.Pakistan declared the JAAC a terrorist organisation and has imposed a communications blackout in the region since 5 June. Its security forces have been accused of fatally shooting at least 30 people during demonstrations last month – charges the government has rejected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe JAAC said Pakistani authorities were trying to suppress dissent and have detained scores of its supporters, who it said were ordinary Kashmiris. It has described the current elections as a “sham”, being held “at gunpoint”.Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in KashmirRead moreWaqas Arif, 38, a British national from Nottingham, was among those detained in the Kashmiri city of Mirpur after protests on 5 June, but his family said he did not take part in the demonstrations.His sister Sumera said: “Waqas was not involved in any kind of protests. But since my other two brothers were involved and they went for the protests with everybody else, the Pakistani forces along with the Rangers came into my house and they took my brothers away.“There is no charge. He hasn’t done anything. This is my brother, but I think there are thousands of other brothers like him from everywhere who they have put in [prison] so they can minimise the protest power … they have not even been taken to court,” she said.Arif’s wife, Varisha Kampulvi, said British authorities had not been able to make direct contact with him since he was taken to the prison in Mirpur.Kampulvi has highlighted Arif’s case to British authorities. A Foreign Office email sent to her on 26 June said: “Consular staff have been able to make contact with officials at the prison where Waqas is currently being held, although we have not had direct contact with Waqas.“The authorities have confirmed that Waqas is in good health, which we were extremely pleased to hear.”Explore more on these topicsKashmirPakistanSouth and central AsiaForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shops | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Vape shops in England and Wales to need planning permission while betting shop law change will also apply in Scotland
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Vape shops in England and Wales to need planning permission while betting shop law change will also apply in Scotland
Content: Two vape shops trading next door to each other on Fargate in Sheffield.Photograph: Katy Blackwood/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenTwo vape shops trading next door to each other on Fargate in Sheffield.Photograph: Katy Blackwood/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.GamblingBurnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shopsVape shops in England and Wales to need planning permission while betting shop law change will also apply in ScotlandAletha AduandAlexandra ToppingMon 10 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCouncils are to be given powers to stop betting and vape shops taking over their high streets under new plans announced byAndy Burnham.Local authorities will be able to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres, while vape shops will be subject to planning permission under plans Downing Street said could be in place from the start of next year.Burnham is promising to scrap the “aim to permit” rule in theGamblingAct 2005, which in effect requires councils to allow new gambling premises where applications meet licensing requirements.This could mark a big shift from changes introduced by Keir Starmer in April that gave councils more scope to consider the number of gambling premises already in an area but stopped short of scrapping the “aim to permit rule”.As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called on Starmer to abolish the rule in January, alongside almost 300 other politicians and campaigners.Burnham said communities should have much more control over their high streets, where traditional shops, pubs and other services have disappeared while vape and gambling shops have expanded.Burnham is attempting to make the first weeks of his prime ministership about tangible changes people can see in their everyday lives.A No 10 source said the government was determined to crack down on vape and betting shops because they were two of the most visible signs of decline on high streets, and local people were genuinely concerned. A fast-tracked consultation on the new measures would take six weeks, with the aim of having the measures in place by the start of 2027.“Local people will actually have more of an input into whether or not those shops should open in the first place, giving them a proper say about how their high streets should look,” they said.The move comes after research suggested Labour would be“washed away in a tide of discontent”at the next general election unless it tackled the decline of Britain’s high streets.Prof Will Jennings, who led the University of Southampton research, said Burnham’s targeting of vape and betting shops was “an important first step”. With nearlyone in three retail salesin the UK now online, it was clear that the policy would “not solve everything”, he said. “But it is speaking to some real area of concern that impacts how people view their local area.”Vape shops currently fall into the same planning category as shops, cafes and banks, meaning they can open without needing a new planning application. Ministers will consult on putting them into their own planning category so councils will be able to consider each new vape shop application individually and reject those they deem not appropriate for the area.The government is also looking at tightening the definition of what a vape shop is, to prevent people saying they were opening a convenience store that had the primary function of selling vapes. It will also make provisions to stop them opening near schools. Angela Rayner said the move addressed problems that had built up over decades. “That’s why we’re giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn’t belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves,” the communities secretary said.Jennings said the government also needed to tackle opaqueownership structuresof high street property, which allows some landowners “who aren’t necessarily that motivated to have shops in their property”.The growth of vape shops is not evenly spread. Research from Health Equity North found that the most deprived communities had three times as many as the most affluent areas.Burnham said high streets had become “unrecognisable” after decades of decline. “The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services and community spaces that people are crying out for.“That’s not on. I said we would improve Britain’s high streets, and that’s exactly what we are starting to do.”The measures are seen as a “first step” on a wider beautification of Britain’s high streets, with Westminster setting clearer expectations for the design and appearance of high street shopfronts.Local leaders will be encouraged to look at blueprints for ideal high streets, and given examples of what works best and how they can improve the look of their own main shopping areas.Dawn Butler, the MP for Brent East, who has campaigned on the issue, said: “It was a real shock to me to discover, during a previous visit to a high street with the Guardian, just how much money gambling machines can generate.“Government analysis of Gambling Commission data found that B3 machines generated an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year. That figure really brought home to me the scale of the gambling industry’s presence on our high streets and why they would want multiple shops on the high street to maximise their profits.“To put it in perspective, the national living wage for someone aged 21 or over works out at around £26,400 a year for someone working 40 hours a week. And in Brent the average wage is less than £35k. That experience underlined for me why urgent action was needed.”Explore more on these topicsGamblingVapingRetail industryEnglandLocal governmentPlanning policyScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘National priority’ to equip UK firefighters amid growing wildfire threat | Firefighters | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: FBU calls for more funding as ‘unprecedented summer’ puts rising demands on already stretched crews
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Exclusive: FBU calls for more funding as ‘unprecedented summer’ puts rising demands on already stretched crews
Content: A firefighter tackels a blaze on Tintwistle Moor.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighter tackels a blaze on Tintwistle Moor.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesFirefighters‘National priority’ to equip UK firefighters amid growing wildfire threatExclusive: FBU calls for more funding as ‘unprecedented summer’ puts rising demands on already stretched crewsCaroline Davies,Matthew PearceandPippa NeillMon 10 Aug 2026 15.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirefighters in the UK are under increased pressure as a result of an “unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires”, the Fire Brigades Union has said, as many parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave of the year.As authorities declared almost three-quarters of England was now in drought, Steve Wright, the FBU general secretary, said the unpredictable environmental challenges the UK was now confronted with meant it was a “national priority” to have enough properly equipped firefighters to “face these threats”.More than 120 firefighters continued to tackle ablaze in the New Forest national parkin Hampshire that began on Sunday. Nottinghamshire fire and rescue service declared a major incident on Sunday as two large fires in woodland near Mansfield put a significant strain on resources there.Emergency calls to the London fire brigade have increased by almost a third this summer as firefighters have battled a surge in wildfires and flooding in the capital, according to an internal briefing seen by the Guardian.The document warned that the brigade had come under mounting pressure from extreme weather and predicted the trend would continue because of the climate crisis. Between 1 April and 9 July, the service received 75,652 emergency calls – 31% more than the previous five-year average – while the number of incidents rose by nearly a quarter to 42,943.London firefighters responded to 392 wildfires during the period, alongside 68 water rescues, the briefing said, as repeated spells of hot weather and heavy thunderstorms stretched the service’s resources.The climate breakdown has been linked to theincreasing frequency of wildfires, burning larger areas, across many parts of the world. The so-called “fire wave” under way in the UK is the most widespread the country has ever seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.In recent weeks, there have been large blazes in places includingDunwich Heath in Suffolk, Headon Warren on the Isle of Wight, Llanwonno in the Rhondda valley in south Wales, and the Cairngorms national park in Scotland.The NationalDroughtGroup, which met on Monday, said 71.3% of England was now experiencing a “flash drought”, which develops very quickly brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures. About 45 million people live in a drought area and more than 27 million are now living under water use restrictions.The group said all regions of the country were experiencing pressure on their water resources, with growing pressure on agriculture, public supplies, navigation and the environment.View image in fullscreenA man fishes from the dried-out bed of Ladybower reservoir in the Derwent valley.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesTony Grayling, the chair of the National Drought Group, said: “Drought conditions are worsening and will continue to do so until we see significant and sustained rainfall. We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment.”He urged everyone to use less water to “make sure our current water reserves last”.No 10 said the dry conditions were having a “significant impact on communities, farmers and businesses across the country”, adding: “Our climate is changing. Droughts are becoming more common.”Country diary: We’ve had fires here in the Cairngorms before. This one has changed things | Amanda ThomsonRead moreThe prime minister’s spokesperson said the government was focused on “both the immediate response and long-term resilience”, including working through the National Drought Group to “protect water supplies and minimise environmental damage”.The spokesperson did not say what threshold would constitute a national emergency. Ministers were monitoring the situation closely, No 10 said, and the Environment Agency had stepped up monitoring and was working with water companies, farmers and local partners to “manage pressure on water resources”.Joanne Smith, the LFB’s deputy assistant commissioner for control and mobilising, said the service had responded to thousands of emergency calls and “hundreds of wildfires alongside water rescues and other significant incidents across the capital”.She said: “We have learned from previous events such as the summer of 2022 and developed our training for firefighters and officers to enhance their knowledge of tactical awareness at wildfires. We’ve invested in new equipment and training to help tackle wildfires, and we will continue to evolve so that we are ready and prepared for future summers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FBU’s Wright called for “increased funding, improved access to the best equipment and better national resilience” to combat rising demands on firefighters. He added: “Our country is facing unpredictable environmental challenges, and it must be a national priority to ensure we have enough properly equipped firefighters ready to face these threats.”He has previously said fire crews had been stretched by staffing cuts, with 12,000 fewer firefighters in the UK today than in 2010.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from a heathland blaze in the New Forest near Ringwood.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAIn Hampshire, hundreds of people were forced to abandon their vehicles and walk after Sunday’s wildfire caused by a van fire on the A31 near Ringwood spread to nearby New Forest heathland and affected an area the size of 140 football pitches.Twenty-six fire engines and four water carriers were called to the scene, which was scaled down to 10 engines and 13 off-road vehicles by Monday.Hampshire fire and rescue said on Monday: “There are more than 120 firefighters on the scene battling the heat and arduous terrain in order to prevent further fire spread. We are monitoring the fire, which is affecting a 1 square kilometre area of heathland off the A31, with police drones.”Amber heat health alerts have been issued for the East Midlands, West Midlands, east of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, London, the north-west, south-east and the south-west, while a yellow heat health alert has been issued for the north-east, from Tuesday at 9am until Friday at 9pm.The Met Office said it was expecting temperatures toexceed 36C in some areaslater in the week, after a relatively cool day on Monday, with the heat peaking on Thursday. England and Wales have had theirdriest July in records dating back to 1836, with 19 counties of England seeing no rain for the entire month, provisional statistics show.Southern England had its hottest July on record, and it was the joint hottest July on record for Wales, while England and the UK as a whole had their second hottest July, Met Office figures show.A spokesperson for the mayor of London said: “The prolonged, extreme heat is presenting incredible challenges for our emergency services, with a huge rise in demand.” They said the mayor had provided record funding to ensure LFB was better equipped and to improve training.Additional reporting byAletha AduExplore more on these topicsFirefightersUK weatherDroughtWildfiresClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ann Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incident | UK news | The Guardian
description: Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home
Content: Ann Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenAnn Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Lucy North/PAUK newsAnn Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incidentPolice looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then homeVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage.Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, was charged with the murder of Widdecombe, 78, who was killed at her Devon home in July, after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.On Friday, police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time, which they have said was an attempted burglary. Other sources describe it as an attempted arson.Police attended the incident, which they initially recorded primarily as a burglary. The Guardian understands detectives are studying fingerprints taken from the scene, as well as video from CCTV cameras in the area and from devices such as video doorbells. They examined the scene to see if an accelerant, such as lighter fluid, was used.On Friday, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said it had referred itself to the police watchdog over the initial investigation of the April 2025 incident.It said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.“In April 2025, the Metropolitan police received a report of an attempted burglary at an address in the Greater London area. Enquiries were carried out by the Metropolitan police, supported by Counter Terrorism Policing London. No arrests were made and the investigation was subsequently closed, pending any new lines of inquiry.“Following the reopening of the attempted burglary investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing London identified a line of enquiry which was not identified and pursued by them at the time, which may have been relevant. As a result, to ensure their support to the initial investigation is thoroughly reviewed, Counter Terrorism Policing London made a mandatory conduct referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct today.”On Monday, Farage said at a press conference: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.”He said he now had confidence in counter-terrorism police and said they were not trying to cover anything up.The Reform leader said of CTP’s decision to refer itself to the IOPC: “The fact they’ve done that shows you they’re not trying to cover up, they’re not trying to ignore, and I have to say I have met Laurence Taylor [the head of CTP] and I did feel a great, great confidence in it.”Widdecombe’s body was found with “serious injuries” by paramedics at her home in Haytor Vale, Devon, at 11.40am on Thursday 9 July.Kerry’s first court appearance in July heard that Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times in her home. Police have said they believed the 78-year-old former minister was attacked the day before her body was found.The attack on Widdecombe has not yet been declared a terrorist incident. CTP took the lead in the investigation because of the possibility there may have been a political motive behind her killing.CTP’s investigations continue.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amber heat-health alerts issued for most of England as temperatures could reach 36C or higher this week – as it happened | UK news | The Guardian
description: The upgraded alerts will be in place from 9am on Tuesday until 9pm on Friday
Author: Yohannes Lowe
Headline: The upgraded alerts will be in place from 9am on Tuesday until 9pm on Friday
Content: 07.32 EDTAmber heath-health alerts issued for most regions in England from Tuesday to FridayAndrew GregoryThe UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has updated heat-health alerts for nine regions in England, warning that rising temperatures this week may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.Amber alerts will be in place for Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands, East Midlands, East of England, South East, London, South West and North West regions from 9am on Tuesday 11 August to 9pm on Friday 14 August. The North East will be under a yellow alert during the same period.Polly Ashmore, acting consultant in Public Health at the UK Health Security Agency, said:double quotation markIt’s important that everyone is aware of the simple steps they can take to stay safe during periods of hot weather. Drinking plenty of water, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day and keeping indoor spaces cool are all things you can do to keep yourself and others safe.For vulnerable groups including older adults and those with existing health conditions, warmer weather than result in serious health outcomes.We urge health and social care services to ensure they are prepared and encourage people to check on vulnerable friends and family to make sure everyone is aware of the forecast, follows the necessary advice and stays safe in this period of hot weather.ShareUpdated at07.37 EDT

title: Labour peer urges Tories to sack former neo-Nazi who abused her | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Badenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana Berger
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Badenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana Berger
Content: Luciana Berger and Joshua Bonehill-Paine.Composite: Getty Images/C4/YoutubeView image in fullscreenLuciana Berger and Joshua Bonehill-Paine.Composite: Getty Images/C4/YoutubeConservativesLabour peer urges Tories to sack former neo-Nazi who abused herBadenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana BergerAletha AduPolitical correspondentMon 10 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Labour peerLuciana Bergerhas urged Kemi Badenoch to “listen to victims” and reverse her decision to give a national advisory role to a former neo-Nazi.Joshua Bonehill-Paine was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, an MP at the time. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.Berger said she was still affected by his crimes more than nine years later, and questioned what safeguarding checks Badenoch and the Conservative party had carried out in relation to his appointment to the party’s culture and integration commission.Berger, who is Jewish, asked whetherBonehill-Paine’s new rolecould bring him to Westminster. She wrote on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?”Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate.View image in fullscreenLuciana Berger said she was still affected by Bonehill-Paine’s crimes more than nine years later.Photograph: Parliament TV/PABerger’s intervention came after the Conservative party leader publisheda lengthy defenceof Bonehill-Paine in the Times, describing questions over his suitabilityto stand as a councillor in Somersetas a “pile-on”.Bonehill-Paine was set to stand as a Tory local councillor but announced last week that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections after Badenoch offered him the advisory role.Badenoch said: “People need to understand that the Conservative party under my leadership is now the party of personal responsibility and law and order. That means insisting on consequences by punishing wrongdoing and protecting the public, especially victims.“We need fewer double standards and instead higher standards in a system that is repeatedly failing to protect the public. We should be tough enough to stand by our beliefs even when politically inconvenient, wise enough to recognise rehabilitation and consistent enough to apply the same principles to friend and foe.”Berger said she had seen the piece late on Saturday night and “tried to ignore it” but after Badenoch shared the article on Monday, the former MP for Liverpool Wavertree accused her of giving insufficient consideration to Bonehill-Paine’s victims.“Badenoch makes one passing reference to the ‘victims’,” Berger wrote. “There were many. And I was one of them. Did Badenoch read the judge’s sentencing remarks? In court we heard the victim impact statements from people unable to testify, whose lives he had destroyed.“His appointment as an adviser to the Conservative party’s culture and integration commission could conceivably bring him to Westminster. Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?“It’s still not too late for Badenoch to listen to victims and reverse her decision.”View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch defended the decision to allow Bonehill-Paine to stand as a Conservative councillor as a ‘pile-on’.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAA spokesperson for Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine had served his time, completed Home Office Prevent (counter-terrorism) courses, and had gone into schools to teach about combatting antisemitism and extremism. But the party did not answer questions about what safeguarding checks it had carried out in relation to his appointment as an adviser, or why Badenoch had not contacted Berger.The abuse Bonehill-Paine directed at Berger included calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He also has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.Berger challenged Badenoch over what consideration had been given to safeguarding: “Badenoch’s article says she wants to safeguard the public and victims, but what safeguarding checks have she and the Conservative party carried out?”If Badenoch or her team had reached out to her, Berger said, “I would say, I don’t think it is ‘harder politics’ for this man to be part of Kemi’s operation. I think it’s the wrong politics.”She added: “I’m all for rehabilitation. But someone convicted of neo-Nazi misogynistic crimes is not suitable for public office less than a decade after his conviction. And neither should he be gifted a national advisory role, even closer to power.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesFar rightLuciana BergerKemi BadenochnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jackie, a beloved bald eagle and livestream star, dies of mysterious illness  | California | The Guardian
description: Thousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestream
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Thousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestream
Content: Jackie the bald eagle is examined on 18 July 2026, at the Los Angeles county Parks San Dimas Raptor Rescue Center in San Dimas, Calif.Photograph: Los Angeles County Parks San Dimas Raptor Rescue Center/APView image in fullscreenJackie the bald eagle is examined on 18 July 2026, at the Los Angeles county Parks San Dimas Raptor Rescue Center in San Dimas, Calif.Photograph: Los Angeles County Parks San Dimas Raptor Rescue Center/APCaliforniaJackie, a beloved bald eagle and livestream star, dies of mysterious illnessThousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestreamMaanvi SinghMon 10 Aug 2026 19.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJackie – the beloved bald eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake whose livestream was followed by millions of viewers as she birthed and raised chicks – died on Monday due to a mysterious illness. She was 14.Jackie had been receiving treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center since mid-July when she was found weak and unable to fly after a scuffle with two younger eagles. Experts at the center had discovered that she was suffering from severe anemia, and suspected she had been sick for weeks before the fight grounded her.“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the raptor center staff wrote in an Instagram post announcing Jackie’s death. “Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her. “Despite administering a number of tests including a CT scan and bone marrow biopsy, experts at the center said they could not determine what had sickened Jackie.The center is in consultation with the US and California fish and wildlife services about Jackie’s condition, and “will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results” at a later date, it said.Thepublic had been watchingJackie’s nest since a livestream was first set up in October 2015 – it was then inhabited by her parents Ricky and Lucy. In 2018, the public watched as Jackie defended her nest against an intruder, dubbed Mr B. Then, Shadow – the male eagle who became her mate – moved in. Greater and greater numbers of viewers tuned in during the pandemic to watch the couple build their lives together and welcome several clutches of fluffy hatchlings.In January, the couple’s clutch of two eggs was eaten by ravens. Jackie laid two more eggs in February, and thousands watched as the couplehatched their two youngest– Luna and Sandy. The latter was named after Sandy Steers, the executive director of Friends of Big Bear Valley, who had recentlydiedfrom cancer.The couple inspired the public to fight for the environment they inhabited. The Friends of Big Bear Lake launched a $10m effort to buy land near the eagles’ nest which had been slated for development – drawing support from the local elementary school, as well as from OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna. The non-profit will now steward 63 acres of the land.Fans of Jackie shared messages of grief following the news of her death – and celebrated her legacy of inspiring a massive public campaign for preserving natural habitat.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastBirdsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ilhan Omar questions whether Trump administration has used ICE to ‘surveil’ critics | Ilhan Omar | The Guardian
description: Congresswoman demands answers after a DHS agent was apparently stationed outside her Minnesota town hall
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Congresswoman demands answers after a DHS agent was apparently stationed outside her Minnesota town hall
Content: Congresswoman Ilhan Omar attends a news conference with members of the congressional progressive caucus on funding and accountability for the Department of Homeland Security on 13 January 2026.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCongresswoman Ilhan Omar attends a news conference with members of the congressional progressive caucus on funding and accountability for the Department of Homeland Security on 13 January 2026.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesIlhan OmarIlhan Omar questions whether Trump administration has used ICE to ‘surveil’ criticsCongresswoman demands answers after a DHS agent was apparently stationed outside her Minnesota town hallMaya YangMon 10 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s administration is facing questions over whether it is using Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to “surveil political opponents” after after an investigative agent was apparently stationed outside Democratic representative Ilhan Omar’s monthly town hall meeting in Richfield, Minnesota.After the incident, Omar demanded the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) clarify whether Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have been used to monitor “any other activity” involving “local, state, or federal officials” in the state.In a letterto Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, the congresswoman said an agent claiming to be conducting an undercover drug operation was parked outside the community center where she was holding an event last Thursday, without prior coordination with local law enforcement.According to Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, a Richfield police officer noticed the agent sitting in a Ford Explorer and “became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building”.“He proceeded to run the plates attached to the vehicle and discovered they were registered to a different vehicle,” said Omar. “He approached the woman in the vehicle to ask about the purpose for her presence there and why the plates on her vehicle did not match the government’s records. Like any reasonable officer, he was concerned that she harbored ill intentions and may be in a stolen vehicle.”The woman initially identified herself as security, but later called her supervisor and said she was an HSI agent conducting an undercover drug operation in the area, Omar said. Richfield police had not been informed of the operation beforehand, according the congresswoman.Omar said that despite a visible sign indicating that a town hall was taking place at the community center, the agent remained parked there until speaking with her supervisor, after which she left the property.“HSI’s actions yesterday evening put an entire community at risk,” she said. “Instead of monitoring the area for those who might wish harm to me and my constituents, Richfield Police were required to devote time to investigating why an HSI agent was outside of a Congressional event in a vehicle with mismatched plates.”Omar added: “It also raises serious and uncomfortable questions about the purpose of HSI’s presence outside of my event. At best, your agent was unable to assess that the parking lot of a community center hosting a congressional event wasn’t the best place to conduct a drug operation.“At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that theTrump administrationuses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy.”In her letter, Omar is demanding answers about why the agent was at the community center, how the agent and her supervisor knew she was holding a town hall there and what action they took in response to that knowledge.The Guardian has contacted DHS for comment.Inside the department, HSI is a federal law enforcement agency and the main investigative branch of ICE. ICE operations in Minnesota have sparked widespread protests across the state this year and have also resulted in the deaths of two Americans, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, who werekilledby federal agents.In January, a mansprayedOmar with an unidentified substance from a syringe during a town hall where she called for ICE to be abolished “for good”.The incident drew widespread condemnation from local and state leaders, with Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey calling it “unacceptable” and saying: “We can disagree without putting people at risk.”Explore more on these topicsIlhan OmarMinnesotaTrump administrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Not your imagination: from backpacks to food, consumer goods are getting worse | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Is it possible to avoid the continuing decline in quality of consumer products brought on by corporate greed?
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: Is it possible to avoid the continuing decline in quality of consumer products brought on by corporate greed?
Content: Wary consumers have noticed a trend in the ‘enshittification’ of products and services.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWary consumers have noticed a trend in the ‘enshittification’ of products and services.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesConsumedRetail industryNot your imagination: from backpacks to food, consumer goods are getting worseIs it possible to avoid the continuing decline in quality of consumer products brought on by corporate greed?Heather TimmonsMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Keyana Sapp, 31, went shopping for a new backpack, the brands he remembered as a kid were just not the same.He researched the companies, from North Face to JanSport and Eastpak, and soon realized they were all owned by the VF Corporation after a wave of acquisitions in the 2000s. After aReddit posthe made about his discovery picked up traction, he started looking at other types of consumer goods – cookware, shoes, tools, clothing.“It seems like that was a story that just repeated in every industry,” Sapp told the Guardian.Angry about fraud or an unsafe product? Here’s how to file a federal complaintRead moreBig conglomerates and private equity were buying up “trusted brands and riding that reputation out until it was a husk of what it was”.From a zipper jam on a nearly new coat to a casserole dish cracking in the oven on its third use, Americans are finding that the quality of many once-beloved name brands is declining. Three-quarters of Americans had a quality or service issue in 2025, theNational Consumer Rage Studyfound, double the rate since the survey started in 1976. And customer complaints havereached record levels, according to the latest University of Michigan American Customer Satisfaction Index.Sapp channeled his personal frustration into building adatabase of hundreds of brandsand ranking them “approved” to “avoid” based in part by their corporate ownership. And as part of his publication,Worse on Purpose, he explains the financial transactions that have undercut the quality of some of the biggest name brands.Sapp sees a structural problem within the consumer retail industry: founders who built brands they love take lucrative offers from big corporations or private equity investors. While they cash in on the decades it took to build their product’s brand, the new corporate owners eventually prove they don’t have the same emotional investment and are distanced from loyal customers.“When you’re running everything from an office building that has no relation to where the product is manufactured and people who are doing the manufacturing”, quality is going to suffer, Sapp said.Big US companies haven’t always been associated with lower-quality products, of course. Purchasing a product from a well-known national brand was often associated with guaranteed quality and consistent customer service for much of the last century.But in recent years, investors have become increasingly “big and powerful” due to the pro-shareholder rights movement and the growth of large institutional investors, explains Dorothy Lund, a law professor at Columbia University. That increased shareholder power can contribute to consumer harm.Thanks to activist investors, many company executives face what feels like “gun-to-the-head pressure to maximize shareholder returns”, or be fired, she said.Shareholder activism targeting CEOs has more than quadrupled since 2018, aDecember 2025 reportby the Conference Board found. Consumer-facing industries have seen “particularly large spikes” in shareholder campaigns that focus on making sure investors get more money.Meanwhile, corporate profitshit an all-time highin the first quarter of 2025, of $3.9tn on an annualized basis.Some brand owners who have sold their companies to big corporations say it’s this relentless pressure to increase profits that intrinsically erodes product quality.“I don’t believe in this idea that you take a sliver off the loaf of baloney and nobody realizes it … and then the next year you take another sliver off, nobody realizes it,” Ben & Jerry’s co-founder Ben Cohen told the Guardian in a recent interview. Cohen isfighting to buy his brand backfrom Magnum, the ice-cream brand sprung out of Unilever, among disagreements over the brand’s social activism.“You keep on doing that, year after year, and all of a sudden, you don’t have any baloney” any more, he added.The news industry in the US used to hold corporations more accountable for the quality of their products and service. But consumer-facing business news wasdecimatedwhen local newspapers disappeared and national news outlets shifted their corporate coverage to focus on investors.‘You can’t make billions without hurting people’: Cory Doctorow on Elon Musk, the AI bubble and bosses’ cruel fantasiesRead moreRecently, a fresh crop of apps and websites, like Worse on Purpose, are taking their place.The progressive non-profit More Perfect Union hasdetailed the impacton food quality as the restaurant supplier Sysco grew through acquisitions, for example, and theBuy’r blog and apptracks the ownership of food and health and beauty brands. Earlier this month, the New York Times’ Wirecuttermappedthe changing ingredients, and taste, of Talenti gelato, after its 2012 takeover by Unilever.Meanwhile, the Reddit groupEnshittification, named aftertech critic Cory Doctorow’s termfor internet decline, has been a clearinghouse for consumers to rant about products and services getting worse since it was started in 2023.So what’s an irate shopper to do? Buy from small companies where possible, Sapp suggests.“The easiest thing any consumer can do is just say, ‘Wherever I can, I’m going to buy independent, rather than from a big conglomerate,’” Sapp recommends. When you’re shopping, “just check who owns the company”.The Guardian is exploring Americans’ frustrations with big companies and how consumer rights have changed in the world’s biggest consumer economy. Disappointed with a product or service, or have a solution to recommend?
