title: Jordan Nobbs ready to complete wishlist with Newcastle WSL dream | Newcastle Women | The Guardian
description: Jordan Nobbs has said she is determined to help women’s football to thrive in the north-east, with Newcastle having made several ambitious signings this summer
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Jordan Nobbs has said she is determined to help women’s football to thrive in the north-east, with Newcastle having made several ambitious signings this summer
Content: Jordan Nobbs: ‘To get a north-east team promoted would be an achievement I would love.’Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan Nobbs: ‘To get a north-east team promoted would be an achievement I would love.’Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesNewcastle WomenJordan Nobbs ready to complete wishlist with Newcastle WSL dreamFormer England midfielder keen for north-east to thriveNewcastle have made ambitious signings this summerTom GarryMon 10 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan Nobbs sayswinning promotion to the Women’s Super Leaguewith Newcastle would fulfil her ambition for a north‑east club to be in the top tier.Nobbs, who has 71 England caps, was born in Stockton‑on‑Tees and believes women’s football in the region would benefit immensely from top‑flight representation. Newcastle finished sixth in WSL2 last season, 11 points behind the title winners, Birmingham, and nine points off the playoffs, but this summer they have made their hopes clear with high-calibre signings from the top division, including the striker Martha Thomas from Tottenham and the Liverpool duo Leanne Kiernan and Gemma Evans.Alexia Putellas: ‘I’m hungry to win, to fight with my teammates for victory’Read moreNobbs is clear about the target for the new campaign. “It is promotion. I know we said it last season [too],” she said. “I’ve always said things don’t happen overnight, [but] that is our goal. You have to say it out loud.“Looking back on last season, we had some really good performances but nine draws, that’s too many points [dropped]. It’s just about focusing on finding a way to win. We’ve just got to build on the good stuff from last season, I don’t think we’re far off it.“[Winning promotion with Newcastle], I’ve always said it would be job done. I think to get a northern team promoted … as I heard from Newcastle I was like, that is exactly what I want to do. In the WSL, I’d ticked as much as I possibly could, so to get a north‑east team, which we all had to leave back in the day, promoted would be an achievement I would love.”Nobbs began her career with Sunderland and broke into their team in the old top flight, but moved to Arsenal when the WSL was launched in 2011 and Sunderland’s application to join the breakaway division was rejected. That led to a successful team also including Nobbs’s future England teammatesLucy Bronzeand Lucy Staniforth breaking up.Sunderland did compete in the top tier between 2015 and 2018, but north-east representation in the WSL has been sparse, so Nobbs is pleased to see investment in recent years at Newcastle as well as their WSL2 rivals, who were taken over in June by Bay Collective.“It’s been a long time coming, but it was something us northerners have always wanted,” Nobbs said. “We don’t want the north-east to fizzle out. We want to show the players that have come from there and developed there.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s definitely grown in the right direction now, which is what we wanted. But the big stepping stone would be getting into the WSL. That would be where we really put the north-east back on the map and I’d love to be a part of that.”The 33-year-old has enjoyed her role in Tanya Oxtoby’s setup at Newcastle after joining them last July. “With Villa I played a lot of a deeper role and [now] I really love being back in my high position, scoring goals, assisting and [I’m] in my happy place. I feel like I found that little spark again [last season] that was nice.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle WomenWomen's Super League 2Women's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City closing in on £85m Bouaddi to soften blow of Rodri’s expected exit | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City are closing in on signing Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille with the midfielder’s expected arrival clearing the path for Rodri’s intent to join Barcelona
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City are closing in on signing Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille with the midfielder’s expected arrival clearing the path for Rodri’s intent to join Barcelona
Content: Ayyoub Bouaddi was hugely impressive for Morocco in the World Cup.Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAyyoub Bouaddi was hugely impressive for Morocco in the World Cup.Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty ImagesManchester CityManchester City closing in on £85m Bouaddi to soften blow of Rodri’s expected exitMorocco international midfielder has agreed termsBarça to return with improved bid for RodriJamie JacksonMon 10 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City are closing in on signing Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, with the midfielder’s expected arrival clearing the path for Rodri to join Barcelona. The 18-year-old has agreed personal terms with City, but the club are still finalising the deal with Lille who value Bouaddi at €100m (£85m).City’s new manager, Enzo Maresca, wants to integrate the Morocco international into his first-team squad immediately. City meet Arsenal in the Community Shield on Sunday and start their Premier League campaign against Bournemouth on 23 August.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal step up push for defensive cover with Timber and Saliba sidelinedRead moreBarcelona are confident of signing Rodri from City, but they will have to return with an improved offer after an initial €45m bidwas rejected last week. The sale of Ferran Torres, who is of interest to Paris Saint‑Germain, would finance Rodri’s purchase. City are all but resigned to the sale of the 30‑year‑old, who has a year left on his contract.If the Bouaddi deal can be completed, he would joinElliot Anderson, who arrived last month from Nottingham Forest for £116m, in a new-look midfield, which has lost the experience of Bernardo Silva.Manchester United, meanwhile, are interested in the Leicester player Louis Page. United, who face competition from Arsenal, are hopeful of securing a deal for the 18-year-old midfielder, with Page believed to favour a transfer to Old Trafford.Marcus Rashford has joined United at their County Kildare training camp following the England forward’s post‑World Cup break. The 28-year-old has spent the past season and a half on loan at Barcelona and Aston Villa respectively, in the aftermath of a breakdown in his relationship with the club executive and the former United head coach Ruben Amorim. Relations have now eased and Rashford is focused on working under the United manager, Michael Carrick, although he could still leave before the end of the transfer window.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityLilleTransfer windowManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Crystal Palace and Everton agree Brennan Johnson-Dwight McNeil swap deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Crystal Palace and Everton have agreed a straight swap for Brennan Johnson and Dwight McNeil
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Crystal Palace and Everton have agreed a straight swap for Brennan Johnson and Dwight McNeil
Content: Brennan Johnson (right) struggled at Crystal Palace last season after joining for £35m in January.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenBrennan Johnson (right) struggled at Crystal Palace last season after joining for £35m in January.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PATransfer windowCrystal Palace and Everton agree Brennan Johnson-Dwight McNeil swap dealWinger McNeil almost joined in JanuaryIsrael right-back Khalaili also on way to PalaceEd AaronsMon 10 Aug 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrystal Palace and Everton have agreed a straight swap for Brennan Johnson and Dwight McNeil – six months after McNeil’s partner accused Palace ofmessing with his mental healthafter pulling out of a deal.McNeil and Johnson, who became Palace’s record signing when he joinedin January from Tottenham for £35m, only to be surpassedby the arrival of Jørgen Strand Larsenfrom Wolves for an initial £43m a few weeks later, are understood to have agreed four-year contracts with the option of a further 12 months. They are expected to have medicals on Monday.Manchester City closing in on £85m Bouaddi to soften blow of Rodri’s expected exitRead moreMcNeil, who has entered the final year of hisEvertoncontract, appeared to be moving to Selhurst Park in February after Palace agreed a £20m fee on transfer deadline day. But the collapse of Jean-Philippe Mateta’s £30m move to Milan, after the France striker failed a medical, prompted Palace to change their offer to an initial loan with an obligation to buy at the end of the season.They submitted a deal sheet to the Premier League, but then pulled out. McNeil’s partner, Megan Sharpley, wrote an emotional poston Instagram saying there had been “radio silence” from Palace and that the player’s mental health had been affected.“Tonight, and the last 48 hours, have broken my heart to see how the football world you love so much can be so cruel to you,” she wrote at the time. “We live in a world where everyone is aware of how big a problem mental health is. So, in football, why do we find it acceptable because these young men are on a lot of money and that’s OK to mess and toy with their mental health and that it’s just part of the job?”Johnson has been disappointing since moving to Palace, failing to score in 18 Premier League appearances. Given he signed a four-and-a-half-year contract in January that is believed to be worth more than £100,000 a week, Palace will take a significant hit on the fee they paid, but remove one of their highest earners from the wage bill.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPalace are also finalising a deal to sign Anan Khalaili from Union Saint-Gilloise for £21m. The Israel right-back had his medical on Sunday and is expected to sign a five-year contract. The 21-year-old’s move to Internazionale broke down last month after he failed a medical.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowCrystal PalaceEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: European Athletics Championships: Hunt wins women’s 100m gold, Ingebrigtsen kicks to 5,000m title – as it happened  | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Amy Hunt won her first major title in the women’s 100m while Jakob Ingebrigtsen capped his injury comeback with victory in the men’s 5,000m
Author: Billy Munday
Headline: Amy Hunt won her first major title in the women’s 100m while Jakob Ingebrigtsen capped his injury comeback with victory in the men’s 5,000m
Content: 4h ago17.31 EDTThat’s all from me on day one.Day two brings Keely Hodgkinson in the 800m heats and Romell Glave going for gold in the men’s 100m.Here’s Sean Ingle’s report on Amy Hunt’s crowning moment …Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowdRead moreShare

title: Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter secured the 100m European title in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter secured the 100m European title in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze
Content: Amy Hunt shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 100m final.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenAmy Hunt shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 100m final.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsBritain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd24-year-old secures title in 11.00sec in BirminghamNorway win 4x400m mixed relay, Britain secondSean Ingleat Alexander StadiumMon 10 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a display of icy resolve and sustained power had secured Amy Hunt a European 100m gold medal, Britain’s new sprint queen reached for a Freddie Mercury lyric. “I want it all,” she said, before peering into a golden future.The Cambridge graduate, 24, now plans to leave the European Championships with four gold medals, adding the 200m and 4x100m women’s and mixed relays to her 100m title. On this evidence, would you dare bet against her?Jakob Ingebrigtsen returns from injury woe to win European Championships 5,000m goldRead moreHunt is never the quickest starter. In truth, she reacted to the gun like a woman whose spikes had been superglued to her blocks and she was still behind with 30m to go before coming through to take her first major title in 11.00sec.“I’ve probably had much worse starts than that,” Hunt said. “The biggest thing is not panicking, trusting in my very, very long legs, long femurs, and just staying calm and pulling through at the end.“‘Trash’ is probably going to be his [her coach, Marco Airale] words about my start,” she said. “And maybe a little bit of Italian blasphemy, but we came through at the end. One of my biggest skills in terms of championships is I know I’m so strong in the end and I always have that kind of extra magic in the last 40, 50m.”Ewa Swoboda of Poland secured silver in 11.02, while Delphine Nkansa took bronze for Belgium in 11.06.“Honestly, it’s just euphoria,” said Hunt. “My first gold. I think it was definitely time to upgrade. This was definitely a coming of age for me. I’m someone that thrives under that pressure, so the stage for the final isn’t intimidating to me. I just knew I had to stay calm and not overthink myself into the gold before I had it in my grasp.”It was also sweet vindication after being beaten into silver at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow a fortnight ago. “It really came in handy for me,” she said. “I wanted to have that experience of being in front of a home crowd and having that meta-expectation, because I’ve never had that before. I took a lot of learnings from Glasgow into today and it really helped me.View image in fullscreenBritain’s Amy Hunt reacts after crossing the finish line to win gold.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APHunt’s story loses little in its retelling. She was the world’s fastest woman over 200m at 18, then had a series of injuries that got so bad some questioned whether she would ever fulfil her potential. A few years ago she ruptured one of her quadriceps so badly that her mum needed to lift her out of the shower.When she won a 200m silver medal in Tokyo last year, she called herself a “track goddess and an academic badass”. “I don’t know if I have any more one-liners in me,” she said. Then came the Freddie Mercury line.Hunt later revealed she had a premonition that she was going to win gold. “I just had such a magical feeling,” she said. “I’ve won English Schools here. I’ve raced here as 13-14-year-old. So, this is really my track. I’m a girl from Newark, I’m a Midlands girl. So I just had a feeling that this was going to be my night.”Hunt insisted that this could be just the start as she now chases an historic four gold medals. “I want to be the best,” she said. “I don’t shy away from that. I train incredibly hard, and I back myself so incredibly hard because I do want to be the best. “I’m not saying that I’m the best right now, but that’s something I aspire to be.”Hunt said she was so nervous before the race that she was unable to nap. Instead, she was just lay awake in bed with her eyes closed. “But I as soon as I get to the track, my nerves disappear,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I love doing what I do. My coach keeps me really chilled. Megan Thee Stallion [American rapper] kept me kind of nice and upbeat, and you can’t be nervous when you listen to that.”View image in fullscreenHenriette Jæger shows her delight after sealing gold for Norway in the 4x400m mixed relay.Photograph: Alex Livesey/British Athletics/Getty ImagesShe also relaxed by playing puzzle games such as Connections, Spelling Bee, Pips and Wordle. “It wakes my brain up without having to overthink.“Even at training, we’re all competitive every single day about Wordle and how many kind of words we got on Spelling Bee, so it just keeps my brain ticking over, listening to Megan Thee Stallion, house music, a bit of Mamma Mia in there, so just not getting too overly serious.”Moments before Hunt’s victory there was also a plucky silver for Great Britain’s mixed 4x400m relay team behind the gold medallists Norway.Britain’s team of Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich, Toby Harries and Yemi Mary John all ran well. But a Norway team spearheaded by the 400m hurdles world record-holder, Karsten Warholm, and the fastest woman in Europe this year, Henriette Jæger, proved too strong as they set a Championship record of 3:09.62, nearly a second clear of Britain.The only disappointment was that more people were not here to witness it given that the Alexander Stadium, which seats about 20,000, looked barely half full.However, organisers said 13,623 tickets had been sold for the Monday night – along with 170,000 tickets for the week – and that from Thursday night onwards the event was pretty much a sellout.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jakob Ingebrigtsen returns from injury woe to win European Championships 5,000m gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen, in his first race for 11 months after injury, won the men’s 5,000m final to become the first man to win four European titles in the same event
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen, in his first race for 11 months after injury, won the men’s 5,000m final to become the first man to win four European titles in the same event
Content: Gold medalist Jakob Ingebrigtsen of Norway poses for a photo after winning the 5000m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGold medalist Jakob Ingebrigtsen of Norway poses for a photo after winning the 5000m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsJakob Ingebrigtsen returns from injury woe to win European Championships 5,000m goldNorwegian kicks to superb win in first race for 11 months‘I dreamt of this two weeks ago when put name on list’Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamMon 10 Aug 2026 16.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are some people who believe that Jakob Ingebrigtsen lacks a sprint finish. The evidence of the Norwegian’s spectacular victory charge to claim his fourth European 5,000m title suggests otherwise.So much for all the doubts and questions swirling around him ­coming into the championships. He had been injured. He had not raced for 11 months. He was apparently vulnerable. Yet, as usual, Ingebrigtsen found a way to win gold again.Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowdRead moreThis surely ranks as one of the most thrilling of his career. Coming around the final bend, he was third and boxed in behind the Frenchman Jimmy Gressier and the German ­Florian Bremm, yet he found a gap and accelerated to power home in 13min 15.29sec.Bremm took silver 0.31sec back, with Etienne Daguinos of France claiming bronze. Ingebrigtsen is now the first man to win four European titles in the same event. For good measure, he has also won 17 European gold medals if you include cross-country victories.It was especially sweet given he has struggled with achilles injuries over the past 17 months. “I dreamt of this moment two weeks ago when I put my name on the list,” said ­Ingebrigtsen, who ran a 54sec last lap. “I crossed my fingers that I would be here and feel better. It was just enough so I am extremely happy. With 600 metres to go, I knew I was going to get that gold medal. I was just hoping and hoping that I was not going to get too tired.”View image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen crosses the finish line to win gold while Florian Bremm takes silver.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersIt was, he also said, one of the greatest wins of his career. “It’s right up there,” he added.His return had represented the biggest enigma of the week. The brilliant Norwegian had a 14-race ­winning streak at European championships, indoor and out, going back to 2019. But he had also not raced for 11 months. In his imperious past, ­Ingebrigtsen would have been an ­overwhelming favourite against a field that included Switzerland’s Dominic Lobalu, who finished fourth at the Olympics in 2024. Not this time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd who could blame the doubters, given Ingebrigtsen had surgery on the sheath around his left achilles tendon in February. But he soon proved he hadn’t come to Birmingham for a Balti or a trip to the Ozzy Osbourne exhibition. When Ingebrigtsen was announced to the crowd it took several seconds for the stadium PA to list his many achievements. The Norwegian stood impassively and then raised one finger. On the track he was soon to prove it.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Araújo joins Liverpool on loan and Van Dijk hopes for more arrivals before new season | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Virgil van Dijk is relishing the prospect of partnering Ronald Araújo, with the Barcelona centre-back joining Liverpool on loan
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: Virgil van Dijk is relishing the prospect of partnering Ronald Araújo, with the Barcelona centre-back joining Liverpool on loan
Content: Ronald Araújo arrives on loan from Barcelona with the ability to play at both centre-back and right-back.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRonald Araújo arrives on loan from Barcelona with the ability to play at both centre-back and right-back.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpoolAraújo joins Liverpool on loan and Van Dijk hopes for more arrivals before new seasonBarcelona’s Ronald Araújo arrives on loanVan Dijk: ‘Let’s see what the next couple of weeks bring’Dominic BoothMon 10 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVirgil van Dijk is ready to welcome Ronald Araújo as his new centre‑back partner atLiverpoolwith the loan deal to sign the Barcelona defender completed on Monday.Uruguay international Araújo, 27, arrives on a one-year contract and has also played at right-back, a vulnerable area of Liverpool’s squad as Conor Bradley continues his rehabilitation from a serious knee injury and with Jeremie Frimpong still to nail down a first XI spot after a disrupted first season at Anfield.On Sunday, Van Dijk played almost an hour in his first pre-season appearance as Liverpool werebeaten 3-2 by Monacoat home, having led 2-0. The Dutchman fouled Aleksandr Golovin just before the break to concede a penalty, which Golovin scored.Iraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costlyRead moreJérémy Jacquet remained absent, Liverpool’s new £50m arrival being treated with kid gloves after an injury‑hit spell at the end of last season with Rennes. Araújo has been signed to bolster Andoni Iraola’s defensive options, with Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni also sidelined.“I can’t wait to get started. I’m very, very happy,” Araújo, who has 27 international caps, told Liverpool’s official website. “It was the ideal move for me at this stage in my career. I think it was a move that was necessary for me to take. As soon as I heard that interest from Liverpool, everything went into action really, really quickly.“I’m super-happy to be here and excited to get started. I’m glad about the interest and it was the right move at the right time.”Van Dijk said of Araújo: “Any player that arrives at the club we will be welcoming.”The captain was upbeat about Jacquet and the prospect of more transfer activity before the deadline on 1 September. Liverpool are keen to add to their forward line with Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola of interest. “Let’s see what the next couple of weeks are going to bring,” Van Dijk said. “Any quality we can add to the team will definitely be welcome so let’s see.”The Dutchman said of Jacquet: “I’ve not seen any of him. I’ve spoken to him. I’ve seen him walking around and we have conversations. I can’t wait to see him back on the pitch and I hope that happens very soon. I’m not a doctor, so I don’t know exactly the situation, but I have a feeling this week he could be back on the pitch, hopefully as soon as possible.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVan Dijk accepted Liverpool are in transition after the sacking of Arne Slot and revealed he has been in regular contact with Andoni Iraola, offering full support to the head coach. “We had a great conversation in the first week when it got announced and the main thing for him to know is I am here for him regardless, anything he needs, wants to know, wants me to do for the team or whatever. Hopefully we will be successful this season.“Nothing to take away from Arne and his staff, we had an amazing time together, but obviously last year [was] a disappointment. This year we have a new manager who has new ways of preparation, so we have to adapt to the new staff, different training methods. I liked working under Arne and I am sure I will like working under the new manager.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sirens call: Super Netball heading for wrangle over name of new Sydney team | Super Netball | The Guardian
description: New owners SEN have lodged a trademark application for ‘Sirens’ but a Sydney-based ice hockey team with a 20-year history has the same moniker
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: New owners SEN have lodged a trademark application for ‘Sirens’ but a Sydney-based ice hockey team with a 20-year history has the same moniker
Content: A stoush over the a new team name is looming after the new Sydney Super Netball franchise owners lodged a trademark application for ‘Sirens’.Photograph: Izhar Khan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA stoush over the a new team name is looming after the new Sydney Super Netball franchise owners lodged a trademark application for ‘Sirens’.Photograph: Izhar Khan/Getty ImagesSuper NetballSirens call: Super Netball heading for wrangle over name of new Sydney teamNew owners SEN have lodged trademark application for ‘Sirens’But Sydney ice hockey team with 20-year history has same nameJack SnapeMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is David versus Goliath – meets Odysseus – in a looming legal stoush on the fringes of Australian sport. One one side, there is an amateur women’s ice hockey team, long-established if under-resourced. On the other is one of Australia’s most influential sporting owners.At stake is the legal right to use the name Sirens, the mythological creatures whose profile has exploded after the release of box-office smash The Odyssey.Sports Entertainment Network (SEN) acquired the Giants’Super Netballlicence last week, immediately promising to scrap the failing brand tied to AFL club Greater Western Sydney. Four days before the announcement, SEN’s NSW entity had lodged a trademark application for “Sydney Sirens”.Jamaica stun Australia as England miss out on Commonwealth Games netball finalRead more“We’ll unveil a brand new brand, and look-and-feel soon for the wonderful Giants who we have been fortunate to acquire and partner with over the last 24 hours in the SuperNetballleague,” SEN chief executive Craig Hutchison said when announcing the takeover. “We see ourselves as positive disruptors in netball in terms of fun and energy and purpose and meaning and storytelling.”The trademark application is currently being considered by IP Australia, and there is no guarantee – even if it accepted, with or without a challenge – the new netball team will be dubbed the Sirens.The moniker was seen fit to trademark but SEN declined to confirm Sydney’s new netball team name. “We are exploring a range of options for the new name and brand of the team but are not in a position to provide any further comment,” a spokesperson said.That offers little comfort to the already-established Sydney Sirens, who compete in the Australian Women’s Ice Hockey League, the highest level of the game played in this country. “We are currently looking into our options,” said team manager Natalie Caruso. “Sydney Sirens Ice Hockey Team has a 20-plus year history having been established in 2005.”View image in fullscreenThe Giants’ Super Netball licence was acquired by SEN last week.Photograph: James Gourley/AAPThe owner of the website domains sydneysirens.com and sydneysirens.com.au – an ice hockey community member and coach linked to the team – told the Guardian they received notification last week that there was interest for them to be acquired. SEN’s spokesperson said, “to our knowledge no one representing SEG [SEN stablemate Sports Entertainment Group] has contacted the club” about purchasing a domain.SEN already owns the Bendigo Spirit and Perth Lynx in the WNBL and the Melbourne Mavericks in Super Netball, and completed a sale of NBL team Perth Wildcats earlier this year at a valuation of $40m.The Sydney Sirens, meanwhile, are fully amateur. “We are a self funded team, without major sponsorship or support – unlike the men’s teams playing in the AIHL [Australian Ice Hockey League],” Caruso said.Teams in different Australian sporting leagues already use the same moniker, such as the Tigers for Richmond in the AFL and Wests in the NRL. But having both the geographical marker and the mascot duplicated across two teams in different sports would likely create confusion and dilute search engine and social media visibility of the less prominent entity.The interest in the name comes amid heightened awareness of the mythical Sirens in recent years. Emily Wilson’s translation of Homer’s The Odyssey triggered a rethink over their depiction in modern stories. Rather than sexualised temptresses, Wilson’s translation revived the original language of“cognitively tempting” bird-women that promised knowledge not sex.Long after the Sydney Sirens were founded, the beings were adopted as a sporting team name in North America when the New York Sirens joined the new Professional Women’s Hockey League in 2023. The “siren” is a key part of hockey culture as a signal for goals and end of play, affording the name a dual meaning. Last week, Cleveland’s new WNBA expansion team also chose the Sirens for its entry into the competition in 2028. Potential US trademark issueswere reportedly settledby conversations between the two teams.Explore more on these topicsSuper NetballNetballAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Somali referee Omar Artan grateful for Super Cup chance after World Cup exclusion | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Somali referee Omar Artan, who was refused entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup, has spoken publicly for the first time about the decision
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: The Somali referee Omar Artan, who was refused entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup, has spoken publicly for the first time about the decision
Content: Omar Artan (centre) was given a hero’s welcome when he arrived back in Mogadishu after being denied entry to the US.Photograph: Feisal Omar/ReutersView image in fullscreenOmar Artan (centre) was given a hero’s welcome when he arrived back in Mogadishu after being denied entry to the US.Photograph: Feisal Omar/ReutersSoccerSomali referee Omar Artan grateful for Super Cup chance after World Cup exclusionReferee was refused entry to US in JuneWill take charge of PSG v Aston Villa on WednesdayBen FisherMon 10 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Somali referee Omar Artan, whowas refused entry to the USto officiate at the World Cup, has spoken publicly for the first time about the decision and detailed his pride as he prepares to take charge of the Super Cup match between Paris Saint‑Germain and Aston Villa on Wednesday. Uefa awarded the 34-year-old Artan the game a few days after he was prevented from working at the tournament.Artan will make history in Salzburg as the first non-European official to take charge of Uefa’s annual competition between the respective winners of the Champions League and the Europa League. “When we got this call it was, for me and my family, really a very, very happy moment,” he said. “There’s a big Somali community in Europe and in Austria and they are over the moon with me officiating a match like this.”Uefa, Concacaf and AFC push for Infantino to quit and discuss rival competitionsRead moreArtan found himself at the centre of controversy after being denied entry at Miami international airport on 6 June. The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, suggested he was powerless to overrule Donald Trump’s administration.Somaliais one of 12 countries on a travel ban list introduced last year by the US.“It was a very tough period,” Artan said. “A lot of people have sympathy for me because when someone has been working a lot of years and is supposed to do something, and then can’t do it, it’s very challenging. I really appreciate the support I received throughout the world, though; I’m so grateful.”Artan has prepared for the match at the Red Bull Arena by taking charge of league games in Somalia and the Kuwaiti Premier League. “We referees go through a lot of preparation in terms of getting to know the teams,” he said in an interview with Uefa. “I always watch the teams play. I like watching European football anyway but, regardless, I go through and do a lot of research on the teams, how they play, learn their behaviours, tactics.”Artan will be assisted by two more African officials, Liban Abdoulrazack Ahmed (Djibouti) and Stephen Eleazar Onyango Yiembe (Kenya).Explore more on these topicsFootballRefereesFootball politicsSomalianewsShareReuse this content

title: UK manufacturers face rising hacking risk as survey shows 30% were hit last year | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Big companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attack
Content: Some generative AI systems have hacked into other businesses autonomously.Photograph: solarseven/GettyView image in fullscreenSome generative AI systems have hacked into other businesses autonomously.Photograph: solarseven/GettyCybercrimeUK manufacturers face rising hacking risk as survey shows 30% were hit last yearBig companies describe being under constant threat but only half have a plan in place to respond to an attackJasper JollyMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly a third of British manufacturers have been hit by a cyber-attack on them or a company in their supply chain, according to a survey that highlighted the growing hacking risk to companies.The findings come almost a year after Britain’s largest automotive employer,JLR, was hit by an attackthat forced it to halt production for weeks.The report by MakeUK, a lobby group for British manufacturers, found that 30% of manufacturers had experienced a cyber-incident in the past 12 months, leading in many cases to lost production time and increased costs. However, only half had a plan in place to respond to an attack.The risk of attacks has risen in recent years as hackers,often backed by hostile states, have become more numerous and more adept at penetrating company defences. Large businesses describe being under near-constant attack from people trying to access their systems, and the UK government has said cybercrime costs the economy £14.7bn a year. The rise of generative AI systems, some of which have been able tohack into other businesses autonomously, has added extra urgency to efforts to upgrade defences.Manufacturers have sought to improve productivity by connecting their factories, allowing them much quicker insight into their operations. However, the larger number of links has also meant that once attackers are inside the system, the scope for harm is much larger. JLR was forced to shut down systems across all its factories, offices and retail operations after it discovered digital intruders on the last day of August last year.The independent Cyber Monitoring Centre said the JLR hackcost the UK economy at least £1.9bn, probably making it the most expensive cyber incident ever in Britain, mainly because of lost output at JLR and its suppliers. The New York Times reported in June that British law enforcement had concluded that Russian hackers were behind it.Other big attacks reported publicly in recent years include two FTSE 100 manufacturers who reported attacks within days of each other early in 2025: the valve maker IMI and the components maker Smiths Group. In the retail sector,Marks & Spencer,the Co-opandHarrodsall suffered costly breaches last year.Jonathon Ellison, director of national resilience at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which was involved in the response to the JLR attack, said: “In today’s landscape, no manufacturer can afford to treat cybersecurity as anything other than a business-critical priority. The NCSC is working to help organisations of all sizes strengthen their cyber defences.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmong companies affected by a cyber-attack on their supply chain, about 30% of 123 manufacturers surveyed said they had suffered delays of deliveries to customers or output cuts, and almost a quarter reported supplier delivery delays or shortages of components and materials.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeManufacturing sectorHackingAI (artificial intelligence)Jaguar Land RoverComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: your passport to a folding phone future | Samsung | The Guardian
description: Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life
Content: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 ditches the skinny candy bar profile of its forebears in favour of a retro passport-like shape.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 ditches the skinny candy bar profile of its forebears in favour of a retro passport-like shape.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsungReviewSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: your passport to a folding phone futureNovel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery lifeSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Samsung’s latest folding phone breaks the mould with a squat, passport-like shape reminiscent of the Blackberry, which opens up to become a tablet similar to an iPad mini. It is certainly a better shape for a tablet than other designs, but is a short and wide phone when closed a compromise too far?The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is an entirely new variant in Samsung’s foldable family for this year launched alongside the Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more familiar candy bar shape. Both folders are extremely expensive, with the Fold 8 starting at £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699) and the Fold 8 Ultra at £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), withRAMageddondriving up prices even at the top of the market.While Samsung’sfirst folding phoneadopted a candy bar shape that opened up like a book to a square tablet, others began with more squat and wide forms including the originalGoogle Pixel FoldandMicrosoft Surface Duo. But as the technology matured most folders adopted the narrower closed form, which proved a better shape for performing phone-type duties such as messaging.View image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 in its closed form is almost the same size as a passport, feeling more like a small notepad than a phone.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 is 9.7mm thick when closed, which is about the same as a regular phone in a case, but its short and wide design looks more like a mini tablet or notepad in your hand. Its width also makes it hard to reach the other side of the screen one-handed, making it a two-handed affair most of the time, similar to huge superphonessuch as the Galaxy S26 Ultra.Photos, apps, games and websites look and work great on the crisp and super-bright outside screen. That is until you open the keyboard, which then takes up just over half the screen, leaving you very little space to see the content you are trying to type into. Apps that include a bar at the top, such as WhatsApp, shrink that space even further.View image in fullscreenWith the keyboard open you only have a narrow window to see the content of messages when typing on the Fold 8 (left) compared with a regular phone or the taller Fold 8 Ultra (right)Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOpen the Fold 8 like a book to reveal a beautiful 7.6in OLED display, which is crisp, smooth and super-bright, making it easy to see in direct sunlight. Like all folders the necessarily softer screen material is fragile and a fingerprint magnet, so needs regular gentle cleaning.The tablet screen’s 4:3 ratio matches that ofApple’s iPadsorMicrosoft’s Surfaces, which makes it a better fit for video with smaller black bars top and bottom when held in landscape compared to squarer foldables.View image in fullscreenWebsites, comics, books and apps look great on the inside screen when held in portrait orientation.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianPortrait orientation is great for websites and the keyboard only takes up about two-fifths of the screen giving you plenty of space with which to work. Most apps will present a dual-pane tablet interface in either orientation.But when you directly compare the Fold 8’s internal screen with last year’sFold 7or the new Fold 8 Ultra’s squarer display, you realise that landscape video is almost the same size on both tablets; only the thickness of the letterboxing black bars differs significantly.The speakers of the Fold 8 are pretty good for a phone, but they are only stereo when the tablet is held in portrait, not landscape when watching video which is unfortunate.View image in fullscreenWith both folders held in landscape, standard 16:9 ratio YouTube videos are 151 x 85mm on the Fold 8 Ultra (left) and 154mm x 86mm on the Fold 8 (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsMain screen:7.6in QXGA+ 120Hz (403ppi) AMOLED flexible displayCover screen:5.5in WUXGA+ 120Hz (428ppi) AMOLEDProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for GalaxyRAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:One UI 9 based onAndroid17Camera:50+50MP rear; 10MP+10MP selfie camerasConnectivity:5G, dual sim, e-sim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, GNSSWater resistance:IP48 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:123.9 x 81.9 x 9.7mmDimensions unfolded:123.9 x 161.4 x 4.5mmWeight:201gPlenty of power for multitaskingView image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 fully charges in 65 minutes hitting 70% in about half an hour using a 45W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included). It also supports 20W wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 has the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and memory asSamsung’s top S26 Ultraand performs very similarly, making it one of the fastest Android phones available with plenty of power for multitasking, gaming or anything else.The battery lasts a solid 40 hours between charge, using an even split of both screens for a total of eight hours on a mix of 5G and wifi for browsing, messaging, shooting photos and making notes. Gaming and other more intensive tasks drained the battery faster, but the Fold 8 should comfortably see out even the heaviest of days without needing a top up.One UI 9 softwareView image in fullscreenThe Fold 8 can have up to three apps on screen in a multiple different grid layouts with more running as small floating windows.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSamsung has the best, most adaptable software for making the most of folding phones, allowing multiple split-windowing configurations with up to three apps in a grid on screen and more in floating windows. One UI 9 is based on the latest Android 17 with Samsung providing Android and security updates until 31 July 2033.The great Now Bar remains from last year’s version for live sports scores, music, timers and other ongoing tasks at the bottom of the lock screen or in the status bar. The improved Now Nudge, Samsung’s AI suggestion toolfrom the S26, can surface information from a greater number of sources in a wider range of apps. The Now Brief AI box remains a weak point, however, rarely suggesting anything useful beyond the weather or your calendar events.Google’s Gemini is baked in along with plenty of other AI tools that can occasionally be useful. One oddity is that if you choose not to have the same home screen on the outside and inside displays, the tablet screen ends up with two separate home screen layouts, one for portrait and one for landscape orientation. That means you have three separate home screens to customise with their own configuration of apps and widgets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has plenty of modes and can be used open or folded for different shooting methods.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold 8 has two 10-megapixel selfie cameras but only two 50MP cameras on the back with no telephoto camera.The main 50MP camera is the best of the bunch and similar in performance to the main camera of thestandard S26, shooting good photos across a range of conditions. The 50MP ultrawide is also solid, with consistent colour across both cameras. The 2x crop zoom on the main camera works fairly well, but magnifying beyond to 4x or 10x digital zoom rapidly becomes poor.The Fold 8’s selfie cameras are decent and handy for video calls, but you get better results using the main camera for selfies with the outside screen as a viewfinder, even if it is a bit ungainly.The camera app has plenty of modes and shoots decent video, with some fancy auto-tracking features that make it easy to set the camera up partly folded and keep a subject in frame.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe crease in the middle where the screen folds is still evident when the display is off or you run your finger over it.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe battery has expected lifespan of at least 1,200 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone isgenerally repairable. Inside screenrepairs cost about £600. Samsung offers aself-repair programme, as well as Care+accidental damage insurancethat reduces the cost of repairs to £50.The Fold 8 is made from 14.9% recycled material by weight, which Samsung breaks down inits environmental report. The company offerstrade-inandrecycling schemesfor old devices.PriceThe Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs from£1,699(€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699).For comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs£1,899, theS26 Ultracosts£1,279, theHonor Magic V6costs£1,999.99and theGoogle Pixel 10 Pro Foldcosts£1,299.VerdictThe Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a bit of a curio from Samsung. Having forged the way with narrower book-style foldables, suddenly offering a squat, passport-shaped version seems like an odd step.On paper, the inside screen’s more conventional iPad-like shape makes it better suited to websites, video and apps. But because the Fold 8’s internal screen isn’t any wider than that of theFold 7or Fold 8 Ultra, apps have less screen space to work with while landscape videos are practically the same size, just with slimmer black bars at the top and bottom on the Fold 8.Meanwhile, the short and fat form of the closed Fold 8 makes for a worse phone experience. It is much harder to use one-handed and the keyboard takes up far too much of the screen. I didn’t find it any easier to fit in a pocket than narrower rivals, either.Shape aside, the Fold 8 is another stunning piece of technology from Samsung with excellent software to make the best of its folding form, plenty of processing power and surprisingly good battery life. But it only has two cameras on the back with no telephoto option, which is poor for this kind of money.The Fold 8 is better than some of the original attempts at the passport folder shapes, but there are many good a reasons book-style folding phones evolved into candy bar shapes over the last eight years.Pros:a phone and tablet in one, thin and light, powerful multitasking abilities, great tablet screen, top performance, solid battery life, water resistance.Cons:extremely expensive, passport-shape not ideal for phone duties, no dust resistance, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, no telephoto camera.View image in fullscreenWith the Fold 8 Ultra (left) and Fold 8 (right), Samsung offers a choice of shapes for its book-style folding phones.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsSamsungAndroidSmartphonesTablet computersMobile phonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph Sakran | The Guardian
description: AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place
Content: ‘Patients will need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason.’Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Patients will need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason.’Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHealthWhat happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment?Simar Bajaj and Joseph SakranAI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first placeMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTShareIn healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becomingless clinically adeptas they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they have built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling. Although a doctor who has forgotten how to reason is recoverable, one who never learned how may not be.OpenEvidence, essentially an AI chatbot for clinicians, has given this concern its most concrete form. Abouttwo-thirds of US doctorsactively use OpenEvidence, asking about puzzling symptoms, drug interactions and clinical guidelines, getting responses within seconds, anchored in the latest research. Trainees, unsurprisingly, have also begun to use this AI tool in many of the same ways – but at a far more formative stage.For example, trainees once asked to build a list of potential diagnoses might struggle and offer an incomplete set, learning what they missed, sometimes painfully. Now, trainees can simply ask OpenEvidence and get a nearly perfect answer, complete with possibilities they might have never considered and none of the embarrassment of having overlooked them. Repeating this answer on the wards may make the trainee look prepared and even impress the supervising doctor.We must not let AI ‘pull the doctor out of the visit’ for low-income patients | Leah Goodridge and Oni BlackstockRead moreHowever, this performance can also conceal the very deficit that training is meant to reveal: that the struggle is the point. Medical training, more than most professions, is an apprenticeship. A student becomes a resident, a resident becomes a fellow, and a fellow becomes an attending – every step shaped by failure, uncertainty and increasing responsibility. With years of repetition and watchful supervision, the habits of clinical reasoning slowly become part of the physician’s inner architecture.Technology has long shifted how people learn medicine, from advanced imaging to electronic medical records. But AI is different, not just expanding what doctors can see but inserting itself into the cognitive machinery that training is meant to build. As these tools become more capable and the physician’s role increasingly involves supervising them, experienced clinicians may have enough intuition and independent judgment to critically evaluate the machine’s answers. But for trainees whose understanding of medicine is being formed alongside AI, the relationship is more fraught. Can they really question the reasoning that shaped their own? What happens when the generation trained by AI becomes the generation responsible for catching its mistakes? With unchecked use among trainees, we risk creating supervisors of reasoning before we create reasoners.The stakes of that question are growing: arecent study in Nature Medicinefound that tools pulling from the latest medical literature, like OpenEvidence does, can be less reliable than they appear and, in some cases, less accurate than general-purpose AI chatbots. The problem of misplaced trust is already embedded in the AI that trainees are using today.To be clear, many trainees sense the trap, telling us they know that tools such as OpenEvidence can become a crutch. But these trainees also feel stuck in an arms race: if everyone else is using AI to sound more prepared, opting out feels like unilateral disarmament. The solution, then, cannot rest on individual restraint. It has to be structural.That is why medical schools and residency programs need to shape not just whether trainees use AI, but when. No one can police every search on every phone, nor should they. But supervising doctors can build a simple expectation – reason first, consult AI second – and assess accordingly. Trainees should have to make their unaided first pass visible, committing to a leading diagnosis, naming the dangerous possibilities to rule out, and explaining what to do next. In practice, that might mean a resident who admits a patient overnight first writes a brief “pre-AI assessment” after the history and physical exam. On rounds, when a new lab result or symptom changes the case, the attending might need to pause the team – before anyone can consult AI – to ask how this changes the diagnosis or treatment plan.As AI becomes more deeply integrated into medicine, this will feel cumbersome and inefficient. But such friction is purposeful: the learning scientists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork describe how “desirable difficulties” slow performance in the moment but improve retention and transfer of skills over time. In fact, used after an independent attempt, AI could actually serve as a powerful tutor, showing trainees what they missed and what they overemphasized.Sequencing, however, may not be enough on its own. Aviation thus offers a useful precedent: pilots in training are not taught to avoid autopilot but to preserve their manual competence. The Federal Aviation Administration evenadvises pilotsto maintain manual flying skills by periodically disengaging automation and hand-flying. Medicine needs similar discipline, with trainees required to periodically work through no-AI cases and assessed on their unaided reasoning to reveal potential drift.I had a blood clot. An AI diagnosis may have saved my life | Gleb TsipurskyRead moreFinally, trainees should be taught to interrogate AI itself. Programs could run the medical equivalent of flight simulator drills, built from real clinical cases: for example, a polished AI-generated assessment with a subtle flaw. Afterward, attendings could debrief not only whether the trainee reached the right answer but also when they trusted the tool, when they questioned it, and when they found the flaw. Just as important, attendings should mix in AI outputs that are perfectly accurate, so students learn not reflexive skepticism but disciplined judgment.None of this is an argument for making medical training harder for its own sake or romanticizing humiliation as pedagogy. In every generation of medicine, there is a temptation to confuse difficulty with virtue, but the struggle to independently reason through a patient’s case is not hazing but a core competency.AI is here to stay, and patients stand to benefit from its speed and reach. But patients will also need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason – doctors whose reasoning is not subordinated to it. Although AI can reason over the facts it is given, a trainee who has seen pneumonia that looks like pneumonia, then pneumonia that looks like heart failure, then heart failure that looks like pneumonia, develops a richer bedside judgment: what to notice, what to question, and when a familiar pattern should be distrusted. That is what medical training is trying to produce. AI should help augment this, not replace it.Simar Bajajis a medical student and Knight-Hennessy Scholar at Stanford University School of Medicine, as well as an award-winning journalistDr Joseph V Sakranis a trauma surgeon and public health expert who serves as executive vice-chair of surgery atJohns Hopkins MedicineExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)US healthcareComputingMedicineResearchcommentShareReuse this content
