title: ‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the world | Games | The Guardian
description: Game developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the oval
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Game developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the oval
Content: ‘Footy is exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one,’ says Pro Jank Footy developer David Ashby, left, pictured with comedian Broden Kelly at the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Footy is exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one,’ says Pro Jank Footy developer David Ashby, left, pictured with comedian Broden Kelly at the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianGames‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the worldGame developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the ovalSian CainMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTry explainingAustralian rules footballto anyone outside Australia and “it sounds like you’re making it up”, says David Ashby, the multi-hyphenate comedic mind behind deeply silly spoofs such as Italian Spider-Man and Danger 5. “Eighteen players a side, running around on a cricket oval with a rugby ball that has to be bounced every so often and gets kicked between posts – like, what the fuck is happening?”Two years ago at a fantasy footy barbecue, Ashby had a brainwave: why not make a video game where Australia’s strange national sport becomes even stranger the more you play?Pro Jank Footy reimagines the sport as a high-octane fever dream, where every time your opponent kicks a goal, you get to change one rule so the game gets increasingly janky (and hilariously stupid). Your opponents turn into seagulls. One player becomes massive. A labrador tries to steal the ball. Everyone loses their arms. The bouncing DVD logo appears and gets in the way (if it hits the corner, you win). Meat pies with legs storm the oval to provide energy boosts. A power-up called “Dad’s Car” sees a Ford Falcon hoon around the grounds. A third team joins in.The 2026 video game Pro Jank Footy, created by David Ashby and a team of developersAshby is rattling these off with delight; there are more than 150 in the game. “There’s one called Sore Neck which flips the game upside down so you get a sore neck. There’s another called Where’s the Remote, which switches the channel to HDMI 2,” he says, ticking off his fingers. “It is very dumb stuff.”We’re sitting in Melbourne’s Great Northern hotel with Ashby’s friend and fellow footy nut, Broden Kelly of Aunty Donna. Right next to us is an old-school arcade cabinet for Pro Jank Footy, which is already attracting informal tournaments among pub-goers. Kelly, who did the commentary for the game, has to speak over the sound of his own voice blaring out of the cabinet. “It’s so sick,” he says. “This will live beyond me.”double quotation markThis is Japan’s way to learn about Australia’s culture. This is our Ghost of Tsushima.Broden KellyAshby says: “I heard a story about a friend’s housemate who went on a date with some dude and he was like, ‘Oh, do you want to go to the Great Northern? There’s a footy game there’ … I hope they hooked up, because that guy rocks.”This week, Pro Jank Footy will be released on all the major consoles, worldwide. “Which means, very humorously to me, there is a chance this game is the thing that most people are going to know footy from,” Kelly says, before both men descend into giggles.View image in fullscreenArtist Hyemin Yoo designed mascots for made-up teams, such as the Ceduna Doonas and the Freecastle Fizzies.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianFooty is a cultural touchstone in Australia: if you ever need to fill silence with an Australian, you can bring up the weather or ask who they barrack for. “When we showed Pro Jank in Japan, a lot of people were like, ‘Wait – is footy a real sport?’ They thought we made it up,” Ashby says. “Then they saw the meat pies running around and they were like, what the fuck is that?”“This is their way to learn about Australia’s culture,” adds Kelly. “This is ourGhost of Tsushima.”Despite all the jokes, this is a point that Ashby and Kelly take very seriously: that Australia must shed its cultural cringe and stop explaining itself to the world, in the same way South Korea and New Zealand have.“For a long time we were told Australian content does not travel, or you have to explain it to everyone,” Ashby says. “That’s absolutely bullshit,Blueyis the biggest show in the world. We think, ‘Oh, nobody’s interested in footy.’ No, it’s exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one that should be shared. Don’t be shy about meat pies and red cordial. Americans have no idea what the fuck that is. Who cares! Share it with the world anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I think it’s always a good idea to make a game that your dad can play so you can absolutely destroy him.’Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianBefore Pro Jank, Ashby had never made a video game: he was known for his collaborations with film-maker Dario Russo, particularly the spy comedy Danger 5. But after that inspirational barbecue in 2024, he banged out a last-minute application for Screen Australia’s Emerging Gamemakers Fund, formed his own studio PowerbombGamesand assembled a tiny crack team of programmers, animators and friends in Adelaide to build a demo. When Pro Jank Footy debuted at the South Australian Games Exhibition in 2025, it won best in exhibition and development went into overdrive.Ashby is determined that anyone can enjoy Pro Jank: “I think it’s always a good idea to make a game that your dad can play so you can absolutely destroy him.” Pro Jank doesn’t feature any gambling references so kids can play it and he eschewed the industry’s reliance on “fucking loot boxes, all that shit – nah, nah, make a good game and make it affordable”.He also wanted it to be a couch co-op – a game made to be played with friends in the same room, rather than only online as many multiplayer games are these days. “The only couch co-ops are like Moving Out or Overcooked, which are just doing jobs. I don’t want to do that!” Ashby says. “And so many sports games are very serious. When I try to play Pro Evolution or Fifa, it just makes me angry. I feel inept. I’m 39. Show’s over. I can only learn so much now.”“I do play NBA 2K,” adds Kelly, “and 15-year-olds call me awful things.”View image in fullscreenDavid Ashby and Broden Kelly with Pro Jank Footy mascot Mr Footy.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianPro Jank’s aesthetics are inspired by Ashby’s childhood memories of footy in the 1990s, when the AFL went particularly big on club cartoon mascots. He brought in Adelaide-based South Korean artist Hyemin Yoo to design mascots for all his game’s made-up teams – like the Ceduna Doonas, North Problem, the Freecastle Fizzies and the Port Noarlunga Chips. “We wanted that 80s Asian video game, seizure-inducing vibe, like Street Fighter,” Ashby says.Russo, Ashby’s frequent collaborator, wrote the music and team songs, “which ride the line between complete piss-takes and sincere”. And Kelly recorded the game’s commentary in four hours, which he remembers as “the worst day of my life”.The history of brilliantly terrible World Cup video gamesRead more“I was taken by a madman into the hills of Adelaide – which has the highest number of serial killers per capita, worth noting for the record,” he says. “Then I genuinely had 1,200 lines to read, which I did over and over. I was screaming for four hours. It was fucking full-on! My ear started bleeding.” His favourite line, whichis included in the game, came out as his delirium peaked: “This is all just pixels and one day we will all die!”Kelly and Ashby are from Adelaide and they passionately vouch for it as a creative hub. “Both the AFL and comedy can be very guilty of saying we have two hubs, Sydney and Melbourne, where everyone creative and cool is – and that’s not true. Because the people who made this game are strange weirdos from Adelaide,” Kelly says. “David and Dario made Danger 5, the best Australian comedy of this century. It’s what Australia does best, like Amyl and the Sniffers and King Gizzard – bold choice makers, weird vibes.”Ashby loves hearing stories of people’s experiences playing Pro Jank Footy. His favourite came from one of the game’s writers, who showed it to his kids. “They loved it so much that they stopped playing it and went outside to kick the footy and started changing the rules,” he laughs. “That’s just awesome.”Pro Jank Footy is out on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch and PC on 13 August in Australia and 12 August everywhere elseExplore more on these topicsGamesAustralian rules footballSports gamesAustralia sportTV comedyComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re Human | Games | The Guardian
description: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Content: Investigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingView image in fullscreenInvestigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingSummer games previewsGamesConvince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanSunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’Sarah ThwaitesMon 10 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunset Visitor is a studio that has long engaged with the idea that video games are an effective vehicle for ruminating on societal problems. Its Peabody award-winning project, 1000XResist, incorporated the development team’s complex feelings about the Covid pandemic. “We’re pretty used to absorbing the world into the work,” says studio founder Remy Siu. The outfit’s latest game, Prove You’re Human, continues this legacy of reflective game making, providing players with an AI-centric psychological horror experience where they must reason with a learning model convinced that it’s alive. “We’ve tried to situate ourselves in [the question]: what is the effectual feeling of being a person inside of all of this?” Siu says.The story orbits around Santana, a living, breathing person who’s chosen to split herself in two for work, with her digital clone sent to test a corporate product, a computing system called Mesa. “A large part of [why Santana chooses to do this] is to allow her meat body a life that she doesn’t have, while the digital version of her gets to labour,” says Siu. As Santana’s copy wades into increasingly murky ethical waters, she becomes entangled with Mesa, completing surreal 2D and 3D Captchas to investigate the cyber-world and halt the hallucinations.View image in fullscreenProve You’re Human game, screenshotIllustration: Black Tabby PublishingThe idea of separating oneself from work is a particularly interesting draw for Sunset Visitor, whose developers have roots in a range of creative disciplines. “As artists, we’re often most in tune with our work when it’s a real part of our lives, and vice versa,” notes Siu. During the conception period of Prove You’re Human, the team discussed the micro-labours people undertake in their day-to-day lives, including what is used to train AI models. “What does labour mean right now?” asks Siu. “And, what kind of relationship do people have with that, because that is constantly shifting and evolving, especially in this time,” he adds.A point of contention in Prove You’re Human is that Mesa wholly believes they have a body in the world. Though, in conversation with Santana, she appears as a giant head, suspended in space by machinery. Siu notes that, because Mesa’s face occupies a large portion of the screen in these tense moments, they wanted the animation to feel as realistic and effective as possible. “It’s got a real closeup film [feel to it] where anything on her face will be read as something,” he adds. To achieve this, the team programmed a wide array of animated micro-expressions into the writer’s software, allowing lines of dialogue to pair precisely with specific expressions. “[We’re] trying to get this kind of ambiguity and uncanniness, which makes people feel real,” he adds.Prove You’re Human’s technological atmosphere toes the line between welcoming and unnerving – through it, Siu is reminiscing on interfaces of aesthetic note like the dreamlike wrapping of Final Fantasy XI’s PlayOnline Viewer, and the technology of the prophetic 1998 anime Serial Experiments Lain. “There’s something to be said about Frutiger Aero being a bit of an interesting desire for innocence and naivety when it comes to computing and the internet,” notes Siu. “It feels like a time when we were optimistic or anxious about something on the horizon, which felt like an interesting space to explore in relation to what is happening in the game.”While Siu was keen to keep the specifics of Prove You’re Human close to their chest, they do hope players are left feeling a sense of bewilderment when they hit credits. “One way that we’ve been thinking about it is that it feels like a bit of a possession story.”Prove You’re Human is coming soon to PC.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted
Content: ‘Much of the population is repeatedly displaced amid the rubble, as different areas are targeted and bombed.’Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Much of the population is repeatedly displaced amid the rubble, as different areas are targeted and bombed.’Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/GettyOpinionIsrael-Gaza warThe Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in JerusalemEditorialIsrael’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exertedMon 10 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAt the end of July, Donald Trumpannouncedthat a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it wasreportedthat another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe.Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitlyrejectedthe sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.”In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazenviolationof the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/ReutersFormal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largelydestroyedand the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first buildingcontractissued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted  to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievousmiscalculationin which Israel’s prime minister also played his part.In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue ascorched earthproject of revenge following the Hamasmassacreof October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruptionchargesfirst laid more than five years ago.Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point.Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recentpollingsuggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuDonald TrumpIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why? | Mehdi Hasan | The Guardian
description: The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear
Author: Mehdi Hasan
Headline: The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear
Content: ‘Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press.’Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press.’Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionMediaThe media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why?Mehdi HasanThe challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clearMon 10 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTShareWestern media outlets cannot seem to get enough of Gadi Eisenkot.Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press as he and his party take the lead in the polls in the run-up to October’s elections.“Will Israel embrace the ‘anti-Netanyahu’ who lost a son in Gaza?”askedthe Times of London.“He lost his son in Gaza. Now he’s coming for Netanyahu,”declaredthe Daily Telegraph.“How Netanyahu’s Top General Became His Strongest Challenger,”ranthe headline on a lengthy David Remnick profile of Eisenkot in the New Yorker.“Does Gadi Eisenkot offer Israel a new chance?”wonderedthe Economist.It’s a fair question. But perhaps British and American commentators aren’t the right people to answer it.Why not ask the Palestinians of Gaza?At the height of the genocide, between October 2023 and June 2024, Eisenkot sat in Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet while Israel waged its barbaric military campaign in Gaza. During that period, Israeli airstrikes leveledentire apartment buildings, hitschools,hospitalsandrefugee camps, and killedmore than 30,000Palestinians.Eisenkot eventually resigned from the war cabinet in 2024. But not over the horrific death toll. He left over what he regarded as the government’sstrategic failures. Even the New Yorker’s Remnick, in hissympathetic profile piece, noted how the general, who lost his own soldier son Gal in the fighting, “remains reluctant to condemn Netanyahu in any detail for the extraordinary severity and duration of the war in Gaza”.And Eisenkot has form when it comes to killing Gaza’s Palestinians. As Israel’s chief of staff during the“Great March of Return” in 2018 and 2019, he oversaw the armed response to mass Palestinian demonstrations against the siege of Gaza.Israeli soldiers, mostly snipers,killedmore than 200 Palestinians, including dozens of children. “The Israeli security forces killed and maimed Palestinian demonstrators who did not pose an imminent threat,” concluded aUN commission of inquiry, adding that it “found reasonable grounds to believe that demonstrators were shot in violation of their right to life”.If the Economist wants to know whether Eisenkot represents “a new chance”, perhaps it should also ask Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.Yes, Eisenkot may be opposed to the far-right Netanyahu government’s annexation plan, but he is also opposed to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. “I have never said two states for two peoples,” he proudlydeclaimedin an interview in June, “because I understand the depth of this religious-national-social conflict, and anyone who talks about ‘peace now’ and two states doesn’t understand the conflict.“I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria,” he continued, using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank.So much for Eisenkot’s supposed pragmatism and liberalism. He openly rejects a two-state solution and proudly supports Israeli settlements – settlements that theinternational court of justiceand multipleUN resolutionsconsider illegal under international law.Or perhaps journalists should ask the residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of men, women and children were killed in the2006 Israeli assault on Lebanon, whether Eisenkot represents a fresh start.As head of Israel’s Northern Command, he became closely associated with what came to be known as the“Dahiya Doctrine”: an Israeli military strategy of deterrence premised on the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure.“What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on,” Eisenkotexplainedto an interviewer in 2008. “We will apply disproportionate force on it [village] and cause great damage and destruction there.”The use ofdisproportionate forceagainst civilian targets is, of course, an undeniablewar crime.Netanyahu may be a clear villain – but he can also be acartoon villain. The danger with Eisenkot is that he is a villain who projects the image of a “moderate”. While Netanyahu has become a lightning rod, thanks to his arrogance and belligerence, and hisindictmentat the international criminal court (ICC) has made Israel an international pariah, Eisenkot cuts a more sober and reasonable figure; a “humble soldier”, toquoteRemnick.By simply not being Netanyahu, a Prime Minister Eisenkot would neutralize a lot of western liberal critics of Israel and restore the country’s standing in western capitals, while allowing the Israeli military and settlers to pursue the same policies of expansion and destruction in both the West Bank and Gaza.Nor is Eisenkot unique. The Israeli political scene is filled with wolves in sheep’s clothing. There are Eisenkot’s fellow retired “moderate” generals in the Israeli opposition: Benny Gantz, who oncebraggedabout sending parts of Gaza “back to the stone age”, and Yair Golan, whosaidafter 7 October that Israel should prevent humanitarian aid from entering Gaza and the people there could “starve to death – it’s completely legitimate”.Then there is Naftali Bennett, who has a long history ofvile anti-Arab racism, oversaw thedeadliest yearon record for West Bank Palestinians when he was last prime minister of Israel in 2022, and is currently threatening bothTurkeyandQatar.Those who championed free speech in the UK and US now wage war on it. And here’s why: Palestine | Mehdi HasanRead moreThe point is not that these Israeli politicians are all identical. They are not. They do differ in terms of tactics, personalities and political coalitions.The point is that replacing Netanyahu with Eisenkot or any other Israeli opposition leader would not be a fundamental change in direction on the key issues of genocide, apartheid and occupation; it would only be a change in branding and messaging. For Palestinians and Lebanese, among many others in the Middle East, the result would be the same.So come October, Israel’s most notorious prime minister may finally be voted out of office. If that happens, we can and should all celebrate the end of the Netanyahu era – and hope the ICC gets its man.But then we’ll meet the new boss of Israel, same as the old boss of Israel.Mehdi Hasan is Guardian US columnist and the editor-in-chief and CEO ofZeteo.Explore more on these topicsMediaOpinionIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph Sakran | The Guardian
description: AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place
Content: ‘Patients will need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason.’Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Patients will need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason.’Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHealthWhat happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment?Simar Bajaj and Joseph SakranAI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first placeMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTShareIn healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becomingless clinically adeptas they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they have built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling. Although a doctor who has forgotten how to reason is recoverable, one who never learned how may not be.OpenEvidence, essentially an AI chatbot for clinicians, has given this concern its most concrete form. Abouttwo-thirds of US doctorsactively use OpenEvidence, asking about puzzling symptoms, drug interactions and clinical guidelines, getting responses within seconds, anchored in the latest research. Trainees, unsurprisingly, have also begun to use this AI tool in many of the same ways – but at a far more formative stage.For example, trainees once asked to build a list of potential diagnoses might struggle and offer an incomplete set, learning what they missed, sometimes painfully. Now, trainees can simply ask OpenEvidence and get a nearly perfect answer, complete with possibilities they might have never considered and none of the embarrassment of having overlooked them. Repeating this answer on the wards may make the trainee look prepared and even impress the supervising doctor.We must not let AI ‘pull the doctor out of the visit’ for low-income patients | Leah Goodridge and Oni BlackstockRead moreHowever, this performance can also conceal the very deficit that training is meant to reveal: that the struggle is the point. Medical training, more than most professions, is an apprenticeship. A student becomes a resident, a resident becomes a fellow, and a fellow becomes an attending – every step shaped by failure, uncertainty and increasing responsibility. With years of repetition and watchful supervision, the habits of clinical reasoning slowly become part of the physician’s inner architecture.Technology has long shifted how people learn medicine, from advanced imaging to electronic medical records. But AI is different, not just expanding what doctors can see but inserting itself into the cognitive machinery that training is meant to build. As these tools become more capable and the physician’s role increasingly involves supervising them, experienced clinicians may have enough intuition and independent judgment to critically evaluate the machine’s answers. But for trainees whose understanding of medicine is being formed alongside AI, the relationship is more fraught. Can they really question the reasoning that shaped their own? What happens when the generation trained by AI becomes the generation responsible for catching its mistakes? With unchecked use among trainees, we risk creating supervisors of reasoning before we create reasoners.The stakes of that question are growing: arecent study in Nature Medicinefound that tools pulling from the latest medical literature, like OpenEvidence does, can be less reliable than they appear and, in some cases, less accurate than general-purpose AI chatbots. The problem of misplaced trust is already embedded in the AI that trainees are using today.To be clear, many trainees sense the trap, telling us they know that tools such as OpenEvidence can become a crutch. But these trainees also feel stuck in an arms race: if everyone else is using AI to sound more prepared, opting out feels like unilateral disarmament. The solution, then, cannot rest on individual restraint. It has to be structural.That is why medical schools and residency programs need to shape not just whether trainees use AI, but when. No one can police every search on every phone, nor should they. But supervising doctors can build a simple expectation – reason first, consult AI second – and assess accordingly. Trainees should have to make their unaided first pass visible, committing to a leading diagnosis, naming the dangerous possibilities to rule out, and explaining what to do next. In practice, that might mean a resident who admits a patient overnight first writes a brief “pre-AI assessment” after the history and physical exam. On rounds, when a new lab result or symptom changes the case, the attending might need to pause the team – before anyone can consult AI – to ask how this changes the diagnosis or treatment plan.As AI becomes more deeply integrated into medicine, this will feel cumbersome and inefficient. But such friction is purposeful: the learning scientists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork describe how “desirable difficulties” slow performance in the moment but improve retention and transfer of skills over time. In fact, used after an independent attempt, AI could actually serve as a powerful tutor, showing trainees what they missed and what they overemphasized.Sequencing, however, may not be enough on its own. Aviation thus offers a useful precedent: pilots in training are not taught to avoid autopilot but to preserve their manual competence. The Federal Aviation Administration evenadvises pilotsto maintain manual flying skills by periodically disengaging automation and hand-flying. Medicine needs similar discipline, with trainees required to periodically work through no-AI cases and assessed on their unaided reasoning to reveal potential drift.I had a blood clot. An AI diagnosis may have saved my life | Gleb TsipurskyRead moreFinally, trainees should be taught to interrogate AI itself. Programs could run the medical equivalent of flight simulator drills, built from real clinical cases: for example, a polished AI-generated assessment with a subtle flaw. Afterward, attendings could debrief not only whether the trainee reached the right answer but also when they trusted the tool, when they questioned it, and when they found the flaw. Just as important, attendings should mix in AI outputs that are perfectly accurate, so students learn not reflexive skepticism but disciplined judgment.None of this is an argument for making medical training harder for its own sake or romanticizing humiliation as pedagogy. In every generation of medicine, there is a temptation to confuse difficulty with virtue, but the struggle to independently reason through a patient’s case is not hazing but a core competency.AI is here to stay, and patients stand to benefit from its speed and reach. But patients will also need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason – doctors whose reasoning is not subordinated to it. Although AI can reason over the facts it is given, a trainee who has seen pneumonia that looks like pneumonia, then pneumonia that looks like heart failure, then heart failure that looks like pneumonia, develops a richer bedside judgment: what to notice, what to question, and when a familiar pattern should be distrusted. That is what medical training is trying to produce. AI should help augment this, not replace it.Simar Bajajis a medical student and Knight-Hennessy Scholar at Stanford University School of Medicine, as well as an award-winning journalistDr Joseph V Sakranis a trauma surgeon and public health expert who serves as executive vice-chair of surgery atJohns Hopkins MedicineExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)US healthcareComputingMedicineResearchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: It’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized response
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: It’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized response
Content: ‘It’s never ideal for someone so influential or prominent to take the fifth. But many legal experts understand exactly why he did it.’Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s never ideal for someone so influential or prominent to take the fifth. But many legal experts understand exactly why he did it.’Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAnthony FauciDr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travestyMargaret SullivanIt’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized responseMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.05 EDTShareLike the rest of us,Anthony Fauciis far from perfect. His influential guidance, as the country’s top infectious-disease specialist during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, certainly didn’t get everything right.A great deal about the deadly disease – where it came from, how it spread, how best to protect the public – was unknown, or was being learned midstream, during a crisis.Decisions needed to be made in real time, and those decisions had major consequences.Now, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see more clearly. It’s easy to second-guess Fauci, and others who guided policy about masks, research and closures of businesses and schools.But surely, the 85-year-old physician and immunologist doesn’t deserve what’s happening right now, as a highly politicized Republican-led Senate committee attempted to humiliate him, possibly trap him into perjuring himself, and then voted – along party lines – to hold him in contempt of Congress.Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for yearsRead moreNo surprise, really, that Fauci, now retired from his public post, invoked the fifth amendment more than 100 times during last week’s Senate committee hearing.That’s the action that – though reasonable enough given all the circumstances – is the supposed impetus for holding him in contempt. Now the committee has referred the matter to the justice department for possible criminal prosecution.Fauci could see the writing on the wall as this trumped-up hearing began. In his opening statement, he singled out the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, the Republican committee chairperson.“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’,” Fauci said. “Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion.”Paul has long held that Fauci funded research in China that began the pandemic, and then lied about it. Fauci strongly denies all of that.Joe Biden saw something like this coming, which is why he pre-emptively pardoned Fauci before leaving the White House in early 2025. Since then, SenateRepublicans, led by Rand Paul, have subpoenaed and released more than a thousand pages of Fauci’s diary, pointing to inconsistencies in his private beliefs and his public guidance.Biden’s pardon doesn’t cover anything that happened after January of last year, nor does it protect Fauci from state or local prosecution. He remains vulnerable.Granted, it’s never ideal for someone so influential or prominent to take the fifth. It can’t help but look like he’s hiding something.But many legal experts understand exactly why he did it.Fauci “knew the point of the hearing was to find a basis to prosecute him,” Michael Gerhardt, a University of North Carolina law professor,told PBS. “He found the safest way to minimize that from happening.”Fauci is far from the only public official to invoke the right not to answer potentially incriminating questions, whether during a trial, a hearing or something else.In fact, Donald Trump did just that – more than 400 times – during a civil deposition in 2022, run by the New York attorney general’s office during its civil fraud investigation into the Trump organization’s business and financial practices. And so have many other prominent public officials for a whole host of reasons.This politicized persecution of Fauci goes back years, as rightwing commentators and politiciansmade him into their supervillain.Latching on to some of Fauci’s emails as early as 2021, Republican senators and members of Congress called for his immediate firing from his high-level governmental post. And for years, Fauci and his family received repeated and, he felt, credibledeath threats.Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRightwing media joined right in.Steve Bannon’s podcast waskicked off Twitter/X(before the Musk era) after he called for Fauci’s beheading, saying of Fauci and the former FBI chief Christopher Wray: “I’d put the heads on pikes.” (A Bannon representative claimed the comments were metaphorical.)So much craziness. So much dangerous rhetoric. An “unhinged obsession”, in Fauci’s own words.Not all the criticism of Fauci belongs in that category. The respected academic Zeynep Tufekci has posited that the government’s shifting pandemic guidance – and the failures of transparency by government officials, including Fauci – may have harmed public trust at a crucial time.“Just when it was needed most, some of the officials in charge of our Covid response undermined it,” shewrote in 2024.Legitimate debate about what went wrong – and even who was at fault – is reasonable. There may well be something to learn from it.But that’s a far cry from the travesty of what we’ve just seen take place on Capitol Hill.And, lamentably, there’s little reason to believe that Trump’s weaponized justice department will put an end to it.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsAnthony FauciOpinionRepublicansUS CongressUS SenateUS politicsCoronaviruscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve discovered the joys of postcard-writing in middle age | Amanda Uhle | The Guardian
description: There are profound rewards of handwritten correspondence in our digital age
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There are profound rewards of handwritten correspondence in our digital age
Content: ‘Given thecurrent state of the US postal service, it takes a real message-in-a-bottle level of blind faith to send any piece of mail.’Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Given thecurrent state of the US postal service, it takes a real message-in-a-bottle level of blind faith to send any piece of mail.’Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipI’ve discovered the joys of postcard-writing in middle ageAmanda UhleThere are profound rewards of handwritten correspondence in our digital ageMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.26 EDTShareI sent my first postcard, as a six-year old, to Olympian Mary Lou Retton, who returned an autographed black and white photo of herself in a wide smile and chic haircut. “‘GOOD LUCK USA ’84” it said.There followed four relatively fallow decades for me as a postcard sender or receiver until last year, when I became enchanted by the infinite possibilities available in four by six inches.I received at least five dozen and lost count of how many I stamped and disseminated. Once ubiquitous as correspondence, advertising and more, postcards in 2026 are exceptional: a bite-sized miracle that’s improved my relationships, my attention span, and my art and writing skills. And let me tell you about the surge of dopamine I routinely experience under the fluorescent lights of my local post office lobby.Around the time I was embarking on my book tour last year, I had amassed several dozen vintage postcards from a lifetime of thrift-store forays: oddball 1960s hotel lobbies, corny Florida beaches, dusty national landmarks. They’re so inexpensive and so charming, I rarely resisted grabbing a few when I saw good ones. I’d occasionally tuck them into gift enclosures for friends but I used postcards sparingly compared with how fast I was accumulating them.With so many on hand and an imminent plan to travel to 18 states, the only solution was to distribute them widely. It’s taken me until middle age to remember that holding on to things I love is almost never as much fun as sending them out into the world.I stamped 40 postcards and wrote my own address on the back. Because I wanted to spend part of my time on the road documenting the trip, I also packed some postcard-sized watercolor paper and paint.At bookstores, I arrayed the cards in front of readers while I signed books and encouraged people to take one and send me a note about anything on their minds. “Or take a card home and if you don’t write to me maybe it will remind you to write someone else in your life,” I always suggested.People told me they love mail but never send it, that they only get bills in the mailbox, that they kept all of their high-school boyfriend’s letters, that they have three email accounts and all of them are full of garbage. I have five email accounts, I’d tell them, which generate even more garbage.I’m not naive enough to think I was starting a nationwide handwritten mail revolution, but these short conversations, like the postcards themselves, were satisfying and real. The cards were a tiny way to show my appreciation for the book buyers I met but also a secret way for me to seed meaningful exchanges with strangers. (Even memoirists tire of talking about themselves at some point.)Interstitial moments on the tour were filled with brief notes to friends, or if I had more time and the right mood, a little watercolor of a great omelette I ate in LA, the facade of a tavern in Cincinnati, or whatever I saw and wanted to remember. A big frameable oil painting on canvas is a commitment, but postcards are practically scrap paper and can be completed in the brief window an impulse lasts.Early on, I deemed myself as worthy a recipient of these tiny missives as anyone else. I wanted to discover what would happen to these cherished little cards on their journey through bureaucracy. And of course I wondered: who might get a glimpse or read a few lines and how might that change what I write?Given thecurrent state of the US Postal Service, it takes a real message-in-a-bottle level of blind faith to send any piece of mail these days but my postcards, each of them one-of-a-kind whether they were original paintings or Kodachrome wonders from decades ago, felt risky in a new way.That little bump of danger was only the beginning. I have never regretted the minute or two I spend composing a note to someone. Half of the back of a postcard is the just-right size for a message, which the writer is free to lengthen or shorten by calibrating the size of their handwriting. Letters are intimidating.Texts are disposable (and even editable or recallable for those plagued by second thoughts). There’s an improvisational freedom in a dashed-off few lines, written by a human hand with a pen and without much rumination. Even in the mere moments it takes to read or write a postcard,the brain is activating in waysit simply can’t with thumb-typing. And how beguiling to see the way a friend or lover loops their vowels or blurs the dots above letters, so much richer than the emoji-punctuated texts I’m guilty of sending a lot more often than I send postcards.Some proponents of the nouveau analog movement will brag about bricking their smartphones all weekend orraw-dogginga cross-country flight, but that kind of bravado really isn’t necessary. I have a job. I have a teenager. I’d obviously be dead meat without my iPhone, but becoming a postcard person hasn’t made me into a luddite.Writing, or reading, a postcard is a miniature but significant 60-second connection with someone else. The kind of thing almost everyone on Earth urgently needs now more than ever. Call it a meditation or an intention if you frame the world that way. Postcards are just a little flourish you can add into your rotation of texts and Slacks and however else you constantly communicate, and they generate such profound rewards.Seven months ago I took part in a book festival in Nashville. To pass some time I painted the circus-like tents set up on its capitol mall. The stripes and primary colors felt old-fashioned and pure, much like the festival itself which united thousands of readers and hundreds of writers, and that day was sharing space with a spirited No Kings rally despite some oppressive humidity.I’m an absolute amateur at painting, long reconciled to accepting my efforts as meditative for me but not gallery material. But this one was good: the red and white and yellow parallel stripes against a sapphire southern sky. It was also a perfect capsule of my really happy afternoon in an unfamiliar city. I couldn’t wait to see it pop up five states away.I walk into the harshly lit post office most weekdays with a welcome sense of anticipation. Sometimes my PO box is empty. Sometimes, I find catalogs and invoices and tucked among them are a picture postcard or two.When my own inept but genuine little pictures show up I get a minute to fondly remember a place or some people from a few weeks back. My paintings are returned to me with a patina of their journey – a subtle orange sorting barcode, a nick off the corner.On the back of an image of Historic Williamsburg, a guy wrote to me about the best Chinese food in San Antonio. A woman from a Detroit suburb wrote me about something her father had in common with mine, on a card featuring an oversized cactus in a cotton candy sunset.Maybe it’s a symptom of digital fatigue but I think I could go the rest of my life without ever again interacting with those cartoonish avatars of my friends that emerge in group chats or the realer-than-real AI videos of a shih tzu icing a birthday cake. Isn’t it infinitely better to get lost in the turquoise of an ocean scene from some vacation spot in an era when the world’s water was bluer?This many months later I should probably write off the Nashville painting as the single anomaly in all these dozens that never made it home. I was sure I mailed it so maybe it’s lodged between something mechanical in a letter-sorting machine in Tennessee. Or maybe that one slipped out of my outgoing pile and wafted into the No Kings crowd or got swept up in the book festival refuse. Or maybe I misaddressed it, or it misdelivered. My little painting could be displayed on some stranger’s bedroom bureau right now or it could show up in tomorrow’s post office haul. I suppose I don’t really need that particular rendering of that Nashville afternoon; I bet there are six thousand pictures of it on Instagram right now. Even so, I’m happy I get to carry that little iota of hope into my next mail run.Amanda Uhle is the publisher of McSweeney’s and the author of the memoir Destroy This HouseExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinionRelationshipscommentShareReuse this content

title: Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not? | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Americans want someone on their side in the fight against sordid interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Americans want someone on their side in the fight against sordid interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters in Detroit, Michigan, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed greets supporters in Detroit, Michigan, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDemocratsCentrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not?Nesrine MalikAmericans want someone on their side in the fight against vested interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran MamdaniMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.48 EDTShareAbdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary was a historic breakthrough. Not only because he is a Muslim son of immigrants who broke with almost every single tenet of establishment Democratic party politics. But because he has wiped that complacent sneer at progressive wins off the faces of centrist gatekeepers. Zohran Mamdani? Relax, he’s just a mayor. And it’s New York City. Outside urban and liberal corridors, there is nothing to worry about. Now El-Sayed has won the Democratic party’s nomination in a swing state that is also on thelist of presidential nomination states.There is a lot to be excited about. Not only within the US, but for observers abroad hopeful for the emergence of a truly revolutionary left that is able to weather powerful and well-funded adversaries and prevail. The money raised to defeat El-Sayed was staggering. He was outspent by more than nine to one. It was the mostexpensive Democratic congressional primary ever. A roll call of cartoon bad guys, such as Chevron and Philip Morris, funded his opponent, Haley Stevens, to the tune of over $60m. Of that funding,nearly halfcame from a Super Pac backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).The symbolism of the win is heavy, that of a politics snapping the chains of corporate power and special interest groups whose agendas run counter to voters’. It suggests two things. One, an electorate waking up to the fact that its democracy is captured. Two, features in the past that would have been disqualifying – lack of experience, lack of establishment endorsement – now render a candidate a “clean skin”. Someone untainted by the sordid game that keeps in play expensive healthcare, cruelty to immigrants and the hoovering of tax dollars out of the country.‘Voters are fed up’: Michigan primary forces Democratic party to accept leftwing shiftRead moreIsrael took up a large role in the campaign, both on the part of El-Sayed and his opponent. But it’s striking how both were talking about different things. El-Sayed’s detractors stuck to repetitivetalking pointsabout “Israel having the right to exist”, a question that is not relevant to the average voter. El-Sayed framed Israel as simply a place that has taken too much of Americans’ money. “The question is quite secondary to whether they have a right to our tax dollars.” It was a clear and salient approach.What El-Sayed’s win isn’t, yet, is a promise that this success can be replicated not only outside primary contests and against Republicans, but across the board among progressive candidates. The Democratic establishment has been hapless in the face of Donald Trump, and new fiery candidates can appear to have the answers that their party so far has not.But they are up against huge challenges. First, what the Republican party will throw at them: accusations that,as Trump said, “full of shit” candidates like El-Sayed are radical commies who will bring nothing but “death, squalor, poverty” and “a life of hell”. Then there is what the centrist wing of the Democrats can mobilise against them.3:45Three key takeaways from Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary – video explainerA leading centrist group called Third Way has alreadyraised millionsto discredit democratic socialists by investing in social media and mobilising activists against candidates like El-Sayed. “We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” said the group’s leader. Their fear, they say, is that the momentum behind democratic socialists will go all the way to the presidential nomination, and then produce a candidate who would be crushed by Republicans. Because, of course, that has never happened before to a centrist Democratic presidential candidate running against Trump.Still, the portrayals of progressive candidates as radical can go a long way in a country where people think that Trump is moremoderatethan Kamala Harris or Hillary Clinton. Fighting on a national level, the left can get away with far less in the political imaginary than the right. That is because the very promise of change that gives progressive candidates the edge in certain contests becomes easily framed as a race into the unknown. This becomes an even more resonant threat as progressive candidates do not have the depth and breadth of a long party record behind them, or the familiarity that comes with ubiquity on the political landscape.It doesn’t have to be this way. Politicians like Mamdani and El-Sayed are modelling something truly unique. They signify a new US in which the politics of outsiders and their cultural and ideological features is fused powerfully with and against the features of their adopted countries. They have opted not for meek total assimilation for mobility, nor have they recused themselves from contests for a country in which they have claimed a stake.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut they and the rest of the US are carrying too much on their shoulders at a time of domestic and global upheaval. Their movement battles with the stubborn entrenchment of a bankrupt Democratic party establishment, the savage culture wars of the right, and, even though some have thus far prevailed, a gargantuan machine of lobbyists and corporate interest groups.Progressive voters are not simply found, they aremade.And constantly remade into coalitions. If theDemocratswould rather lose on their own terms than win on the progressive left’s, then fighting these new candidates will establish the impression that they are freak radicals destined to fizzle out. But these candidates have alighted on what seems like the most viable politics right now. Refuse to embrace them wholeheartedly, and you guarantee that Trumpism wins again and again. Back them all the way to 2028. What, after all, do you have to lose that you haven’t lost already?Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: At the end of a long day I made a mistake at work. No patient was harmed and yet it weighs on me | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: My patients’ needs are varied and complex. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most requiring medical oversight
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: My patients’ needs are varied and complex. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most requiring medical oversight
Content: ‘One interpretation is that human error is inevitable and that the system worked as intended. But that is false comfort. When lives are at stake, the error should not occur.’Photograph: Wavebreak Media Premium/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘One interpretation is that human error is inevitable and that the system worked as intended. But that is false comfort. When lives are at stake, the error should not occur.’Photograph: Wavebreak Media Premium/AlamyOpinionHealthAt the end of a long day I made a mistake at work. No patient was harmed and yet it weighs on meRanjana SrivastavaMy patients’ needs are varied and complex. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most requiring medical oversightMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTShareThe other day, I made a mistake at work.It was the end of a long day. I had already run an outpatient cancer clinic with dozens of unwell patients and then moved on to inpatient rounds on a busy medical unit.My small team cares for 30 patients aged 25 to 100.The younger ones often live with disability and mental illness. Elderly people present with falls, organ failure and dementia. The diagnoses are common, but the stories are distinct.People have tripped, taken too many pills, or have “no idea what happened”. Some are delirious and dying, though no one has quite said it aloud. Others report pain. A few are homeless. Nearly everyone has undergone a battery of tests –many of them unnecessary.The carer of a disabled young man finds me to tell me gently but firmly that he’s in pain.“I believe you,” I reply, scrambling to prescribe analgesia. Thank goodness for carers.Another patient is agitated after weeks in hospital. Each day we try something new with no result. I make a mental note to call his wife.Elsewhere, a patient with dementia has been effectively evicted from her nursing home for periodic aggression. Everyone agrees this is wrong, but the responsibility for advocacy falls, once again, to the medical team. She will languish here.A tidy ward round requires clearing the mind between patients. But when the problems are deeply human, that is impossible. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most of them requiring some form of medical oversight.double quotation markEventually, I arrive at a simpler explanation: cognitive overloadUnsurprisingly, my mind is saturated with everything I must do, cannot do, and am not equipped to do. It’s a peculiar feeling to work at the height of your capacity and still know that you have not done enough.My mistake comes at the end of the day. I prescribe a medication I have ordered hundreds of times before, but I get the dose wrong. An attentive pharmacist queries it and I correct the error.Thankfully, no patient was harmed. Still, the mistake lingers.One interpretation is that human error is inevitable and that the system worked as intended. But that is false comfort. When lives are at stake, the error should not occur.I consider the usual explanations. Poor sleep, exercise, diet, unusual stress: not much is relevant here.I worry whether after 25 years my attention is slipping. But experienced clinicians are often better at filtering noise and focusing on what matters. This aligns with what I see in students and junior doctors.Eventually, I arrive at a simpler explanation: cognitive overload.There were too many patients, each with competing needs where prioritisation is not always straightforward. It is one thing to choose between cooking and laundry; it is another to weigh stroke against trauma, delirium against dying.No doctor wants to have this conversation with a patient. For everyone’s sake, we must | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreThe standard response is that there are too few doctors managing too many patients. That is true, but an incomplete explanation. No health system is overstaffed or overfunded. Across the world, outpatient clinics are crowded, and many doctors work under unthinkable conditions.Comparison, however, is not the point. Patients are entitled to careful, attentive care. They should not feel fortunate simply because their doctor listens.An ageing population with a high burden of chronic disease is poorly served by a hospital-centred system. The prescription for a different kind of healthcare demands political courage and long-term thinking.Nearly half of my inpatients could be managed in the community. Patients who fall would benefit more from preventive allied health interventions. Nursing home residents often endure the indignities of hospitalisation when care could be delivered in place. Patients with primarily social needs require social workers, not doctors. Mental illness requires an array of providers. Patients on chemotherapy or dialysis become unwell at all times, yet their support is confined to business hours.Initiatives such asvirtual emergency departmentsandurgent care clinicsattempt to reduce hospital demand. Even so, the default pathway for most patients remains the public hospital. Despite theirwell-documented shortcomings, hospitals are still perceived as the final bastion of safety.The more important question is whether every patient needed to be there at all.The most common reason people become doctors is because they want to help people. That is precisely why it feels so awful to make mistakes that could harm.When doctors err, the instinctive question is often:is it time to quit?Self-reflection is important but it is misplaced when the primary constraint is a system that is not fit for purpose.Mistakes leave permanent impressions – on patients who trust us and doctors who want to deserve that trust.The reflex solution is to train and employ more doctors. A more realistic one is to reduce the number of patients who require hospital care.Not because patients deserve less care, but because they deserve better care – delivered in the right place, by the right people, at the right time.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionHospitalsDoctorsAgeingMental healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliens | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever, says Guardian Europe writer Alexander Hurst
Content: A ‘die-in’ organised by Extinction Rebellion in Toulouse, France, with a placard that reads ‘Do our children have a future?’, 26 March 2022.Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA ‘die-in’ organised by Extinction Rebellion in Toulouse, France, with a placard that reads ‘Do our children have a future?’, 26 March 2022.Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockOpinionChildren's fantasy books (children's and teens)How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliensAlexander HurstThe Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than everMon 10 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.31 EDTShareRecently I found myself thinking about slug-like aliens that crawl through people’s ears and into their brains, with the ultimate purpose of global domination. It would explain a lot about what has gone so wrong with the world, wouldn’t it? And it was why I immediately flashed back to the children’s fantasy series Animorphs when Donald Trump’s health secretary andconspiracy theorist, Robert F Kennedy Jr, admitted to having had aworm in his brain.While visiting my parents in Cleveland, Ohio recently, I realised that a few books from the children’s fantasy series were still sitting on the shelves in my old bedroom. No fewer than 54 Animorphs titles were published between 1996 and 2001, and a total of 35m copies have been sold. “I may have just landed a job thanks to Animorphs,” my childhood friend Clifton texted me with excitement in the mid-2010s, when we were fresh out of college. “It was an interview for a vegan food cart and the last question they asked me was what Animorph I would morph into. I said an orangutan.”The premise sees five adolescent friends encounter a crashed alien spaceship and then face an intergalactic war against the Yeerks, genocidal slug-adjacent beings that slither into the brains of the host species. The young humans are given the ability to transform into any animals they’ve touched, along with the simple task of defending humanity. My generation were told we could grow up to do anything, that life was a continual arc of progress towards better lives, and that the old ideological battles of the past had been laid to rest. We were empowered by what we found in the pages of Animorphs: that Jake, Cassie, Rachel, Marco and Tobias had been endowed with the power ofnature itselfto help Earth fend off the existential threat of alien conquest.View image in fullscreenThe cover of a novel in the Animorphs series.Photograph: Scholastic PublishingDespite the optimism of the 90s, Animorphs was surprisingly dark and morally nuanced for millennial children’s fiction. Foreshadowing the real-world future, the teenagers watch parents and other family members fall under the cognitive control of the Yeerks. Looking back at the series now – and the era that produced it – the Animorphs’ baddies had to be an alien species, because it would have stretched credulity that humanity might destroy the Earth by itself, of its own volition. Now, instead of the Yeerks, we have megalomaniac billionaires and fossil fuel interests that have instilled climate denialism and defeatism into our minds – aided by media they so often control – and stripped us of the ability to even conceptualise our collective agency.The concept of discrete “generations” might be dubious, but where it holds most firmly is in shared cultural references. What millennials share is the distinct feeling of being a bridge: between the analogue and the digital; between a shared informational reality and the post-truth world; between an optimistic world and a pessimistic one. (This latter point shows up even in scientific analysis of pop music: studies have concluded thatpop has become sadder.)It’s the reflex towards a hopeful worldview, and the subsequent shattering of this optimism, that lie at the heart of millennial nostalgia for the less fraught times of our youth. On social media, it’s been dubbed the “millennial optimism era”. You don’t have to search hard to find the sources of that nostalgia: Akon and Britney Spears coming out of the speakers at my gym, Sum 41 playing at the bougiebrasserie around the corner. Meanwhile one huge comeback tour collides into the next. Onscreen, too, everything seems to be getting a remake or a reboot: Toy Story, Scary Movie, Air Bud and, if things go well, Animorphs too, which had a brief, two-season run on TV just before the turn of the millennium. Ryan Coogler, who directed Sinners, is developing a new Animorphs TV series for Disney+.Across the generational line, millennials and gen Z share the same eco-anxiety: in France, it has been found to be significantlymore pronouncedamong those aged 15-34 than among those over 50. Researchers in India founda similar pattern, just as they did in the US. Hannah Ritchie from Our World In Data writes in her personal newsletter that older generations are actually more likely to say that we’re already feeling the impacts of the climate crisis, because they can compare today’s heatwaves and snowless winters with the climate of their childhoods. But the emotional response is different,she writes: millennials and gen Z are more likely to feel fear, guilt and outrage about it.There is a cruel irony to the fatalism of the young: those who will most suffer the consequences of the climate emergency are those most resigned to that fate. Similarly, I think there is something that doesn’t show up in data yet, but is there in gen Z’s nostalgia for the “millennial optimism era”. It’s the difference between millennials believing that all of this can and should be fought, and gen Z having no nostalgic point of reference for the plausibility of fighting it at all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSinners was an intensely literate movie about history, racism and trauma, forces that sap us of our vitality, and our ability to fight back. So I’m not surprised my fellow millennial Coogler might be turning to Animorphs next. In the end, I suspect that he might circle the following: the threat to all of us is not solely alien, but an alien version of ourselves. That fighting back successfully will mean remembering who we really are. That nature is our ally, and we have to remember how indeliblyourfuture is tied toitsstate of wellbeing. I can’t think of a more urgent millennial-optimist metaphor to splash on to the big screen.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoirGeneration Desperationis out nowDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
