title: Prison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him that | Simon Hattenstone | The Guardian
description: Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives, says Guardian writer Simon Hattenstone
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives, says Guardian writer Simon Hattenstone
Content: A new review into indeterminate prison sentences has been announced.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA new review into indeterminate prison sentences has been announced.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianOpinionPrisons and probationPrison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him thatSimon HattenstonePolitical leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own livesMon 10 Aug 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTShareIn January 2015, Tommy Nicol told his family that he was suffering “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years”. Nicol had been given an imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentence six years earlier for stealing a car from a garage and injuring the owner. He was alreadytwo years beyond his four-year tariff– the minimum time you can serve in prison before being considered for release. Nicol was given another two-year knock-back from the Parole Board and was in despair. If and when he got released, he would be on a lifelong licence. Eight months later, aged 37, Nicol hanged himself at The Mount prison in Hertfordshire, England.By the time he took his own life, the inhumane IPP sentence had already been abolished for three years. The problem is, it didn’t apply retroactively. Those already serving IPP sentences stayed on them. This, despite David Blunkett, who devised and introduced them as home secretary in 2005, calling it “the biggest regret” of his political career. And this despite UN special rapporteur on torture Alice Edwardsagreeing with Tommy Nicolthat the sentence was “psychological torture”. Astonishingly, more than 2,000 people are still serving IPP sentences in England and Wales.Last week prime minister Andy Burnham announced anew reviewinto indeterminate sentences as part of his plan to reduce the prison population. Reviewing a sentence that was abolished 14 years ago seems Kafkaesque. And what exactly is left to review? We all know IPPs are wrong – they are no longer handed down, and those serving them should be resentenced. Review after review has said so. Surely it makes more sense to simply introduce legislation to make that happen?IPPs were given to people who didn’t merit life sentences, but were regarded as a risk to society. With an IPP, once prisoners have served their tariff, they have to apply to the Parole Board for release. The Parole Board only grants release if satisfied that the offender no longer poses a risk to the public. This means that an IPP prisoner could be detained indefinitely.It was expected that very few prisoners would receive IPPs (an estimated 900 at any one time) and only for serious crimes.The reality couldn’t have been more different. Between 2005 and 2013 (a handful of people were sentenced after the cut-off of 31 December 2012),8,711 people were given an IPP sentence. While some had long tariffs, most were on low tariffs for minor crimes. Nevertheless, many never got released. Or if they did, they were recalled to prison for the slightest breaches of their licence, such as being late for appointments with probation officers.Often the people who were imprisoned on an IPP were already vulnerable. Not surprisingly, many prisoners lost hope, like Nicol did. Ninety-four peoplehad taken their own lives up to March 2025 while serving the sentence in prison. Forty-four people are known to have taken their own lives while out on licence, though these community-based figures have only been tracked since April 2019, so are likely to be higher.The IPP horror stories are legion, and many concern young people such as Martin Myers, whoserved 18 yearsfor attempting to steal a cigarette, despite having an original tariff of just 19 months and 27 days when sentenced aged 24; Ronnie Sinclair served16 years in jail on a three-year IPP tarifffor stealing a flowerpot at the age of 17; and Wayne Bell was 17 when he was imprisoned on an IPP for punching a boy and stealing a bike in 2007 on a tariff of one year and 350 days. He is still in prison 19 years later.Although the lifelong licence was removed for IPP prisoners in 2024, many are still serving the sentence. As of June 2026, there were2,271 IPP prisonersjailed in England and Wales –856 unreleased prisoners and 1,415 recalled prisoners.This proposed review would be the third since 2022 when the cross-party Justice Committee Inquiry concluded IPP sentenceswere “irredeemably flawed”and recommended resentencing. Nothing was done. Last year the Howard League expert working grouprecommended fixed-release windowsfor IPP prisoners. Nothing was done. A private member’s bill sponsored by (Lord) Anthony Woodley urged a comprehensive, retrospective resentencing exercise forall prisoners still subject to an IPP. The bill passed its second reading in the House of Lords and progressed to the committee stage, but the government blocked it.The campaign groupUngrippfears that any new review will have the same outcome as previous ones. “Each review meant more wasted time, more people on IPP despairing and inevitably, more suicides,” it says. “How can we be confident this will be any different?”Shockingly, all but three of the 2,271 people serving IPP sentences in prison are past their tariff. With resentencing, these three prisoners would be given a fitting determinate sentence, while the 2,268 remaining IPP prisoners would gradually be released with appropriate social care and housing to ensure they were safe within the community and the community safe with them. The£60,000 a year savedin prison costs would go a considerable way towards paying for this.So why hasn’t it yet been done? Simple. Political leaders are terrified of looking soft on crime – so they have consistently kicked the IPP can down the road. Yet IPP sentences are universally recognised as unjust. Not a single mainstream politician defends this barbaric sentence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast year Keir Starmer said: “It is right that the IPP sentence has been abolished”, but he wasn’t brave enough toresentence IPP prisoners. Andy Burnham must be braver.The former supreme court justice Lord Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood called IPP “the greatest single stain on our criminal justice system” in a2020 reportfor the Prison Reform Trust. If Burnham wants to show he means business, he will not bother with another review and will simply legislate to get this shaming stain removed once and for all.Resentencing is too late for Tommy Nicol and the many others IPP prisoners who took their own lives, but it’s not too late for those still behind bars, tortured by not knowing whether their imprisonment will ever end.Simon Hattenstone is a Guardian features writerIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionSentencingUK criminal justicecommentShareReuse this content

title: A TikTok PM may seem laughable – but reaching young people like me might just keep Labour in office | Lucy O’Brien | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham and his social media team know how to connect with us. We’re no fools, though – this has to be backed by serious policies, says Guardian deputy audience editor Lucy O’Brien
Author: Lucy O’Brien
Headline: Andy Burnham and his social media team know how to connect with us. We’re no fools, though – this has to be backed by serious policies, says Guardian deputy audience editor Lucy O’Brien
Content: Andy Burnham with Alstom apprentices in Derby as he unveiled new technical educational routes to tackle youth unemployment, 28 July 2026.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Alstom apprentices in Derby as he unveiled new technical educational routes to tackle youth unemployment, 28 July 2026.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamA TikTok PM may seem laughable – but reaching young people like me might just keep Labour in officeLucy O’BrienAndy Burnham and his social media team know how to connect with us. We’re no fools, though – this has to be backed by serious policiesMon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareStrapped up in his navy suit, blue tie and charmingly nerdy glasses, Andy Burnham entered No 10 newly appointed as our fifth prime minister in four years. I didn’t watch this historic scene live on BBC News. Instead, I saw a10-second clip on TikTok, with a viral Love Island soundbite: “A hot new bombshell has entered the villa.” Not exactly the introduction you might expect from a world leader – or is it?The video sent millions of eyes rolling backwards and many flocking to the comments, cringing at the idea of British politics succumbing to ridiculous social media trends. Critics have called his social media strategy“trivial” and a “distraction”. After years of leadership turmoil and a flailing Labour government under Keir Starmer, should we really be making light of yet another transfer of power on a platform designed for teenagers?More than a month into the job, Burnham’s team has continued the shenanigans on his own accounts (where he has more than a million followers acrossInstagramand TikTok combined). Scroll down his feed and you will still find a fair amount of silliness, but the tide is starting to change.One video starts with thePM defending “barms”– the northern-preferred nickname for a bread roll (it’s definitely abap, sorry Andy) – before seamlessly flowing into a metaphor for his strategy of devolution and handing back power to local councils. It now has more than 850,000 views.Similarly, when he talked through his education strategy on TikTok, cheekily transitioning between holding a graduation cap and hard hat, his audience listened.That videohas 3m views and is flooded with comments of people feeling alarmingly inspired by his plans. “Have we actually maybe finally got a good one?” one user said. Finally, it seems we have a politician who comes across like areal personwho knows how to talk to otherreal people(even if it does remind you of your dad trying to prove he’s down with the kids) – and for gen Z members like me, it’s working.Social media popularity isn’t the end goal, but it is the first hurdle. If you want young people to vote for you, you have to find a way to make them care. You have to meet them where they are. And in today’s attention-span economy, that is the hardest job of all.Reuters’ 2026 Digital News Reportfound that, globally, 52% of 18- to 24-year-olds use social media, video networks and AI chatbots as the main way of getting their news.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIf you’re over 30, Burnham’s videos may seem clumsy – embarrassing, even. But don’t get it twisted, the PM’s team knows exactly what it’s doing. Burnham has tapped into something I have long understood: if we have any chance of overturning the general sense of misery in this country, we need to get young people to believe in politics again. This is the first time in my adult life I have heard my peers say they actuallylikewhat the PM is doing, that they think he’s a decent guy, and that there’s a reason to hope again.Since the Brexit referendum in 2016, I’ve witnessed my generation become increasingly disillusioned with politics. Faced with crippling student loans, the risk of becoming a Neet, or the seeming impossibility of getting on the property ladder, young people have had little to hope for under previous governments. Rebuilding the PM’s trust among the young is the only way to dismantle more than a decade of political alienation.What Burnham is doing is nothing new. Labour understood the power of social media to rally younger voters during the 2024 general election, and it paid off.YouGov pollingdocuments that 41% of those aged 18-24 voted Labour, rising to 45% among those aged 25-29. Keir Starmer was the first British PM to launch a personal TikTok profile, where he tried – and failed – to maintain Labour’s initial momentum. Ultimately, his stuffy and ineffective communication style ended up alienating the very voters that handed him his mandate in the first place. Hopefully, Burnham won’t make the same mistake.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTikTok fame won’t buy Burnham unwavering support. Nor should it. We might be a fickle generation, but we’re not stupid. No one really thinks a few viral videos equates to the PM effecting real and lasting change. But getting young people on side is essential work; work that could keep Labour in government for a generation, if he plays his cards right.Lucy O’Brien is a deputy audience editor at the GuardianExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionSocial mediaYoung peopleTikTokInstagramDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaos | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: Matt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APView image in fullscreenMatt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APOpinionPoetryIt’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaosCharlotte HigginsFrom Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enoughMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe biggest sales of poetry since records began are expected this year. The reason? The movies, of course. UK print sales ofThe Odysseyincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period last year. In the US, year-to-date sales of The Odyssey areup 76% so far. Christopher Nolan is doing miracles for Homer – whatever problems one might have with the movie (and Emily Wilson, who made the most popular recent translation,has a few).Strip out the Odyssey factor, though, and poetry is still doing exceptionally well, driven by writers whose work is often mildly denigrated as “Instapoetry”, such asLucas Jones. His is a kind of versifying that delivers immediate uplifting aphorisms rather than either the kind of dense, allusive play with language that might reward repeated reading; or the sort of limpid, performable music that propels a well-translated Homeric epic. But even so, the poets of Instagram reach for something that can’t quite be expressed through everyday speech. And readers respond to it.Sales figures are a rough and insubstantial metric, though. They don’t tell us how someone feels when they read a good poem, what it expands for them, what memories it brings, what connections to other times and places. What shiver of alienation it offers; what moment (often) of puzzlement.Poetrycan be baffling; it can refuse to unfurl all of itself to the reader. Better, I think, to sink into the sensations that a poem creates than always to worry at it like a puzzle. By its nature, poetry expresses what can’t be said in prose; it can be resistant, you can snag on it. Poetry is needed in an emergency, when ordinary ways of writing or speaking can’t get at the moment, or the feeling, or the thought.What poetry is not, however, is peripheral to human life. What I have learned by reporting from Ukraine is that when catastrophe hovers overhead rather than looms from a distance, poetry seems more, rather than less, vital. The mostrapt poetry readingI have ever attended was in the frontline city of Kharkiv, the border with Russia only 30km away, when one poet described scratching poems into the wall of her Russian prison cell and audience members silently mouthed the learned-by-heart words of writer Serhii Zhadan’s poems as he performed them.The foreign correspondent Lindsey Hilsum, who has covered wars and humanitarian crises for decades, has long understood this, which is whyI Brought the War with Me, her anthology of work by poets across time and geographies, accompanied by her stories, is such a treasure. The poetry emerging from Gaza, and from Palestinian poets scattered across the world – figures such as the young writerHaia Mohammed, or the Palestinian-American poetFady Joudah– collectively provides the most arresting document of lives lived amid cataclysm: such poetry is composed with an urgency, vividness and compression that no other art form can quite achieve.It is true, as the Ukrainian poet Halyna Kruk said in 2022, that “no metaphors work against a man with a machine gun … no poetry can save you from a tank”. It is true, as her fellow Ukrainian writer Kateryna Iakovlenko has put it, that the poetry created most obviously by war is asemic, ugly and inscribed into the very land: “Ruins and abandoned houses, devastated forests, burnt land and roads carved up by tanks and armoured personnel carriers began to resemble letters and unwritten sentences.”View image in fullscreenSerhii Zhadan reads a debut book by Yulia Paevska, call-sign ‘Taira’, at a poetry festival in Kharkiv last year. They are both serving in the Khartia brigade.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAnd yet, with remarkable speed, and despite its failure either to deflect bullets, or keep its writers and readers physically safe, poetry quickly began to be written inUkraineafter the full-scale invasion. Poetry was the form that could grapple most effectively with the collapse in meaning brought about by the shock of violence, the feeling that time had ceased to carry significance, the future ripped away. Poems could be written relatively quickly, with limited means, and even in inhospitable places (the shelter, the trench).The novelist Victoria Amelina, who was later killed by a Russian bomb that targeted the restaurant where she was eating, stopped writing novels (which both take time to write and contain time as an ingredient) and started writing poetry. Some of it denied its own status as poetry, as if it were just the shrapnel-hit remnants of language. One poem, Not Poetry, translated by Uilleam Blacker, contains the lines, “But the reality of war / devours punctuation / plot structure / structure …”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘After the reading, the poets hold each other’: what happens when Ukraine’s largest literary festival comes under Russian attackRead morePoems were written at the front. The young writer Artur Dron’, who served in the Ukrainian armed forces for more than three years,did not writeabout bravado or heroism, but made small, delicate memorials for fellow soldiers who had been killed. Or sometimes he built encapsulations of seemingly insignificant moments.One of his poems is about a child in some unnamed village near the frontline, who becomes the unofficial mascot of the soldiers posted there. At Christmas, they leave the young boy “a bag with our crushed Snickers bars / and tangerines. / The ones with seeds, / but oh so sweet.” It was a fleeting incident: not newsworthy, not impressive, nothing for the history books – but it was material for a poem. Yaryna Chornohuztold methat her work as asoldier poetwas the “documentation of feelings”.In the midst of a cataclysm, poems survive, often stripped back to their most essential forms, which are surely universal and primordial human forms of expression: the lament for the dead, the lullaby for the child, the curse. In the end, humans need those things: those songs, those poems. They are proof of life. They may not be remembered; but poetry has a better chance at survival than much else that humans do or make. They may become memorials more lasting than bronze.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, is published on 20 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOn Wednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. With Olia Hercules, Sasha Dovzhyk, Olesya Khromeychuk and Shaun Walker. Book ticketshereDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPoetryOpinionUkraineThe OdysseyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Sam Neill on making Hunt for the Wilderpeople: ‘We were attacked by a puppet pig!’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatised
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatised
Content: ‘It felt like both of us were 12’ … Julian Dennison and Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Piki Films/AllstarView image in fullscreen‘It felt like both of us were 12’ … Julian Dennison and Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Piki Films/AllstarHow we madeMoviesSam Neill on making Hunt for the Wilderpeople: ‘We were attacked by a puppet pig!’Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatisedWarning: contains spoilersInterviews byChris BroughtonMon 10 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Neill, played Hector FaulknerTaika Waititi’s filmBoyis one of my favourites ever, so when I got the Wilderpeople script I was already well disposed to it. Hec is sort of a New Zealand archetype. When I was at university, during the holidays I’d work at cutting hay and shifting sheep and fertiliser. There was always a Hec driving the truck. They were men of very few words, but when they did say something it meant a lot. It was clear I was never going to have many lines in the film.Hunt for the Wilderpeople is based on Wild Pork and Watercress, a novel by Barry Crump, a legendary figure when I was growing up. A lot of his stuff is very amusing, but not this one – it took Taika to make it funny. Just about every comedian inNew Zealandis in the film. I was probably the only non-comedian, but the film has a complexity beyond the humour. A lot of that comes, I think, from Rima Te Wiata. She plays Hec’s wife Bella with such warmth, compassion and empathy that when she dies both Hec and Ricky are suffused with grief. That grief gives a powerful dimension to the remainder of the film.View image in fullscreen‘When Bella dies both Hec and Ricky are suffused with grief’ … Sam Neill, Rima Te Wiata and Julian Dennisonin Hunt for the WilderpeopleThe Ricky Baker birthday songseems to have become a sort of informal national anthem, but it’s only in the film because the traditional Happy Birthday song wasn’t then in the public domain. The scene was all set up with Rima about to play the conventional version on her little keyboard when the producer came running in and said: “We can’t use that, we don’t have copyright!” Rima, Taika and I had to write something new in 10 minutes, but it was mostly Rima. Sometimes, working under pressure produces the best things.I didn’t have the best relationship with the canine actor that played Hec’s hunting dog, Zag. I’m a dog guy, but he wasn’t the pal you would expect a dog to be – he had other things on his mind. The wild boar that wounds Zag was realised on screen in a mixture of ways. But on location we were reacting to a couple of guys operating a kind of puppet pig! The finished scene is pretty full-on. A lot of people have to comfort their children after it.People often stop me and say it’s their favourite film. They remember it with affection, and when something is taken to heart, that’s a wonderful thing to have in your CV. The only thing that irritated me after its release was some people saying Julian stole the film from me. I don’t think there was any theft involved – the film was always his in the first place.Sam Neill gave this interview in June, a monthbefore his death on13 July.Julian Dennison, played Ricky BakerI’d worked with Taika before on an anti-drugs advert and didn’t have to audition. Ricky is this broken kid stuck in a system of foster care that’s failing him. I come from a community where that happens a lot with young people – I had cousins who acted like Ricky Baker, I had friends who dressed like him and my brother listened to Tupac.I knew Sam Neill was big and lots of people liked him, but I didn’t really know who he was. Knowing there were going to be all these scenes of just him and me in the bush, I thought: “Man, I hope he’s not lame …” He turned out to be very young at heart, like an older cousin. I had the best time and loved hanging out with Sam – sometimes it felt like both of us were 12 years old.I grew up in a religious home and went to Sunday school, and I wasn’t a big swearer like Ricky. When it came to lines like: “Shit just got real!” I was like: “Am I allowed to say this?”double quotation markI said: ‘Wouldn’t it be funny if Sam opened the door and realised he hadn’t dug the tunnel yet?’Rachel House, who played the child welfare officer leading the hunt for Hec and Ricky, was also my acting coach. She taught me tricks like recording my lines and listening back to them the night before we shot a scene. I still do that today. The movie is full of pop-culture references from way before I was born which I didn’t get while I was making it, but I see the bigger picture now.Taika was open to ideas, which often arrived while we were all practising our lines in a hot tub. In the scene where Ricky and Hec are trying to come up with an escape plan with Rhys Darby’s character, Psycho Sam, there was a line in the script about an underground bunker. I said: “Wouldn’t it be funny if Sam opened the door and realised he hadn’t dug the tunnel yet?” That ended up in the movie.The big car chaseat the end was shot on the ancestral land of the Ngāti Rangi tribe, who were really welcoming and helpful, as were the army, who use some of their territory as a training ground. We had to travel in a truck with army people when we went from the filming base to the location. I guess they’d lost some of their mines or something – they’d be like: “If you see metal things sticking out of the ground, just let us know.” If anything was spotted, someone would come over with bright pink spray paint and draw a circle around it, like some people do to draw attention to dog poo.The 10th anniversary release of Hunt for the Wilderpeople in 4k is in cinemas and on digital platforms now, with UHD and Blu-ray editions on 17 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeSam NeillTaika WaititiNew ZealandComedy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is asking a lot of the buttocks’: my 23-hour Wagner marathon on a rock hard seat in a heatwave | Opera | The Guardian
description: How does it feel to be locked into a venue notorious for its unpadded seating to experience a full-throttle Ring cycle and more? Our critic found out at the 150th anniversary of the mighty Bayreuth festival
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: How does it feel to be locked into a venue notorious for its unpadded seating to experience a full-throttle Ring cycle and more? Our critic found out at the 150th anniversary of the mighty Bayreuth festival
Content: ‘How’s your 19th-century German?’ … Rienzi at this year’s festival, which never uses surtitles.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreen‘How’s your 19th-century German?’ … Rienzi at this year’s festival, which never uses surtitles.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOpera‘This is asking a lot of the buttocks’: my 23-hour Wagner marathon on a rock hard seat in a heatwaveHow does it feel to be locked into a venue notorious for its unpadded seating to experience a full-throttle Ring cycle and more? Our critic found out at the 150th anniversary of the mighty Bayreuth festivalFlora WillsonMon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Liszt and Bruckner were there from the start. Debussy, Mahler and Puccini all subsequently made the journey. So did writers from Virginia Woolf and Thomas Mann to WEB Du Bois, not to mention choreographer Sergei Diaghilev, anarchistEmma Goldman, British fascist Diana Mosley (wife of Oswald) and – most notoriously and fanatically – Adolf Hitler.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Culturally and politically, Germany’sBayreuth festivaldoesn’t so much have baggage as its own industrial-scale luggage hangar. But it’s also prized as the ultimate place to hearRichard Wagner’s operas. One hundred and fifty years after the composer launched the festival with the premiere of his epic Ring cycle, tickets for this summer’s edition sold out within 90 minutes. No mean feat for a theatre with famously uncomfortable seats, no air conditioning and only one man’s music on the menu. Theshortestwork lasts two-and-a-half hours without a break.double quotation mark‘You mustn’t move,’ an old hand told me. ‘I once got told off for uncrossing my legs’So perhaps it was inevitable that I had mixed feelings about my own first trip. Admittedly, I’ve taught generations of students about Wagner and Bayreuth and have been aware of the theatre’s acoustic – revered among opera-lovers – since I was myself an undergraduate. Of course I seized the opportunity to experience it in situ. The brief was to review six operas across seven days: intensive, but not off the scale for a critic covering a festival. Then I did the maths. That’s almost 23 hours of Wagner, not including intervals, in a single week. During a heatwave.View image in fullscreenComplaining about stagings is a festival pastime … Das Rheingold in 2013.Photograph: Enrico Nawrath/Bayreuther Festival“They lock you in, you know,” a friend tells me when I mention that I’ll be reviewing there this year. “And it’s done with a real theatrical flourish!” I block out a terrifying image of being imprisoned by an opera cult and focus instead on remembering his tip: borrowing a cushion is vital. Wagner and his architects modelled the auditorium on the ancient Greek amphitheatre, after all. The idea was to promote a communal artistic experience through unbroken rows of seats stretching in a wide arc from one side of the theatre to the other. There are no private boxes, no restricted-view tickets and minimal padding. This fantasy of democratic opera-going asks a lot of the buttocks.That’s no excuse for wriggling, it seems. “You mustn’t move in the auditorium,” warns one Bayreuth old hand when we get chatting at Nuremberg airport. “I got told off once when I uncrossed my legs.” My heart sinks. Sure enough, I witness a set-to about someone twitching their walking stick. Rustling attracts pointed stares and jabbing fingers. But even an audience this committed to self-policing can’t hold the modern world entirely at bay. Every evening features the clatter of phones falling from laps on to the wooden floor. Several text messages arrive with a ping. There are even a couple of incoming calls.So much for Wagner’s struggle to create the ideal conditions for music drama. But there’s much at Bayreuth that hasn’t changed. The original orchestra pit, for instance, which is exceptionally deep and almost entirely covered,descending in steps beneath the stage. Wagner and his collaborators intended the design to create what they grandly called a “mystic gulf”: a seamless, uncluttered view of the stage that would draw the audience fully into the action.View image in fullscreenFlamboyant re-imaginings … an outdoor choreography rehearsal for Tannhäuser in 1930.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./ullstein bild/Getty ImagesOne happy by-product is Bayreuth’s unique acoustic, which gives the orchestral sound both a luminous sheen and a beguiling sense of perspective as the low brass and percussion filter through the strings sitting metres above them. Less welcome is the pit’s oppressive heat. When I’m ushered in ahead of a performance one afternoon, the musicians already in their seats are wearing T-shirts and shorts. It’s the only feasible concert attire, I’m told. In one of the few modifications made since Wagner’s time, a tiny air-con unit has been fitted. But the contraption looks like spare parts for a vacuum cleaner and apparently helps only the conductor.It says something about the opera world that such discomfort is considered worth enduring for the sake of Bayreuth’s sound. Another legacy of Wagner’s desire for an ultra-immersive operatic experience has more doubtful value: unlike most major opera houses in the world today, Bayreuth has no surtitles. Your grasp of poetic 19th-century German isn’t what it could be? You struggle to pick out the words from the average Wagnerian’s full-throttle delivery? You’re even – horror of horrors – new to opera? Tough. You’ll have to work out what’s going on from the staging.Good luck with that this year. The new “AI Ring” involves a set of constantly shifting projections, behind which the singers stand – sometimes invisible and all wearing the same costume. I spot people wisely reading the libretto before curtain-up. “Didyouknow there wouldn’t be surtitles?” one despairing American visitor asks me during an interval partway through the second opera. He has seen the Ring before but is totally, furiously lost here. “I’m off to Munich tomorrow,” he fumes. “There’s no point staying to see the rest of this.”View image in fullscreenThe ultimate place to hear Wagner … Das Rheingold in 2006.Photograph: Jochen Quast/APNeedless to say, I stay put. Bolt upright, in fact, which seems to be the only way to survive the Ring’s almost 15-hour span in these seats (slumping is fatal), at least if you want to reach Götterdämmerung’s apocalypse with any sensation left in your lower body. It helps that I am as swept up as ever in Wagner’s mad, miraculous marathon of a score, which yes, sounds even more spectacular in this acoustic. There are moments when the orchestral sound glows, and others when it rises from the pit – thrilling in its power – to break over us like a slow-motion wave. ButI’m left dry-eyed through the drama’s betrayals and its meet-cutes, the hope, the fury, the usually heartbreaking self-sacrifice of its heroine. Not even this lineup of world-class singers can persuade me to invest in their characters when they’re hidden behind an avalanche of visual dross. There’s no storytelling here, just an extended spot-the-past-production game for Wagner nerds.At a time when many opera companies are trying to make the art form more broadly inviting, Bayreuth’s determination to cater purely to insiders stands out. Particularly given that the town’s other theatre – the exquisitely preserved 18th-centuryMargravial Opera House, now a Unesco world heritage site – boasts an interactive museum that has “accessibility” written all over it. When I pop in, I find a crowd enthralled by a scale model of the theatre’s machinery that allows visitors to move scenery and create waves, wind and thunder.From the archive: The Manchester Guardian reports on the first ever Bayreuth festivalRead moreYet no other opera house besides Wagner’s has such a dependably loyal audience or such a restricted repertory – just 10 of his mature operas. (Perhaps that’s just as well: this year’sexceptional anniversary-year production of the composer’s sprawling earlier opera Rienzi– Hitler’s favourite, no less – attempts to recast it as a contemporary political thriller. Let’s just saymy review isn’t wholly positive.) But no wonder, given the tiny number of works on the roster, that most Bayreuth productions since the 1950s have involved the flamboyant re-imaginings and conceptual gambits ofRegietheater(allowing a director free rein). And no wonder complaining about stagings is a major festival pastime.View image in fullscreen‘Smiling, improbably’ … Flora Willson is toasted by Wagner himself.Photograph: Ditlev Rindom“I don’t hate it as much as I thought I would,” one woman ventures ofJay Scheib’s staging of Parsifal. She has come with a group of friends, she explains, after one of them “found a cheap schloss”. Perhaps staying in a castle would’ve improved matters for me, too.I dislike the production far more than I had expectedand come dangerously close to needing to leave the theatre to escape the stomach-turning gore-fest – filmed in closeup – that dominates its two-hour first act. Another day, when I pass Wagner’s grave en route to the theatre, I find two men in their 50s comparing stories about the worst Wagner stagings they’ve seen. “What the hell?” explodes one in accented English, outraged by the other’s report of inappropriate animatronics, before returning to German. “What does that have to do with Wagner?”You could ask the same thing of Bayreuth’s tackier side. Interval drinks are available from “Richard’s Spritz Bar”. A balloon labelled “Wagner Mania” flies over the box office and a lifesize cutout of the composer – smiling, improbably – is available for red-carpet photos. Elsewhere, there are statues, awalking trail of mini-Wagnerson plinths and gold figurines in shop windows. It takes me several days of waiting at traffic lights near the theatre to notice that the green man holds a baton and wears the composer’s floppy hat.Call it theme-parkification, call it kitsch. Either way, such homegrown attempts to cash in on or send up Wagner’s image make for a surreal contrast to the earnest aesthetic debates on and off stage at Bayreuth. But both ultimately betray the same preoccupation with itself that characterises the festival today: the ongoing internal tussle over what it is, who it’s for – and how to come to terms with its deeply troubled past.TheBayreuth festivalcontinues until 26 AugustExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRichard WagnerBayreuth festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Cameron Mitchell: ‘It’s punk to turn off your phone – you’re walking away from the herd’ | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The writer, director and star of Hedwig and the Angry Inch on turning down David Bowie, falling off a Broadway stage, and a cringeworthy moment with Nicole Kidman
Author: Dee Jefferson
Headline: The writer, director and star of Hedwig and the Angry Inch on turning down David Bowie, falling off a Broadway stage, and a cringeworthy moment with Nicole Kidman
Content: John Cameron Mitchell: ‘One career regret that I cannot live down is that Bowie asked me to consider Ziggy Stardust for the stage, and I said no.’Photograph: Festival of Dangerous IdeasView image in fullscreenJohn Cameron Mitchell: ‘One career regret that I cannot live down is that Bowie asked me to consider Ziggy Stardust for the stage, and I said no.’Photograph: Festival of Dangerous Ideas10 Chaotic QuestionsTheatreJohn Cameron Mitchell: ‘It’s punk to turn off your phone – you’re walking away from the herd’The writer, director and star of Hedwig and the Angry Inch on turning down David Bowie, falling off a Broadway stage, and a cringeworthy moment with Nicole KidmanDee JeffersonMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe film adaptation of Hedwig and the Angry Inch has such a cult following. What’s been your most memorable interaction with a fan?It’s interesting, Hedwig wasn’t famous, it was a film that so many people found because a friend told them about it. So people don’t come up to you because you’re famous, it’s because they were touched. The most intense interaction was when I was on the subway platform and a kid gave me a tiny piece of paper and hopped on a train. I opened it and it said, “Thank you. Hedwig saved my life”. I don’t know what happened – maybe they felt lonely and then the film made them feel like “There’s other people for me out there”.You recently starred inOh, Mary!onBroadway– doing eight shows a week – what was your post-show wind-down ritual?I’ve become a late-era pothead – just a night-time pothead – and there was a great comfort in coming home, after a long night making people laugh, to a nice bliss. Then I’d settle down with an episode of The Wire. I watched it all over again for the first time since it came out – and it’s still great.You’re bringing your Bowie song cycle, I’m Afraid of Americans, to Australia. What’s your favourite Bowie song, and why?I keep coming back to Heroes: it’s so unique and rousing, and so complex. It’s not just heroic – he’s like, “I’ll drink all the time”, it’s dark. It’s inspired by him watching his producer, Tony Visconti, have an affair and kiss a woman under the Berlin Wall – that’s where the lyrics came from. It’s his most moving song.Adam Liaw: ‘The most famous person I’ve cooked for? Gordon Ramsay. My wife spilled a jug of water over him’Read moreIn terms of song cycles, I would say Ziggy Stardust. One career regret that I cannot live down is that Bowie asked me to consider Ziggy Stardust for the stage and I said no. I’d just finished a decade of Hedwig, which is a rock star on stage, and I couldn’t take it any more. But later, I’m like, “Why didn’t I just fucking do it? It’sDavid Bowie.”View image in fullscreenJohn Cameron Mitchell as Hedwig in Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001).Photograph: New Line/AllstarYou’re also bringing your punk masterclass to Australia. Who is a contemporary punk icon that inspires you?The entire population of Minneapolis who fought back [against ICE raids]. That’s neo-punk: standing up to the so-called system for the right reason. Punk is not a hairstyle you saw on TikTok, it’s a way of making things that has the same goals as leftist identity politics – harmony, empathy, justice – but the tactics are wildly different. These days our sensitivities, especially for young people – it’s like, “I don’t want to see that. I’m triggered”. But punk is about facing the ugliness to get through it. The ugliness isn’t the point – the original punks, like Sex Pistols and Patti Smith, were trying to get through the dark into something else.What’s one punk thing we can all do right now?Turn off your phone. I think letting go of digital technology opens you up to your natural punk, to your natural self, whereas when we’re mediated by this thing all the time it changes your attention span. When your attention span shrinks, you feel less empathy, and you get numbed out. How do you get back to your real self? Through punk, through music, through art – in my view. It was art that helped me. You’ll feel better when you keep the phone as a tool toget tothe IRL, not tobethe IRL. And the more we get into fucking AI, you’re not going to want to trust [your phone] anyway, so why not get off it now? It’s punk to turn off your phone; you’re walking away from the herd.What’s been your most cringe-worthy encounter with a celebrity?I worked with Nicole Kidman on a couple of films, and we had a good working relationship, but it wasn’t like a cuddly “let’s hang out” relationship. And I don’t know if that’s her way; she seems socially a little bit nervous, you know? I think she’s happier on a horse, on her farm. Anyway we were in her apartment in the West Village, and I had a CD recording for a certain scene I wanted her to hear – this is in the old days – and she didn’t know where the CD player was. It was a white room, and we couldn’t find the stereo, it was just a blank wall. Nicole and I were like, “Let’s hunt for it”. And we were trying to trip the trigger that would open the stereo – our hands were all over the wall.Were you stoned?No, I wish I was! It was almost like a performance piece. Eventually she touched something and the CD player flipped out, and I played the song, and she’s like, “I like it” and then I was off. Another one: I voiced a character in a 90s commercial for Dunkaroos, an Australian-themed cookie that you dip in frosting. I was Sydney the kangaroo, with a terrible Australian accent. So I said to Nicole, “Hey, how do you doyourDunkaroos?” in the accent, and she’s like, “No.”Thatwas cringe.Virginia Gay: ‘Shakespeare’s most overrated play? Hamlet. Too long’Read moreWhat’s the strangest job you’ve ever had?Around the late 80s, I was a ticket cashier at a film festival where I was acting in three films that were in it, but had to pay the bills. My favourite job before acting was janitor for the military thrift shop in Albuquerque, New Mexico, because I could just take anything I wanted. And there were a lot of gay books – it was the 70s, so even the military hadThe Joy Of Gay Sex. So I kind of learned about being gay from being a janitor and reading these books.What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened on stage?Well, I did fall off the stage in Oh, Mary! I was being a good boy and picking up someone’s prop in the dark, which made me rush and then fall off the stage in the dark into the audience. The lights came up, and I was climbing back on, and the audience applauded like, “Oh Mary, the drunk!” Everyone [in the show] was horrified. I actually had a hairline fracture from that, but I went back two days later, because for me, the show must go on. I always get injured in shows. In Hedwig, my knee went out.If you had to fight a famous person, who would it be and how would you fight them?Right now, I’d say Pete Hegseth. I’d fight him with giant plastic hands – not to hurt him, just to slap him until he’s silly. There’s this sort of male peacocking that he does, that he somehow connects to Jesus, and how Jesus wants “lethality-maxxing” or whatever Clavicular language he’s using. He’s an avatar of the manosphere, he’s not real – he’s just a collection of ticks of the worst of the worst of American manhood. And his deep lack of empathy seems to be a plus in the Elon Musk world. You know, I actually heard a Christian preacher talking about “the sin of empathy” recently. This is America, we can change Christianity into whatever we want. It is fucked up, and it’s repulsive. Having a British mother, and having lived in Britain and around the world, I don’t feel as American as I used to.I used to love the idea of America as a refuge: come on over; make your life here; we don’t care where you’re from. I love that. I grew up in the military, and that’s the vibe in the US military. No one cares where you’re from.Theatreis the same way, and New Orleans, where I live, is the same type of thing. They don’t care where you’re from; it’s like, “What you got to bring to the party?”John Cameron Mitchell is appearing at Melbourne international film festival for a25th anniversary screening of Hedwig and the Angry Inchon 21 August, and at theFestival of Dangerous Ideasat Sydney’s Carriageworks on 22 to 23 August.
