title: Lesbians, latex and $2,000 condoms: why are this summer’s movies so obsessed with sex? | Movies | The Guardian
description: From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacy
Content: Olivia Wilde in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesView image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesMoviesLesbians, latex and $2,000 condoms: why are this summer’s movies so obsessed with sex?From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacyRafaela BassiliMon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThefirst alarm bellssounded nearly 10 years ago, and since then, a deluge of books, podcasts androundtableshas tried to get at the bottom of the problem: why is gen Z not having sex?Recently it’s as though culture has been recalibrated to make up for the youth’s apparent frigidity. “Smut” literature is on the rise, prestige TV is nowdepictingOnlyFans models, and indie films have taken a turntowardskink. This summer, through confused young protagonists and their sexual misadventures, the movies are zeroing in on generational attitudes about sex.One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcomRead moreThere is acontradictionbehind gen Z chastity: despite being the most sexually progressive generation ever, zoomers live under the influence of rampant sexual conservatism. After the 2022 overturning of Roe v Wade, for instance, 16% of single gen Z adults are more afraid to date. This tension is at the heart ofOne Night Only, a new romcom that imagines a world in which Congress has outlawed premarital sex. For one night of the year, the government lifts the ban, essentially enacting the purge for single people’s sexual freedom. On this night, after a series of missed encounters and wrong turns, Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (Monica Barbaro) meet cute.View image in fullscreenCallum Turner and Monica Barbaro in One Night Only.Photograph: Nicole Rivelli/Universal Pictures/APDespite its political tenor, One Night Only’s vision of dystopia is not a comment on America’s rapid hurtle toward authoritarianism. It merely presents obstacles for Allie and Owen to overcome – such as the $2,000 price tag for the condoms Owen attempts to procure – much like the missed connection brought about by a busy phone line in a 90s romcom. We know nothing about what these characters’ lives were like before the ban, which means that Allie’s complaints about the difficulty of finding her “Prince Charming” come off generic, indistinguishable from any number of complaints that I, a married zoomer, have heard from my single friends about dating in the age of apps.‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken starRead moreSilly hijinks aside, One Night Only misunderstands today’s sex recession as libidinal, when really, it’s existential. It’s not that zoomers aren’t horny, or can’t find a man: they are the first generation to grow up fully under the influence of the internet, with its attendant alienations; worse, its youngest members came of age during the pandemic. Knowing how to relate to one another is hard enough, let alone how to initiate sex – a process often awkward, if not outright painful, foreveryoneno matter their age (This much, at least, One Night Only gets right.)Other films this summer understand that sex can’t solve the fundamental alienation brought about by modern life. It’s loneliness that ails Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), the flush-cheeked studio assistant to the provocative artist Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde) inGregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex. For the most part Araki’s characters stay in their boxes, with Erika the worldly provocateur to Elliot’s gullible dork. But in the film’s best moment, a doomed threesome with Elliot’s sexually confused roommate Apple (Chase Sui Wonders), that order is disturbed. The arrival of a third person with her own muddled desires – does Apple want Erika, Elliot, or both? Do they wanther? Does she want to be wanted? – leads Erika to lose her grip, and Elliot to rebel against his part. Standing there half naked, they might as well be worlds apart.View image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in The Invite.Photograph: Black Bear/PAI Want Your Sex shares a dynamic withThe Invite(in which Wilde also stars, and which she directed) and Jane Schoenbrun’sTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a younger and less experienced person (or couple) becomes entangled with an older, sexy woman who shows them the path to self-knowledge through desire. But whereas sex is an all-consuming problem for the characters in The Invite and I Want Your Sex, Camp Miasma presents sex, death and art as intertwined human impulses that are impossible to separate from one another. Tasked with rebooting the Camp Miasma slasher franchise that first prompted her “queer awakening”, 29-year-old film-maker Kris (Hannah Einbinder) has one theme on her mind: “DESIRE”, as she scrawls in her journal, in big block letters.By letting us into Kris’s process of self-discovery, Miasma addresses generational concerns in more nuanced ways than its counterparts this summer. Through her relationship with her muse Billy Presley (a wonderfulGillian Anderson), Camp Miasma’s original final girl, Kris learns that to arrive at artistic epiphany or sexual climax, one must let go of control, let the movie play out. To Billy, slashers are as elemental as sexual desire: she teaches Kris that sex, like art, is a visceral experience not easily theorized.View image in fullscreenGillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Ryan Plummer/Mubi/APWhile One Night Only plays threats tobodily autonomyfor laughs and I Want Your Sex’s Erika rolls her eyes at gen Z’s “wokeness”, Camp Miasma strikes a more sincere tone. Kris is initially drawn to reboot the Camp Miasma films to correct the franchise’s transphobia, but only discovers a physical and emotional experience of art when she learns to stop overintellectualizing slashers. It’s only then that she can really connect with Billy, and it’s only through their connection that she can make a film that is true.These movies don’t exactly present zoomers with a model for how to be a young person who has sex; if anything, they’re more like cautionary guides showing what kinds of behavior to avoid. But that’s precisely where their value lies. After decades of unrealistic depictions of sex on screen and a fewworrisome yearswhen it seemed likely that sex would disappear from the movies altogether, it’s a relief to see sex return to screen – messy awkwardness and all.Explore more on these topicsFilmSexOlivia WildeGregg ArakiSeth RogenRoe v WadeRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘For this record, I took an edible and said, screw it’: jazz pianist Sullivan Fortner on confronting the trauma of Hurricane Katrina | Jazz | The Guardian
description: The New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivors
Author: Hugh Morris
Headline: The New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivors
Content: Finding his keys … Sullivan Fortner (centre) with drummer Kayvon Gordon (left) and bassist Tyrone Allen.Photograph: Youri LenquetteView image in fullscreenFinding his keys … Sullivan Fortner (centre) with drummer Kayvon Gordon (left) and bassist Tyrone Allen.Photograph: Youri LenquetteJazzInterview‘For this record, I took an edible and said, screw it’: jazz pianist Sullivan Fortner on confronting the trauma of Hurricane KatrinaHugh MorrisThe New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivorsMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Black music is forwardandupward in movement, you know? Never forwardorupward,” pianist Sullivan Fortner declares. “It’s a tornado that’s always getting bigger and moving faster,” he adds, whizzing his fingers around with delight.On a video call between sets at Rotterdam’sNorth Sea jazz festival, the 39-year-old speaks like he plays, with quirkiness, subtlety and mischief. A three-time Grammy winner – including for 2025’s Southern Nights – Fortner also recently received the Larry J Bell award, a prize of $300,000 (£225,000) given every four years to a standout jazz pianist, which gave him the confidence to present an all-encompassing version of himself on Leave That in There, his sixth album. “I’ve tried the self-editing way,” he says of previous albums involving multiple takes and endless post-production tinkering. “For this record, I took an edible and I just said, screw it.”Fortner’s sweep is wide and idiosyncratic. On album opener Sugarcane, Kayvon Gordon’s criss-crossing bàtá drumming helps root the record in Louisiana’s history as a centre for the sugar trade, the “white gold” extracted by slave labour that made the area one of the richest in the 19th-century US. But the record travels: through Latin acoustic piano, journeying Hammond organ lines, Thelonious Monk tributes and whirling Moog synths, it ends with Fortner singing a wordless, Stevie Wonder-like hymn to a late friend, Linda Payne.Leave That in There is also rooted in 2005’s Hurricane Katrina, which devastated New Orleans, Louisiana’s biggest city, where Fortner grew up. The album takes its title from a moment in Spike Lee’sWhen the Levees Broke: A Requiem in Four Acts, the epic 2006 documentary that underlined just how much the US failed New Orleans during and after the disaster.Lee relays events with a brutal fury. Dead bodies float face down in flooded boulevards; out of the water pokes a sign for Humanity Street. But Fortner’s title derives from a more understated moment. A woman exits her car, and when she’s told she’s left her purse behind, she tersely replies: “Leave that in there.”Fortner evolves her words into an artistic manifesto against self-censorship. “Music to me is a kind of a place of safety, where anything can happen,” he says. “Rather than saying, ‘OK, these are the things that I’m going to hide,’ it’s more a case of, ‘these are the things I want to keep with me.’”View image in fullscreen‘A place of safety’ … Sullivan Fortner at Newport jazz festival in 2022.Photograph: Douglas Mason/Getty ImagesFortner was 18, and preparing for another year at Ohio’s Oberlin Conservatory, when he got a phone call from a fellow New Orleanian student who told him their city was under water. Fortner shrugged – the area floods regularly – but his friend persevered and Fortner rushed to his dorm. “I turn on CNN, and the first thing I see, in a panning shot of the Convention Center, is my girlfriend and her mother waiting on buses to show up.” Phone lines and emails were down. “So I was panicking. Finally, I got a phone call from my sister, and it lasted like five seconds.” The call cut off, but she confirmed her family were safe, evacuated to nearby Baton Rouge; his girlfriend’s family, meanwhile, were bussed seven hours to Arkansas.Two tracks – A Poignant Time, and Another Poignant Time – reference a Wynton Marsalis quote from the documentary: “I think that this is a great moment in American history, because in this moment we see a lot of what’s wrong with us.” Lee’s film particularly emphasises the debilitating impact of Katrina’s aftermath: of denied insurance claims, substandard accommodation, and sluggishness by federal disaster agency Fema. “People are still dealing with the trauma of that time, even now,” Fortner says. “Not just through people losing their homes, but their mental and physical health – still dealing with grief.”“But it also showed the resilience of the people,” he adds. “There was still that crop of people that’s just like, ‘I’m coming back. This is my city. I ain’t going anywhere.’” His family – an oil rigger dad (“gone basically half the year”) and a mother who was “everything to us” – remained, a half-hour drive from the city centre. For his family, “singing is kind of our love language,” he says. There are around 40 singers among his relatives, and he’s working on an album featuring all of them.His formative musical experiences came with them in the church, but a flash of inspiration came, aged 11, through local organist Ronald Markham. “He got on the organ and started playing Bach.” Fortner had never heard anything like it. “He said, ‘man, it’s classical music.’ Then he goes and plays Latin, then gives me a 30-second demonstration of all these different genres. I didn’t know anything about any type of music other than gospel. But he had the key, and opened the door to this world I’m in now.”View image in fullscreen‘A statement of the moment’ … Fortner at work in the studio.Photograph: Artwork RecordsMarkham suggested he attend theNew OrleansCenter for Creative Arts. In his year were other musicians who have also become Grammy mainstays: Chief Adjuah, Trombone Shorty and Jon Batiste. Later, in New York, Batiste double-booked himself, meaning Fortner filled in on piano with legendary trumpeter Roy Hargrove.While in Hargrove’s band, Fortner began studying with another legend, pianist Fred Hersch. Fortner would turn up to lessons having practised tunes during the week. “Fred’d be like, ‘No, you prepared that, that was a drag. Just play something for me, and then we’ll go from there.’” The trust in intuition that Hersch impressed on Fortner would become among his biggest strengths.‘He used the trumpet as a songbird’: 100 years of Miles Davis, by jazz greats Sonny Rollins, Yazz Ahmed and moreRead moreFor all the power of the albums Fortner has recorded since, his most characterful work today is arguably with US singer Cécile McLorin Salvant. In rough sketches posted to social media, they sit down, hit record and play through Sting, Noël Coward or upturned Great American Songbook tunes. The performances embody a looseness that defines Fortner’s work: always moving forward and upward, never hemmed in. “Just because it’s permanent, doesn’t mean it has to be precious,” he says. Recording, whether in a studio or on Instagram, “is just a statement in the moment: of how we feel and where we’re going.”Leave That in There is released 28 August via Artwork RecordsExplore more on these topicsJazzHurricane KatrinaNew OrleansfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Men have 30 seconds to get a laugh. Women have 10’: standup Bella Hull on proving herself in rough clubs | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: She started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedy
Author: Rachael Healy
Headline: She started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedy
Content: ‘Comedy’s what I’m alive to do’ … Hull spent formative years with her grandma who liked to garden naked.Photograph: Michael JulingsView image in fullscreen‘Comedy’s what I’m alive to do’ … Hull spent formative years with her grandma who liked to garden naked.Photograph: Michael JulingsEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Men have 30 seconds to get a laugh. Women have 10’: standup Bella Hull on proving herself in rough clubsRachael HealyShe started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedyMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComedy isn’t just a career for Bella Hull. It’s a compulsion. “Standup for me is like – Ihaveto do it,” says Hull, who first picked up a mic aged 17. “Regardless of what the response is.”A decade in, the response is resoundingly positive. The 28-year-old had a sell-out show at last year’s Edinburgh fringe (Doctors Hate Her, which explored a break-up, insanity and the occult), appearances on Have I Got News For You and The News Quiz, and a coveted role as writer on the new UK version of Saturday Night Live. “There’s something symbolic about being the person with the voice,” she says of standup. “A lot of situations in my personal life, I don’t feel like that at all.”double quotation markA famous older male comic made jokes about how they were going to rape me after the show. Everyone was laughingHull was a shy child, constantly on edge amid her parents’ “messy” marriage breakdown, an outsider at a private girls’ school where she was “mixed race and overweight”. She lived in London and Kent, including formative years with her “expressive” grandma, who was often found barefoot or gardening naked. Comedy provided solace and she would watch standup specials and record her observations in a journal, until the urge to do it herself became too strong to ignore.The decade since has been spent “in some of the most unsafe basements you could possibly imagine”, Hull jokes, as she threw herself into the comedy circuit. She studied history of art at Cambridge, drawn there by its comedy heritage. But the ubiquity of Footlights’ alumni among the comedy pantheon led Hull to the grittier world of comedy clubs. “I was obsessed with paying my dues,” she says. “I met a lot of people at Cambridge that had ‘golden boy syndrome’. They would sit back and think, ‘Where’s my TV show?’ Well, you don’t fucking deserve a TV show because you’re not good enough. Can you make a stag party in Nottingham laugh? I don’t think so.”View image in fullscreen‘Golden boy – can you make a stag party in Nottingham laugh? I don’t think so’ … Hull on stage.Photograph: Stephen Keable/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.On stage, she melds a compelling persona – a woman on the edge, fixed smile concealing a spikier centre – with formidable craft, tightly written gags peppering every topic. “I just got a personal trainer,” goes a line from Doctors Hate Her that made this paper’sbest jokes listfrom last year’s Edinburgh festival. “She’s horrible to me but my body goal is a thicker skin.”Among the neat punchlines, her shows traverse disordered eating, family breakdown, relationship issues and mental health. As the old meme goes, inside Hull there are two wolves: one, the club-drilled comic subduing audiences with an unprecedented gag rate; the other, a tortured artist forging meaning from her darkest experiences.Her parallel obsessions as a teenager were comedy and art, her idols Ali Wong and Tracey Emin. She now recognises Emin’s influence on her comedy: “She’s so unapologetically intense.” This year’s Fringe show, Mad Cow Disease, will be “very Emin-coded”, a collection of “feminine shameful detritus” ranging from ant infestations and the dread of revealing her true self to a new boyfriend, to fears of inheriting mental health conditions and yearning for a baby “which I think is very taboo for a female comedian”. That she can turn something “sad or dark or heartbreaking” into laughs has always felt magical.View image in fullscreenA chance to try some weirder stuff … Hull (third from right front row) with fellow Saturday Night Live UK writers.Photograph: Saturday Night Live UK/PAHull’s love for club comedy is clear and it’s been a “rigorous” training ground for her joke-writing and stage confidence. Initially, she’d shake and even vomit with nerves before shows. Yet it forced her to inhabit a version of womanhood that audiences would accept. “You’ve got 30 seconds to make them laugh when you get on stage,” Hull says. “If you’re a woman, you’ve maybe got 10.”She was told never to wear revealing clothes and found out why after being “horrendously heckled and wolf-whistled”. Aged 21 and in a remote part of England, she had a famous older male comic making “consistent jokes about how they were going to rape me after the show. Everyone was laughing. That was the norm.” Many women don’t last long in that environment, she says, but she doesn’t regret this path.“I love having something to push against,” Hull says. “I love proving people wrong. You have to have a bit of teeth.” They were on full display in her HIGNFY appearances, where she playfully roasted Ian Hislop and scored an off-the-cuff zinger at the expense of Russell Brand. “Gags are your armour,” Hull says, and so she became used to hiding behind punchlines.Increasingly though, she’s pushing against that club instinct, exploring her poetic, sillier side, and introducing surreal monologues, act-outs and props into her shows. On SNL, she spent six-day weeks hammering out topical jokes and sketches, but it was also a chance to try “weirder” stuff. There was a sketch set at baggage claim where a scatty hun (Aimee Lou Wood) admits that her lost suitcase contains a bomb. Or the Weekend Update dating correspondent Scrimpch, a “really sexual Italian man who was stuck in London because they’d left him on a school trip”.“I love when she’s written a feature that a cast member is going to do with me because I know I’m going to find it really funny,” says Ania Magliano, star of Weekend Update, who first met Hull at Cambridge. Even back then, Hull was naturally funny and daringly honest, says Magliano. “She is a true weirdo, a real eccentric, and she’s confident leaning into that. All of us girls go through a phase of thinking we have to be ‘cool’ and she’s a great example to embrace your weirdness and follow your instincts.”Hull seems genuinely surprised that she got the SNL job – initially, she didn’t even want to apply – but being part of something bigger, so different from the solo world of standup, has been “so meaningful”.Scrimpch was a hit on TikTok and Instagram: Hull’s own posts often do big numbers (one video about a fashion disaster has24.6m views), but social media’s growing presence in comedy doesn’t always sit comfortably. “There’s something about having to show everyone everything all of the time that can upset the artistic process,” she says. “Working away in the darkness makes it much more likely that it will be authentic.” There’s also a pressure to virtue signal and “stand for something”, but she’s drawn towards riskier, more divisive jokes. “I want to be horrified. That’s what I find impressive, when people can scoop out their shame and make it funny. It’s not brave to have the right opinion.”After August in Edinburgh, then series two of SNL in September, what’s Hull up to next? “I don’t want it to stop,” she says. “But if it does, I’ll be OK, because I’ll go back to the clubs. Being able to make people laugh is the meaning of my life. It’s what I’m alive to do.”Bella Hull: Mad Cow Disease is atMonkey Barrel Comedy, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaos | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough, says Guardian chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: Matt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APView image in fullscreenMatt Damon as Odysseus in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APOpinionPoetryIt’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaosCharlotte HigginsFrom Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enoughMon 10 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe biggest sales of poetry since records began are expected this year. The reason? The movies, of course. UK print sales ofThe Odysseyincreased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period last year. In the US, year-to-date sales of The Odyssey areup 76% so far. Christopher Nolan is doing miracles for Homer – whatever problems one might have with the movie (and Emily Wilson, who made the most popular recent translation,has a few).Strip out the Odyssey factor, though, and poetry is still doing exceptionally well, driven by writers whose work is often mildly denigrated as “Instapoetry”, such asLucas Jones. His is a kind of versifying that delivers immediate uplifting aphorisms rather than either the kind of dense, allusive play with language that might reward repeated reading; or the sort of limpid, performable music that propels a well-translated Homeric epic. But even so, the poets of Instagram reach for something that can’t quite be expressed through everyday speech. And readers respond to it.Sales figures are a rough and insubstantial metric, though. They don’t tell us how someone feels when they read a good poem, what it expands for them, what memories it brings, what connections to other times and places. What shiver of alienation it offers; what moment (often) of puzzlement.Poetrycan be baffling; it can refuse to unfurl all of itself to the reader. Better, I think, to sink into the sensations that a poem creates than always to worry at it like a puzzle. By its nature, poetry expresses what can’t be said in prose; it can be resistant, you can snag on it. Poetry is needed in an emergency, when ordinary ways of writing or speaking can’t get at the moment, or the feeling, or the thought.What poetry is not, however, is peripheral to human life. What I have learned by reporting from Ukraine is that when catastrophe hovers overhead rather than looms from a distance, poetry seems more, rather than less, vital. The mostrapt poetry readingI have ever attended was in the frontline city of Kharkiv, the border with Russia only 30km away, when one poet described scratching poems into the wall of her Russian prison cell and audience members silently mouthed the learned-by-heart words of writer Serhii Zhadan’s poems as he performed them.The foreign correspondent Lindsey Hilsum, who has covered wars and humanitarian crises for decades, has long understood this, which is whyI Brought the War with Me, her anthology of work by poets across time and geographies, accompanied by her stories, is such a treasure. The poetry emerging from Gaza, and from Palestinian poets scattered across the world – figures such as the young writerHaia Mohammed, or the Palestinian-American poetFady Joudah– collectively provides the most arresting document of lives lived amid cataclysm: such poetry is composed with an urgency, vividness and compression that no other art form can quite achieve.It is true, as the Ukrainian poet Halyna Kruk said in 2022, that “no metaphors work against a man with a machine gun … no poetry can save you from a tank”. It is true, as her fellow Ukrainian writer Kateryna Iakovlenko has put it, that the poetry created most obviously by war is asemic, ugly and inscribed into the very land: “Ruins and abandoned houses, devastated forests, burnt land and roads carved up by tanks and armoured personnel carriers began to resemble letters and unwritten sentences.”View image in fullscreenSerhii Zhadan reads a debut book by Yulia Paevska, call-sign ‘Taira’, at a poetry festival in Kharkiv last year. They are both serving in the Khartia brigade.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAnd yet, with remarkable speed, and despite its failure either to deflect bullets, or keep its writers and readers physically safe, poetry quickly began to be written inUkraineafter the full-scale invasion. Poetry was the form that could grapple most effectively with the collapse in meaning brought about by the shock of violence, the feeling that time had ceased to carry significance, the future ripped away. Poems could be written relatively quickly, with limited means, and even in inhospitable places (the shelter, the trench).The novelist Victoria Amelina, who was later killed by a Russian bomb that targeted the restaurant where she was eating, stopped writing novels (which both take time to write and contain time as an ingredient) and started writing poetry. Some of it denied its own status as poetry, as if it were just the shrapnel-hit remnants of language. One poem, Not Poetry, translated by Uilleam Blacker, contains the lines, “But the reality of war / devours punctuation / plot structure / structure …”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘After the reading, the poets hold each other’: what happens when Ukraine’s largest literary festival comes under Russian attackRead morePoems were written at the front. The young writer Artur Dron’, who served in the Ukrainian armed forces for more than three years,did not writeabout bravado or heroism, but made small, delicate memorials for fellow soldiers who had been killed. Or sometimes he built encapsulations of seemingly insignificant moments.One of his poems is about a child in some unnamed village near the frontline, who becomes the unofficial mascot of the soldiers posted there. At Christmas, they leave the young boy “a bag with our crushed Snickers bars / and tangerines. / The ones with seeds, / but oh so sweet.” It was a fleeting incident: not newsworthy, not impressive, nothing for the history books – but it was material for a poem. Yaryna Chornohuztold methat her work as asoldier poetwas the “documentation of feelings”.In the midst of a cataclysm, poems survive, often stripped back to their most essential forms, which are surely universal and primordial human forms of expression: the lament for the dead, the lullaby for the child, the curse. In the end, humans need those things: those songs, those poems. They are proof of life. They may not be remembered; but poetry has a better chance at survival than much else that humans do or make. They may become memorials more lasting than bronze.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, is published on 20 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOn Wednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. With Olia Hercules, Sasha Dovzhyk, Olesya Khromeychuk and Shaun Walker. Book ticketshereDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPoetryOpinionUkraineThe OdysseyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Amanda Knox in Cartwheel review – rookie standup acquitted of murder tells her story | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show
Content: Knox brings off some adroit jokes while staying respectful to the memory of Meredith Kercher, who was murdered in 2007.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKnox brings off some adroit jokes while staying respectful to the memory of Meredith Kercher, who was murdered in 2007.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAmanda Knox in Cartwheel review – rookie standup acquitted of murder tells her storyGilded Balloon TeviotPerformer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy showBrian LoganMon 10 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Welcome to themost controversial show on the fringe!” Some audiences will diagnose self-regard in that intro by rookie standup Amanda Knox. For others, as for Knox herself, it merely acknowledges the continuing efforts to silence her. But then, Knox is “the human version of the blue/gold dress”, a canvas on to which we all project guilty, innocent – or weird. Her innocence now proved, it’s the last of these charges she takes on in this fringe outing, retelling her oft-told tale through the lens of new motherhood.Is it a disgrace that she’s telling it at all – and profiting from it, some would say. (Although they’ve presumably never taken a show to the Edinburgh fringe.) Classifying Cartwheel as comedy may be a misstep; it risks looking insensitive and inaccurately describes the show. But, judging by the evidence, Knox would be damned whatever she did. Now at least she can tell her story in her own way, articulating a growing anger at her treatment and a determination to raise her daughter, not to be silenced and scared but “to be the exact girl I was punished for being”.View image in fullscreenAmanda Knox in Cartwheel at The Wine Bar at Gilded Balloon.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf we’re here for an insight into what it’s like to beAmanda Knox, we get it, as episodes from the 39-year-old’s “extremely prolonged and public trauma” are recounted while folding children’s clothes and maintaining a dialogue with the voice of her four-year-old daughter. How can she tell her kids about her wrongful imprisonment? As a Dr Seuss story: “Knox the fox in a box with locks”? How to react when her baby’s birth is greeted with hateful online abuse? Becoming a mum has refined Knox’s understanding and sharpened her fury at everything she, and her own mother, have been put through.More power to her for peppering this account with several adroit jokes – even if they elicit more rueful smiles than laughs. She’s an inexperienced comedian, this isn’t a “show” – but she shapes and performs this umpteenth telling of her story well. I found its spirit of defiance stirring, I found it respectful to the memory of her murdered roommate, and as well judged an effort by Knox to reclaim her awful story as we have any right to expect.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Amanda KnoxComedyEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C Smith | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Writer-director Eilidh Loan takes inspiration from her grandmother for this portrait of grief and religion
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Writer-director Eilidh Loan takes inspiration from her grandmother for this portrait of grief and religion
Content: Inspired … Elaine C Smith in Cathy.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenInspired … Elaine C Smith in Cathy.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewCathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C SmithTraverse theatre, EdinburghWriter-director Eilidh Loan takes inspiration from her grandmother for this portrait of grief and religionMark FisherMon 10 Aug 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEilidh Loan marked her arrival as a playwright withMoorcroft, a tremendous male-centred comedy inspired by her father’s amateur football team. Now she has moved up a generation to write a female-centred family comedy inspired by her grandmother.It was the older woman who stipulated that her character – the Cathy of the title – should be played by Elaine C Smith, a decision so spot on it suggests that she missed her calling as a casting director. It’s hard to imagine an actor who could better embody Loan’s vision of a newly widowed working-class woman whose grief is veering towards depression. She lands Loan’s jokes – acerbic and sharp – with battle-hardened precision.This is a woman who craves the love of neither the audience nor anyone else on stage. She has reached a point in life where her every discomfort is voiced – sod the consequences. Her waspish tongue and world-weary sourness go down several layers before we see the vulnerable person beneath. Deflated and disillusioned, she cannot see herself making it as far as Christmas.The setting is the aftermath of the funeral of Tommy, Cathy’s husband of 50 years, and the play begins with the kind of gallows humour characteristic of such events. Any mention of death makes one person laugh and another burst into tears.There is Flo (Michele Gallagher), grieving for her father; Flo’s husband, Colin (Alan Orr), a Protestant intruder to this Catholic clan; and Amy (Chloe Hodgson), heavily pregnant and hoping for a less acrimonious future for her growing family. The set, designed by Kenny Miller, switches between Cathy’s front room and the charity shop where Amy works. Here, the similarly bereaved Lizzie (Sally Reid) helps push the story along – an indication that life goes on even when grief persists.Sanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisisRead moreAs social comedy it is snappily observed, but it is also dramatically underpowered. The only thing at stake is the family’s cordial relations in the absence of the placatory Tommy, and it hardly seems to matter whether Cathy and Flo can patch up their mother-daughter conflicts by the end of the play. New life and a Christmas resolution provide a touching ending, but even with the big laughs, it covers limited emotional ground.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisis | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jacob Sparrow’s award-winning two-hander finds hope and humanity amid the prejudice and loss of the 1990s
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Jacob Sparrow’s award-winning two-hander finds hope and humanity amid the prejudice and loss of the 1990s
Content: Light in darkness … Matthew Tennyson (left) and Richard Cant in Sanctuary at Pleasance Dome, Edinburgh.Photograph: Andrew PerryView image in fullscreenLight in darkness … Matthew Tennyson (left) and Richard Cant in Sanctuary at Pleasance Dome, Edinburgh.Photograph: Andrew PerryEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisisPleasance Dome, EdinburghJacob Sparrow’s award-winning two-hander finds hope and humanity amid the prejudice and loss of the 1990sArifa AkbarMon 10 Aug 2026 02.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the highlights of the Edinburgh international festival is a revival of Tony Kushner’s Angels in America, an era-defining play set at the height of the Aids crisis. In a smaller room of the same city is Jacob Sparrow’s debut – an award-winning two-hander that captures the desperation and hope of young men with Aids in the 1990s.It is a miniature piece, relatively speaking, and surprisingly uplifting, given the subject matter. The setup is apparently inspired by the real-life public furore around plans to build an Aids hospice in a Suffolk village. Sparrow’s characters, both gay and at close quarters with HIV, ruefully mention the fears in this village around the potential contamination of their cows if the hospice were to be built.View image in fullscreenDelicately emotional … Matthew Tennyson (left) and Richard Cant in Sanctuary at Pleasance Dome, Edinburgh.Photograph: Andrew PerryInside a house owned by a well-meaning, off-stage woman who is inviting people with HIV/Aids to seek sanctuary here instead, two men meet in the kitchen. Michael (Matthew Tennyson) is young, infected and angry, while the other (Richard Cant) is older, unnamed and more mysterious, but happily living with his partner in retirement, he says.They get talking and it is really an opportunity for Michael to reveal his backstory: his first, incandescent love, the moment he was told he was HIV positive, losing friend after friend to Aids and his feelings towards the narrow-minded villagers who seem to care about the welfare of cows over humans.In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreDirected by Josh Seymour, both actors give delicately emotional performances which become deeply moving. Amid the darkness is Michael’s barely whispered hope for more life, and a greater sense of joy in living – and loving – as a gay man despite the death around him.There are plot twists and contrivances which you see coming from the start. These jar, as does the warm tying up of the story at the end, which feels tonally at odds with this abject moment of prejudice in the history of the illness. But Sparrow still captures a moment, his play determined not to simply paint everything black. There are also some lovely, lyrical passages in his script that showcase the potential of his talent.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreAids and HIVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl review – a smart swipe at the mess made by men | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tenderness
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Jessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tenderness
Content: Bare-faced bravado … Jessica Aszkenasy’s Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl is at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreenBare-faced bravado … Jessica Aszkenasy’s Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl is at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTitclown: Daddy’s Little Girl review – a smart swipe at the mess made by menSummerhall, EdinburghJessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tendernessKate WyverMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the 2025 debut of her breast-forward stage persona Titclown, Jessica Aszkenasy’s second grubbily smutty clowning show rolls around sardonically in daddy issues and the messy disappointment of men these days.The straight dating pool is running dry. All this clown wants is a boyfriend, but none of them are enough like her father. As voice notes to friends unpack the feminist implications of wanting a man while generally disliking them, thePhilippe Gaulier-trainedclown wriggles around on the floor in an oversized suit with something bulging down below. Directed by Cecily Nash, Daddy’s Little Girl is divided neatly between these two forms: half wry analysis told with a bitter laugh, half nude-heavy clowning that bares its teeth at the ease with which men command praise, affection and power.This tightrope walk leads to some smart contrasts, as Aszkenasy nuzzles a wobbling dildo while her voiceover worries about the worship of the male ego.Comedyis built into her bones. She hunches backwards to whip out a wobbling penis with grinning bravado, then crumples in shame to put on a pad.Olga Koch: Fat Tom Cruise review – surefire standup pirouettes through the punchlinesRead moreThese playful, inventive fragments are most striking in their specificity, though they later give way to the broader fury of what men are allowed to get away with, as more nuanced details are sidelined for the straightforward egging of abusers everyone can agree are scum. Her point is about the slippery slope of the bad behaviour we allow men to get away with, but it feels less artfully done than the rest.At the end of the greased-up, egg-covered 18+ show, what resonates most isn’t the dick-swinging audience participation, nor the groin thrusting to the front row. What sticks is the sense of longing that underlies the bravado and the analysis. It’s the slow, tender hug of the suited inflatable man who accompanies her throughout the performance, standing in for the flesh-and-blood version she’s still waiting to come along.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ofcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarks | GB News | The Guardian
description: Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia
Content: Caroline Farrow describes herself as a Catholic commentator.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCaroline Farrow describes herself as a Catholic commentator.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockGB NewsOfcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarksRegulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophiliaMichael SavageMedia editorMon 10 Aug 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia.The remarks are thought to have set a new record for individual complaints about a GB News programme, with more than 12,000 people raising concerns about comments made by the guest Caroline Farrow.Those to speak out included the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, andBimini, the star of RuPaul’s Drag Race UK.Farrow, who describes herself as a Catholic commentator and is a campaigns manager for theultra-conservative advocacy group CitizenGO, made the remarks during a discussion after the Pride in London march in July.Speaking on the Alex Armstrong Tonight show, Farrow said the march was “not about gay rights” and had instead “become about celebrating every single sexuality that isn’t heterosexuality”.She said this included “some very bizarre and unhealthy kinks and quirks, you know, like furries and bestiality and even minor-attracted, they call themselves minor-attracted people, you know, paedophiles”.The remarks prompted an open letter signed by Polanski and Bimini calling onOfcomto deal with the “dangerous” disinformation.Ofcom confirmed to the Guardian that it was investigating the show over potential breaches of broadcasting standards. The rules dictate that “material which may cause offence is justified by the context”.The edition of the show containing the remarks has since been removed from YouTube.Armstrong, the show’s presenter, challenged the comments at the time, saying “the overwhelming amount of people at pride were there for good reasons”.He added: “I don’t think it was full of paedophiles and everything, I’m sure there are nefarious people.”He went further on a later show, saying: “Comments made by guests last weekend conflated gay pride with the celebration of paedophilia. This is an age-old gay trope that’s been used over a number of years to demonise and slander gay people. Those comments by guests had no place in that discussion.”TheGreen partydeputy leader welcomed Ofcom’s latest decision to investigate Farrow’s comments.“Zack was right to complain about it at the time,” Rachel Millward said. “The suggestion that gay people are somehow a particular threat to children is baseless, irresponsible and deeply harmful.“GB News is a regulated broadcaster, and broadcasters are supposed to meet basic professional standards. That should include not using their platform to spread hateful lies about a marginalised group.”GB News has been approached for comment. At the time, it said: “These comments were expressed within a live debate by a contributor. They were her own views, and do not reflect the views or editorial position of GB News.“Anyone watching the debate would have noted the comments were robustly and repeatedly challenged by two other contributors.”GB News has previously been criticised by Ofcom for similar remarks on another programme. Last year, the regulator concluded that the channel breached the broadcasting code after a presenter, Josh Howie, said the “full inclusion of LGBTQ+ persons” at a church would “include paedos”.On that occasion, sanctions were not imposed on GB News because it had already broadcast an apology and a fuller discussion about the context of the comment within weeks of the original broadcast.The investigation comes amid increased pressure on Ofcom to enforce broadcasting rules.While the regulator is also investigating a GB News repeat of itsinterview with Donald Trump, it declined to investigate a claim by a GB News presenter that there had been noriot in Belfastin June, despite cars and houses being set alight, attacks on police and families fleeing their homes.The previous Ofcom chair, the Conservative peer Michael Grade, who left the post in April, accused GB News’s critics of seeking to restrict free speech to a“liberal, Islington consensus”.Explore more on these topicsGB NewsPrideOfcomLGBTQ+ rightsTelevision industryTelevisionZack PolanskinewsShareReuse this content

title: Tupac Shakur: jury selection begins in trial of ex-gang boss for rapper’s killing | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors allege Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis ordered killing and provided gun in Las Vegas drive-by shooting 30 years ago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prosecutors allege Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis ordered killing and provided gun in Las Vegas drive-by shooting 30 years ago
Content: Tupac Shakur backstage after a performance in 1994. The proceedings in LA will open with jury selection, which is expected to take a week.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTupac Shakur backstage after a performance in 1994. The proceedings in LA will open with jury selection, which is expected to take a week.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesTupac ShakurTupac Shakur: jury selection begins in trial of ex-gang boss for rapper’s killingProsecutors allege Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis ordered killing and provided gun in Las Vegas drive-by shooting 30 years agoGuardian staff and agenciesMon 10 Aug 2026 14.02 EDTFirst published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJury selection began on Monday in Las Vegas as the murder trial of a former gang leader finally got under way decades after the shooting of the rapperTupac Shakur, one of the most high-profile unsolved killings in the US.It was thought likely to take at least the rest of the week to seat a jury for the trial of Duane “Keffe D” Davis, in which prosecutors aim to show that Davis, 63, the one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang in California, ordered the killing and provided the gun for the fatal attack on Shakur.About 75 potential jurors were called to the courthouse on Monday to be questioned ⁠about their ability to be fair and impartial in such a high-profile trial. Davis faces a potential life sentence without parole if convicted.Shakur, 25, was gunned down at the height of his career, on 7 September 1996, as he sat in the passenger seat of a black BMW with the music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight in the Nevada tourist city, where the rap star had watched a boxing match featuring Mike Tyson and was on his way to a club to perform. Knight survived the shooting.Davis is the only person to be charged in the killing and is accused of murder with a deadly weapon – even though he is not alleged to have fired the shots himself.The proceedings are expected to last a month to five weeks before the judge, Carli Kierny. However, the trial remains unlikely to make clear who fired the fatal shots.William Lesane, who said he was Shakur’s cousin, told reporters outside the courtroom that the trial was the culmination of 30 years of grief and trauma for his family.“Hopefully we’ll find out some new information. And more importantly, the right person is charged and convicted for Tupac’s murder,” Lesane said.View image in fullscreenDuane Davis appearing at a hearing before his trial.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesDavis is the only person still alive out of the group that prosecutors believe attacked Shakur and Knight that night. They plan to present as evidence material from Davis’s tell-all book, Compton Street Legend, which was published in 2019 and gives a vivid account of the shooting.The death of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has prompted endless debate among music fansover who did it and why. The rapper was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US east coast against the west coast.Known for hits such as California Love and All Eyez on Me, Shakur – the son of a Black Panther – was raised in the New York City neighborhood of Harlem and Baltimore, Maryland, but quickly became the epitome of a California bad boy when he signed with the Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.The trial will revisit the battle between Death Row, founded by Marion “Suge” Knight, and Bad Boy Records, the east coast label created bySean “Diddy” Combsand featuring Christopher “the Notorious BIG” Wallace, who was murdered in March 1997.View image in fullscreenTupac Shakur, left, with the Death Row Records chair Marion ‘Suge’ Knight in Los Angeles the month before the killing.Photograph: Frank Wiese/APProsecutors say Death Row Records was protected by Mob Piru, a Los Angeles gang that was part of the wider Bloods alliance. Knight was affiliated with the group. Bad Boy Records had hired the rival group South Side Compton Crips, led by Davis, as bodyguards.After the Tyson fight at the MGM Grand casino, Knight and Shakur attacked Davis’s nephew, the Crips member Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, in retribution for an alleged assault on a Death Row employee. Davis was out for revenge, the prosecution says.Later that night, a white Cadillac carrying Davis, Anderson and others pulled up beside Shakur’s car inLas Vegas. Shots were fired from the Cadillac and Shakur was fatally wounded.View image in fullscreenSean ‘Diddy’ Combs (left) and the Notorious BIG at an awards ceremony in New York in 1995.Photograph: Al Pereira/Getty ImagesThe investigation sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the cold case was revived after Davis’s memoirs, in which says he handed a pistol from where he was in the front seat to those in the back seat of the Cadillac, which had pulled up alongside Shakur’s BMW.These compromising revelations were consistent with remarks Davis had made previously to reporters. But this time, theyled to his arrest, in September 2023.Davis has since backtracked andpleaded not guilty,saying there is no evidence against him and his co-author merely inflated a tale.In May, the rapper’s stepbrother Maurice Shakurfiled a wrongful death lawsuit in civil court.“There remain individuals who were involved in Tupac’s murder who, for 30 years, have not been held accountable for their crimes,” his complaint says.The suit cites a recent TV documentary series titled Sean Combs: The Reckoning, in which Davis says in an interview with police that Combs, now in prison himself, offered him $1m to kill Shakur.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurLas VegasRapnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Potter fans force relocation of £430m undersea cable to avoid Dobby’s ‘grave’ | Harry Potter | The Guardian
description: Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beach
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beach
Content: The elf Dobby, who was buried on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire during the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe elf Dobby, who was buried on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire during the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.Photograph: ReutersHarry PotterHarry Potter fans force relocation of £430m undersea cable to avoid Dobby’s ‘grave’Power cable linking UK and Ireland now passes near Bronze Age human burial remains instead of fictional grave on Welsh beachHelena HortonMon 10 Aug 2026 03.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Potter fans have forced a new multimillion-pound power cable between the UK and Ireland to be relocated after complaining it would desecrate the “grave” of Dobby, a fictional elf.The character was laid to rest on Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire,Wales, in the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows. Fans of the wizard series come to leave stones reading “Here Lies Dobby” despite being asked not to by the land owner, the National Trust, because the beach is an ecologically sensitive site.View image in fullscreenDobby’s ‘grave’ at Freshwater West.Photograph: Sam Cuthbertson/AlamyThe £430m Greenlink interconnector, which links the National Grid to Ireland, was initially going to pass through the site of the “grave”, the project manager Simon Ludlam told theEnergyRevolution podcast.Fans became aware of the plans after Ludlam pointed out where the 125-mile (200km) cable to County Wexford would go underground at Freshwater West during a BBC interview. “We did the shot, we finished, I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later. And we got hundreds of calls, I mean, hundreds of calls.”Ludlam said he did not know who Dobby was, and became confused by the calls the company received, saying a colleague told him: “Apparently we’re going to go straight through Dobby’s grave”.“I said: ‘Dobby, who’s Dobby? I don’t know Dobby?’ I said: ‘He’s a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?’”He said the colleague told him: “No it’s very, very serious.”The firm then enlisted planners to find a new route that avoided the supposed grave. “A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby’s happy.”In the end, he said, “we went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby’s grave”.The Bronze Age remains include urns associated with human burial.Explore more on these topicsHarry PotterEnergyWalesHeritageUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Odyssey becomes Christopher Nolan’s highest grossing film as it passes $1.1bn at box office | Christopher Nolan | The Guardian
description: The film-maker’s take on Homer’s epic has beaten his previous record holder The Dark Knight Rises
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The film-maker’s take on Homer’s epic has beaten his previous record holder The Dark Knight Rises
Content: Jimmy Gonzales as Cepheus, Matt Damon as Odysseus and Himesh Patel as Eurylochus in The Odyssey. The film has become Christopher Nolan’s top-earning film at the box office after less than a month in cinemas.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenJimmy Gonzales as Cepheus, Matt Damon as Odysseus and Himesh Patel as Eurylochus in The Odyssey. The film has become Christopher Nolan’s top-earning film at the box office after less than a month in cinemas.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesChristopher NolanThe Odyssey becomes Christopher Nolan’s highest grossing film as it passes $1.1bn at box officeThe film-maker’s take on Homer’s epic has beaten his previous record holder The Dark Knight RisesPress AssociationSun 9 Aug 2026 21.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 23.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has become the highest grossing film of Christopher Nolan’s career, having made more than US$1bn at the global box office less than a month after its release.The blockbuster, which was released on 17 July, is an adaptation of Homer’s ancient Greek epic and follows Matt Damon as Odysseus, the Greek king of Ithaca, on his perilous 10-year journey home after the Trojan war.The film, which has receivedstrong reviewsfrom critics, has grossed $1.104bn (£819m, A$1.56bn) worldwide, making it the most successful of Nolan’s career.‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summerRead moreIt has beaten his previous record-holder, the 2012 Batman film The Dark Knight Rises, which earned $1.085bn (£805.7m), while its 2008 predecessor The Dark Knight grossed $1.005bn (£745m).The Oscar-winning film-maker has directed blockbusters such as Tenet, Dunkirk and Interstellar, with his movies having now grossed more than US$7bn (£5.198bn) globally.The 56-year-old wrote and directedThe Odyssey, which he also produced alongside his wife, Emma Thomas.The film features a star-studded cast including Damon, Anne Hathaway and Robert Pattinson – and has become the highest-grossing of all three actors’ careers.The three-hour-long epic also stars Zendaya, Tom Holland, Charlize Theron and Lupita Nyong’o.The Odyssey debuted at number one globally and it remained in the top position for two consecutive weekends.It was made with production companies Syncopy and Universal Pictures, and is one of three Universal films to have grossed US$1bn globally this year, alongside The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and the Michael Jackson biopic Michael.Jim Orr, president of domestic theatrical distribution at Universal Pictures, said: “Christopher Nolan has earned audiences’ trust by consistently delivering must-see theatrical events, and The Odyssey is him operating at the peak of his powers.“Nolan’s epic film has been at the forefront of culture, with audiences seeking out premium formats and repeat viewings for this once-in-a-lifetime cinematic journey.”Veronika Kwan Vandenberg, president of distribution at Universal Pictures International, hailed the film as “a global epic that has resonated with audiences everywhere with its massive scope and uncompromising vision”.The Odyssey had a reported production budget of US$250m (£185m, A$353m) excluding marketing costs, making it one of the most expensive films of Nolan’s career.Explore more on these topicsChristopher NolanThe OdysseynewsShareReuse this content

title: Movie paradise? How Malta became a magnet for big film shoots | Malta | The Guardian
description: EU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annually
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: EU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annually
Content: Pedro Pascal, director Ridley Scott and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II in Malta.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APView image in fullscreenPedro Pascal, director Ridley Scott and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II in Malta.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APMaltaMovie paradise? How Malta became a magnet for big film shootsEU’s smallest country has played ancient Rome, the Land of Spells and Bay of Pentos and draws more than 30 productions annuallyPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorMon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 03.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat links the Caribbean, ancient Rome, Enid Blyton’s Land of Spells, the south of France and the Bay of Pentos from Game of Thrones? They are all places that have been portrayed in recent and forthcoming films by a sunny archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea, no bigger in size than Sheffield.Malta has over the last decade risen to become one of the most popular places inEuropefor American and British film-makers to set their works in, taking a lead in what has been described as an “arms race” to lure big movie productions with tax incentives.The EU’s smallest country has hosted more than 30 film and TV productions each year in each of the last three years, including a record 36 in 2023 and 2025. They includeJurassic World RebirthandGladiator II, this spring’s Blyton adaptationThe Magic Faraway Treeand the new Jason Statham action thriller Mutiny, out at the end of this month.On the screen,Maltahas stood in for Greece (in the BBC’s recent Two Weeks in August), 1980s Sicily (Heidi Ewing’s forthcoming British feature The Travel Writer), rural southern France (Channel 5’s cosy crime drama The Madame Blanc Mysteries) and the Caribbean (Guy Ritchie’s forthcoming Layer Cake follow-up Viva la Madness).View image in fullscreenSally Lindsay (in red) as Jean White in The Madame Blanc Mysteries, set in southern France and filmed in Malta.Photograph: Mark Cassar/Clapperboard/Channel 5 TelevisionThe island is even starting to represent itself: the third season of Netflix’s detective drama Enola Holmes decamps from Victorian London to the then British-occupied island, and principal photography is due to start next year for TV auteur Stephen Poliakoff’s The Order, set on the eve of the 1565 siege of Malta by Ottoman forces.“For such a small European country, Malta is really punching above its weight,” said Adrian Wootton, the chief executive of the British Film Commission. “It’s been very aggressive, in a positive way, about diversifying its industry.”The microstate’s history of hosting cinematic productions dates back to 1925’s silent maritime drama Sons of the Sea, and since the 1970s it has hosted two of the world’s largest water tanks designed to allow film-makers to shoot maritime scenes in a controllable environment.But in the past its film industry was essentially seasonal, said Johann Grech, Malta’s film commissioner. “Now, we have an industry that is working every day, all year round.”Its success is largely due to the broader global upheaval of how film-making is financed. Until the early 2000s, audiovisual productions in Europe were mostly funded by direct funding, such as film funds or selective grants.Over the last few decades, however, films are increasingly made possible by tax incentives, such as cash rebates that production companies are reimbursed after filming if they hire local crews or rent facilities.View image in fullscreenNicola Coughlan in the Enid Blyton adaptation The Magic Faraway Tree.Photograph: Entertainment Film DistributorsSuch financial incentives now make upalmost half of European fiction films’ budgets, and mean that “films and series no longer simply occupy locations, they are engineered around them”, as a recent report by the European Audiovisual Observatory noted.Malta, which introduced a cash rebate mechanism in 2005, has aggressively ratcheted up its offering over the last decade, to what the Napoleon and Gladiator II producerdescribedas “probably the most generous cash rebate in the world”.All of the 36 major productions that filmed in Malta in 2025 qualified for a 40% cash rebate, which, unlike in some competing states, can also be applied to crew and equipment coming in from abroad if it can’t be sourced locally.At the Mediterrane film festival on the island in June, Grech announced his intention to further improve the rebate model, which runs out in 2028, and to find private investment to build an €80m (£70m) studio complex. “Every euro that we invest in the rebate, the industry generates back four,” he said in an interview. “The film industry is becoming an economic pillar for our country.”Some critics in Malta say the country’s rise as a filming location has come at the cost of neglecting local cinematic talent. Examples of Maltese films engaging audiences outside its borders are few and far between: Alex Camilleri’s 2021 film Luzzu, which contended for the grand jury prize at Sundance, is a rare exception.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe narrow streets of Malta’s capital, Valletta, are beloved by film-makers.Photograph: Alina Zienowicz/Getty ImagesWith local crews in demand from international production companies, Maltese directors often find themselves being outbid by Hollywood, said Teodor Reljić, a Malta-based screenwriter and former film critic. “There’s a bit of a parallel universe: people in servicing are thriving, but local film-makers can’t pay a DOP [director of photography] because they are expecting Jurassic World fees.”The Malta Film Commission is focused on courting international productions, while nurturing domestic film is left to the arts council, which operates on a smaller budget. Malta does not match funding for financial incentives to its homegrown film funding, which is something that countries such as Estonia have done.“Without incentives, smaller European countries would simply be excluded from the global production market,” said Edith Sepp, the head of the Estonian Film Institute. “They can be gamechangers.”“At the same time, we need to ensure our own films are seen, exported and remembered. Otherwise, we risk becoming a place to shoot the films, but our own stories struggle to find their funding.”Film in Europe is booming, but the gongs and glamour only tell one side of the story | Moritz PfeiferRead moreThere are also signs that Malta’s infrastructure is being tested to the limits as its cities, towns and villages regularly turn into film sets. Road closures and parking restrictions have become a bugbear for local people. “What are Valletta residents supposed to do – stay confined in their homes?”, one resident of Malta’s capital asked news outlet MaltaToday recently.Last month, equipment linked to a film being shot in Valletta knocked over and damaged a 100-year-old statue and a historic pedestal in St George’s Square, causing anger among Malta’s religious community.“There are signs of a pushback against overtourism, like in Barcelona or Venice,” said Reljić. “But in Malta we have online gambling, construction and tourism – for now, film-making is the least toxic of our big industries.”Explore more on these topicsMaltaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles / György  Kurtág’s Kafka Fragments review – Bristol Proms reach for the heavenly | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Sunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wife
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Sunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wife
Content: Hearing the world in a grain of sand … Sakari Oramo and Anu Komsi perform György Kurtág’sKafka Fragmentsat Bristol Beacon.Photograph: Jessie MyersView image in fullscreenHearing the world in a grain of sand … Sakari Oramo and Anu Komsi perform György Kurtág’sKafka Fragmentsat Bristol Beacon.Photograph: Jessie MyersClassical musicJoby Talbot’s Path of Miracles / György  Kurtág’s Kafka Fragments review – Bristol Proms reach for the heavenlyTenebrae, Nigel Short / Anu Komsi and Sakari OramoSt George’s Bristol / Bristol BeaconSunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wifeAlexandra CoghlanMon 10 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRitual can be a choir in procession in a great cathedral or the simple act of putting down a violin bow. At the BBC Proms’ Bristol performances this weekend, it was both – and to strikingly different effect.First, grandeur and spectacle, as Nigel Short and his chamber choir Tenebrae celebrated their 25th anniversary with a return to their 2005 commission: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles. Inspired by the Catholic pilgrimage to Santiago, it’s a piece with a cult following, a phenomenon as much as a score, and one that only comes to life fully in live performance.We start in musical darkness. A low drone gradually swells and rises, growls becoming notes. Then, suddenly, a chord flares bright from behind us. Singers surround the audience, clustering in circles, moving down the aisles, forming and reforming into quartets, duets. Talbot’s hypnotic music – post-minimalist patterns and dances, chants and road songs – is designed to inhabit space, physically as well as musically dramatising the journey along the Camino.It’s hard to imagine it better sung. High sopranos and low basses performed unearthly feats of endurance, and the precision of the whole – a musical mosaic constructed before our eyes – was utterly compelling. But it’s a piece conceived (as Short explained) with “wonderful cathedrals” in mind – cathedrals without the creaking wooden floors and overpowering heat of St George’s Bristol, where the scuffling and banging business of movement (and a faint from an audience member, derailing much of the choreography) overpowered the rite. It’s hard to keep your eyes on heaven when your ears keep getting dragged back to the here and now.No such problems down the road at Bristol Beacon, where the BBC Symphony Orchestra’s chief conductor Sakari Oramo swapped baton for bow, joined by soprano Anu Komsi for a ritual they’ve performed for nearly 40 years – since before they were married.Scored for just violin and voice, György Kurtág’s 1986Kafka Fragmentsmines the novelist’s diaries and letters not just for gold but lead and copper too – 40 shards of text that range from the tender and philosophical to the banal, erotic and absurd. In the composer’s100th birthday year, it’s the perfect distillation of the Hungarian’s music: playful and infinitely rich, hearing the world in a grain of sand.Are the Fragments an argument? A love story? A camouflaged opera? In Komsi and Oramo’s hands – calm, matter of fact, intensely focused – they feel, above all, like a search for truth: tantalisingly beyond reach in slippery, striving near-octaves, rejected in the simplicity of “The good march in step”, the lyricism of “The flower hung dreamily” and the bravura excesses of “Scene on a tram”. They try each musical door with equanimity, never demanding or forcing interpretation. Why rush to the answer when there are 40 more years of questions ahead?Available on BBC Sounds until 12 October. The Proms continueuntil 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicGyörgy KurtágPromsProms 2026FestivalsShareReuse this content
