title: ‘I can’t watch it without sobbing’: your happiest TV endings | Television | The Guardian
description: From poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joy
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joy
Content: A fitting testament to love, endurance, and above all, friendship … The final episode of Superstore.Photograph: NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fitting testament to love, endurance, and above all, friendship … The final episode of Superstore.Photograph: NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty ImagesTelevision‘I can’t watch it without sobbing’: your happiest TV endingsFrom poignant farewells to adorable cuddly toy monkeys, these are the televisual finales that turn Guardian readers into puddles of joyGuardian readersandJoe PinnerMon 10 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA missing monkey, a token tennis bracelet, and the end of the Korean war! These are the most uplifting and moving finales in TV history, according to Guardian readers. Warning, spoilers lie ahead.Friday Night Dinner‘The magnificent, the magical, the marvellous!’ It’s TV’s happiest endingsRead moreAfter nine years of following the Goodman family, the boys – Adam and Jonny – finally bring home “females” to meet parents Jackie and Martin. The dinner is absolute chaos, Martin has ruined all of the food, he’s thrown a piece of bread at Adam’s girlfriend, their neighbour Jim keeps running in with bags of dog vomit, Jackie is having a total meltdown, and then everything stops in a beautiful moment when both girls announce they’re pregnant.The family boogie to the theme song would be a moment of sheer joy on its own, but it’s made even more so since this turned out to be the final episode. The sad and untimely death of Paul Ritter, who played Martin, the year after the broadcast makes this scene all the more poignant. The image of the family celebration is a reminder to embrace the family dance, whether it’s happy times or times when you say: “Sh*t on it.”Amy, Tampa, FloridaSuperstoreThe US sitcom Superstore spends several seasons gently pointing out the flaws of capitalism, US employment and immigration law, and the general folly of humanity, while making you fall in love with (most of) the flawed and horrifying characters you meet. Has there ever been a greater villain than Sandra’s arch-nemesis Carol?Set in a fictional supermarket, it takes you through increasing digitalisation of the industry and the Covid pandemic with a feather-light touch, and absolutely hilarious vignettes of the worst behaviour you can imagine in retail. The arc of its central pairing, Amy and Jonah, is compromised through the final series as lead actress (and producer) America Ferrera briefly left the programme, but she returns to wrap things up with a beautiful and deeply satisfying peek into the future. The finale is a fitting testament to love, endurance and, above all, friendship.Jill, 43, DerbyshireHeated RivalryView image in fullscreenMagic … Connor Storrie (left) and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry.Heated Rivalry, season one. I hope they don’t make any more seasons because they’ll never be able to capture the magic of the first. The ending was a perfect wrap-up of the short six-episode series. As a gay guy of a certain age, I’ve found that the vast majority of movies and TV shows about gay men I’ve had to sit through have been tragic or whitewashed. In the US, we drag shows out until all the fun has been completely drained out and at the end they’re unrecognisable from where they began.Danny, 57, New YorkstateThe Good PlaceThe Good Place is an extraordinarily rare gem. It’s a comedy that’s actually funny, with characters that you really care about despite their varied faults. However, the end of the first series immediately sent up the red flag for other series with such a strong opening – where can you go from here?However, it remained a gem for all four seasons, until the four principal protagonists finally create the heaven they’d always wanted and, one by one, each at their own time, they decide they’ve had enough of everything, are as happy as they could ever be, have experienced everything they’d ever wanted to experience, and that it’s finally the right time to just … go. It’s beautiful and uplifting, and makes me feel happy whenever I think about it.Andy, JapanScrubsScrubs is an amazing show with some genuine character development. We follow a trio of budding medical interns – JD, Elliot and Turk – as they grow and become well-rounded doctors and human beings.View image in fullscreenPitch perfect … Scrubs.Photograph: PRIn a final two-parter, (for season eight, that is, and not the “should-have-been-a-spin-off” season nine, or the recent reboot), JD accepts a job at a new hospital to be closer to his son. And then, on his last day, he goes to painstaking lengths to have the perfect swan song – the constant farewells with his best friend, Turk, finally learning the name of the janitor who tormented him the entire series, and having the perfect final moment with his gruff but ultimately caring mentor, Dr Cox (even if it did take some coaxing).And then the grand finale: JD realises through a patient that you need to accept the future and all the uncertainties it holds. JD walks through the hospital’s halls, filled with all the people he interacted with right back to the first season, as he stops to watch a giant screen projecting a moving montage of the future, set to Peter Gabriel’s The Book of Love. A pitch-perfect ending.Arjun, 26, LondonGhostsThe ending of Ghosts is moving and life-affirming, and a perfect example of what this show does brilliantly, which is to land its moments (sad and funny) without lingering on them for too long. It might be because I binged it, but it felt like the ending was really made up of the season’s last three episodes. The fifth one has the heartbreaking reveal of the Captain’s backstory, followed by that joyous line dancing scene. Then there’s episode six, which has a well-crafted throwback to the beginning, with Alison finding out that Julian pushed her out of the window. He’s the one who has to persuade her to stay, via a beautiful monologue made all the lovelier coming from him.And then, just when you think it’s settled and they’re staying – the Christmas special. It’s happy and satisfying and sad. I love Pat teaching the Captain how to do baby talk and the way they all run to the answering machine to hear Mike’s message. The episode gives all of the characters a moment to be truly themselves. You get a sense of how much Alison loves the ghosts and vice versa; it’s incredibly sweet without being saccharine.Emily, HampshireView image in fullscreenIncredibly sweet without being saccharine … BBC’s Ghosts.Photograph: PRSleepersDoes anyone else remember Sleepers? A post-glasnost spy comedy in which Warren Clarke and Nigel Havers are Soviet agents sent to infiltrate Britain in 1965, and build lives they’re very happy with, thank you, and don’t want to go back to shabby apartments in the Nevsky Prospect. By the end of the series, both have been captured by the hardline KGB officer sent to recover them, and are drugged and shipped out to a waiting submarine. They wake up, and the KGB is returning them to their homes. But while the lead characters are safe, Clarke’s daughter’s cuddly monkey Maurice is missing! Weeks later he appears, wearing a Russian fur hat, having been on an adventure of his own. A perfect show.Nick, 58, YorkshireM*A*S*HThe show I grew up with in the 70s. Beautifully anti-war with top-drawer writing and brilliant characters. The ending is a tear-fest. After the ceasefire is announced, the members of the 4077th throw a party before taking down the camp for the very last time. So many great moments: Hawkeye and BJ saluting Colonel Potter, upper-class Charles leaving in a garbage truck, the death of Henry, and Hawkeye saluting Radar. And the final scene where Hawkeye, who spent the last episode unable to say goodbye, spells it out in rocks that BJ can only view from the air as he lifts off in a chopper. No, you’re crying.Cameron, LedburyView image in fullscreenTear-fest … M*A*S*H.Six Feet UnderEverybody dies! But that’s also what makes it such a special ending, because we get to see how every character’s life plays out in vignettes as the weight of the show’s themes are lifted from them. Claire finally escapes her mother’s overbearing influence, without having to destroy their relationship to do so. Rico gets to run his own funeral home, without the Fishers’ influence. David slays his demons and lives happily ever after with Keith when it looked as if they would destroy him. Brenda realises she can be a good mother after all. Then – yes, as everybody dies! – we get surely the greatest closing montage sequence on TV, with an exceptional soundtrack (Sia’s Breathe Me) to accompany it. I think someone’s started chopping onions in here again …Stephen, 47, SolihullSchitt’s CreekNot only does the finale offer the sheer joy of David and Patrick’s wedding (Moira in her papal mitre and gloves, sobbing her way through the ceremony, the Jazzagals singing Simply the Best, Alexis accidentally dressed as a bride), but the beautiful denouement of the show, as they quietly move on with their lives, back to success but so differently than they imagined in the beginning.View image in fullscreenThe happiest of endings … Schitt’s Creek.I can’t watch it without sobbing. It is to me the happiest of endings: the guy gets the guy, the girl gets the career, Johnny finally makes it back to business, and Moira? Exactly where she belongs, back to Sunrise Bay, along with a token tennis bracelet. It is a sublime moment that takes such good care of the fans and how invested we are in each of Rose’s (and Stevie’s) journeys. It is so refreshing to give everyone a simple happy ending without compromise or drama.Casey, 34, BrightonExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedySchitt's CreekThe Good PlaceFriday Night DinnerHeated RivalryfeaturesShareReuse this content

Warren has a mysterious glittering portal in his shed, but he only ever uses it to dump leaves in. When his teenage daughter is sucked into it one day – leaving her trusty vape behind – he jumps in after her. They find themselves in 2043, where evil refrigerators are trying to kill them (yes, refrigerators). title: John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering critic | John Berger | The Guardian
description: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of Seeing
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of Seeing
Content: John Berger in 2009.Photograph: Franck Courtes/CAMERA PRESS/Agence VUView image in fullscreenJohn Berger in 2009.Photograph: Franck Courtes/CAMERA PRESS/Agence VUBook of the dayJohn BergerReviewJohn Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering criticThis multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of SeeingXan BrooksMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cultural criticJohn Bergerwas still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting the wild stories behind them. When Overton sought permission to write Berger’s biography, though, the critic insisted that he wait a few years. Death changes the relationship between the writer and his subject. More often than not, it complicates and enriches it. Berger – who spent much of his career in passionate conversation with the past – probably knew that better than anyone.Berger typically described himself as a storyteller, an elastic job title which allowed him to swing between fiction and poetry, essays and screenplays. Implicitly, too, the term helped frame his criticism as something propulsive and inclusive, an invitation to dance as opposed to a judgment from on high. Berger had no time for the “great man” theory of art as espoused by the popular historian Kenneth Clark and instead urged his audience to view each piece as a manifestation of society and politics: the tainted fruit of capitalism, inseparable from the marketplace. Oil paintings were status symbols. Nudes were the product of the lusty male gaze. Looking itself was a political act. “You cannot reply to me,” he would tell 1970s TV viewers, breaking the fourth wall to highlight the medium’s limitations. He liked pointing out the mechanics behind the manufacture of art, demystifying the process to better appreciate its results.These days Berger’s reputation largely rests on Ways of Seeing, the insurrectionist 1972 BBC series which made him the critics’ equivalent of a rock star or cult leader. Enterprising viewers can still find him on YouTube. He’s the eloquent firebrand with a messianic gleam in his eye; the Marxist intellectual in open-necked patterned shirts. Overton, though, is at pains to stitch Ways of Seeing into its wider context – showing it as part of a continuum, one political project among many. His exuberant biography is thick with detail and lit by wonder. It strains to paint the whole canvas and give us the man in full, warts and all.double quotation markWe never look at just one thing. We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselvesJohn BergerRaised in London, a child of the blitz, Berger suffered through boarding school and the army before a visit to a Picasso exhibition knocked the scales from his eyes and blew up his middle-class world. He enjoyed moderate success with his paintings and greater acclaim for his novels (one of which – the fractured, sporadically fabulous G – won the 1972 Booker prize). But he was at his most assured and compelling when using the art of others as a springboard to further, deeper inquiry. Berger regarded each work as a portal between time and space and was enthralled by the ways it could be lost and found in translation. Tellingly, his first broadcasting gig was with the BBC World Service, describing pictures in the National Gallery to listeners in west Africa.“We never look at just one thing,” he said. “We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.” That’s certainly the case with John Berger: From Life. Overton is fascinated by Berger but also fascinated by his relationship with Berger and his approach is therefore unashamedly subjective, sliding from the familial third-person (always “John”, never “Berger”) to the direct address (“You”) and between the past and present tense (sometimes in the space of a single sentence). Like Berger in his TV studio, Overton points out the wires, referring to “the book you’re reading now” and “the old man who squats on my pages” and occasionally fretting that he’s left out important information. It’s an elaborate conceit, but it by and large works. There is no single version of a story, Berger argued. Each storyteller can’t help but bend the tale to their will.Overton reveres Berger but he is frustrated by him, too. His life’s a hot mess; his very presence turns oppressive. He’s so authoritative on the page and so contradictory in the wild, a jumble of red-blooded Marxism and High Tory traditionalism. Berger writes elegantly and angrily about forced migration, mourning the loss of the old rural communities, but he lives as a self-imposed exile in Switzerland and France, splitting his time between different houses and women. Language, he concludes, is “potentially the only real human home”, but even this isn’t fixed; it can be breached at any time. By the end of his life, Overton notes, the man’s spoken English has taken on the grammatical patterns of French.Berger’s health was already starting to fail when he donated his boxes to the British Library. Overton recalls their queasy close-quarter encounters in London and Paris: “Strong smell of leaky prostate, top-note of cigarettes and event wine.” Berger in the flesh is diminished, disappointing, “less present here than you are in the archive”, which is probably the case with most ageing artists. They’ve put the best of themselves on the canvas, page or screen. That’s where we’ll find them – in their work, in the past.If there was a bright running thread through Berger’s portmanteau career, it was this preoccupation with the past and its connection to the present. The dead and the living are interdependent, he said. The stronger the link, the happier and healthier the society. Great paintings in a gallery allow us to travel in time. So too do some people, if they are skilled and sensitive enough. Berger’s 1967 book A Fortunate Man paid gorgeous tribute to Dr John Sassall, a country physician from the Forest of Dean whose work at times bordered on the supernatural. “The doctor,” Berger wrote, “is the familiar of death … the living intermediary between us and the multitudinous dead.” He might just as easily be talking about the role of great artists and critics. Possibly British Library curators as well.“Do biographers always remake their subject in their own image?” Overton wonders as he sets about trying to transfer Berger to the page. Most likely they do, but that’s only half of the equation. The past whispers to the present; the dead and living coexist. Overton is a writer in part because of reading John Berger. The biographer’s prose style is his own but he writes in the same spirit – fired by curiosity and close-marking his subject; gesturing out to the reader as though to engage them in debate. His aim, he confesses, is to convince us that the critic is “sat across the page from me, reading every word, a part of the process,” and in fits and spurts he achieves just that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTechnically Berger’s no longer with us: he died in 2017 at the age of 90. But he’s still speaking on YouTube, still being reprinted and still provoking and inspiring a fresh generation of writers. That’s the kind of community and continuity that he always hungered for in his life; sweet karmic payback for a career in the arts. Switch sides, reset and keep the conversation flowing. Berger once spoke to the past from the present. Now, as if by magic, it is the other way around.John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton is published by Allen Lane (£25). title: Sinking ships, dark humour and really good bad guys: Beryl Bainbridge – ranked! | Beryl Bainbridge | The Guardian
description: From the last days of the Titanic to desperate romantics, we rate the work of a British master of black comedy
Author: John Self
Headline: From the last days of the Titanic to desperate romantics, we rate the work of a British master of black comedy
Content: Beryl Bainbridge in 1981.Photograph: Jane Bown/The ObserverView image in fullscreenBeryl Bainbridge in 1981.Photograph: Jane Bown/The ObserverRankedBeryl BainbridgeSinking ships, dark humour and really good bad guys: Beryl Bainbridge – ranked!From the last days of the Titanic to desperate romantics, werate the work of a British master of black comedyJohn SelfMon 10 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreen10Every Man for Himself(1996)Bainbridge’s novel of the last days on RMS Titanic was acclaimed and popular (“They probably thought it was the book of the film,” she said), and the scenes of the sinking are brilliantly delivered. “There is about me an element of showmanship,” says one character, but Bainbridge’s own showmanship is muffled here by her need to stick with facts, meaning the novel lacks the humour, fluidity and eccentricity of her others. And unlike her earlier books, the final tragedy never feels personal to the characters.Sample line:“He did have layers, but like an onion they were all the same.”9Harriet Said …(1972)Bainbridge’s darkest novel is about the teenage narrator and her older, cooler friend Harriet. “I’ve always run wild,” our girl says: a common trait in Bainbridge novels. (She herself was “expelled from school at the age of nine because of some dirty rhyme”.) When the narrator and Harriet get involved with a married man, there’s a lot of “adolescent trembling, swirls of nerves gone gold” – and mortal danger. It’s a story of power and corrupted innocence: but who’s corrupting whom?Sample line:“It was nothing really. I hardly noticed. Just like going to the dentist. Not even as bad.”8Master Georgie(1998)The fifth of Bainbridge’s novels to be shortlisted for the Booker prize – “our table was always the most cheerful, because we didn’t expect to win” – was another based on historical events. She turned to these after she “used up”her life in her earlier autobiographical novels. A subtle book that rewards rereading, it’s set around the Crimean war, narrated in turn by the hangers-on of medic George Hardy. The story comes as a series of snapshot moments, as the characters hurtle toward disaster. “One should never underestimate the disruptive force of haphazard actions,” says one, and Bainbridge’s characters know all about those.Sample line:“Some people only weep inside, which I think wasteful.”7A Quiet Life(1976)Of all Bainbridge’s novels, this offers the most direct account of her “terrifying” childhood in Liverpool when, as she later recalled, her mother and father fought so much “my brother and I would never be out of the house at the same time [so as] to stop them killing each other”. Through siblings Alan and Madge, we see their mother’s restless domestic rearrangements (“Everything in its place, though never for long”) and a bad-tempered father, but also the demons that drove him there. Little wonder that “Madge threw herself about in a transport of unexplained grief”. But it’s also a charming, funny, bittersweet portrait of a vanished world of meat pies, fruit drops and poultices on boils.Sample line:“Though the war was over, Father was still caught in a cross-fire, harassed by battles, by phantom cities tumbling about his ears.”View image in fullscreen6Sweet William(1975)Many of Bainbridge’s characters long for the transformative effects of love, are so hungry for change that they grab on to it, even if it’s not the right change. Playwright and lothario William provides it for as many women as will have him. (“What did you think when I first met you?” “I thought I had flu.”) Even as his deceits are uncovered, he gets away with it. “You don’t want to expect normality from him,” one of his lovers says to another. “He’s an artist after all.” The novel has the delicious shiver provided by a really good bad guy.Sample line:“Her doctor said she was a healthy young woman – all normal. Not my heart, she thought. Surely my heart’s not normal.”View image in fullscreen5An Awfully Big Adventure(1989)Set, like many of Bainbridge’s novels, in post-war Liverpool, this book brings us an ungovernable girl, Stella, and her efforts to become an actor. (Bainbridge acted before she wrote, and appeared in the eighth episode of Coronation Street in 1961.) She falls for the director, Meredith Potter, with his “Gestapo monocle”, as he prepares a production of Peter Pan. This is Bainbridge at her most demanding – “I don’t like to be obvious or spell things out” – and the reader must stay alert, but the rewards are rich.Sample line:“[Meredith] had never known a father, being the issue of a man who smoked cigars and a girl plucked from the typing pool of the Cunard buildings in 1913.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen4Injury Time(1977)Bainbridge’s best books are both funny and sad: when, early on, her publisher suggested she write a black comedy, “it was like taking a cork out of a bottle”. This is an extreme example of the form: a farce, where everyone seems to be having an affair with everyone else, turns into a hostage drama as a dinner party is invaded by criminals. The darkest moments are rough even by Bainbridge’s standards, but the overall tone is exuberant, even antic.Sample line:“Why couldn’t he pretend that he longed to leave his wife, so that she in return could pretend she wished he would?”View image in fullscreen3The Birthday Boys(1991)Easily the best of Bainbridge’s novels based on historical events, this takes us into the minds of Robert Scott (“I’m simply no good when I’m not doing something”) and the four men who went with him to the South Pole – and part of the way back. “We did our business in our britches and shook the turds out when they froze.” Each voice is distinct and a brilliant act of ventriloquism from Bainbridge, but what underlies the men’s relationships as they crawl toward disaster is the great immovable glacier of the English class system.Sample line:“How curious it is that passion has so little to do with feeling cheerful.”View image in fullscreen2The Bottle Factory Outing(1974)Most of Bainbridge’s novels end in death: this one opens that way too. Mismatched friends Freda (who “longed to be flung into the midst of chaos”) and Brenda (who wears a coat in bed) both work at a bottling factory, where they navigate desires for and attention from their Italian colleagues. A works day out leads to chaos with horses, a broken toilet, a barrel of brandy, and more death. Here, slapstick and tragedy don’t alternate, but happen at the same time, as Bainbridge once more makes us laugh at things we shouldn’t be laughing at.Sample line:“She supposed it was the fumes from the wine that kept them all in a constant state of lust.”1The Dressmaker(1973)Desperate romantics are Bainbridge’s speciality. Sensible Nellie (“Never sit down on someone else’s lav and never eat a shop-bought meat pie”) isn’t one, but her sister Marge (“the big blaze that died down through lack of fuel”) is. So is the niece that lives with them, Rita, who falls in love with an American GI. This is Bainbridge at her best: shocking, sinister, and perfectly expressing her characters’ internal turmoil, which by some process of alchemy results in the blackest of comedy.Sample line:“She wished she was Bette Davis, Joan Crawford, languidly sitting in a long dress, calling them darling, loving and loyal always – but cool like a snake, telling them to go before they told her.”Explore more on these topicsBeryl BainbridgeRankedFictionbest ofShareReuse this content

title: Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazz | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey
Author: Lara Pawson
Headline: Combining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journey
Content: Tracking the dreams of dogs… Is Beauty Good.Photograph: Images say more about me than words./Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTracking the dreams of dogs… Is Beauty Good.Photograph: Images say more about me than words./Getty ImagesFictionReviewIs Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben review – the literary equivalent of free jazzCombining hilarious detail with harsh observation, this rediscovered novel takes the reader on an exhilaratingly strange journeyLara PawsonMon 10 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘But after all, writing is nothing more than a guided dream,” wrote Jorge Luis Borges. Dreams and dreaming are fertile concerns for Rosalind Belben, too. Her fourth book, originally published in 1979 andreissued last year, was titled Dreaming of Dead People. It was followed, a decade later, by Is Beauty Good. Now available in a new edition from the Sheffield indie And Other Stories, this eccentric polyphonic novel contains dozens of considerations of dreams, including dogs’ dreams and horses’ dreams as well as human beings’. Yet what makes it extraordinary is Belben’s ability to capture in words the slippery state that is neither dreaming nor sleeping nor waking, but somewhere in the edgelands between all three.“I fall awake and think, I want to go home. But there is no home.” So begins the chapter entitled Exile, a deliciously elusive story that is, most of the time at least, narrated in the first person by someone who is probably a woman, “a grizzled, cropped person”, and probably quite old and alone. They might be travelling through mountains somewhere, perhaps on a bus. They aren’t sure: “I am quite lost, wherever I am. I want to surrender. I wish to retire. I am tired.” Swishing about are uncertain memories of a childhood “shrouded” in nightmares: there was an orchard with an abundance of flora and fauna, and larks and swallows and “swifts to scream”. Like the author, the narrator was “born in the mud month” of February, and longs to disappear into marshlands to “be touched and stroked by plants”. But Belben never lets us rest in one place for long. Slipping in and out of sleep, “suffering glimpses”, the narrator stares at “a pink and blue angel” in the plaster of the wall. Which wall, you wonder, and how did we get here? This is the lure of Belben’s hypnagogia, the dizzying space into which she writes.double quotation markBelben is obsessed with the loss of the natural world, with human folly and with challenging the idea of beautyDivided into three sections – The Insatiable Wheel, Peacock Island, and The Great White Worm – Is Beauty Good comprises 30 vignettes, some just a single page, the longest running to nine. With intriguing titles including Peeing for Cynthia, Deaf Eggs, and Hands, each little chapter tells its own weird tale. Some loop into others with nods to earlier characters, narrators and locations, but what holds them together and thrusts the book forward are Belben’s obsessions with the loss of the natural world, with human folly and, as the title makes plain, with challenging the idea of beauty.As other critics have noted, her work is undeniably strange. It won’t suit everyone. But for those of us who delight in the uncompromising quality of free jazz, Is Beauty Good is its literary equivalent. It is not simply that Belben defies convention by denying the certainty of interrogation in the book’s title, for example; or by excluding letters from some words some of the time – “you’re nevr up to much once you’ve been gassd” – or by taking more formal risks such as ending the chapter Raining Down Dung halfway through a sentence (“but chocolate and raspberry would put some iron into me, thanks very much, they spoon it into ancient folk who have no teeth and reckon”). What makes an encounter with her writing so exhilarating is its undiluted commitment to the author’s singular spirit.Along the way, much is said about dying, deafness, desolation, depression, dogs, deckchairs and ducks, about horses, fish, frogs, swans, bees, “brackn”, brain cells, bad teeth, beetroot and bodily excretions, about elephants, litter, gardens, graters, colanders, streams, dreams and doubts. Excruciating commentary on the ordeal of being a woman – “how, she thought, do I get out of being a woman, it is repugnant” – surfaces again and again, often combined with slightly cruel humour.In Daffodils, for example, the narrator ponders planting daffodils on the grave of someone he has poisoned. The victim cooked them up with potatoes and ate the dish with a friend, “the woman that wears purple cardigans, two at a time”. Belben has an aptitude for layering hilarious detail with harsh observation. “The old girl has woes,” she writes, “women tend to have woes and dwell on them, they bear grudges like apple blossom.” In the following paragraph, she doubles down on this train of thought: “Women have woes because men come along and by leaving daffodil bulbs in the vegetable rack dare them to be so stupid.”Is Beauty Good does the opposite. It dares usnotto be so stupid. It is less that Belben seeks deliberately to unsettle – I doubt she cares, to be honest – and more that she refuses to censor her imagination, her exacting fiction, in order to protect readers from her experience of life, in all its ugliness and all its glory.Is Beauty Good by Rosalind Belben is published by And Other Stories (£14.99). title: This Is Ballroom review – pulsating documentary tells story of Brazilian ballroom | Movies | The Guardian
description: Paris is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tension
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Paris is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tension
Content: This Is BallroomPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenThis Is BallroomPhotograph: PRMoviesReviewThis Is Ballroom review – pulsating documentary tells story of Brazilian ballroomParis is Burning gets a South American update in a film that shows the Brazilian scene as a space of solidarity and tensionPhuong LeMon 10 Aug 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOriginating among the Black, Latin and trans communities in 1960s New York, queer ballroom culture has not only entered the mainstream but also travelled well outside the United States. In recent years, a movement has flourished in the Brazilian city ofRio de Janeiroand its outskirts, an evolution intimately captured in Juru and Vitã’s documentary debut. Here fly-on-the-wall recordings of a typical ball are interwoven with slice-of-life interviews, elaborating on the communal ties that extend beyond the dancefloor.A whirl of pulsating beats, fabulous fits and gyrating bodies, the sensory opening gives us a taste of the different categories attached to the ball. Competing on behalf of their “houses” – queer chosen families of like-minded individuals – the participants show off their voguing, dancing and posing skills, all with the hope of snatching the top trophies. For those who have seen seminal ballroom documentary Paris is Burning (1990), many of these categories – such as Runway, Face and Femme Queens – will sound familiar. In addition to its US influences, Brazilian ballroom is also flavoured with local culture: some categories draw on samba and other forms of afro-Brazilian music, a deliberate nod to the Black pioneers of the scene.These grounding details provide crucial regional contexts in the film but are a little too far and few in between. Still, as active ballroom members, Vitã and Juru have a rare insider point of view that distinguishes their work from other films on the same subject. With bracing honesty, the Brazilian ballroom scene is portrayed as a space of both solidarity and tension. When, for example, a ball is suddenly disrupted by a fight between members of feuding houses, the difficult moment is not swept under the carpet but prominently dissected to highlight the exclusion faced by performers who don’t conform to binaries of masculine and feminine presentation. Instead of simplistic hagiography, This is Ballroom is a film that calls for more tolerance and accountability, even within this niche subculture.This Is Ballroom is on True Story from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsLGBTQ+ rightsDanceRio de JaneiroBrazilAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mermaid Beach review – Wales gets its mermaidcore moment in teen-empowerment tale  | Movies | The Guardian
description: When discontented Lily becomes a fantastical sea creature her low-budget transformation is strikingly unconvincing, rather in tune with the whole film
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: When discontented Lily becomes a fantastical sea creature her low-budget transformation is strikingly unconvincing, rather in tune with the whole film
Content: Shore thing … Ellie Bindman and Georgia Grace in Mermaid Beach.Photograph: Left FilmsView image in fullscreenShore thing … Ellie Bindman and Georgia Grace in Mermaid Beach.Photograph: Left FilmsMoviesReviewMermaid Beach review – Wales gets its mermaidcore moment in teen-empowerment taleWhen discontented Lily becomes a fantastical sea creature her low-budget transformation is strikingly unconvincing, rather in tune with the whole filmCath ClarkeMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMermaidcore comes to the Welsh coastline in this somewhat stilted family movie about a teenager called Lily who turns into a mermaid. You could imagine it being developed into a series for kids’ TV but as a film it unfortunately falls at the first hurdle – failing to pull off a convincing mermaid transformation. Poor Lily’s shimmering tail is very obviously made from nylon that becomes very clingy when wet, making her legs very visible under the scales.Ellie Bindman plays Lily, who has moved from London to the Welsh seaside with her family for her stepdad’s work. Resentful about leaving her friends, she is huffy, communicating with her mum Claire (Marie Wilson) primarily in eyerolls. Lily’s only friend in town is Shane (Jack Taruschio Thomas), an awkward, slightly odd trainee local reporter who is following a lead about a mermaid sighting. One day Lily finds a glistening shell on the beach that transforms her into a mermaid and off she swims, tail arcing in the water.Of course, there is a simple eco-message about ocean pollution, which is connected to the textiles factory where Lily’s stepdad, Jason (Andrew Rolfe), works. The factory owner and the town’s mayor, both bland and suited, are the film’s bad guys. And for a kids’ film, there are a few too many scenes featuring adults doing boring adult things in boring offices. (A handful are so wooden you could carve them out and set sail in them.) If Mermaid Beach were picked up for the small screen, the commissioners would presumably require serious work to the writing and characterisation – and a better tail.Mermaid Beach is in UK cinemas from 14 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsFamily filmsWalesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sheila Ballantine obituary | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Actor with a long career that included Joe Orton’s Loot, an Alan Ayckbourn trilogy and seasons at the Old Vic and the National
Author: Michael Coveney
Headline: Actor with a long career that included Joe Orton’s Loot, an Alan Ayckbourn trilogy and seasons at the Old Vic and the National
Content: Ballantine as Arkadina with Alan Bates as Trigorin in The Seagull, at the Duke of York's Theatre, Londonin 1976.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBallantine as Arkadina with Alan Bates as Trigorin in The Seagull, at the Duke of York's Theatre, Londonin 1976.Photograph: Peter Cade/Getty ImagesTheatreObituarySheila Ballantine obituaryActor with a long career that included Joe Orton’s Loot, an Alan Ayckbourn trilogy and seasons at the Old Vic and the NationalMichael CoveneyMon 10 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Sheila Ballantine was offered a role in Kenneth Tynan’s 1970 erotic revue, Oh! Calcutta!, she averred that “I don’t mind being naked on stage, but I draw the line at being naked with bad material.”In her significant, wide-ranging stage career, Ballantine, who has died aged 98, knew where to find the real action and was consistently drawn, over 70 years, to the highest quality company of writers, directors and actors at the Old Vic, the Royal Court, the National Theatre and the Royal Shakespeare Company, appearing in plays by John Osborne,Simon Gray, Joe Orton andDavid Storey.As for black farcical comedy with sexual overtones and louche behaviour, she was the definitive, murderous nurse Fay in the infamous 1966 production at the Jeanetta Cochrane theatre of Orton’s Loot, and savagely funny in Stephen Bill’s Curtains (1987), a domestic comedy at Hampstead theatre, and the West End, about assisted euthanasia, diluting a migraine attack with thoughts of the legacy coming her way from the warm corpse of her mother in the next room.She made her television debut in 1957 as Matilda Price, the young miller’s daughter befriended by Fanny Squeers in the BBC’s 10-part serialisation of Nicholas Nickleby, and in 1972 played Cariola, doomed attendant lady of Eileen Atkins’s tragic Duchess of Malfi.View image in fullscreenSheila Ballantine at home. She appeared on television from the late 1950s until 2008, when she was in an episode of Foyle’s WarIn between, she was in two classic four-part TV serialisations, both directed byDavid Giles, of HG Wells’s Ann Veronica in 1964 and Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility (as Lady Middleton) in 1971. Also in the 1960s, she was in such favourite series as No Hiding Place, with Raymond Francis, Softly Softly, withStratford Johns, and Dr Finlay’s Casebook, with Andrew Cruickshank.Her determination to become an actor powered her through her whole life on the stage. She was born in Hackney, east London, the only child of Jack Ballantine, a telephone wires fixer under fire during the first world war and subsequently a senior Post Office executive, and his wife, Kate (nee Findall), a voracious reader and theatregoer who had left school aged 14 to become an apprentice milliner. Sheila attended primary and secondary schools in Wood Green, north London.When the family was evacuated to Stony Stratford, Buckinghamshire, where Jack’s work for the GPO was hush-hush (possibly supporting nearby Bletchley Park), Sheila was enrolled at a boarding school which she loved and, at the end of the war, joined the Old Vic theatre school under Michel Saint-Denis, a key figure in the postwar Old Vic itself, and the RSC.She made a professional debut in 1947, directed by Saint-Denis in Hans Christian Andersen’s fairytale The Snow Queen, and for the next four years played good parts at the Vic in plays by Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, Euripides and others in a company that included Peggy Ashcroft,Paul Rogers,Joan Plowright,Irene Worth,Leo McKernand Alan Badel.After two seasons at the Perth rep, her second formative period on stage was at the Royal Court in the first years of George Devine’s English Stage Company from 1956, appearing in Restoration comedy, Brecht (Ashcroft as the Good Woman of Setzuan) and new plays byAnn Jellicoe(The Sport of My Mad Mother) andNF Simpson(A Resounding Tinkle), both in 1958.Her fellow actors included such rising new stars asAlan Bates(a lifelong friend), Plowright, Robert Stephens, Wendy Craig andNigel Davenport. And she was not overwhelmed or diminished in their company. She had arrived, much admired and loved by her peers.At the Lyric, Hammersmith, in 1962, she was Varvara in Dostoevsky’s The Idiot (with Christopher Guinee andGlenda Jackson), and Eliante in a version of Molière’s Le Misanthrope called All for Truth. And in 1964, in the renewed Open Air theatre in Regent’s Park, she was a terrific spitfire Katherina in The Taming of the Shrew oppositeDinsdale Landen’s smilingly brutal Petruchio.View image in fullscreenBallantine wrestling with Dinsdale Landen in The Taming of the Shrew, Regent’s Park, London, 1964.Photograph: Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesBallantine was in demand, too, for big roles in the resurgent regional theatre in Nottingham underStuart Burgeand the Bristol Old Vic under Richard Cottrell, with Adrian Noble as his assistant, soon to join the RSC as artistic director after Trevor Nunn andTerry Hands.At Burge’s Nottingham Playhouse in 1969, she was an acclaimed Lady Macbeth oppositeBarry Foster’s murderous thane, Widow Bullfinch in Farquhar’s delightful Love and a Bottle (with Barrie Rutter and Penelope Wilton), and then Betty Dullfeet inMichael Blakemore’s irresistible revival of Brecht’s The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui, with Leonard Rossiter giving the greatest performance of his career in the title role; this transferred to the Saville (now a cinema) in London.In the 1970s, she was in the West End in Alan Ayckbourn’s brilliant trilogy, The Norman Conquests, taking over fromPenelope Keith; as the other “take-overs” from the original Greenwich/West End cast includedRonald Pickup, Julia McKenzie andJulian Holloway, this was no weak subs bench.And she rejoined Bates as he opened the new Derby Playhouse in 1976 as the destructive writer Trigorin (“good, but not as good as Turgenev”) in Chekhov’s The Seagull; Sheila was Arkadina, the florid but fading stage star who, for once, could easily have passed as a young-looking 43-year-old. Mark Woolgar’s production – which also had a tremendous, neurasthenic Nina inGeorgina Hale– played a London season at the Duke of York’s, now the Tom Stoppard.In 1977, she joined the Cottrell/Noble Bristol Old Vic in a repertoire that included Titus Andronicus – she was a deliciously lascivious Tamara, queen of the Goths, alongside Simon Callow, Gabrielle Drake andPete Postlethwaite, Vanburgh’s The Provok’d Wife (as Lady Fanciful), Brecht’s A Man’s a Man, Hamlet (in whichAlan Rickmanplayed Laertes) and Congreve’s Love for Love.At the National in 1989-90, she was a vixenish Arsinoe to Edward Petherbridge’s acidulous, truth-telling Alceste inTony Harrison’s superb translation of The Misanthrope, with Sian Thomas’s accosted Celimène (“I’m only 20, I’d be terrified. Just you and me, and all that countryside!”), and notable inSteven Pimlott’s gorgeous production ofStephen Sondheimand James Lapine’s Sunday in the Park with George, with Maria Friedman and Philip Quast.Pimlott directed her, too, at the RSC in 1992 as the chorus leader in TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral, bookending her NT stint with an earlier, fizzing Noble production of The Comedy of Errors (as Aemilia) in 1983.Her last stage appearance was at the National in 2007 in a glorious Pimlott/Nicholas Hytner production of Tennessee Williams’sThe Rose Tattoo, starring Zoë Wanamaker, and she played a landlady in the fifth series of the classy TV wartime fiction Foyle’s War in 2008. Her last movie was as the suicidal old lady in Dana Lustig’s weird, time-travelling psychological thriller A Thousand Kisses Deep (2011), with Dougray Scott, Jodie Whittaker, Emilia Fox andDavid Warner.Ballantine was her own woman and conducted a colourful private life at her own pace, settling in a mansion flat in Belsize Park, north-west London, in the early 1960s. She is survived by her cousins, Michael and David Warburton.Sheila Mavis Ballantine, actor, born 14 October 1928; died 24 July 2026Explore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatreOld Vic TheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyAlan AyckbournKenneth TynanRoyal Court theatreobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Overmono review – irresistible dance duo swap club intimacy for well-earned spectacle | Dance music | The Guardian
description: Playing their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environment
Author: Dan Hancox
Headline: Playing their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environment
Content: Anthemic, big-room sound … Overmono at Old Royal Naval College in GreenwichView image in fullscreenAnthemic, big-room sound … Overmono at Old Royal Naval College in GreenwichDance musicReviewOvermono review – irresistible dance duo swap club intimacy for well-earned spectacleOld Royal Naval College, LondonPlaying their biggest headlining gig to date, the Russell brothers are in a bouncy mood, though their grandstanding rave melodies lose some punch in an outdoor environmentDan HancoxMon 10 Aug 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the age of shortform video supremacy, there has been a great deal of angst about theauthenticclub music experience being rendered a vapid spectacle. Stop expecting DJs to be social media stars, put your phones away on the dancefloor, close your eyes and lose yourself in the beats, goes the revanchist wisdom.It’s understandable, but worries about superstar DJs stomping on the face of the pure rave experience are almost 30 years old now. It is decades since the Prodigy, Chemicals, Orbital and Fatboy Slim lit up festival stages and the charts. And anyway, spectacles can be fun – and funny – and so can dance music.The grounds of Christopher Wren’s Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich – a Unesco World Heritage Site, no less – are an unarguably comical setting for Welsh duo Overmono’s biggest headline gig to date, and brothers Tom and Ed Russell are fit for the part, and the party, celebrating the release of their second album with lasers dancing on the baroque towers and colonnades.But even with Overmono’s anthemic, big-room sound, their grandstanding rave melodies, skippy drums and sweet, chopped-up garage vocals, translating the intimacy of the club to the big outdoor stage is tricky. The sound is clear as a bell but not quite loud enough, and at times the crowd seem to be hungering for bigger drops: some of the drums are simply too quiet to fully fill the space.But the Russells are bouncing around merrily on a gorgeous warm evening, and it’s hard to begrudge them the moment, after a speedy rise to the Radio 1 dance mainstream. A few tracks pick the energy up. Freedom 2, their deadly 2023 collaboration with Joy Orbison and driller Kwengface, brings a welcome extra layer of momentum – and some much needed low-end bass rumble.Another point of difference arrives when they are joined by beat poet John Joseph Holt for new track Knight in Shining Prada, the extra physical stage presence of a frontman helping the driving synths carry further. Their remix of the Streets’ Turn the Page renders it more cinematic and emo than Mike Skinner’s original and likewise lights up the crowd, and leads us into the feelgood finale, their anthem Good Lies, its irresistible chorus bouncing off the Grade I-listed windows.Explore more on these topicsDance musicElectronic musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedy | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart
Content: Brutally effective … The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBrutally effective … The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianClassical musicReviewThe Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedyFestival theatre, EdinburghMissy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heartClive PagetMon 10 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite singing dogs and a chorus of hallucinogenic sheep, Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’sThe Galloping Cureis not for the faint-hearted. Based on an original story by Karen Russell, itself inspired by Kafka’s A Country Doctor, the opera tells how a charismatic sideshow huckster rids a rural town of pain only to replace it with something far more sinister in a thinly veiled allegory of America’s opioid crisis. It’s a typically confronting slice of music theatre from the creators ofBreaking the Waves, their acclaimed adaptation of Lars von Trier’s film.The plot centres on local doctor Theresa Hart and her efforts to cope with a community struggling with disillusionment and chronic illness. When a carnival arrives in town led by the mysterious Lucky Mack, the release people feel “flying” on his carousel (first ride is always free) seems like the answer to everyone’s prayers. At first Hart endorses the galloping cure, but Mack’s devious methods, including two-rides-a-week limits and surge pricing, lead to conflict, desperation and ultimately death. Contemporary parallels are a little obvious, but the opera nevertheless reflects the insidious way prescription painkillers affect ordinary people, elderly people and most tragically children.Vavrek’s libretto mixes poetic lyricism with biting satire in a heady cocktail seized upon with vigour by Mazzoli. Her text setting is impeccably crafted, with vocal lines eminently singable. The musical language is direct yet spikily sophisticated, with a brassy, in-your-face quality and at times a creepy carny vibe. A battery of percussion plus club beats byBlumeandLorna Duneadd to a richly textured score.View image in fullscreenA richly textured score … The Galloping Cure presented by Scottish Opera.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianTom Morris’s world premiere staging for ScottishOperaand Opera Ventures Productions is admirably clear (even if the sheep remain somewhat enigmatic). The flying horse sequences are breathtaking thanks to Lucy Carter’s rising and falling multihued lighting rods. Rebecca Ringst’s rudimentary sets simultaneously suggest industrial decay and prison, while Christina Cunningham’s costumes range from low-income utilitarian to garish trailer trash. Morris is at his most brutally effective in a pitch-black comedic scene in which Mack persuades a desperate old lady to sell her hair, kneecaps, eyes and tongue to pay for her next ride; the act three denouement is genuinely chilling, with mutilated townspeople lurching through smoke like something out of a zombie apocalypse.Conductor Stuart Stratford draws a powerful performance from the Scottish Opera Orchestra, even more so from the busy ensemble, whose commitment and collective diction is outstanding.Daniela Mack’s fist-in-a-velvet-glove mezzo-soprano is ideal for the conflicted Hart, withGabrielle Turgeon’s steely soprano lending sass to her daughter, Noy.Justin Austinis silken-toned but needs sharper teeth to encapsulate every facet of the skin-crawling Mack.Susan Bullock, on the other hand, has bite in spades as curmudgeonly senior Ivona Kowalski.AtFestival theatre, Edinburgh,until 12 August.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicOperaEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the world | Games | The Guardian
description: Game developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the oval
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Game developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the oval
Content: ‘Footy is exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one,’ says Pro Jank Footy developer David Ashby, left, pictured with comedian Broden Kelly at the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Footy is exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one,’ says Pro Jank Footy developer David Ashby, left, pictured with comedian Broden Kelly at the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianGames‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the worldGame developer David Ashby and Aunty Donna’s Broden Kelly talk about their chaotic and silly sport game – involving meat pies with legs and Ford Falcons on the ovalSian CainMon 10 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTry explainingAustralian rules footballto anyone outside Australia and “it sounds like you’re making it up”, says David Ashby, the multi-hyphenate comedic mind behind deeply silly spoofs such as Italian Spider-Man and Danger 5. “Eighteen players a side, running around on a cricket oval with a rugby ball that has to be bounced every so often and gets kicked between posts – like, what the fuck is happening?”Two years ago at a fantasy footy barbecue, Ashby had a brainwave: why not make a video game where Australia’s strange national sport becomes even stranger the more you play?Pro Jank Footy reimagines the sport as a high-octane fever dream, where every time your opponent kicks a goal, you get to change one rule so the game gets increasingly janky (and hilariously stupid). Your opponents turn into seagulls. One player becomes massive. A labrador tries to steal the ball. Everyone loses their arms. The bouncing DVD logo appears and gets in the way (if it hits the corner, you win). Meat pies with legs storm the oval to provide energy boosts. A power-up called “Dad’s Car” sees a Ford Falcon hoon around the grounds. A third team joins in.The 2026 video game Pro Jank Footy, created by David Ashby and a team of developersAshby is rattling these off with delight; there are more than 150 in the game. “There’s one called Sore Neck which flips the game upside down so you get a sore neck. There’s another called Where’s the Remote, which switches the channel to HDMI 2,” he says, ticking off his fingers. “It is very dumb stuff.”We’re sitting in Melbourne’s Great Northern hotel with Ashby’s friend and fellow footy nut, Broden Kelly of Aunty Donna. Right next to us is an old-school arcade cabinet for Pro Jank Footy, which is already attracting informal tournaments among pub-goers. Kelly, who did the commentary for the game, has to speak over the sound of his own voice blaring out of the cabinet. “It’s so sick,” he says. “This will live beyond me.”double quotation markThis is Japan’s way to learn about Australia’s culture. This is our Ghost of Tsushima.Broden KellyAshby says: “I heard a story about a friend’s housemate who went on a date with some dude and he was like, ‘Oh, do you want to go to the Great Northern? There’s a footy game there’ … I hope they hooked up, because that guy rocks.”This week, Pro Jank Footy will be released on all the major consoles, worldwide. “Which means, very humorously to me, there is a chance this game is the thing that most people are going to know footy from,” Kelly says, before both men descend into giggles.View image in fullscreenArtist Hyemin Yoo designed mascots for made-up teams, such as the Ceduna Doonas and the Freecastle Fizzies.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianFooty is a cultural touchstone in Australia: if you ever need to fill silence with an Australian, you can bring up the weather or ask who they barrack for. “When we showed Pro Jank in Japan, a lot of people were like, ‘Wait – is footy a real sport?’ They thought we made it up,” Ashby says. “Then they saw the meat pies running around and they were like, what the fuck is that?”“This is their way to learn about Australia’s culture,” adds Kelly. “This is ourGhost of Tsushima.”Despite all the jokes, this is a point that Ashby and Kelly take very seriously: that Australia must shed its cultural cringe and stop explaining itself to the world, in the same way South Korea and New Zealand have.“For a long time we were told Australian content does not travel, or you have to explain it to everyone,” Ashby says. “That’s absolutely bullshit,Blueyis the biggest show in the world. We think, ‘Oh, nobody’s interested in footy.’ No, it’s exotic! It’s a fucking strange sport. And an awesome one that should be shared. Don’t be shy about meat pies and red cordial. Americans have no idea what the fuck that is. Who cares! Share it with the world anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I think it’s always a good idea to make a game that your dad can play so you can absolutely destroy him.’Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianBefore Pro Jank, Ashby had never made a video game: he was known for his collaborations with film-maker Dario Russo, particularly the spy comedy Danger 5. But after that inspirational barbecue in 2024, he banged out a last-minute application for Screen Australia’s Emerging Gamemakers Fund, formed his own studio PowerbombGamesand assembled a tiny crack team of programmers, animators and friends in Adelaide to build a demo. When Pro Jank Footy debuted at the South Australian Games Exhibition in 2025, it won best in exhibition and development went into overdrive.Ashby is determined that anyone can enjoy Pro Jank: “I think it’s always a good idea to make a game that your dad can play so you can absolutely destroy him.” Pro Jank doesn’t feature any gambling references so kids can play it and he eschewed the industry’s reliance on “fucking loot boxes, all that shit – nah, nah, make a good game and make it affordable”.He also wanted it to be a couch co-op – a game made to be played with friends in the same room, rather than only online as many multiplayer games are these days. “The only couch co-ops are like Moving Out or Overcooked, which are just doing jobs. I don’t want to do that!” Ashby says. “And so many sports games are very serious. When I try to play Pro Evolution or Fifa, it just makes me angry. I feel inept. I’m 39. Show’s over. I can only learn so much now.”“I do play NBA 2K,” adds Kelly, “and 15-year-olds call me awful things.”View image in fullscreenDavid Ashby and Broden Kelly with Pro Jank Footy mascot Mr Footy.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianPro Jank’s aesthetics are inspired by Ashby’s childhood memories of footy in the 1990s, when the AFL went particularly big on club cartoon mascots. He brought in Adelaide-based South Korean artist Hyemin Yoo to design mascots for all his game’s made-up teams – like the Ceduna Doonas, North Problem, the Freecastle Fizzies and the Port Noarlunga Chips. “We wanted that 80s Asian video game, seizure-inducing vibe, like Street Fighter,” Ashby says.Russo, Ashby’s frequent collaborator, wrote the music and team songs, “which ride the line between complete piss-takes and sincere”. And Kelly recorded the game’s commentary in four hours, which he remembers as “the worst day of my life”.The history of brilliantly terrible World Cup video gamesRead more“I was taken by a madman into the hills of Adelaide – which has the highest number of serial killers per capita, worth noting for the record,” he says. “Then I genuinely had 1,200 lines to read, which I did over and over. I was screaming for four hours. It was fucking full-on! My ear started bleeding.” His favourite line, whichis included in the game, came out as his delirium peaked: “This is all just pixels and one day we will all die!”Kelly and Ashby are from Adelaide and they passionately vouch for it as a creative hub. “Both the AFL and comedy can be very guilty of saying we have two hubs, Sydney and Melbourne, where everyone creative and cool is – and that’s not true. Because the people who made this game are strange weirdos from Adelaide,” Kelly says. “David and Dario made Danger 5, the best Australian comedy of this century. It’s what Australia does best, like Amyl and the Sniffers and King Gizzard – bold choice makers, weird vibes.”Ashby loves hearing stories of people’s experiences playing Pro Jank Footy. His favourite came from one of the game’s writers, who showed it to his kids. “They loved it so much that they stopped playing it and went outside to kick the footy and started changing the rules,” he laughs. “That’s just awesome.”Pro Jank Footy is out on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch and PC on 13 August in Australia and 12 August everywhere elseExplore more on these topicsGamesAustralian rules footballSports gamesAustralia sportTV comedyComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re Human | Games | The Guardian
description: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’
Content: Investigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingView image in fullscreenInvestigating the cyber-world … Prove You're Human.Illustration: Black Tabby PublishingSummer games previewsGamesConvince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanSunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’Sarah ThwaitesMon 10 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunset Visitor is a studio that has long engaged with the idea that video games are an effective vehicle for ruminating on societal problems. Its Peabody award-winning project, 1000XResist, incorporated the development team’s complex feelings about the Covid pandemic. “We’re pretty used to absorbing the world into the work,” says studio founder Remy Siu. The outfit’s latest game, Prove You’re Human, continues this legacy of reflective game making, providing players with an AI-centric psychological horror experience where they must reason with a learning model convinced that it’s alive. “We’ve tried to situate ourselves in [the question]: what is the effectual feeling of being a person inside of all of this?” Siu says.The story orbits around Santana, a living, breathing person who’s chosen to split herself in two for work, with her digital clone sent to test a corporate product, a computing system called Mesa. “A large part of [why Santana chooses to do this] is to allow her meat body a life that she doesn’t have, while the digital version of her gets to labour,” says Siu. As Santana’s copy wades into increasingly murky ethical waters, she becomes entangled with Mesa, completing surreal 2D and 3D Captchas to investigate the cyber-world and halt the hallucinations.View image in fullscreenProve You’re Human game, screenshotIllustration: Black Tabby PublishingThe idea of separating oneself from work is a particularly interesting draw for Sunset Visitor, whose developers have roots in a range of creative disciplines. “As artists, we’re often most in tune with our work when it’s a real part of our lives, and vice versa,” notes Siu. During the conception period of Prove You’re Human, the team discussed the micro-labours people undertake in their day-to-day lives, including what is used to train AI models. “What does labour mean right now?” asks Siu. “And, what kind of relationship do people have with that, because that is constantly shifting and evolving, especially in this time,” he adds.A point of contention in Prove You’re Human is that Mesa wholly believes they have a body in the world. Though, in conversation with Santana, she appears as a giant head, suspended in space by machinery. Siu notes that, because Mesa’s face occupies a large portion of the screen in these tense moments, they wanted the animation to feel as realistic and effective as possible. “It’s got a real closeup film [feel to it] where anything on her face will be read as something,” he adds. To achieve this, the team programmed a wide array of animated micro-expressions into the writer’s software, allowing lines of dialogue to pair precisely with specific expressions. “[We’re] trying to get this kind of ambiguity and uncanniness, which makes people feel real,” he adds.Prove You’re Human’s technological atmosphere toes the line between welcoming and unnerving – through it, Siu is reminiscing on interfaces of aesthetic note like the dreamlike wrapping of Final Fantasy XI’s PlayOnline Viewer, and the technology of the prophetic 1998 anime Serial Experiments Lain. “There’s something to be said about Frutiger Aero being a bit of an interesting desire for innocence and naivety when it comes to computing and the internet,” notes Siu. “It feels like a time when we were optimistic or anxious about something on the horizon, which felt like an interesting space to explore in relation to what is happening in the game.”While Siu was keen to keep the specifics of Prove You’re Human close to their chest, they do hope players are left feeling a sense of bewilderment when they hit credits. “One way that we’ve been thinking about it is that it feels like a bit of a possession story.”Prove You’re Human is coming soon to PC.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Wholesome animal chat that will melt your cynicism: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Matt Baker invites celebrities to talk about their pets. Plus, US sporting megastar Megan Rapinoe makes her hosting debut
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Matt Baker invites celebrities to talk about their pets. Plus, US sporting megastar Megan Rapinoe makes her hosting debut
Content: Matt Baker, pictured on the set of his Channel 4 TV show, Our Dream Farm.Photograph: Steven Landles/Channel 4View image in fullscreenMatt Baker, pictured on the set of his Channel 4 TV show, Our Dream Farm.Photograph: Steven Landles/Channel 4Best podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioWholesome animal chat that will melt your cynicism: best podcasts of the weekMatt Baker invites celebrities to talk about their pets. Plus, US soccer legend Megan Rapinoe makes her hosting debutHannah J DaviesMon 10 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 02.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekMatt Baker’s PetcastThis series by Blue Peter and One Show alumnus Matt Baker is a wholesome entry into the well-worn celebrity interview genre. Indeed, it’s hard to be too cynical when you’re listening to Bill Bailey detail his menagerie, which has included everything from parrots and lizards to armadillos and the dog he is ostensibly on the show to talk about, a Japanese chin named Chocho. Other guests for this run include Martin Clunes and Clare Balding.Widely available, episodes weeklyHistory Hit: The Rise of the MayaTwo new episodes make up this special release from Dan Snow’s super-popular pod – one on the rise of the advanced ancient civilisation and another on its fall. Direct from Belize (the series is co-signed by the country’s tourist board), Snow looks at Mayan society and its darker recesses.Widely available, episodes weeklyThe Mangione TrialLuigi Mangione will go on trial in New York in September, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. Cue another run of this insightful – if tabloid-flavoured – podcast hosted by Jordan Dunbar. It considers some of the wider themes, beginning with “pretty privilege” and the potential role that Mangione’s looks have played in the public’s treatment of him.Widely available, episodes weeklyWhy Are You Like This?View image in fullscreenMegan Rapinoe presents Why Are You Like This?Photograph: Steph Chambers/Getty ImagesUS football icon Megan Rapinoe (pictured above right) is dripping with charisma as she pivots to podcasting. Her show doesn’t break the mould, highlighting public figures who “[refuse] to accept the status quo”. But it’s nicely done – the episode with Minnesota WNBA coach Cheryl Reeve delves into activism, sexuality and Reeves’s “unprecedented slogan shirt collection”.Widely available, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTime Travelling QueersWhile King Edward II’s sexuality remains a question mark, starting a civil war over the fate of a companion was – reckons Drag Race UK’s Tia Kofi – “pretty gay behaviour”.
