title: Broth, tart and salad: Kirk Haworth’s vegan tomato recipes for summer | Food | The Guardian
description: A smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatin
Content: Karl Haworth’s tomato tarte tatin.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenKarl Haworth’s tomato tarte tatin.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.FoodBroth, tart and salad: Kirk Haworth’s vegan tomato recipes for summerA smoky tomato broth, a grilled peach, tomato and almond ‘ricotta’ salad scattered with roast almonds, and a sparky tomato tarte tatinKirk HaworthMon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAugust is peak tomato season. This most versatile of fruits can be put to just about any use, from raw to slow-cooked and from oven- or sun-dried to desserts (believe it or not, they go incredibly well with summer berries, especially strawberries and raspberries). Not only that, but tomatoes have high glutamate levels that rise even further as they ripen, which gives them an umami kick. However you prepare them, though, the key thing isneverto keep tomatoes in the fridge: the chill breaks down their cell structure and, even more importantly, affects their flavour in an alarming way.Tomato tarte tatin (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minCook45 minServes4500g cherry tomatoes20ml balsamic vinegar50ml extra-virgin olive oil10g maple syrupFlaky sea saltPlain flour, for dusting250g vegan puff pastry15g harissa10ml lemon juice½ tsp dijon mustard100g mixed salad leavesBasil leavesHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, and put the whole cherry tomatoes in a large bowl.In a small bowl, whisk the balsamic vinegar with 30ml of the oil, the maple syrup and a good pinch of salt, then pour over the tomatoes and toss to coat.Dust a work surface with flour, then roll out the pastry to a 30cm circle. Leaving a border all around the edge, spread out the harissa in a 24cm circle over the centre of the pastry.Spoon the tomatoes and their dressing into a 24cm oven-safe frying pan, lay the pastry harissa-side down on top, then tuck it in all around the edge of the tomatoes. Bake for half an hour, until the pastry is cooked through and golden.Once the pastry’s cooked, remove the pan and leave it to cool for a few minutes. Meanwhile, make a dressing by whisking the remaining extra-virgin oil with the lemon juice and mustard.To serve, carefully invert the tarte tatin on to a large plate or board. Dress the salad leaves and basil lightly, season with salt, and serve alongside.Barbecue tomato brothWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenKirk Hayworth’s barbecue tomato broth.Prep10 minCook1 hr 45 minServes41whole garlic head4 shallots, peeled and sliced (300g net)4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilSalt1kg cherry tomatoes½ tsp smoked paprika2 heaped tbsp white misopaste5g kombu(roughly 1 sheet)2 vegetable stock cubesHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Wrap the garlic bulb in foil and roast for 45-60 minutes, until soft (while you’re at it, and seeing as the oven’s on anyway, you might as well roast a few more, because you can never have too much roast garlic in the fridge). Remove, leave to cool, then squeeze out the flesh from the papery skins.Light the barbecue and, while it’s getting hot, put a large saucepan on a medium heat and gently sweat the shallots in the oil with a healthy pinch of salt for about 10 minutes, until soft but not coloured. Stir in the roast garlic flesh and paprika, and take off the heat.Barbecue the tomatoes on only one side until blackened, then tip them into the shallot pan. Stir in the miso and kombu, crumble in the stock cubes, then add three litres of water and bring to a boil. Turn down to a steady simmer and cook for about half an hour, until reduced by a third.Leave to cool, then pass through a sieve and season with more salt to taste. Serve chilled or reheat gently, and finish with a drizzle of good olive oil.Grilled peach, tomato, almond ‘ricotta’ and roast almond saladWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenKirk Hayworth’s grilled peach, acidulated tomato, almond ‘ricotta’ and roast almond salad.Prep10 minSoak4 hr+Cook30 minChill2 hr+Serves4For the almond ‘ricotta’200g blanched almonds, soaked for at least 4 hours and up to overnight30ml lemon juice, plus extra to tasteSaltFor the salad4ripe peachesNeutral oil, for grillingExtra-virgin olive oilFlaky sea salt50g blanched almonds300g mixed tomatoes1 tbsp sherry vinegar1 tbsp lemon juiceBasil leaves, to serveDrain and rinse the soaked almonds, then put them in the jug of a blender with 600ml cold water and blend smooth. Fine strain through muslin or a nut milk bag (or your thinnest tea towel at a pinch!), and really squeeze out as much liquid as you can. Pour the resulting nut milk into a saucepan, put it on a medium heat and slowly bring up to 85C, stirring occasionally. Once the milk is up to temperature, take the pan off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and leave to cool. Once cooled, strain the milk through a muslin-lined sieve into a bowl or container, cover and chill for at least two hours, and preferably overnight, during which time the “milk” will separate into curds and whey. Taste the almond “ricotta” and season with salt and a squeeze of lemon juice to taste.Light the barbecue or put a griddle pan on a high heat. Cut the peaches in half, remove and discard the stones, then cut each half in half again and brush the cut sides with neutral oil. Grill the peaches flesh-side down, flipping as necessary until all the flesh sides are nicely charred and slightly softened, then brush the flesh with extra-virgin olive oil and season with a pinch of sea salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, put the blanched almonds on a baking tray and roast for 10 minutes, giving them a shake halfway through. Remove, leave to cool, then roughly chop.Depending on the size of your tomatoes, cut them in half, quarters or leave them whole, and put them in a large bowl. In a small bowl, whisk the sherry vinegar, lemon juice and a tablespoon of olive oil until emulsified, then pour the dressing over the tomatoes.To serve, dot a few spoonfuls of almond ricotta across four plates, then arrange the peaches and tomatoes in between. Tear the basil over the top, scatter on the almonds and serve.Kirk Haworth is chef/owner ofPlates, London EC1Explore more on these topicsFoodTomatoesSummer food and drinkSaladVegan food and drinkVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for spiced sticky chicken with plums and pancakes | Chinese food and drink | The Guardian
description: A quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or rice
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or rice
Content: Georgina Hayden’s spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakes.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakes.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easyChinese food and drinkGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for spiced sticky chicken with plums and pancakesA quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or riceGeorgina HaydenMon 10 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a real aversion to the term “fakeaway”. I don’t know why. But as much as I resist the terminology, I guess it’s exactly what this dish is – it’s 100% based on and inspired by a Chinese takeaway classic: crispy duck pancakes. A real people pleaser, and something my girls adore. Making this with pan-fried chicken takes next to no time and is the perfect after-school/work quick dinner. And for a different ending, I sometimes serve the chicken and plum sauce over jasmine rice instead. With the same accompaniments, of course.Spiced sticky chicken, plums and pancakesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook35 minServes42 skinless chicken breasts(about 150g each)Sea salt1 tsp freshly ground white pepper1½ tsp Chinese five-spiceGroundnut oil10cmpiecefresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped3 plums, halved and stoned, flesh roughly chopped2 star anise3 tbsp soft dark brown sugar1 tbsp rice vinegar2 tbsp soy sauce1 bunchspring onions, trimmed and cut into 5cm strips½ cucumber, trimmed and cut into matchsticks12 Chinese-style pancakesPut the chicken breasts in a bowl and add some sea salt, the white pepper and Chinese five-spice. Add a drizzle of groundnut oil and toss to coat.Put a medium frying pan on a medium-high heat and add a little more oil. Lay in the chicken breasts, scraping any of the marinade from the bowl on to the meat, too, and cook for about eight minutes, until the chicken is charred. Flip over the meat and cook for another six to eight minutes, until cooked through and gnarly. Transfer the chicken to a plate to rest.Meanwhile, wipe the pan clean and put it back on the hob on a medium heat. Add two tablespoons of groundnut oil and the chopped ginger, and fry for a minute. Add the chopped plums, star anise and four tablespoons of water, then bring to a boil and cook for a couple of minutes, until the fruit softens. Add the sugar, rice vinegar and soy sauce, stir well, then bring to a simmer and leave to bubble and soften for a further five to 10 minutes, until the sauce is sticky and rich; if the sauce is thickening but the plums haven’t softened enough, add a splash more water.When the sauce is ready, slice and shred the chicken, then transfer to a platter. Warm the pancakes, then serve with the chicken, sliced spring onions, cucumber and a bowl of the sauce on the side.Explore more on these topicsChinese food and drinkQuick and easyFoodChickenMeatMain courseFruitHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Riffing on classic British comfort food | Food | The Guardian
description: Jimi Famurewa, restaurant critic and food journalist, travels to Edinburgh, London and Manchester eating at the female-fronted cafes and bistros reviving regional favourites, passed down through generations.
Author: Jimi Famurewa
Headline: Jimi Famurewa, restaurant critic and food journalist, travels to Edinburgh, London and Manchester eating at the female-fronted cafes and bistros reviving regional favourites, passed down through generations.
Content: 13:42Feed with Jimi FamurewaFoodRiffing on classic British comfort foodJimi Famurewa, restaurant critic and food journalist, travels to Edinburgh, London and Manchester eating at the female-fronted cafes and bistros reviving regional comfort food favourites, passed down through generations. Starting with soda bread and a fry-up cooked by Irish-born owner Claire Hanrahan at her bistro Norah, named after her late grandmother. Onwards to Bara, where Cecily Dalladay and Zoë Heimann are celebrating the Welsh ingredients they grew up with and feed Jimi a hearty Caerphilly cheesesteak. Finally he visits Auntie Lou’s, where Emily Witts recreates her grandmother’s recipe for scones with apricot jam and cheese.Jimi Famurewa,Jess Gormley,Nicole Jackson,Tim LusherandJimi OtukoyaMon 10 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsFoodFeed with Jimi FamurewaComfort foodBritish food and drinkIrish food and drinkChefsSocial mediaRestaurants
